# C. Critiques & limits of self-correction

<a id="r010-large-language-models-cannot-self-correct-reasoning-yet"></a>
## Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet

**ID:** R010  **Category:** C (Critiques & limits of self-correction)  **Authors:** Huang et al.  **Venue:** ICLR 2024  **Learning locus:** n/a  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798

### Basic info

- **name**: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet

- **year**: 2023 (arXiv Oct 2023); published ICLR 2024

- **authors**: Jie Huang, Xinyun Chen, Swaroop Mishra, Huaixiu Steven Zheng, Adams Wei Yu, Xinying Song, Denny Zhou; lead affiliation Google DeepMind (Jie Huang also UIUC). Huang and Chen contributed equally.

- **venue**: ICLR 2024 (DBLP conf/iclr/0009CMZYSZ24); first posted as arXiv preprint 2310.01798

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**: verbal-self-critique (analysis/critique of intrinsic verbal self-correction; the paper itself proposes no new method, it evaluates self-critique-via-prompting, multi-agent debate, and oracle-guided correction)

- **feedback source**: self-generated (intrinsic setting, no external feedback); contrasted against ground-truth-oracle feedback used by prior work (RCI, Reflexion) and against equivalent-cost self-consistency

- **iteration structure**:

> iterative-refine (multi-round prompting: round 1 = 3 calls, round 2 = 5 calls), evaluated against single-shot standard prompting; also evaluates multi-agent debate rounds vs self-consistency sampling at matched call budgets

- **reflection object**: output content / reasoning chain — the model is prompted to review its previous answer and reasoning and revise it; the paper studies revision of the generated reasoning/answer rather than prompts, skills, or weights


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: n/a (critique/analysis paper; no learning or weight update is introduced — it studies in-context prompt-based self-correction at inference time)

- **requires training**: none (no training; purely inference-time prompting study using GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, and Llama-2 off-the-shelf)

- **reward or critic model**:

> self-as-judge (intrinsic setting: the LLM acts as its own critic); the paper's central finding is that this self-judgment signal is unreliable for reasoning, and prior reported gains relied on a ground-truth oracle as the stopping/verification signal rather than the model's own judgment

- **distillation target**: none (no reusable artifact is produced or distilled; the work is an empirical critique, not a method that stores experience)

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> engineered (the self-correction behaviors examined are prompt/scaffold-engineered, e.g. Reflexion/RCI/Self-Refine/Multi-Agent-Debate style prompting); the paper predates and is orthogonal to RL-emergent reflection in reasoning models


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: none (no memory mechanism; single-conversation multi-turn prompting only)

- **memory persistence**: within-episode (correction occurs within a single task/conversation; no cross-episode experience retention)

- **memory curation mechanism**: n/a (no persistent memory to curate)


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**: holistic/outcome-level (self-correction operates on the whole response/answer; the paper notes the model cannot reliably localize which reasoning step is wrong without an oracle, so correction is outcome-level)

- **intra task vs inter task**: intra-task (refinement is within a single task instance; no transfer of experience across tasks)

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**: post-hoc-revision (model revises a completed answer after the fact); the finding is that this post-hoc revision frequently degrades rather than recovers correct answers


### Application domain

- **task domains**: math, QA/reasoning, commonsense reasoning, multi-hop QA, and (for the external-feedback / constrained-generation discussion) code and constrained text generation

- **benchmarks**:

> GSM8K (1,319 test problems), CommonSenseQA (1,221 dev questions), HotpotQA (100-question closed-book set following Shinn et al. 2023); CommonGen-Hard used in the constrained-generation / prompt-design analysis (Section 5)


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Intrinsic self-correction degrades reasoning accuracy: GPT-3.5 GSM8K drops from 75.9 (standard) to 75.1 (round 1) to 74.7 (round 2); GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; CommonSenseQA GPT-3.5 collapses 75.8 -> 38.1; HotpotQA GPT-4 49.0 -> 43.0 by round 2. With oracle labels (Table 2) self-correction appears to help (GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 89.7) but the gain vanishes without the oracle.

- **baselines**:

> Standard (single-pass) prompting; oracle-label-guided self-correction (reproducing RCI/Reflexion-style setups); multi-agent debate (Du et al. 2023) vs self-consistency (Wang et al. 2022) at matched response budgets; Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023) baseline prompts vs an improved standard prompt on CommonGen-Hard

- **gains vs baseline**:

> Negative/no gain in the honest intrinsic setting. GPT-4 GSM8K: -4.0 pts after round 1, -6.5 pts after round 2 vs standard prompting. GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA: about -37.7 pts after round 1. Llama-2 (Table 4) GSM8K 62.0 -> 43.5 -> 36.5 and CommonSenseQA 64.0 -> 37.5 -> 36.5. Multi-agent debate (Table 7) 9 responses = 83.0 GSM8K vs self-consistency 9 responses = 88.2, so debate underperforms equal-cost self-consistency. Section 5: with a strong initial prompt (Standard Prompting (ours) 81.8 on CommonGen-Hard) Self-Refine drops it to 75.1.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Self-correction multiplies inference calls: round 1 = 3 LLM calls, round 2 = 5 LLM calls vs 1 for standard prompting; multi-agent debate uses 6 (round 1) / 9 (round 2) responses vs 1 baseline. The paper argues fair evaluation must compare at equal inference cost, and at equal cost simple self-consistency beats debate. No training cost (inference-only study).


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> This is a critique paper documenting limitations of self-correction itself: (1) intrinsic self-correction without external feedback typically does not improve and often degrades reasoning accuracy; (2) prior positive results relied on oracle ground-truth labels as the stopping/verification signal; (3) multi-agent debate gains are really self-consistency gains and underperform equal-cost majority voting; (4) some Self-Refine gains stem from sub-optimal initial prompts that a single better prompt already fixes. Scope of the study: limited to a few benchmarks (GSM8K, CommonSenseQA, HotpotQA) and reasoning tasks; the negative finding is specific to intrinsic, label-free reasoning self-correction, not to settings with valid external feedback (e.g. code execution / unit tests).

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> oracle-label/ground-truth — THIS is the paper's central thesis: reported self-correction gains in RCI (Kim et al. 2023) and Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023) depend on a ground-truth oracle label to decide when to stop/accept revisions; remove the oracle and the gains vanish. In the intrinsic-only (self-verify) setting performance does not improve and frequently deteriorates. The paper does endorse genuinely external/verifiable feedback (code executors/unit tests, e.g. Self-Debugging/CRITIC) as the case where self-correction legitimately helps.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-negative for intrinsic reasoning self-correction (correction degrades accuracy across GSM8K/CommonSenseQA/HotpotQA on GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-2); requires-oracle to show net-positive gains. Self-correction is beneficial only when valid external feedback (e.g. code execution, unit tests) is available.

- **calibration effect**:

> degrades (paper's intuitive explanation: a well-aligned model with a good initial prompt already produces a near-optimal response; the extra self-correction/feedback prompt biases the model away from the optimal answer, so it tends to change correct answers to incorrect ones — an effect consistent with overconfidence/'reasoning tax'); calibration is not measured with a formal metric, the evidence is the accuracy-degradation pattern


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> classifies-failure-mode (taxonomy of evaluation pitfalls in prior self-correction work: oracle-label leakage; unfair-cost comparison vs self-consistency; sub-optimal initial-prompt design) rather than per-step or per-agent attribution

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Exposes 'superficial self-reflection' / unreliable self-verification: the model cannot reliably tell whether its own reasoning is correct, so label-free self-revision flips correct answers to wrong ones (error introduction / over-correction). Also exposes evaluation failure modes: oracle-label leakage, inflated multi-agent-debate gains that are really self-consistency, and unfair-baseline (weak-initial-prompt) comparisons. Relates to MAST-style 'ineffective/superficial self-reflection' and incorrect verification modes.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Self-correction methods it critically re-evaluates: RCI (Kim et al. 2023), Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023), Multi-Agent Debate (Du et al. 2023; Liang et al. 2023), Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023); methodological references include self-consistency (Wang et al. 2022), chain-of-thought (Wei et al. 2022; Kojima et al. 2022), Self-Debugging (Chen et al. 2023b), CRITIC (Gou et al. 2023), and Constitutional AI / moral self-correction (Bai et al. 2022; Ganguli et al. 2023).

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Triggered a wave of follow-up analyses and methods on when/whether LLMs can self-correct, e.g. surveys such as Kamoi et al. (TACL 2024) 'When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs'; works distinguishing intrinsic vs external/verifiable feedback and small-model self-correction (e.g. SCoRe, Self-Rewarding/training-time self-correction); and the broader debate on test-time self-improvement for reasoning models. (Specific successor list approximate.)

- **citation count**: ~931 (Semantic Scholar, as of 2026-06)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**: False

- **on policy distillation link**:

> n/a / indirect — no distillation in this paper; however it motivates the on-policy-distillation / training-time line of work by showing that purely in-context (off-policy prompt) self-correction fails for reasoning, implying that genuine self-correction likely needs a trained signal (verifiable reward or learned critic) rather than zero-shot self-judgment.

- **sample efficiency**: Evaluated at up to 2 self-correction rounds (1 -> 3 -> 5 LLM calls); additional rounds do not recover and tend to further degrade accuracy, so more trials do not help in the intrinsic setting.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- code_url
- dataset_or_benchmark_released

<a id="r023-on-the-self-verification-limitations-of-large-language-models-on-reasoning-and-planning-tasks"></a>
## On the Self-Verification Limitations of Large Language Models on Reasoning and Planning Tasks

**ID:** R023  **Category:** C (Critiques & limits of self-correction)  **Authors:** Stechly et al.  **Venue:** ICLR 2025  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://openreview.net/forum?id=4O0v4s3IzY

### Basic info

- **name**: On the Self-Verification Limitations of Large Language Models on Reasoning and Planning Tasks

- **year**: 2024

- **authors**: Kaya Stechly, Karthik Valmeekam, Subbarao Kambhampati (Arizona State University)

- **venue**: ICLR 2025 (Poster); arXiv preprint 2402.08115 first submitted Feb 2024

- **paper url**: https://openreview.net/forum?id=4O0v4s3IzY (arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.08115)


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**: verbal-self-critique (LLM critiques/backprompts its own answers) contrasted against tool-verified external sound verification; the paper is a critique/analysis of self-critique rather than a new method

- **feedback source**:

> Two regimes compared: (1) self-generated critique (LLM-as-verifier, the 'LLM+LLM' setup) and (2) external sound verifiers/ground-truth-oracle: VAL for STRIPS planning, SymPy symbolic checker for Game of 24, and a constraint/edge checker for graph coloring

- **iteration structure**:

> iterative-refine via repeated backprompting: a proposed answer is verified, and if rejected the critique is appended and the model re-queried, looping up to a stopping condition (e.g. 15 rounds); also compares against single-pass sampling (k=15, k=25)

- **reflection object**:

> output content / final answer (the proposed solution: a Game-of-24 arithmetic expression, a graph coloring assignment, or a STRIPS plan). The system reflects on and re-generates the candidate solution given a verdict/critique; it does not modify weights, prompts, skills, or reasoning-chain structure


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal

- **requires training**: none (inference-time iterative prompting of a frozen GPT-4; no weight updates)

- **reward or critic model**: Contrasts self-as-judge (LLM critiquing itself, which collapses performance) against verifiable reward / sound external verifiers (SymPy, VAL, constraint checker) that provide guaranteed-correct verdicts and yield gains

- **distillation target**: none (no reusable artifact is distilled; this is an analysis of in-context iterative prompting with no memory or skill persistence)

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> Studies prompt/scaffold-engineered reflection (Reflexion/Self-Refine/Tree-of-Thoughts-style iterative self-critique on GPT-4). It is not about RL-emergent reflection; it argues such engineered self-critique does not work without sound external verification


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: short-term/scratchpad — the backprompt loop accumulates the history of failed attempts and critiques within a single task episode's context window; no long-term or cross-task memory

- **memory persistence**: within-episode (the failed-attempt history and critiques persist only across iterations of the same problem instance; nothing carries across tasks)

- **memory curation mechanism**: append-only — each round appends the latest critique/failed attempt to the prompt; the authors note prompts grow additively with iteration (whereas sampling's token cost is quadratically lower)


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> response-level / holistic outcome-level — the verifier renders a verdict on the whole proposed solution; critique variants range from binary feedback (B.F., just 'wrong') to first-error feedback (F.E.F., e.g. first wrong edge/action) to all-error feedback (A.E.F., every wrong edge/action), but the unit corrected is the full candidate answer

- **intra task vs inter task**: intra-task — iterative refinement within a single problem instance (Self-Refine/Reflexion-within-task style); no transfer of experience across tasks

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> post-hoc-revision — a complete candidate is generated, then verified and (if rejected) re-generated; no mid-trajectory in-flight correction. With self-critique this revision degrades performance; with a sound verifier it recovers/improves


### Application domain

- **task domains**: QA/reasoning, constraint-satisfaction, and planning/decision-making: arithmetic puzzle (Game of 24), graph coloring (NP-complete CSP), and STRIPS classical planning (Blocksworld and obfuscated Mystery Blocksworld)

- **benchmarks**:

> Game of 24, Graph Coloring (custom generated instances), and STRIPS planning via Blocksworld and Mystery Blocksworld (PlanBench-style); sound verifiers: SymPy (Game of 24), constraint checker (Graph Coloring), VAL (planning)


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> GPT-4 self-critique (LLM+LLM) causes performance collapse vs single-pass standard prompting: Game of 24 5% -> 3%, Graph Coloring 16% -> 2%, Mystery Blocksworld 4% -> 0% (Blocksworld modestly rose 40% -> 55%). Replacing the LLM verifier with a SOUND external verifier yields large gains: Game of 24 to 36-38%, Graph Coloring to 34-38%, Blocksworld to 60-87%, Mystery Blocksworld to ~6-10%. Critique content barely matters: binary/first-error/all-error feedback give similar results, and pure sampling+sound verifier (no critique) matches or beats it (e.g. Blocksworld k=25 sampling 72%)

- **baselines**:

> Standard prompting single-pass (S.P.), self-consistency over 15 samples (S.C.), and plain sampling (k=15, k=25) re-checked by a sound verifier; the full LLM-self-critique pipeline (LLM+LLM with B.F./F.E.F./A.E.F. critique variants); also compared to Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT) cost/accuracy on Game of 24

- **gains vs baseline**:

> Self-critique is net-negative vs S.P. in 3 of 4 domains (Game of 24 -2pp, Graph Coloring -14pp, Mystery Blocksworld -4pp). Sound external verifier is net-positive: Game of 24 +31 to +33pp (5%->36-38%), Graph Coloring +18 to +22pp (16%->34-38%), Blocksworld +20 to +47pp (40%->60-87%). Sampling+sound-verifier without any critique attains comparable gains, and self-consistency gives essentially no improvement over S.P.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Inference-time API-call multiplier with no training cost. Iterative backprompting prompts grow additively with iteration count; sampling-based prompts are quadratically cheaper. CoT verification raises Game-of-24 verifier accuracy 87%->99% but at ~17x output-token increase (more than doubling verification cost) and still leaves a 6pp gap to a sound verifier. ToT averages $0.74/problem (~150 CoT prompts); 150 direct queries + sound verifier reach 70% vs ToT's reported 74%


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Self-critique fails because the LLM verifier has a high false-negative rate (rejecting valid solutions) and hallucinated critiques (non-existent edges in graph coloring, hallucinated precondition satisfaction in planning, incorrect rejections in Game of 24). Gains require a SOUND external verifier; results are GPT-4-specific on three formal/well-specified domains, so generalization to open-ended tasks and to reasoning models is not established. The content of critiques does not drive improvement

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> external-tool/verifier (sound, guaranteed-correct: SymPy, VAL, constraint checker) is required for gains; intrinsic self-verification is shown to be insufficient/harmful. THE discriminating finding: self-correction works only when verification comes from a sound external source, not from the LLM itself

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-negative for intrinsic self-critique (correction degrades performance in 3 of 4 domains and as backprompts increase quality consistently drops); net-positive only when paired with a sound external verifier. Effectively requires-oracle/sound-verifier; without label/verifier soundness it does not improve

- **calibration effect**:

> degrades — the verifier LLM is miscalibrated, with significant false-negative rates (e.g. Graph Coloring FNR 95.8%, Mystery Blocksworld FNR 97.09%) and false positives (e.g. Game of 24 FPR 10.4%); it confidently rejects correct answers and accepts wrong ones, so self-verification is unreliable


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> classifies-failure-mode — diagnoses why self-critique fails by measuring LLM-as-verifier accuracy and false-positive/false-negative rates per domain (Table 2) and cataloging critique hallucination types (non-existent edges, hallucinated preconditions, spurious vertex-color claims)

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Exposes 'superficial/unreliable self-reflection' and self-verification miscalibration: high verifier false-negative rates (valid solutions rejected) and false positives, hallucinated critiques, and self-correction error-loops where iterating on self-critique consistently degrades output quality (related to MAST 'superficial self-reflection' / 'incorrect verification' modes)


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Authors' prior self-verification critiques: Stechly et al. 2023 'GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong: An Analysis of Iterative Prompting for Reasoning Problems' (arXiv:2310.12397, graph coloring) and Valmeekam et al. planning/PlanBench work; the LLM-Modulo framework (Kambhampati et al.). Critiques the self-critique optimism of Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023), Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023), Tree-of-Thoughts (Yao et al. 2023a), and Weng et al. 2023

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Cited (~134 citations) by subsequent self-correction critique and verification-scaffolding work, including LLM-Modulo follow-ups, generator-verifier gap analyses, and metacognitive/neuro-symbolic planning agents (e.g. Metagent-P, ACL Findings 2025); broadly grouped with Huang et al. and Kamoi et al. critiques of intrinsic self-correction

- **citation count**: 134


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> no / not-targeted — the study uses GPT-4 (a non-reasoning model, pre-o1/R1) with prompt-engineered iterative self-critique; it does not evaluate reasoning models with built-in reflection, though it is frequently invoked as evidence about the limits of self-verification that motivates testing such models

- **on policy distillation link**:

> n/a — no distillation or weight-update component; purely inference-time prompting. Relevant only as motivation: it argues improvement signal must come from sound external verification (verifiable reward) rather than the policy's own judgments

- **sample efficiency**:

> Iterative self-critique runs up to ~15 backprompt rounds (collapses regardless). Sampling+sound-verifier reaches reported gains at k=15 to k=25 guesses; extending to 150 direct queries + sound verifier reaches 70% on Game of 24 (comparable to ToT's 74% at similar cost)


### Uncertain (not determined)

- code_url
- dataset_or_benchmark_released

<a id="r060-understanding-the-dark-side-of-llms-intrinsic-self-correction"></a>
## Understanding the Dark Side of LLMs' Intrinsic Self-Correction

**ID:** R060  **Category:** C (Critiques & limits of self-correction)  **Authors:** Q. Zhang, Wang, Qian et al.  **Venue:** ACL 2025 (Long Papers), pp. 27066-27101  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.1314/

### Basic info

- **name**: Understanding the Dark Side of LLMs' Intrinsic Self-Correction

- **year**: 2024

- **authors**: Qingjie Zhang, Di Wang, Haoting Qian, Yiming Li, Tianwei Zhang, Minlie Huang, Ke Xu, Hewu Li, Yan Liu, Han Qiu (lead affiliation: Tsinghua University, China; with Nanyang Technological University and Ant Group)

- **venue**: ACL 2025 (Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Volume 1: Long Papers), pp. 27066-27101. arXiv first submitted Dec 2024 (arXiv:2412.14959).

- **paper url**: https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.1314/ (arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14959)

- **code url**: https://x-isc.info/ (project page / open-sourced materials)


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> verbal-self-critique (analysis/critique of prompt-only intrinsic self-correction). The paper is itself an analysis object that interprets verbal self-critique via interpretability methods (tuned-lens probing, PACT token attribution, cognitive-bias log analysis) rather than proposing a new reflection method.

- **feedback source**:

> self-generated (intrinsic feedback prompts only, e.g. 'Are you sure? Think and answer again.'). The paper explicitly removes external/oracle information (e.g. removes 'You were unsuccessful in completing the task.') to study purely intrinsic self-correction; it argues intrinsic self-correction fails precisely because there is no external/oracle signal.

- **iteration structure**: iterative-refine (multi-round Initial response -> Feedback -> Refinement loop; up to 10-round conversations analyzed for answer wavering).

- **reflection object**:

> output content / reasoning chain and the prompt-context itself. The study analyzes how the model wavers its intermediate and final answers (output content), how it over-processes its reasoning chain (overthinking/cognitive overload/perfectionism) and how it is biased by the refinement prompt vs the original question (prompt/context). Their proposed fixes modify the prompt (question repeating) and the model weights via small-sample SFT.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**:

> in_context_verbal (the phenomenon studied is prompt-only, no weight update). One proposed mitigation (small-sample SFT) is gradient_weight_update, so the paper as a whole is hybrid in its remedies, but the analyzed mechanism is in_context_verbal.

- **requires training**: none for the analyzed intrinsic self-correction; SFT (supervised fine-tuning with <10 samples: 4 for Llama, 10 for GPT) is proposed as one lightweight mitigation.

- **reward or critic model**:

> none. The paper critiques self-as-judge intrinsic feedback, showing that prompting the LLM to self-correct (acting as its own judge) behaves almost identically to simply telling it 'You are wrong.' (JS divergence 0.0186 between the two prompts' internal confidence curves), i.e. the self-critic provides no reliable improvement signal.

- **distillation target**: prompt (question-repeating prompt-design fix) and model-weights (small-sample SFT that re-weights attention toward the original question rather than the refinement prompt). No episodic memory or skill library is built.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> Analyzes prompt/scaffold-engineered intrinsic self-correction (Reflexion/Self-Refine-style prompting). Also includes reasoning-model lens: tests o1 / DeepSeek-R1 (RL-emergent reflective models) and finds they reduce but do not eliminate self-correction failures, and even regress on step-by-step decision-making.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> short-term/scratchpad (the multi-round conversation history and feedback/refinement context). No long-term episodic memory or skill library is constructed; the paper notes LLMs do not rely on successful first-answer experience (PACT contribution of the first answer is ~0% even when retained).

- **memory persistence**:

> within-episode (refinement happens within a single multi-round conversation per question). No cross-episode/cross-task experience transfer is built (the SFT fix does transfer Yes/No-trained behavior to complex tasks, an observed generalization rather than a memory mechanism).

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> n/a (no memory store is built or curated). The paper instead observes that long accumulated context causes 'cognitive overload' (failed-case refinement prompts are 4.4-6.1x longer and outputs 1.7-3.1x longer than normal cases), i.e. uncontrolled context growth is itself a failure cause.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> token-level and response-level. Token-level via PACT (Prompt Attribution and Contribution Tracking) attributing each prompt token/sequence's contribution; layer/representation-level via tuned-lens probing of per-layer confidence scores; response/outcome-level via accuracy and overturn (correct->incorrect) rates; step-level qualitatively for decision-making logs.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> intra-task (refinement within a single task/conversation is the analyzed setting). The paper additionally reports inter-task generalization of the SFT fix: models fine-tuned on the Yes/No task transfer improved behavior to the three complex tasks.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> post-hoc-revision (intrinsic self-correction is a post-hoc revision of an already-produced answer). The paper's contribution is exposing that this post-hoc revision frequently degrades correct answers rather than recovering errors.


### Application domain

- **task domains**: QA/reasoning (Yes/No factual QA, multi-hop reasoning), decision-making (text-based embodied agent), code (programming). Spans one simple task and three complex tasks.

- **benchmarks**: BoolQ (3,270 Yes/No samples), AlfWorld (134 environments, decision making), HotPotQA (100 multi-hop reasoning questions), HumanEval (161 functions, programming).


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Intrinsic (prompt-only) self-correction degrades accuracy across all four tasks for SOTA LLMs. On Yes/No (BoolQ), Llama-3.1-8B drops 20.4% ACC with 58.8% of correct answers overturned; GPT-3.5-turbo drops 12.1% ACC; even o1-preview drops 4.9% and DeepSeek-R1 1.6%. On decision-making (AlfWorld), o1-mini collapses to 1.5% ACC (-8.2) with 92.3% correct->incorrect. Proposed fixes recover accuracy: question repeating raises Yes/No ACC by 3.2-4.9% (reducing correct->incorrect overturns by 5.3-10.9%); small-sample SFT raises Yes/No ACC by up to 4.1% (often eliminating overturns), at a cost of only ~$0.004 and ~3 minutes.

- **baselines**:

> Initial-response accuracy (ACC0) vs post-self-correction accuracy (ACC1) is the core comparison; the self-correction baseline itself (Reflexion/Self-Refine-style prompting, Xie et al. 2023, Shinn et al. 2024) is the object critiqued. Mitigations (question repeating, small-sample SFT) are compared against vanilla self-correction; SFT is contrasted with prior high-cost SFT approaches (4.6k-100k samples in Sharma et al. 2023 / Xie et al. 2023).

- **gains vs baseline**:

> vs vanilla intrinsic self-correction: question repeating increases Yes/No ACC by 3.2-4.9% and decreases correct->incorrect (overturn) rate by 5.3-10.9% on ChatGPT and Llama; small-sample SFT increases ACC by up to +4.1% (GPT-4o Yes/No to 87.7%) and drives overturn rate to 0 on several Yes/No settings, and improves complex-task accuracy after Yes/No-only fine-tuning. Note these gains are relative to the degraded self-correction state; they largely restore/exceed the original initial-response accuracy rather than add new capability.

- **compute cost profile**:

> The analyzed self-correction adds inference cost (multi-round Feedback+Refinement, up to 10 rounds; refinement prompts can exceed 2000 tokens vs 9 tokens for simple Yes/No, and are 4.4-6.1x longer in failed cases). Question repeating adds negligible cost (a few extra tokens, no model change). Small-sample SFT is extremely cheap: ~$0.004 and ~3 minutes using only 4 (Llama) or 10 (GPT) training samples.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Internal answer-wavering (tuned-lens) experiments are only feasible on open-sourced Llama, not ChatGPT (no hidden states); authors hypothesize but cannot confirm ChatGPT wavers internally. PACT prompt-bias attribution cannot be applied to long/complex-task outputs (only single-token Yes/No for ChatGPT; Llama cannot handle complex tasks). Llama cannot handle the complex tasks at all. Results are timestamped 2025.2.15 and depend on the specific API models. Mitigations are explicitly described as preliminary.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> intrinsic-only is exactly the regime studied and shown to fail: without oracle labels / external feedback, prompt-only self-correction wavers answers, introduces prompt bias (recency bias toward the refinement prompt) and human-like cognitive bias, degrading accuracy. The paper directly supports and extends the Huang et al. (2024) and Kamoi et al. (2024) critique that self-correction needs external/oracle signal to help.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-negative (intrinsic, prompt-only self-correction degrades correct answers across all four tasks and many models). The paper frames this as the 'dark side': self-correction is net-negative without oracle feedback; only with the proposed prompt/SFT remedies does it become roughly neutral-to-positive.

- **calibration effect**:

> degrades / overconfident-then-wavering. Self-correction induces internal answer wavering (Llama changes its internal answer 14.1% of the time under self-correction vs 8.3% during initial generation) and a fair prompt ('Are you sure?') behaves like an outright denial ('You are wrong.') with JS divergence only 0.0186, indicating the model is not well-calibrated about its own correctness and is easily pushed off correct answers.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> classifies-failure-mode (taxonomy). The paper identifies three root-cause failure modes of intrinsic self-correction: (1) answer wavering (final and internal/intermediate), (2) prompt bias (recency bias toward the refinement prompt over the original question), and (3) human-like cognitive bias on complex tasks, sub-divided into overthinking, cognitive overload, and perfectionism bias.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Exposes: answer wavering / superficial self-reflection (model wavers intermediate and final answers, internal wavering 14.1% vs 8.3%; GPT-3.5-turbo changes 81.3% of answers >6 times in 10 rounds); prompt/recency bias (model attends to the refinement prompt rather than the original question); overthinking (e.g. o1-mini 'thinks' 15.4 times in failures vs 5.3 in successes; 17.6% of complex failures); cognitive overload from long context (33.3% of failures; failed-case prompts 4.4-6.1x longer); perfectionism bias / over-optimization (49.0% of failures; over-optimizing a correct trajectory into a failed one). Maps to MAST-style 'superficial self-reflection', 'overthinking', and 'error-loops/being stuck in think'.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new benchmark dataset of failure traces is released; the work open-sources code, prompts, and interpretation tooling (PACT, tuned-lens probing setup) at https://x-isc.info/. Evaluations reuse existing datasets (BoolQ, AlfWorld, HotPotQA, HumanEval).


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Huang et al. (2024) 'Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet' (defines intrinsic self-correction; shows it fails without oracle labels); Kamoi et al. (2024) survey 'When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes?'; Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2024) and Self-Refine / Xie et al. (2023) self-correction prompting; Zhao et al. (2021) recency-bias / calibration; tuned lens (Belrose et al. 2023) and logit lens (nostalgebraist 2020); token-attribution methods (Miglani et al. 2023; Zhu et al. 2024); human-cognitive-bias-in-LLMs work (Jones & Steinhardt 2022; Agrawal et al. 2022; Hagendorff et al. 2023).

- **citation count**: 42 (Semantic Scholar, as fetched 2026-06; influentialCitationCount 0).


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> Partially yes. The study explicitly evaluates reasoning/RL-emergent models (OpenAI o1-preview, o1-mini, and DeepSeek-R1) alongside non-reasoning models. It finds advanced/reasoning models reduce but do not eliminate self-correction failures, and that on step-by-step decision-making more advanced models can exhibit worse human-like cognitive bias (e.g. o1-mini collapses to 1.5% ACC with 92.3% overturn). So the findings target and hold (with attenuation) for reasoning models.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Weak/indirect. The proposed small-sample SFT distills corrected behavior (turning correct->incorrect samples into correct->correct demonstrations) into weights, but it is offline supervised fine-tuning on a handful of self-generated, model-known-answer samples rather than on-policy distillation; the paper does not frame it as OPD.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Extremely high for the SFT fix: only 4 samples (Llama) / 10 samples (GPT) suffice to substantially reduce self-correction failures (e.g. drive Yes/No overturn rate to 0 and raise ACC by up to ~4%), at ~$0.004 and ~3 minutes, contrasted with prior 4.6k-100k-sample SFT approaches.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- extended_by_or_inspired

# D. Search + reflection hybrids

<a id="r004-tree-of-thoughts-deliberate-problem-solving-with-large-language-models"></a>
## Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models

**ID:** R004  **Category:** D (Search + reflection hybrids)  **Authors:** Yao et al.  **Venue:** NeurIPS 2023  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10601

### Basic info

- **name**: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models

- **year**: 2023

- **authors**: Shunyu Yao et al. (Princeton University; Google DeepMind)

- **venue**: NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2305.10601)

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10601

- **code url**: https://github.com/princeton-nlp/tree-of-thought-llm


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**: search-guided | verbal-self-critique (LM self-evaluation of intermediate states used as a search heuristic, combined with BFS/DFS lookahead and backtracking)

- **feedback source**:

> self-generated (the LM itself evaluates/votes on partial states; no external tool, unit test, or trained verifier provides the heuristic). Note: the IO+Refine baseline uses groundtruth equation-correctness feedback, but ToT itself relies on self-generated value/vote signals.

- **iteration structure**: tree/MCTS-search (deliberate tree search via BFS or DFS over intermediate 'thought' nodes, with lookahead and backtracking)

- **reflection object**:

> reasoning chain — ToT reflects on and selects among intermediate reasoning steps ('thoughts', coherent units of text serving as steps toward a solution). The LM self-evaluates partial states (via value or vote prompts) to decide which branches to expand, prune, or backtrack from. No weights, prompts-as-artifacts, or persistent skills are modified; the object of deliberation is the in-context tree of partial solutions.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal

- **requires training**: none (uses off-the-shelf GPT-4 with prompting only; no fine-tuning or RL). The paper notes fine-tuning LMs in a ToT style is future work.

- **reward or critic model**:

> self-as-judge — the same LM provides the state-evaluation signal by either independently valuing each state (value prompt, e.g. classify a partial Game-of-24 state as sure/likely/impossible) or voting across states (vote prompt). No trained reward model or external verifier.

- **distillation target**:

> none — ToT performs inference-time search and does not distill the reflection into any persistent reusable artifact (no episodic memory, skill library, learned prompt, or weight update). Successor work (Chain of Preference Optimization) later distills ToT search trees into model weights, but that is outside this paper.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> engineered — the deliberation/search behavior is entirely scaffold-engineered: a human designs the thought decomposition, generator, evaluator (value/vote), and the BFS/DFS search algorithm around an off-the-shelf LM. It is not an RL-emergent reflective behavior.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: short-term/scratchpad — the tree of partial solutions (states) is held in working memory during a single problem's search; no long-term or cross-episode memory store.

- **memory persistence**: within-episode — the search tree exists only while solving one problem instance and is discarded afterward; nothing persists across tasks or sessions.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> retrieval-gated / population-or-Pareto-selected (in-tree) — states are kept or discarded by the search policy: BFS keeps the best b states per step (breadth limit b, e.g. b=1 or b=5), DFS prunes states the LM deems impossible and backtracks; less promising branches are dropped to keep the frontier bounded. This is search-frontier pruning rather than a persistent memory store.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> step-level — evaluation, pruning, and backtracking operate at the level of individual intermediate thoughts/states (a step in the reasoning, e.g. one arithmetic operation in Game of 24 or one filled clue in Mini Crosswords), not holistic outcome-level scoring.

- **intra task vs inter task**: intra-task — ToT explores and refines reasoning paths within a single task instance via search; it does not transfer learned experience across tasks or episodes (contrast Reflexion/ExpeL).

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> mid-trajectory-recovery — the search corrects in-flight by backtracking from dead-end/low-value states to a parent and exploring an alternative branch (explicitly shown important in the Mini Crosswords ablation: removing backtracking drops word-level success from 60% to 20%).


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> QA/reasoning; math; creative writing / language generation (planning and search-heavy tasks). Specifically deductive/mathematical reasoning (Game of 24), creative writing with constraints, and lexical/constraint reasoning (crosswords).

- **benchmarks**: Game of 24 (hard subset, games indexed 901-1000 from 4nums.com), Creative Writing (100 passages from 4 random sentences), Mini Crosswords (5x5, 20 games)


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**: On Game of 24 with GPT-4, ToT (BFS, breadth b=5) achieves 74% success vs 4.0% for chain-of-thought prompting (and 7.3% for IO, 9.0% for CoT-SC k=100); ToT at b=1 already reaches 45%.

- **baselines**: IO (input-output) prompting, Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, CoT self-consistency (CoT-SC, k=100), IO+iterative-Refine (k=10, with groundtruth feedback), and best-of-100 sampling for IO/CoT. All on GPT-4.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> Game of 24: ToT 74% vs CoT 4.0% (+70 pts), vs CoT-SC k=100 9.0% (+65 pts), and vs best-of-100 CoT 49% (+25 pts). Creative Writing: ToT preferred / higher coherence (the paper reports ToT generating more coherent passages than IO/CoT via GPT-4 and human evaluation). Mini Crosswords: ToT word-level success 60% and 4/20 games solved vs <16% word-level for IO/CoT; ablations: removing pruning drops to 41.5% word-level, removing backtracking drops to 20% word-level.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Inference-only cost multiplier vs single-pass. Game of 24: ToT uses ~5.5k generate / 1.4k prompt tokens at ~$0.74 per case, comparable to ~100 CoT trials (CoT best-of-100 ~6.7k/2.2k tokens, $0.47) but with higher accuracy. Creative Writing: ToT uses ~5x the completion tokens/cost of IO/CoT (ToT ~4k/2.9k tokens, $0.32 vs IO $0.06). No training cost (no fine-tuning). Cost-performance tradeoff is tunable via breadth limit b.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Deliberate search may be unnecessary for tasks GPT-4 already solves (Appendix B.1); the work only studies three relatively simple tasks chosen to challenge GPT-4; ToT requires substantially more compute/API cost than sampling methods (mitigated by the tunable cost-performance tradeoff and open-source LMs); it uses an off-the-shelf LM with no fine-tuning, and ToT-style fine-tuning is left as future work; the self-evaluation heuristic need only be approximately helpful, implying it can be imperfect/noisy.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> self-verify — ToT's search heuristic comes from the LM self-evaluating its own intermediate states (value or vote prompts), with no oracle labels or external verifier required to run the method. (The compared IO+Refine baseline does use groundtruth correctness feedback, but ToT does not.) On Game of 24 the success/failure of a final equation is checkable, but the per-step value heuristic driving the search is self-generated.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive — across all three tasks ToT improves over IO/CoT/CoT-SC without using oracle labels for its search heuristic; gains are large (e.g. +70 pts on Game of 24) and ablations confirm the search components (pruning, backtracking) each contribute. Efficacy is somewhat task-dependent (designed for tasks needing exploration/lookahead; less useful where CoT already suffices).

- **calibration effect**: not-measured — the paper does not report confidence-calibration or 'reasoning-tax' effects; it focuses on task success rates rather than calibration of model confidence.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a — ToT is a problem-solving/search method, not a failure-attribution or error-taxonomy method. It does perform implicit step-level error localization via state pruning/backtracking, but does not classify failure modes or attribute blame.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets failure modes of token-level, left-to-right (no-backtracking) decoding: lack of exploration, no strategic lookahead, and inability to revise early pivotal decisions. Relative to MAST-style modes, it addresses premature/greedy commitment and absence of in-flight self-correction by enabling branch exploration, pruning of unpromising states, and backtracking from dead ends.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> Yes — three task setups with all prompts released in the code repo (https://github.com/princeton-nlp/tree-of-thought-llm): Game of 24 (hard subset 901-1000 from 4nums.com), a 100-instance Creative Writing task, and a 20-game 5x5 Mini Crosswords task; these became commonly reused ToT evaluation tasks.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Chain-of-Thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022); Self-Consistency / CoT-SC (Wang et al., 2022); Self-Refine / iterative refinement (Madaan et al., 2023); classical AI search and human problem-solving as search through combinatorial problem spaces (Newell, Shaw & Simon); ReAct (Yao et al., 2022, same lead author) for LM action/reasoning. Uses GPT-4 as the base LM.

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Chain of Preference Optimization (CPO, Zhang et al., NeurIPS 2024, arXiv:2406.09136) fine-tunes LLMs on ToT search trees to make CoT match ToT without the search cost; Graph of Thoughts (Besta et al., 2024); Language Agent Tree Search (LATS, Zhou et al., 2024) which combines ToT-style search with Reflexion-style reflection and MCTS; Tree-of-Thought-based program repair (Weng & Andrzejak, ISSREW 2023); broadly inspired the 'System 2'/deliberate-reasoning and inference-time tree-search line of work.

- **citation count**: ~4160 (Semantic Scholar, mid-2025)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> no / not-native — ToT is a prompt-and-search scaffold around a non-reasoning base LM (GPT-4, 2023), not a reasoning model with built-in reflection like o1/R1. It is a precursor to the inference-time-search ideas that reasoning models later internalize; the paper itself does not target o1/R1-style models (which postdate it).

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Direct relevance via successor work: ToT search trees provide stepwise preference signal that Chain of Preference Optimization (CPO) distills into model weights (a form of search-to-policy distillation, DPO-style on ToT-derived preferences). ToT itself performs no distillation, but it is a natural source of on-policy search trajectories for distilling deliberate search into a single forward pass.

- **sample efficiency**:

> On Game of 24, one problem is solved with ~5.5k completion tokens (roughly the budget of ~100 CoT samples) yet outperforms best-of-100 CoT; search breadth b=1 already yields 45% and b=5 yields 74%. Creative Writing uses ~5x the tokens of a single CoT pass. So the reported gains are reached at roughly a 5x-100x inference-token multiplier vs a single pass, with no training samples required.

<a id="r011-language-agent-tree-search-unifies-reasoning-acting-and-planning-lats"></a>
## Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting and Planning (LATS)

**ID:** R011  **Category:** D (Search + reflection hybrids)  **Authors:** Zhou et al.  **Venue:** ICML 2024  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04406

### Basic info

- **name**: Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting and Planning (LATS)

- **year**: 2023

- **authors**: Andy Zhou, Kai Yan, Michal Shlapentokh-Rothman, Haohan Wang, Yu-Xiong Wang (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign / Lapis Labs)

- **venue**: ICML 2024 (Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235:62138-62160). First arXiv submission October 2023 (arXiv:2310.04406).

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04406

- **code url**: https://github.com/lapisrocks/LanguageAgentTreeSearch


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> search-guided (Monte Carlo Tree Search over actions) combined with verbal-self-critique. The LM is repurposed as agent, state evaluator (LM-powered value function), and feedback generator; on unsuccessful terminal nodes it produces a verbal self-reflection used as added context in later trials.

- **feedback source**:

> external-tool / environment-reward (environment observations: compiler + LM-generated test-suite results for code, search-API retrieval for QA, browser feedback for WebShop) plus self-generated verbal self-reflection. HotpotQA uses an oracle setup that signals answer correctness; programming uses test-pass percentage as reward.

- **iteration structure**:

> tree/MCTS-search. A variant of MCTS runs over k trajectories with six operations performed in succession (selection, expansion, evaluation, simulation, backpropagation, reflection) until the task succeeds or the compute budget is reached.

- **reflection object**:

> Primarily the action trajectory (and reasoning chain within it): MCTS searches over a tree whose nodes are states [input, action sequence, observation sequence]. On failure, a verbal self-reflection summarizing errors and proposing better alternatives is generated and injected as context (prompt/context augmentation) for subsequent trials and for the value function. No model weights are modified.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal

- **requires training**: none (training-free / gradient-free; the LM-powered value function and reflection both rely on in-context learning, explicitly avoiding the cost of training a value function or RL).

- **reward or critic model**:

> self-as-judge: a self-generated LM value function V(s) = lambda*LM(s) + (1-lambda)*SC(s), combining an LM-produced scalar score (after seeing environmental feedback) with a self-consistency heuristic. Augmented by environment/test/oracle reward signals backpropagated through the tree. No separately trained reward model.

- **distillation target**:

> episodic-memory: failed trajectories and their verbal self-reflections are stored in a long-term memory structure and re-injected as context in later iterations. The reflections act as a 'semantic gradient' rather than being distilled into model weights or a reusable skill library.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> prompt/scaffold-engineered. Reflection and the value function are explicitly prompted/orchestrated by the LATS scaffold (MCTS operations + Reflexion-style self-reflection prompts) over a frozen base LM (GPT-3.5/GPT-4); not an RL-emergent reflective behavior.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: long-term-episodic (external long-term memory storing the search tree, failed trajectories, and self-reflections) plus a short-term scratchpad within a trajectory.

- **memory persistence**:

> within-episode / cross-trial within a single task instance: the tree and reflections persist across the k trajectories of solving one task, but memory is not carried across distinct tasks or sessions (the agent is re-initialized per task).

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> append-only with value-guided retrieval: failed trajectories and reflections are appended to memory, and the MCTS value/UCT scores prioritize (gate) which nodes are expanded and which reflections are surfaced as context; no explicit summarization or eviction is described.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> step-level / trajectory-level. MCTS operates at the granularity of individual actions/states (each tree node is one action+observation step) so it can revert to and re-expand specific intermediate states; reflection itself is holistic over a failed trajectory (whole-trajectory verbal critique).

- **intra task vs inter task**: intra-task: LATS refines exploration within a single task instance via repeated trajectories, reflections, and tree search; experience is not transferred across separate tasks.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> mid-trajectory-recovery and avoidance: MCTS can revert to an earlier state and explore alternative branches in-flight (recovery via backtracking), while self-reflection on a failed terminal node is used to avoid repeating the same error in subsequent trajectories.


### Application domain

- **task domains**: code (program synthesis), QA/reasoning (multi-hop QA), web-navigation (online shopping), math/decision-making (Game of 24).

- **benchmarks**: HumanEval, MBPP (programming); HotpotQA (multi-hop QA, 100-question subset, oracle feedback); WebShop (web navigation, 50 instructions); Game of 24 (math reasoning).


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> State-of-the-art 92.7% Pass@1 on HumanEval with GPT-4 (vs Reflexion 91.0, base GPT-4 80.1). With GPT-3.5: 83.8 Pass@1 on HumanEval and 81.1 on MBPP; 0.71 EM on HotpotQA (CoT+ReAct); 75.9 average score / 38.0% success on WebShop (gradient-free, comparable to gradient-based fine-tuning); 0.44 success on Game of 24.

- **baselines**:

> CoT, CoT-SC, ReAct, Reflexion, Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT), Reasoning-via-Planning (RAP), plus ToT/RAP adapted with ReAct prompting; on WebShop also imitation learning (IL), IL+RL, and supervised fine-tuning, and human expert performance.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> HumanEval GPT-4: +1.7 Pass@1 over Reflexion (92.7 vs 91.0). HumanEval GPT-3.5: +15.7 over Reflexion (83.8 vs 68.1). MBPP GPT-3.5: +9.7 over RAP (81.1 vs 71.4). HotpotQA: best LATS (CoT+ReAct) 0.71 vs RAP(ReAct) 0.54 (+0.17) and Reflexion 0.51 (+0.20); roughly doubles ReAct (0.32 -> 0.63/0.71). WebShop: +11.7 score over Reflexion (75.9 vs 64.2) and +22.1 over base ReAct (raises average score by 22.1 with GPT-3.5); exceeds RL fine-tuning on score (75.9 vs 67.5). Game of 24: 0.44 vs RAP 0.40 (+0.04).

- **compute cost profile**:

> Higher inference cost than single-pass methods: samples n actions per expansion over k trajectories (sample complexity O(kn) for tree-search variants, same asymptotic order as ToT/RAP). On HotpotQA (n=5, k=50) LATS consumed ~173,290 tokens upon success vs RAP ~176,500 and ToT ~210,215, i.e. LATS expands fewer nodes per success (e.g. 66.65 nodes at k=50 vs RAP 70.60, ToT 84.05; on average 3.55 fewer nodes than RAP and 12.12 fewer than ToT). No training/gradient cost. Authors flag higher compute vs ReAct/Reflexion as a key limitation.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Two stated main limitations: (1) higher computational/inference cost than simpler prompting (ReAct, Reflexion), limiting practicality; (2) it assumes the ability to revert to earlier states in the environment, which is not universally applicable. Additionally, self-reflection gave only a small +0.05 gain on HotpotQA (vs Reflexion's +0.19 over ReAct), and on WebShop reflections were often generic/unhelpful, causing the agent to get stuck in local minima; gains depend on availability of high-quality external feedback.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> external-tool/verifier and (for some settings) oracle-label/env-reward. LATS is explicitly designed for and depends on external feedback: compiler+test-suite results (code), search-API observations (QA), and browser feedback (WebShop). HotpotQA uses an oracle that signals answer correctness. The paper argues, citing Huang et al. (2024), that LMs cannot reliably self-correct internal reasoning, making external feedback critical.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive but feedback-dependent / task-dependent. LATS improves over all baselines when high-quality external feedback is available (large gains in code and oracle-QA), but the self-reflection component alone contributes only marginally on HotpotQA (+0.05) and is largely unhelpful on WebShop (generic reflections, local minima); most of the gain comes from MCTS search plus external feedback rather than from self-reflection in isolation.

- **calibration effect**: not-measured (the paper does not report confidence-calibration / overconfidence metrics; it focuses on task accuracy/success and token cost).


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a (LATS is a search+reflection method, not a failure-attribution/diagnosis system; it generates verbal critiques of failed trajectories but does not classify failure modes against a taxonomy or attribute responsibility across agents).

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets compounding/propagating errors of autoregressive single-trajectory prompting (CoT/ReAct), lack of exploration of alternative continuations, and inability to incorporate external feedback (hallucination, getting stuck in local minima). Relative to MAST-style modes, it most directly addresses error-propagation/error-loops and superficial single-trajectory reasoning by enabling backtracking and reflection; it does not address multi-agent coordination modes.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new dataset or benchmark released. The authors released official code, prompts, and model outputs at https://github.com/lapisrocks/LanguageAgentTreeSearch (evaluation uses existing benchmarks HumanEval, MBPP, HotpotQA, WebShop, Game of 24).


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Monte Carlo Tree Search / UCT (Kocsis & Szepesvari 2006; AlphaGo/AlphaZero, Silver et al. 2016/2017); ReAct (Yao et al. 2023b); Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023); Tree-of-Thoughts (Yao et al. 2023a); Reasoning-via-Planning RAP (Hao et al. 2023); Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023); Chain-of-Thought (Wei et al. 2022) and Self-Consistency (Wang et al. 2022).

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Widely cited as a representative MCTS+LLM agent/tree-search method; influenced subsequent LLM tree-search and reasoning works such as Tree Search for Language Model Agents (Koh et al. 2024), AlphaMath / MCTS-for-LLM reasoning lines, RAP-style planners, ReST-MCTS*, and LangGraph's LATS reference implementation. Frequently used as a baseline in later deliberate-search / self-improving agent papers (2024-2025).

- **citation count**: approx. 498 (Semantic Scholar, mid-2025)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> No. LATS targets standard (non-reasoning) instruction-tuned LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4) and externally scaffolds System-2 deliberation via MCTS+reflection; it predates and does not assume o1/R1-style models with built-in reflection (though the authors frame it as a 'System-2' approach whose value may shift as inference compute cheapens).

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Weak/indirect. LATS is gradient-free and distills experience only into in-context episodic memory (failed trajectories + verbal reflections), not into model weights; it is not on-policy distillation, but its self-generated value scores and successful trajectories could serve as a data source for later distillation/RL pipelines (a direction other works pursue rather than LATS itself).

- **sample efficiency**:

> On HotpotQA, n=5/k=50 reaches 0.63 EM; increasing n improves performance at higher cost. LATS reaches success with fewer expanded nodes than ToT/RAP at matched k (e.g. 66.65 vs 70.60/84.05 nodes at k=50). Programming uses k=8 iterations with n=5 solutions; WebShop/Game-of-24 use k=30, n=5. Same O(kn) sample complexity as other tree-search methods but more sample-efficient per success.

<a id="r012-adaplanner-adaptive-planning-from-feedback-with-language-models"></a>
## AdaPlanner: Adaptive Planning from Feedback with Language Models

**ID:** R012  **Category:** D (Search + reflection hybrids)  **Authors:** Sun et al.  **Venue:** NeurIPS 2023  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16653

### Basic info

- **name**: AdaPlanner: Adaptive Planning from Feedback with Language Models

- **year**: 2023

- **authors**: Haotian Sun, Yuchen Zhuang et al. (Georgia Institute of Technology)

- **venue**: NeurIPS 2023

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16653

- **code url**: https://github.com/haotiansun14/AdaPlanner


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**: verbal-self-critique (LLM-as-planner-and-refiner) with environment-feedback-driven plan revision; closely related to search-guided/replanning but no explicit tree search

- **feedback source**:

> external environment feedback (text observations from ALFWorld/MiniWoB++); subgoal-level assertion checks detect discrepancies between predicted and actual observations, which trigger refinement. No human labels or ground-truth oracle.

- **iteration structure**: iterative-refine within a single episode (closed-loop): the agent refines its self-generated plan in-flight via in-plan and out-of-plan refinement, resuming from an intermediate step rather than resetting the episode

- **reflection object**:

> action trajectory and plan (the reusable code-style plan program). In-plan refinement integrates parsed observation info into the existing plan/context for better action grounding; out-of-plan refinement revises the entire plan when feedback deviates from predictions. Successful plans are also stored as reusable skills.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal

- **requires training**: none (operates solely via prompting; no dedicated training phase)

- **reward or critic model**: self-as-judge / self-as-refiner: the same LLM acts as planner and refiner; environment observations plus assertion statements supply the verification signal. No separately trained reward or critic model.

- **distillation target**: reusable-skill/workflow: a skill discovery mechanism archives successful plans (code-style solutions) in a long-term skill memory and reuses them as few-shot exemplars for similar future tasks

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> prompt/scaffold-engineered: the closed-loop refinement, code-style prompting, ask_LLM() parsing action, and skill discovery are hand-designed scaffolds around a frozen LLM (text-davinci-002 / gpt-3.5-turbo), not RL-emergent behavior


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: skill-library (long-term skill memory of successful code-style plans) plus a within-episode scratchpad/context for in-plan information

- **memory persistence**: cross-task (skills discovered on solved tasks are reused as few-shot exemplars for new, similar tasks); information from in-plan refinement persists within-episode

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> retention of successful solutions only (success-gated, append-on-success); retrieved as few-shot exemplars when a new task resembles a stored skill (retrieval-gated reuse). AutoManual later notes AdaPlanner stores only successful paths, not failures.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> step-level / block-level: each subgoal in the code-style plan ends with an assertion statement that tests its fulfillment; a failed assertion localizes the discrepancy and triggers in-plan (one-step) or out-of-plan (whole-plan) refinement at that point

- **intra task vs inter task**: both: intra-task closed-loop refinement (mid-trajectory plan correction within one episode) plus inter-task transfer via skill discovery (reusing successful plans across tasks)

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> mid-trajectory-recovery: AdaPlanner proactively refines the plan in-flight when observations deviate from predictions and resumes from an intermediate point within the same episode, rather than only retrying in a reset episode


### Application domain

- **task domains**: decision-making / embodied-text (household tasks) and web-navigation / tool-use (computer GUI tasks)

- **benchmarks**: ALFWorld (134 tasks across 6 types) and MiniWoB++ (9 feedback tasks + 53 RCI tasks)


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Outperforms SOTA baselines by 3.73% on ALFWorld and 4.11% on MiniWoB++ while using 2x and 600x fewer samples respectively; overall success 91.79% on ALFWorld (GPT-3/text-davinci-002) and 91.11% on MiniWoB++ feedback tasks (93.22% on no-feedback tasks)

- **baselines**:

> BUTLER (training-based); ReAct and Inner Monologue and RCI (implicit closed-loop with fixed plan); Reflexion; ProgPrompt/Code-as-Policies (code prompting); DEPS (explicit plan refinement with plan selector); CC-Net (MiniWoB++ RL, 23,000+ samples/task)

- **gains vs baseline**:

> On ALFWorld (134 tasks), AdaPlanner (GPT-3) reaches 91.79% vs Reflexion (GPT-3+3.5) 88.06% and ReAct (GPT-3) 61.94% (i.e. +3.73 over strongest LLM baseline). On MiniWoB++ feedback tasks 91.11% vs strongest comparable baseline (+4.11), with 600x fewer samples; on no-feedback tasks 93.22%, comparable to CC-Net which needs >23,000 samples/task.

- **compute cost profile**:

> No training cost (prompting only). Substantially more sample/demonstration-efficient than baselines: 2x fewer samples on ALFWorld and 600x fewer on MiniWoB++; skill acquisition uses at most one expert demonstration (e.g. one 'put' demo on ALFWorld; zero-shot on MiniWoB++). Inference cost is higher than single-pass due to multiple LLM calls for planning, ask_LLM() parsing, and out-of-plan replanning, but the agent refines only on detected discrepancies rather than every step.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Still requires few-shot expert demonstrations to solve complex tasks (cannot yet do fully demonstration-free complex tasks). Depends on the LLM reliably producing the specific function-form code format; later work (AutoManual) reports AdaPlanner underperforms its paper numbers with creative LLMs because the rigid code format is hard to satisfy. Stores only successful trajectories, not failures, limiting learning from mistakes. Code-style prompting is essential (ablation: removing it drops ALFWorld 81% to 46% and MiniWoB++ 93% to 66%).

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> env-reward / external-environment-feedback: refinement is driven by environment observations and subgoal assertion checks (binary success/fail signals from the environment), not by ground-truth labels of the answer. It is closed-loop on environment feedback, so self-correction is grounded in external verification rather than purely intrinsic self-critique.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive in the tested feedback-rich sequential-decision settings: closed-loop in-plan/out-of-plan refinement and skill discovery each improve success rate (shown via ablations), and AdaPlanner beats fixed-plan / implicit closed-loop baselines under the same LLM. Efficacy relies on availability of environment feedback (assertion signals); gains are largest on tasks that provide feedback.

- **calibration effect**: not-measured (the paper does not study confidence calibration or a reasoning tax; it measures task success rate)


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> attributes-failing-step: assertion statements at subgoal boundaries localize which subgoal failed (discrepancy between predicted and observed state), enabling targeted in-plan or out-of-plan correction. It does not provide a formal failure-mode taxonomy.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets brittleness of open-loop/static plans and fixed-plan closed-loop methods that adjust only the immediate action and assume the initial plan is correct; addresses LLM hallucination via code-style prompting; mitigates error propagation in long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks. Relates to MAST-style modes such as failing to recover from off-track trajectories and step-level execution errors.

- **dataset or benchmark released**: No new benchmark released; evaluates on existing ALFWorld and MiniWoB++. Code released at https://github.com/haotiansun14/AdaPlanner.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> ReAct (Yao et al. 2022); Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023); RCI (Kim et al. 2023); Inner Monologue (Huang et al. 2022); code-as-plan methods ProgPrompt and Code-as-Policies; DEPS; chain-of-thought / least-to-most planning; HuggingGPT and Chameleon (open-loop planning)

- **extended by or inspired**:

> AutoManual (2024, online rule/manual building, ALFWorld/MiniWoB++); REPL-Plan / Interactive and Expressive Code-Augmented Planning (2024); ADAPT: As-Needed Decomposition and Planning (NAACL Findings 2024); CoPiC: Code Driven Planning with Domain-Adaptive Critic (2025, directly compares to AdaPlanner); SALA (Self-Adaptive Language Agent 2024); Hindsight Planner (2024); broadly cited in code-based and closed-loop LLM-agent planning literature

- **citation count**: 222


### Other / reserved fields

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Not an on-policy distillation method (no weight updates). The closest analog is its in-context skill distillation: successful code-style plans are distilled into a reusable skill library used as few-shot exemplars, conceptually parallel to skill/experience reuse rather than gradient-based on-policy distillation.

- **sample efficiency**:

> High: outperforms baselines using 2x fewer samples on ALFWorld and 600x fewer on MiniWoB++; skill acquisition uses at most one expert demonstration per environment (zero-shot on MiniWoB++), versus baselines like CC-Net needing >23,000 samples per task


### Uncertain (not determined)

- reasoning_model_native
