# E. Parametric / learned reflection (training-based)

<a id="r013-retroformer-retrospective-large-language-agents-with-policy-gradient-optimization"></a>
## Retroformer: Retrospective Large Language Agents with Policy Gradient Optimization

**ID:** R013  **Category:** E (Parametric / learned reflection (training-based))  **Authors:** Yao et al.  **Venue:** ICLR 2024  **Learning locus:** gradient_weight_update  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.02151

### Basic info

- **name**: Retroformer: Retrospective Large Language Agents with Policy Gradient Optimization

- **year**: 2023

- **authors**: Weiran Yao, Shelby Heinecke, Juan Carlos Niebles, Zhiwei Liu, Yihao Feng, et al.; Salesforce AI Research

- **venue**: ICLR 2024 (arXiv preprint Aug 2023, arXiv:2308.02151; DBLP conf/iclr/YaoHNLFXNC0AXMW24)

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.02151

- **code url**: https://github.com/weirayao/Retroformer (project page: https://Retroformer.github.io/)


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**: learned-critic-model (a small retrospective LLM is trained to generate verbal self-reflections that improve a frozen actor LLM)

- **feedback source**:

> environment-reward (episode returns / success rate from HotPotQA, AlfWorld, WebShop environments); the reward signal is the difference in episode returns between two consecutive trials, used to fine-tune the retrospective model

- **iteration structure**:

> episodic-retry-with-reset (agent retries the same task across N trials; reflections from failed trials are appended as long-term memory before each retry, and the retrospective model is fine-tuned offline from collected rollouts)

- **reflection object**:

> prompt/context plus model weights: the retrospective model edits the actor LLM's prompt (verbal reflection summarizing root cause of prior failed attempts + proposed action plan), and the retrospective model's own weights are updated by policy gradient. The frozen actor LLM's weights are never touched; learning is localized to the small retrospective model.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: gradient_weight_update

- **requires training**: RL (PPO via standard RLHF pipeline, trl/trlx framework, with LoRA fine-tuning of the retrospective model and KL regularization to a frozen reference model)

- **reward or critic model**:

> separate retrospective model trained with a reward defined from environment returns: the reward is the difference in episode returns between consecutive trials (credit-assignment-style shaping), optimized with PPO against the environment reward; the actor LLM is treated as part of the (frozen) environment

- **distillation target**:

> model-weights: the reflection-generation capability is distilled into the fine-tuned retrospective model's parameters (LoRA adapters on LongChat-7B-16k); per-task reflections themselves are still passed as prompt text to the actor

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> engineered/scaffold-based reflection loop (Reflexion-style actor + reflection + memory architecture), but the quality of the reflective behavior is RL-optimized rather than purely prompt-engineered: the retrospective model is trained to produce better reflections, so reflection quality is learned via gradients


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: long-term-episodic plus short-term/scratchpad, plus a replay buffer of (instruction, response, episode-return) tuples used for training

- **memory persistence**:

> cross-episode within a task (long-term memory of prior failed trials appended to the actor prompt) and cross-task (replay buffer aggregates good/bad reflections across tasks and environments for fine-tuning the retrospective model)

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> append-only for the long-term reflection memory (reflections from failed trials appended to actor prompt); the training replay buffer is sampled (retrieval-gated by sampling) to fine-tune the retrospective model, providing demonstrations of good and bad reflections across tasks


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**: holistic/outcome-level (reflection summarizes the root cause of a failed trial / episode and assigns credit to actions affecting future rewards); operates at trajectory/episode level rather than token- or step-level

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> both: intra-task refinement across retries of a single task via appended reflections, and inter-task transfer because the retrospective model is trained on a replay buffer spanning multiple tasks and environments and acts as a reusable plug-in

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**: avoidance-only via episodic retry: the agent reflects after a failed trial and retries the task from reset in the next episode (it does not correct mid-trajectory in-flight)


### Application domain

- **task domains**: QA/reasoning (search-based question answering); embodied/games (text-based embodied robotics); web-navigation / decision-making (web shopping); tool-use (search/click action APIs)

- **benchmarks**: HotPotQA (distractor dev, 100 validation tasks), AlfWorld (134 tasks), WebShop (100 tasks)


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Improves success rate over Reflexion baseline by +18% on HotPotQA (with 4 retries), +36% on AlfWorld (with 3 retries), and +4% on WebShop, using a frozen GPT-3/GPT-4 actor with a LongChat-7B retrospective model fine-tuned via policy gradient. With GPT-4 actor and LoRA r=4, Retroformer reaches 54% (HotPotQA, N=4), 100% (AlfWorld, N=4), and 46% (WebShop, N=4).

- **baselines**: ReAct, Reflexion (frozen-LLM verbal reflection, Shinn et al. 2023), and SAC (a Soft Actor-Critic RL baseline); also positioned against Self-Refine and RAP in related work

- **gains vs baseline**:

> vs the strongest comparable baseline Reflexion (N=4): HotPotQA GPT-3 50% -> 53-54%, GPT-4 52% -> 53-54%; AlfWorld GPT-3 84.33% -> 100%, GPT-4 85.07% -> 100%; WebShop GPT-3 35% -> 36%, GPT-4 44% -> 45-46%. The paper emphasizes faster learning (larger gains in the first few trials, e.g. +18% HotPotQA at trial 4, +36% AlfWorld at trial 3). Gains are largest on AlfWorld and smallest on WebShop (verbal feedback is suboptimal for the exploration-heavy WebShop environment).

- **compute cost profile**:

> Inference: episodic retries (N up to 4) multiply rollout cost over a single pass, plus an extra retrospective-model forward pass per episode. Training cost is small and parameter-efficient: only the retrospective model is fine-tuned with LoRA (learnable params 0.53M for r=1, 2.25M for r=4) using offline RLHF/PPO; the large actor LLM (GPT-3/GPT-4) is frozen and requires no gradients, and gradients are not propagated through the actor.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Verbal-feedback reflection is suboptimal for exploration-heavy environments such as WebShop (only +4%), which require precise search queries and extensive exploration (also observed for Reflexion); gains on HotPotQA are modest (a few points); the approach still relies on environment reward signals and per-environment fine-tuning of the retrospective model; method tested only on three benchmarks with relatively small validation sets (100/134/100 tasks).

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> env-reward: improvement relies on environment reward / task success signals (episode returns) to both append-trigger reflections and train the retrospective model; it does not depend on ground-truth answer labels at inference, but the retrospective model's training reward comes from environment returns (verifiable environment feedback rather than self-verification alone).

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive (and environment/reward-dependent): training the retrospective model with environment reward yields consistent gains over frozen-LLM verbal reflection (Reflexion) across all three environments, with the benefit being task-dependent (large on AlfWorld, small on WebShop). Because correction is driven by external environment reward rather than intrinsic self-verification, it avoids the label-leakage critique while still being limited by reward informativeness.

- **calibration effect**: not-measured (the paper does not report confidence calibration or a 'reasoning tax'; it focuses on success-rate gains)


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> attributes-failing-step (implicitly): the retrospective model is explicitly trained to perform credit assignment, summarizing the root cause of prior failed attempts and assigning credit of actions to future rewards, but it does not output a formal failure-mode taxonomy or per-step attribution scores

- **failure mode addressed**:

> targets superficial/uninformative self-reflection (the motivating failure: a frozen LLM produces reflections that merely rephrase failed action sequences, causing repetitive incorrect actions and goal-forgetting over long interactions) and the credit-assignment problem in long multi-step trajectories; addresses error-loops/repetitive-action failures

- **dataset or benchmark released**: No new benchmark dataset released; code and project page released (github.com/weirayao/Retroformer). Uses existing HotPotQA, AlfWorld, and WebShop; collects an internal replay buffer for training.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023); ReAct (Yao et al., 2023); RLHF / PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) and the trl/trlx pipeline; LoRA (Hu et al., 2021); related verbal-refinement work Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023) and RAP (Hao et al., 2023); LongChat (longchat-7b-16k) as the base retrospective model

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Cited (~126 citations) by follow-ups on RL-trained reflection / verbal reinforcement and agent optimization, e.g. FinCon (synthesized LLM multi-agent with conceptual verbal reinforcement, 2024), GLoRe (when/where/how to improve LLM reasoning via global and local refinements, 2024), and self-reflective LLM stock-prediction work; surveyed in agent-memory and LLM-agent reflection surveys (e.g. A Survey on the Memory Mechanism of LLM-based Agents, 2024). Part of the lineage that distills/optimizes reflection signals rather than using frozen-LLM reflection.

- **citation count**: 126 (Semantic Scholar, as of 2026)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> No: predates and does not target o1/R1-style reasoning models; the actor is a non-reasoning frozen LLM (GPT-3 text-davinci-003 / GPT-4) and reflection ability is added via an external trained retrospective model rather than emerging from RL on the actor itself

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Related conceptually: distills reflection/credit-assignment skill into a small model's weights via offline policy-gradient (RLHF/PPO) on rollouts of the frozen actor; it is an early example of optimizing an auxiliary policy (the retrospective model) rather than the actor, conceptually adjacent to on-policy distillation / skill-optimization of a reusable reflection module, though training is offline from a replay buffer rather than strictly on-policy

- **sample efficiency**:

> Reported as a 'faster learner' than Reflexion: most of the gain appears in the first few retries (e.g. +18% on HotPotQA by trial 4, +36% on AlfWorld by trial 3); offline RL training data collected by rolling out the base policy for N trials per training task (exact rollout/gradient-step counts in Appendix C not fully specified here)

<a id="r015-star-bootstrapping-reasoning-with-reasoning"></a>
## STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning with Reasoning

**ID:** R015  **Category:** E (Parametric / learned reflection (training-based))  **Authors:** Zelikman et al.  **Venue:** NeurIPS 2022  **Learning locus:** gradient_weight_update  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.14465

### Basic info

- **name**: STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning with Reasoning

- **year**: 2022

- **authors**: Eric Zelikman*, Yuhuai Wu* (Stanford + Google Research), Jesse Mu, Noah D. Goodman; lead affiliation Stanford University Department of Computer Science (Zelikman and Wu contributed equally).

- **venue**: NeurIPS 2022 (36th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems); also arXiv preprint 2203.14465. Semantic Scholar CorpusID:247762790.

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.14465 (proceedings: https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/hash/639a9a172c044fbb64175b5fad42e9a5-Abstract-Conference.html)

- **code url**: https://github.com/ezelikman/STaR (official code release stated in the NeurIPS camera-ready).


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> learned-critic-model is NOT used; the closest fit is a self-improvement training loop with an answer-conditioned 'rationalization' repair step. There is no verbal in-context self-critique at inference. The corrective signal is a ground-truth-answer-checked filter plus a backward 'reason-from-the-answer' (rationalization) generation step, distilled into weights via SFT. Best categorized as: outcome-verified self-training with answer-hinted rationalization (not verbal-self-critique, not multi-agent-debate).

- **feedback source**:

> ground-truth-oracle. The improvement signal is the binary correctness of the model's final answer checked against the dataset's ground-truth label (indicator reward 1(y_hat = y)). Correct-answer rationales are kept; for problems answered wrong, the correct answer is fed back as a hint to generate a rationalized rationale. No external tool/compiler, no unit tests, no human-in-the-loop, no learned reward model.

- **iteration structure**:

> population/evolutionary is NOT it; it is an iterative bootstrapping outer loop (expert-iteration style): each outer iteration (1) generates rationales for the whole training set with the current model, (2) filters by answer correctness (+ rationalization on failures), (3) fine-tunes a FRESH copy of the original pre-trained model on the accumulated correct rationales, then repeats. Crucially each iteration RE-TRAINS from the original pretrained checkpoint rather than continuing the previous checkpoint. Runs up to ~36 iterations (arithmetic ~20; GSM8K capped at the 30th iteration / 7912 steps).

- **reflection object**:

> model weights (primary). STaR modifies the model's parameters via SFT on self-generated reasoning chains; the artifact being improved is the policy that produces reasoning chains. Secondarily the unit being generated/curated is the reasoning chain (rationale/scratchpad), and the rationalization step reflects on a failed answer by reasoning backward from the correct answer. It does NOT modify prompts, action trajectories, or maintain an episodic memory store.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**:

> gradient_weight_update. STaR's improvement is realized entirely through fine-tuning (gradient updates) on filtered self-generated rationales; there is no in-context-only / test-time-only mechanism. The authors frame the loop as approximating an RL-style policy-gradient objective implemented with standard LLM training machinery.

- **requires training**:

> SFT (supervised fine-tuning) on filtered self-generated rationales, applied iteratively. The authors note STaR can be viewed as approximating an RL policy-gradient objective (with greedy decoding to reduce variance and multiple gradient steps per batch, akin to PPO-style reuse), and rationalization as an off-policy estimate of that objective, but the concrete implementation is iterated supervised fine-tuning, not an explicit PPO/DPO/RL optimizer. Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 1e-6 (searched 1e-7 to 1e-4), batch size 8 x length 1024, on a single TPU-v3 node.

- **reward or critic model**:

> verifiable reward (binary answer-correctness against ground-truth labels) acts as the filter; equivalently a fixed 'expert' check rather than a trained reward/value model. The paper explicitly states it uses a fixed expert and does NOT train a separate value function (contrast with full Expert Iteration / AlphaZero-style value nets). No self-as-judge, no learned reward model, no separate retrospective model.

- **distillation target**:

> model-weights. Each outer iteration distills the set of answer-correct (and rationalization-repaired) reasoning chains back into the base model's weights via fine-tuning; the reusable artifact is the improved reasoner itself, not an external memory, skill library, prompt, or constitution.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> engineered (algorithmically engineered self-training loop), not RL-emergent in the R1 'aha' sense. The bootstrapping loop, the answer-correctness filter, and especially the rationalization repair step are hand-designed scaffolding around standard fine-tuning. However, the resulting capability (a model that learns to produce better, sometimes-novel rationales by training on its own successful reasoning) is an emergent product of the loop; the paper's human eval found STaR rationales preferred 30% more often than few-shot rationales (p=.039) and 74% more often than human-written rationales (p<.001).


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> skill-library is NOT used; closest is none / cumulative-training-set. There is no external memory module. The only 'persistence' is the accumulating fine-tuning dataset of correct rationales used to retrain weights each iteration, plus the fixed few-shot prompt set used during sampling.

- **memory persistence**:

> cross-task within the training distribution: the learned reasoning skill is baked into weights and transfers across all problems in the dataset and to held-out test problems (and, for arithmetic, to out-of-distribution 9-10 digit sums never seen in training). There is no per-episode scratchpad retained across inference calls; persistence is at the parameter level, not an episodic store.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> self-summarized/curated via correctness-filtering and re-training from scratch. Curation = keep only reasoning chains whose final answer matches ground truth (line 5 filter), augmented with rationalization-generated chains for failures; the fine-tuning dataset grows across iterations (e.g., CQA final model trained on 78.2% via rationale generation + 8.5% via rationalization). Each iteration RE-TRAINS the original pretrained model on the accumulated set rather than continuing the prior checkpoint, which prevents compounding drift; few-shot prompting during sampling is reported to reduce rationale 'drift' away from the seed rationale style.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> holistic/outcome-level. The corrective signal is the binary correctness of the final answer only; there is NO step-level, token-level, or block-level credit assignment within a rationale. A wrong final answer discards the entire rationale's gradient (the indicator reward zeroes it out); rationalization then regenerates a whole new chain conditioned on the correct answer. The paper notes a confound: in high-chance settings (e.g., 5-way CQA ~20% random, binary tasks) correct answers can come from bad reasoning, which outcome-level filtering cannot catch.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> inter-task. STaR learns transferable reasoning ability by training on successful chains across the whole dataset; the improvement generalizes to held-out test problems and even out-of-distribution arithmetic lengths. It is not an intra-task within-one-instance refinement loop (contrast Self-Refine); it is a dataset-level, weight-update self-improvement loop.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> post-hoc-revision via rationalization (recover from a failed attempt by reasoning backward from the provided correct answer, then training as if the model produced that chain unaided), which is a form of avoidance for future episodes (the repaired chain teaches the model to solve similar problems next time). It is NOT mid-trajectory in-flight recovery; correction happens between attempts/iterations, not during a single rollout.


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> math (symbolic arithmetic and grade-school word-problem math) and QA/reasoning (commonsense multiple-choice QA). Specifically: n-digit integer addition (symbolic/arithmetic), CommonsenseQA (commonsense reasoning), and GSM8K (grade-school math word problems). No code, web-navigation, embodied, or dialogue domains in this paper.

- **benchmarks**:

> Arithmetic (n-digit summation, dataset built following Nye et al. 2021 'Show Your Work' scratchpads), CommonsenseQA (CQA; Talmor et al. 2019, 5-way multiple choice), and GSM8K (Cobbe et al. 2021; 7,473 train / 1,319 test grade-school math word problems requiring 2-8 calculation steps).


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> On CommonsenseQA, STaR with rationalization reaches 72.5% dev accuracy with a 6B GPT-J base, vs 60.0% for GPT-J fine-tuned to directly predict answers (+12.5 absolute) and comparable to a 30x larger GPT-3 (175B) direct-finetuned baseline at 73.0%. On GSM8K, STaR with rationalization reaches 10.7% test accuracy vs 5.8% for GPT-J direct-finetuned (+4.9 absolute, ~1.8x) and 3.1% few-shot CoT GPT-J. On 2-digit arithmetic, accuracy jumps from <1% to 32% after one fine-tuning iteration with rationalization.

- **baselines**:

> Few-shot Direct GPT-J (no rationale), Few-shot CoT GPT-J (with rationale), Few-shot CoT LaMDA 137B (Wei et al. 2022 chain-of-thought), GPT-J fine-tuned to directly predict the answer ('GPT-J Direct Finetuned', trained on 100% of data), and GPT-3 (175B) fine-tuned to directly predict the answer (Xu et al. 2021, for CQA). STaR-without-rationalization vs STaR-with-rationalization is the internal ablation.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> CQA: STaR-with-rationalization 72.5% vs strongest comparable same-size baseline GPT-J Direct Finetuned 60.0% = +12.5 absolute, using only 86.7% of training data; STaR-without-rationalization = 68.8% (+8.8). STaR (72.5%) approaches the 30x larger GPT-3 at 73.0%. GSM8K: STaR-with-rationalization 10.7% vs GPT-J Direct Finetuned 5.8% = +4.9 absolute (~1.84x), using only 28.7% of training data; STaR-without-rationalization 10.1% (rationalization gives little extra on GSM8K). Arithmetic: rationalization enables learning many digit-lengths at once (2-digit <1% -> 32% in one iteration) and OOD generalization to 9-10 digits unseen in training. Few-shot prompts during fine-tuning add ~+8 on CQA (60.9->68.8 without rationalization; 69.9->72.5 with).

- **compute cost profile**:

> Training-dominated: an iterated SFT loop with full-dataset rationale sampling per outer iteration plus repeated fine-tuning from the original checkpoint. Arithmetic ran ~20+ iterations; GSM8K capped at the 30th iteration after 7,912 cumulative training steps (36 iterations for STaR-without-rationalization plus 10 more with rationalization). Training starts at ~40 steps in iter 1 and grows ~20% per outer loop (arithmetic variant: 300 steps then +20/iter). All on a single TPU-v3 node, batch 8 x len 1024, Adam, lr 1e-6. Inference is single-pass greedy (low temperature) — STaR explicitly REJECTS high-temperature multi-sampling as an alternative to rationalization because generating 10 samples is ~10x slower and degrades reasoning quality; rationalization is the cheaper data-expansion mechanism.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> (1) Cold-start floor: the base model's few-shot performance must be above chance for iteration 1 to bootstrap — GPT-2 could not bootstrap even on arithmetic; the initial model must be large enough to have some reasoning ability. (2) High-chance/low-answer-cardinality settings (e.g., binary decisions, 5-way MC) yield many correct-answer-but-bad-reasoning chains; outcome-only filtering cannot screen these out (an open filtering problem). (3) Requires ground-truth answers for the (large) unlabeled-rationale dataset; the hint-construction for rationalization 'does not follow immediately from the question and answer' and may be nontrivial in some domains. (4) Re-training from scratch each iteration is expensive and the gradient-signal effects are hard to measure. (5) Faithfulness: the model can reach correct answers via flawed reasoning / logical fallacies (documented CQA failure patterns: question-implies-answer, individual-vs-general statements), and on GSM8K sometimes 'accidentally' answers correctly with fewer/skipped steps.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> oracle-label/ground-truth. STaR fundamentally depends on access to the correct final answer for every training problem: it both filters generated rationales by answer-correctness AND uses the gold answer as the hint for rationalization. This is the discriminating variable — STaR's self-improvement is gated on ground-truth answer labels (not on intrinsic self-verification). The authors note self-consistency majority-vote (Wang et al. 2022) could relax this to question-only data, but that is future work and yields lower performance (later shown by Huang et al. 2022 LMSI).

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive but requires-oracle. With ground-truth answer labels, the loop reliably and substantially improves reasoning across all three tasks; rationalization further accelerates and improves learning (decisive on arithmetic, modest on GSM8K, ~+3.7 on CQA over no-rationalization). It is NOT an intrinsic self-correction method — improvement is contingent on the answer-correctness oracle; without labels the method as-presented does not apply.

- **calibration effect**:

> not-measured. The paper predates the reasoning-model calibration / 'reasoning tax' lens and reports no confidence-calibration metrics. It does discuss a related pathology: low-temperature sampling makes correct-without-rationalization examples the ones the model is 'most confident' in, giving a weaker gradient signal — but this is a training-signal observation, not a calibration measurement.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a. STaR is a self-improvement training method, not a failure-attribution/diagnosis system; it does not classify failure modes, attribute a responsible agent, or perform counterfactual step localization. It only uses coarse outcome-correctness to filter data (it does, qualitatively, catalog CQA reasoning failure patterns in an appendix, but does not localize or attribute errors algorithmically).

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets the data-bottleneck failure of reasoning models (no rationale-annotated data and weak few-shot reasoning) and the 'no training signal from failed problems' failure of naive self-training (which rationalization fixes by injecting backward-derived chains for hard/failed problems). In MAST-style terms it most relates to mitigating under-exploration / failure-to-solve-hard-problems and, via rationalization, avoiding the self-training plateau; conversely it can entrench 'superficial reasoning' (correct answer, unfaithful chain) because filtering is outcome-only.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new reusable benchmark/dataset of failure traces is released; STaR uses existing datasets (CommonsenseQA, GSM8K) and a generated arithmetic dataset (following Nye et al. 2021). The contribution released is the method and code (https://github.com/ezelikman/STaR), not a labeled failure-trace corpus.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022); scratchpads / 'Show Your Work' (Nye et al. 2021); explanation-based commonsense QA and rationalization seed idea (Rajani et al. 2019 'Explain Yourself!'); few-shot in-context learning (Brown et al. 2020 GPT-3); finetuned instruction following (Wei et al. 2022 FLAN); Expert Iteration / ExIt (Anthony et al. 2017) and its formal-math use (Polu et al. 2022) as the iterated-learning/self-play inspiration; policy-gradient / PPO framing (Schulman et al. 2017); self-consistency (Wang et al. 2022) as a discussed extension; GPT-J 6B base (Wang/Mesh-Transformer-JAX 2021).

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Directly seeds the rejection-sampling / self-training-for-reasoning lineage: LMSI / Huang et al. 2022 (self-improve with majority-vote pseudo-labels), RFT rejection fine-tuning (Yuan et al. 2023), ReST (Gulcehre et al. 2023) and ReST-EM (Singh et al. 2023, EM-style RL fine-tuning), V-STaR (Hosseini et al. 2024, trains a DPO verifier on correct+incorrect STaR traces for best-of-N), Quiet-STaR (Zelikman et al. 2024, token-level latent thoughts), TRICE (Hoffman et al. 2024, marginal-likelihood over multiple traces), Iterative Reasoning Preference Optimization (Pang et al. 2024), B-STaR (Zeng et al. 2025, exploration/exploitation balance + PRM), Lean-STaR (Lin et al. 2025, theorem proving), AdaSTaR (2025, adaptive data sampling / FLOPs reduction), CARE-STaR (2025, constraint-aware), process-supervision (Uesato et al. 2022). Widely cited as the ancestor of RL'd self-improvement of reasoning (precursor framing for o1/R1-style training).

- **citation count**: ~909 (Semantic Scholar, paperId 23dd78e424d32f6a48660dcd67ce994b8a7db8be / CorpusID:247762790, as of June 2026).


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> no (predates). STaR uses a 6B GPT-J base and predates o1/R1-style models with built-in/RL-emergent reflection. However, it is widely regarded as the conceptual ancestor of the train-on-your-own-correct-reasoning paradigm underlying modern reasoning models; Quiet-STaR (same lead author) is a closer step toward native always-on reasoning.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> strong / foundational. STaR is essentially self-distillation: the model generates rollouts and is fine-tuned (distilled) on its own answer-correct traces. The authors explicitly frame it as approximating a policy-gradient objective with greedy (low-variance) decoding and multiple gradient steps per batch (PPO-like reuse); rationalization is framed as an OFF-policy estimate (sampling from a hint-augmented proposal distribution p(r|x,y) instead of on-policy p(r|x)). It is a canonical predecessor to on-policy distillation / RL fine-tuning of reasoners (ReST-EM makes the EM/RL view explicit).

- **sample efficiency**:

> Data-efficient relative to direct-answer fine-tuning: STaR matches/beats baselines while training on a fraction of available labels (CQA: STaR-without-rationalization uses 69.7% and with-rationalization 86.7% of train; GSM8K: 25.0% without and 28.7% with rationalization vs 100% for direct-finetune baselines). Iteration count is the cost axis: arithmetic improves within 1 iteration on 2-digit (with rationalization), full runs ~20-36 iterations; GSM8K capped at 30 iterations / 7,912 steps. Rationalization markedly improves per-iteration sample efficiency on structured tasks (learning multiple digit-lengths simultaneously instead of stage-wise).

<a id="r016-self-rewarding-language-models"></a>
## Self-Rewarding Language Models

**ID:** R016  **Category:** E (Parametric / learned reflection (training-based))  **Authors:** Yuan et al.  **Venue:** ICML 2024  **Learning locus:** gradient_weight_update  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10020

### Basic info

- **name**: Self-Rewarding Language Models

- **year**: 2024

- **authors**: Weizhe Yuan, Richard Yuanzhe Pang, Kyunghyun Cho, Xian Li, Sainbayar Sukhbaatar, Jing Xu, Jason Weston (Meta AI / NYU); lead affiliation Meta

- **venue**: ICML 2024 (also arXiv preprint 2401.10020, Jan 2024)

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10020

- **code url**: No official code release from authors; method reproduced in community implementations (e.g., HuggingFace/Oxen.ai). Authors did not release official training code or model weights.


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> learned-critic-model (the model itself acts as an LLM-as-a-Judge reward model / self-critic); the judge ability is itself improved by training, so it is a self-generated learned critic rather than a separate frozen reward model

- **feedback source**:

> self-generated (LLM-as-a-Judge: the same model assigns scalar rewards 0-5 to its own candidate responses via an additive 5-criteria scoring prompt). No external tool, unit test, or ground-truth oracle is used for the reward signal; a small human-authored seed set (IFT + EFT) bootstraps the judge.

- **iteration structure**:

> iterative-refine across training rounds (population of model generations) within an Iterative DPO framework: starting from seed model M0, each iteration generates self-instruction data, self-judges it to build preference pairs, and trains the next model via DPO (M1 -> M2 -> M3); 3 iterations run.

- **reflection object**:

> model weights (the reflective/judgment signal is distilled into the next iteration's parameters via DPO). The proximate object reflected on is the model's own output content / candidate responses (judged by LLM-as-a-Judge), but the persistent locus of improvement is the weights — both the policy and the embedded reward/judge capability.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: gradient_weight_update (preference data generated by self-judging is consumed by DPO, updating model weights each iteration).

- **requires training**: DPO/preference (Iterative DPO: each iteration builds a preference dataset from self-rewarded pairs and runs DPO; seeded by SFT on IFT+EFT data).

- **reward or critic model**: self-as-judge (the policy model itself, via LLM-as-a-Judge prompting, provides the reward). No separate trained reward model or external verifiable reward; the judge improves alongside the policy across iterations.

- **distillation target**: model-weights (self-generated preference judgments are distilled into the next iteration's parameters via DPO; no external memory or skill library is produced).

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> scaffold-engineered: the self-rewarding loop is an explicitly engineered pipeline (LLM-as-a-Judge additive-scoring prompt + Iterative DPO), not an RL-emergent reflective behavior. However, the improvement of the reward-modeling ability across iterations is an emergent training-dynamics effect within that engineered scaffold.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: none (no explicit episodic memory, scratchpad, or skill library). 'Memory' is implicit: experience is absorbed into model weights and the growing AIFT preference datasets used for the next iteration.

- **memory persistence**: cross-task / cross-iteration in the sense that learning accumulates in weights across training rounds; there is no within-episode or cross-session inference-time memory store.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> n/a (no inference-time memory). At the data level, each iteration appends newly self-generated and self-judged preference pairs to form the training set (AIFT(M1)=3,964 pairs to train M2; AIFT(M2)=6,942 pairs to train M3); pairs are selected as highest-vs-lowest scored among candidates (append-and-select per round).


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> holistic/outcome-level / response-level: the LLM-as-a-Judge assigns a single additive 0-5 score to a whole candidate response (criteria: relevance, coverage, usefulness, clarity, expertise); no step-level, token-level, or block-level credit assignment.

- **intra task vs inter task**: inter-task: the method is an offline training procedure that improves the model across newly generated instruction-following prompts and iterations; it is not within-task in-context refinement of a single response.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> avoidance-only / training-time improvement: there is no mid-trajectory recovery or post-hoc revision of a single answer at inference; the model improves future behavior via weight updates. The DPO loss pushes away from lower-scored (worse) self-generations.


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> general-alignment / instruction-following (primary); also evaluated on QA/reasoning and standard NLP benchmarks (math GSM8K, MMLU, ARC, HellaSwag, etc.) and MT-Bench multi-turn categories (math, coding, roleplay, writing).

- **benchmarks**:

> AlpacaEval 2.0 (win rate vs GPT-4 Turbo), MT-Bench, head-to-head GPT-4 judged win rates on 256 IFT test prompts, human evaluation, and 9 NLP benchmarks: ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, SIQA, PIQA, GSM8K, MMLU, OBQA, NQ. Reward-modeling accuracy measured on a held-out Open Assistant preference evaluation set.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Fine-tuning Llama 2 70B (seeded on Open Assistant) over 3 iterations of self-rewarding Iterative DPO raises AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate vs GPT-4 Turbo from 9.94% (M1) to 15.38% (M2) to 20.44% (M3); the M3 model outperforms Claude 2, Gemini Pro, and GPT-4 0613 on the AlpacaEval 2.0 leaderboard. Reward-modeling pairwise accuracy with humans also improves across iterations (65.1% -> 78.7% -> 80.4% -> 81.7%).

- **baselines**:

> SFT Baseline (Llama 2 70B fine-tuned on IFT seed data only), the seed model M0, Self-Rewarding iterations M1/M2/M3 against each other, and external leaderboard systems (Claude 2, Gemini Pro, GPT-4 0613, GPT-4 Turbo as the AlpacaEval reference); also IFT-only vs IFT+EFT ablation for the judge.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate vs GPT-4 Turbo: M1 9.94% -> M3 20.44% (about +10.5 points across iterations; each iteration of self-rewarding DPO gives further gains, M2 15.38%). Head-to-head: SFT baseline is on par with M1; M2 beats M1 and SFT; M3 beats M1, M2 and SFT by a large margin. Reward-model pairwise accuracy: SFT/M1 65.1% -> M2-style 78.7% (IFT+EFT effect), and over self-training iterations 65.1% -> 78.7% -> 80.4% -> 81.7%; Spearman corr. 0.253 -> 0.349. MT-Bench overall: SFT 6.85 -> M3 7.25. Standard NLP benchmarks remain comparable to the Llama 2 70B base/SFT (no degradation; e.g., GSM8K M1 60.27 vs SFT 50.72).

- **compute cost profile**:

> Training-side cost: 3 iterations of generation + self-judging + full DPO fine-tuning of a 70B model. Each iteration generates candidate responses (4 per new prompt) and runs the judge 3 times per response (averaged) to assign rewards, then builds preference pairs (AIFT M1 = 3,964 pairs; AIFT M2 = 6,942 pairs) and runs DPO. No quantitative GPU-hour/FLOP cost reported in the paper. At inference the final model is a single standard model with no added pass overhead (the self-rewarding cost is incurred only during training data generation).


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Authors call results preliminary: only 3 iterations in a single setting (Llama 2 70B), so scaling laws of iterative self-improvement are unknown and gains may saturate/bottleneck. Observed increase in generation length with known length-quality correlation (possible length bias / reward hacking not ruled out). Potential reward-hacking and shared-bias risk since both the training reward and part of the evaluation use LLM judges (GPT-4 for AlpacaEval, model-as-judge for training), even if different models. No safety evaluation or safety training conducted. Relies on a human-authored seed set (IFT+EFT) to bootstrap the judge.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> self-verify / intrinsic-only for the reward signal: rewards come entirely from the model's own LLM-as-a-Judge with NO ground-truth oracle, external tool, or verifiable reward in the loop. A small human-authored seed set (IFT instructions + EFT judge examples) bootstraps the judge, and GPT-4 is used as an external evaluator at test time (but not as a training signal). This places it in the 'self-verify without oracle labels' regime — distinct from oracle-dependent self-correction methods.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive within scope: unlike intrinsic single-shot self-correction (which Huang et al. find degrades without oracle feedback), here the self-judging signal drives genuine measured gains in BOTH instruction following (AlpacaEval 9.94%->20.44%) and reward-modeling accuracy (65.1%->81.7%) across iterations. Efficacy is amplified because the judge itself is trained/improved (EFT data) and improvement is realized via weight updates rather than in-context revision; long-run efficacy is unverified (only 3 iterations, possible saturation/reward-hacking).

- **calibration effect**:

> not-measured: the paper does not report confidence-calibration metrics. Indirect signal: the model's reward-judgment quality (agreement with human rankings, Spearman/Kendall correlation) improves with iterations, but predictive calibration / overconfidence ('reasoning tax') is not evaluated.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**: n/a (this is a training/self-improvement method, not a failure-attribution or trace-analysis object; it does not classify failure modes or attribute responsible agents/steps).

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets the human-feedback bottleneck of frozen reward models in RLHF/DPO (reward model cannot improve during training and is capped at human level). Self-reported risk it may introduce: length-bias / superficial-quality reward hacking and shared-judge-bias (relevant to MAST-style 'superficial self-reflection' / reward-hacking failure modes). It does not address multi-agent coordination failure modes.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new reusable benchmark or dataset released by the authors. Uses existing resources: Open Assistant (seed IFT/EFT and reward-model eval set) and AlpacaEval 2.0 / MT-Bench for evaluation. Self-generated AIFT preference datasets were not publicly released.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Iterative DPO (Xu et al., 2023, 'Some things are more cringe than others' / Pairwise Cringe Optimization); DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023); LLM-as-a-Judge (Zheng et al., 2023, MT-Bench); RLHF/InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., 2022); Constitutional AI / RLAIF (Bai et al., 2022); instruction self-creation (Self-Instruct, Wang et al. 2023; Li et al. 2024 Self-Alignment with Instruction Backtranslation). Seed model: Llama 2 70B (Touvron et al., 2023) on Open Assistant (Köpf et al., 2023).

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Meta-Rewarding Language Models (Wu et al., 2024, arXiv 2407.19594, adds a meta-judge to improve the judge itself); Self-Rewarding correction / self-rewarding reasoning for math (e.g., 'Self-rewarding correction for mathematical reasoning', 2025); CREAM (Consistency Regularized Self-Rewarding, 2024); numerous self-rewarding / label-free RLVR follow-ups (e.g., Co-rewarding 2025) and self-rewarding extensions to vision/text-to-image (Class-Conditional self-reward, 2024). Broadly cited as a foundational self-improvement / self-alignment method.

- **citation count**: 611 (Semantic Scholar, as of 2026-06; paperId 04d64be16fb402f28348faffef484bd419c8bd8f)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> no: the method predates and does not target o1/R1-style reasoning models with built-in reflection. It is an alignment/instruction-following self-improvement method on Llama 2 70B; reflection here is an engineered LLM-as-a-Judge scaffold, not RL-emergent chain-of-thought reflection. Its self-rewarding idea has, however, been adapted in later self-rewarding reasoning work.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Strong conceptual link to self-distillation / on-policy improvement: each iteration generates on-policy samples from the current model, self-scores them, and distills the preference signal back into weights via DPO — a self-bootstrapping loop closely related to on-policy self-improvement and skill self-optimization. It is not classic teacher->student distillation (no external teacher); the model is its own teacher and student.

- **sample efficiency**:

> 3 training iterations (M1->M2->M3) suffice to reach the reported headline gains; preference data scale ~3,964 pairs (AIFT M1) and ~6,942 pairs (AIFT M2) plus ~3,200 IFT + ~1,775 EFT seed examples. Gains continue across the 3 iterations but the number of iterations to saturation is unknown (authors flag this as future work).
