<a id="r029-meta-rewarding-language-models-self-improving-alignment-with-llm-as-a-meta-judge"></a>
## Meta-Rewarding Language Models: Self-Improving Alignment with LLM-as-a-Meta-Judge

**ID:** R029  **Category:** E (Parametric / learned reflection (training-based))  **Authors:** Tianhao Wu, Weizhe Yuan et al.  **Venue:** arXiv 2024; EMNLP 2025  **Learning locus:** gradient_weight_update  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.19594

### Basic info

- **name**: Meta-Rewarding Language Models: Self-Improving Alignment with LLM-as-a-Meta-Judge

- **year**: 2024

- **authors**: Tianhao Wu, Weizhe Yuan, Olga Golovneva, Jing Xu, Yuandong Tian, Jiantao Jiao, Jason Weston, Sainbayar Sukhbaatar (Meta FAIR; UC Berkeley; New York University). Lead affiliation: Meta FAIR (work led with UC Berkeley).

- **venue**: EMNLP 2025 (main conference, pages 11537-11554, Suzhou, China; DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.emnlp-main.583). Originally arXiv preprint 2407.19594 (July 28, 2024).

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.19594 (also https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.583/ ; OpenReview https://openreview.net/forum?id=lbj0i29Z92)

- **code url**:

> No official code/model release identified from the authors. The ICLR 2025 OpenReview submission certified no public GitHub/URL, and the paper does not announce a code release. Only community reimplementations of the predecessor Self-Rewarding exist (e.g., lucidrains/self-rewarding-lm-pytorch, Oxen-AI/Self-Rewarding-Language-Models).


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> learned-critic-model with a meta-level critic: the same model acts as judge (LLM-as-a-Judge scoring its own responses) and as meta-judge (LLM-as-a-Meta-Judge, judging its own judgements). The judging/meta-judging ability is itself improved by training, so it is a self-generated learned critic refined by a meta-critic rather than a separate frozen reward model.

- **feedback source**:

> self-generated. All three roles (actor, judge, meta-judge) are the SAME model; no external tool, unit test, human label, or ground-truth oracle is used for the training reward. A small human-derived seed (EFT data built from Open Assistant, used for SFT) bootstraps the judge. GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106-preview) is used only as an external evaluator/proxy at test time, never as a training signal.

- **iteration structure**:

> iterative-refine across training rounds within an Iterative DPO framework. Starting from an SFT (on EFT) seed of Llama-3-8B-Instruct, 4 iterations are run (M1->M2->M3->M4); each iteration generates on-policy responses, self-judges them, meta-judges the judgements, builds preference pairs, and trains the next model via DPO. (Iters 1-2 train BOTH actor and judge preference pairs; Iters 3-4 train actor pairs only.)

- **reflection object**:

> model weights are the persistent locus of improvement (via DPO). The proximate objects reflected on are two-fold: (1) the actor's output content / candidate responses (reflected on by the judge), and (2) the model's own reasoning-as-judge, i.e. the judgements themselves including their rubric scores (reflected on by the meta-judge). The key novelty over Self-Rewarding is reflecting on the judgement (the critique reasoning chain), not just the response.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: gradient_weight_update. Self-generated preference data (response pairs + judgement pairs) is consumed by DPO to update the model's weights each iteration; there is no inference-time in-context reflection loop.

- **requires training**:

> DPO/preference (Iterative DPO). Each iteration constructs preference pairs from self-rewarding (actor) and meta-rewarding (judge) signals and runs DPO. Seeded by an SFT stage on the EFT (LLM-as-a-Judge) dataset; the actor is not re-trained on human responses because the seed is already instruction-tuned.

- **reward or critic model**:

> meta-judge plus self-as-judge: the policy model is its own judge (assigns 0-5 scores via an additive 5-criteria LLM-as-a-Judge rubric, averaging N=11 judgements) AND its own meta-judge (pairwise LLM-as-a-Meta-Judge comparing two judgements, with Elo/MLE scoring to derive meta-rewards). No separate trained reward model or external verifiable reward is used in the loop.

- **distillation target**:

> model-weights. Both the self-rewarding (response) signal and the meta-rewarding (judgement-quality) signal are distilled into the next iteration's parameters via DPO; no external memory, skill library, or persisted prompt/rule artifact is produced.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> scaffold-engineered: the actor/judge/meta-judge self-play loop, the LLM-as-a-Meta-Judge prompt, the length-control selection, and the Elo-based meta-reward are all explicitly engineered pipeline components, not RL-emergent reflective behavior. The improvement of the judging ability across iterations is an emergent training-dynamics effect within that engineered scaffold.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: none. No explicit episodic memory, scratchpad, or skill library. 'Memory' is implicit: experience is absorbed into model weights and into the per-iteration self-generated preference datasets.

- **memory persistence**: cross-task / cross-iteration: learning accumulates in weights across the 4 training rounds. There is no within-episode or cross-session inference-time memory store.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> n/a for inference-time memory. At the data level, each iteration regenerates training data on-policy from the current model (sampling 5,000 of 20,000 seed prompts per iteration, K=7 responses, N=11 judgements per response) and SELECTS preference pairs via score-based selection with length-control (top/bottom quality tiers, parameter rho) for the actor and via meta-judge Elo ranking (highest vs lowest Elo judgement) with a verbosity length-filter for the judge. This is regenerate-and-select per round rather than append-only accumulation.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> response-level for the actor (a single averaged 0-5 score per whole candidate response; no step/token/block-level credit assignment) and judgement-level for the judge (the meta-judge does pairwise comparison of two whole judgements). Granularity is thus holistic at the response level and holistic at the critique level; no fine-grained intra-response error localization.

- **intra task vs inter task**: inter-task: an offline training procedure that improves the model across newly generated instruction-following prompts and iterations; it is not within-task in-context refinement of a single response at inference.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> avoidance-only / training-time improvement: there is no mid-trajectory recovery or post-hoc revision of a single answer at inference. The DPO loss pushes the policy away from lower-scored responses and the judge away from lower-quality (lower-Elo) judgements, improving future behavior via weight updates.


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> general-alignment / instruction-following (primary). Also probes QA/reasoning-flavored categories within AlpacaEval (science, gaming, literature, etc.) and multi-turn dialogue (MT-Bench). Not applied to code, math benchmarks, web-navigation, or embodied tasks (math is one weak category).

- **benchmarks**:

> AlpacaEval 2 (length-controlled win rate vs GPT-4-Turbo), Arena-Hard, MT-Bench (Turn 1 / Turn 2). Reward-modeling quality measured by judge agreement/Spearman correlation with GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106-preview) and with human rankings on a held-out Open Assistant split (190 samples / ~580 responses).


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> On Llama-3-8B-Instruct with NO additional human data, 4 iterations of Meta-Rewarding raise AlpacaEval 2 length-controlled (LC) win rate from 22.92% (seed) to 39.44% (Iter 4), outperforming GPT-4-0314 and approaching Claude-Opus level; Arena-Hard score rises from 20.6% to 29.1% (+8.5). It beats both Self-Rewarding+length-control (35.49% LC) and SPPO (38.77% LC, which uses a reward model trained on human+GPT-4 data).

- **baselines**:

> Seed Llama-3-8B-Instruct; SFT-on-EFT; Self-Rewarding LLM (Yuan et al., 2024c) equipped with the same length-control (the key ablation isolating the meta-judge contribution); SPPO (Wu et al., 2024) as a strong external-reward-model baseline; an external-reward-model variant using Starling-RM-34B; and GPT-4 / Claude-Opus as leaderboard reference points.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> AlpacaEval 2 LC win rate: 22.92% (seed) -> Iter1 27.85% -> Iter2 32.66% -> Iter3 35.45% -> Iter4 39.44% (about +16.5 points over seed). Versus the strongest comparable baseline Self-Rewarding+LC: 35.49% (Iter4) vs 39.44%, i.e. ~+3.95 points attributable to the meta-judge. Versus SPPO 38.77% (which uses human+GPT-4 reward data): +0.67. Arena-Hard: 20.6% (seed) -> 29.1% (Iter4), +8.5; vs Self-Rewarding+LC Iter4 27.3%, ~+1.8. MT-Bench Turn 1: 8.319 -> 8.738 with <=0.1 drop in Turn 2 (Self-Rewarding+LC drops >0.2 in Turn 2 without improving Turn 1). Reward-modeling: judge agreement-without-ties with GPT-4 improves up to +12.34% (Self-Chosen Pairs, Iter 2) and >+6% (GPT-4-Chosen Pairs) over Self-Rewarding at matched iterations.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Training-side only; no inference overhead at deployment (final model is a single standard 8B model). Per iteration on 5,000 prompts: actor samples K=7 responses (~35,000 responses) and judge generates N=11 judgements per response (~385,000 judgements), then meta-judge does pairwise battles on judgement pairs (each compared twice for positional debias) followed by Elo/MLE scoring, then DPO fine-tuning of the 8B model. 4 iterations total. Substantial generation/judging cost during data creation (N=11 judgements and O(N^2)-style judgement battles are the dominant cost); no GPU-hour/FLOP figure reported in the paper.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> (1) The 5-point judging system produces frequent ties and saturates toward the maximum score as training progresses (scores drift to 4.5/4.75/4.9), making further improvement hard to detect; a more nuanced multi-aspect or comparison-based scoring is suggested. (2) Judge-training limitations: meta-judge positional bias persists despite debiasing and hindered further gains in Iteration 3; the judge develops a strong score-bias (prefers higher-score judgements ~97.7% by Iter 2), accelerating score saturation. (3) The judge shows limited improvement on NON-self-generated (out-of-distribution) responses, and its correlation with human rankings is not sustained over later iterations (distribution shift). (4) Length-bias requires explicit length-control mechanisms in both response and judgement selection. (5) Only evaluated up to 8B / 4 iterations on Open-Assistant-distribution prompts.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> self-verify / intrinsic-only for the training signal: rewards and meta-rewards come entirely from the model's own LLM-as-a-Judge and LLM-as-a-Meta-Judge with NO ground-truth oracle, external tool, or verifiable reward in the loop. A small human-derived EFT seed (Open Assistant ranked responses) bootstraps the judge in the SFT stage, and GPT-4 is used as an external evaluator at test time but not as a training signal. This is the 'self-verify without oracle labels' regime, distinct from oracle-dependent self-correction.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive within scope: unlike intrinsic single-shot self-correction (which degrades without oracle feedback), the self+meta judging signal drives genuine measured gains in BOTH instruction following (AlpacaEval LC 22.9%->39.4%) and judging quality (higher agreement with GPT-4 and human rankings) via weight updates. Efficacy is amplified specifically by training the JUDGE (the meta-judge contribution: +~4 LC points over Self-Rewarding+LC). However, gains are not unbounded: judge correlation with humans is not sustained in later iterations and score saturation/positional bias cap improvement (notably blocked further judge gains at Iteration 3).

- **calibration effect**:

> degrades / overconfident on the judging side (a documented 'judging-tax'): after training, the meta-judge almost always prefers higher-score judgements (63.0% Iter1 -> 97.7% Iter2) and the judge's score distribution concentrates toward the maximum (mean 4.1 -> 4.7+), reducing discriminative ability and reflecting score-bias and overconfidence. The paper does not report standard confidence-calibration metrics for the actor's answers, so actor-side calibration is not-measured; the judge-side miscalibration is explicitly analyzed as a limitation.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a: this is a training/self-improvement method, not a failure-attribution or trace-analysis object. It does not classify failure modes or attribute responsible agents/steps. (It does, however, analyze its own induced biases: judge score-bias and meta-judge positional bias.)

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets the saturation/reward-hacking failure mode of Self-Rewarding, where training only the actor while the judge stays static causes rapid saturation or overfitting to a non-improving reward (a form of 'superficial self-reflection' / reward-hacking in MAST-style terms). It explicitly co-trains the judge to keep the reward signal improving. It also surfaces and partially mitigates length-bias (verbosity reward hacking) and positional bias. It does not address multi-agent coordination failure modes.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new reusable benchmark or dataset released. Uses existing resources: the EFT seed data and 20,000 instruction prompts from Self-Rewarding (Yuan et al., 2024c) (originally generated by Llama-2-70B-Chat), Open Assistant for judge/reward-modeling evaluation, and AlpacaEval 2 / Arena-Hard / MT-Bench for actor evaluation. Self-generated preference datasets were not publicly released.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Self-Rewarding Language Models (Yuan et al., 2024c, ICML 2024) — the direct predecessor it extends by adding the meta-judge; Iterative DPO (Xu et al., 2023, Pairwise Cringe Optimization); DPO (Rafailov et al., 2024); LLM-as-a-Judge / MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2024); RLHF/InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., 2022); RLAIF / Constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022); length-bias mitigation work (Singhal et al., 2023; Dubois et al., 2024; Park et al., 2024; length-following Yuan et al., 2024b); Elo/MLE ranking from LLM-as-a-Judge (Zheng et al., 2024). Seed model: Llama-3-8B-Instruct; SPPO (Wu et al., 2024) as a contemporaneous comparison.

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Cited as a foundational self-improvement / self-judging method in subsequent self-rewarding and label-free RLVR / self-alignment work and surveys (e.g., 'Sailing by the Stars: A Survey on Reward Models and Learning Strategies for Learning from Rewards', Wu 2025, arXiv 2505.02686; broader self-rewarding reasoning, CREAM consistency-regularized self-rewarding, Co-rewarding, and meta-judge / judge-training follow-ups). The meta-judge / judging-skill-training idea informs later work that trains the critic as well as the actor.

- **citation count**: 194 (Semantic Scholar, paperId df90ee11ed6378635f22e6d0061cf67dd0bacd13; as of 2026-06)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> no: predates and does not target o1/R1-style reasoning models with RL-emergent built-in reflection. It is an alignment / instruction-following self-improvement method on Llama-3-8B-Instruct; the reflection is an engineered LLM-as-a-Judge / LLM-as-a-Meta-Judge scaffold with chain-of-thought judgements, not RL-emergent reasoning. The meta-judge does elicit CoT reasoning in its critiques, but the model is a standard instruct model, not a reasoning model.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Strong conceptual link to on-policy self-improvement / self-distillation: each iteration generates on-policy samples (responses and judgements) from the current model, self-scores them with its own (meta-)judge, and distills the resulting preference signal back into weights via DPO — a self-bootstrapping loop where the model is its own teacher and student. The distinctive twist is distilling improved JUDGING skill (critique quality), closely related to self-optimizing the critic/skill rather than only the policy. It is not classic teacher->student distillation (no external teacher).

- **sample efficiency**:

> 4 DPO iterations (M1->M4) reach the headline gains, with judge co-training active only in Iters 1-2; most actor gains continue through Iter 4 while judge-quality gains plateau / are blocked by Iteration 3 (positional bias, score saturation). Per iteration: 5,000 prompts, K=7 responses, N=11 judgements per response. Number of iterations to full saturation is not characterized; gains over Self-Rewarding are modest in absolute terms (~+4 LC points) but achieved without any added human data.

<a id="r034-self-adapting-language-models"></a>
## Self-Adapting Language Models

**ID:** R034  **Category:** E (Parametric / learned reflection (training-based))  **Authors:** Zweiger, Pari et al. (MIT)  **Venue:** NeurIPS 2025  **Learning locus:** gradient_weight_update  **URL:** https://papers.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/6b41e04c41726e2a60e456d0a2b961ab-Abstract-Conference.html

### Basic info

- **name**: Self-Adapting Language Models

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Adam Zweiger, Jyothish Pari (equal contribution), Han Guo, Ekin Akyürek, Yoon Kim, Pulkit Agrawal; MIT (CSAIL / Improbable AI Lab)

- **venue**: NeurIPS 2025 (poster); also arXiv:2506.10943

- **paper url**:

> https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10943 (NeurIPS proceedings: https://papers.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/6b41e04c41726e2a60e456d0a2b961ab-Abstract-Conference.html; OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=JsNUE84Hxi)

- **code url**: https://github.com/Continual-Intelligence/SEAL (project page: https://jyopari.github.io/posts/seal)


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> learned-critic-model (the policy itself is RL-trained to generate effective 'self-edits'; the improvement signal is the downstream task reward of the updated model rather than a verbal self-critique). The reflective act is meta-learned self-directed adaptation rather than verbal self-critique of an output.

- **feedback source**:

> environment-reward / verifiable downstream performance: the reward is the post-update model's accuracy on the held-out evaluation task (QA accuracy for knowledge incorporation, ground-truth output match for few-shot ARC). Requires ground-truth labels on the downstream task tau to compute the binary improvement reward.

- **iteration structure**:

> Nested-loop / episodic: an outer RL loop (ReST-EM rounds) optimizes the self-edit generation policy, and an inner update loop applies the self-edit via SFT (a round of test-time training) and evaluates it. Within the knowledge-incorporation single-passage setting, results are reported after two rounds of ReST-EM. Self-edits are sampled on-policy (M candidates per context).

- **reflection object**:

> model weights (primary) plus prompt/context: the model reflects on an input passage/task context and emits a 'self-edit' (synthetic finetuning data + optimization directives such as learning rate, epochs, data augmentations, selective loss over token types); the self-edit is then applied as a persistent gradient-based weight update via SFT. So the modified target is the model's own weights, parameterized through generated training data.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: gradient_weight_update

- **requires training**:

> nested-RL+SFT: an outer RL loop (ReST-EM = filtered behavior cloning / rejection-sampling + SFT) trains the self-edit generation policy; the inner loop applies SFT to perform the actual weight update. GRPO and PPO were tried but found unstable, so ReST-EM (an EM-style approach) is used.

- **reward or critic model**:

> verifiable reward: the model itself acts as the policy, and the reward is the measured downstream task performance of the updated model (binary reward = 1 if adaptation via the self-edit improves performance on tau, else 0). No separate trained reward model or learned critic network; relies on ground-truth task labels.

- **distillation target**:

> model-weights: reflection/self-edits are distilled into persistent parameter updates (the self-generated synthetic finetuning data is the intermediate artifact, but the durable distillation target is the model's own weights). Stands in contrast to in-context-only methods.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> engineered/scaffold-trained: the self-edit format is defined per domain via human-designed templates (e.g., 'generate implications' for knowledge incorporation, a JSON config of augmentations/hyperparameters for ARC), and the RL outer loop trains the model to produce effective self-edits within that scaffold. The adaptation behavior is meta-learned via RL rather than RL-emergent in the R1 'aha' sense.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> model-weights as memory (parametric): there is no external episodic memory store, scratchpad, or skill library; new knowledge/skills are written directly into the weights via self-edits. The self-edit text and synthetic data are transient within an episode.

- **memory persistence**:

> cross-task / persistent within the model: weight updates are lasting (the paper demonstrates generalization from single-passage TTT episodes to a continued-pretraining regime with 200 passages, and a continual-learning experiment applying sequential edits). Persistence is in parameters, not an external memory log.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> overwrite/evolution (self-relinking) via gradient updates with no explicit retention mechanism — this is exactly the weakness the paper flags: repeated self-edits overwrite earlier knowledge (catastrophic forgetting). Curation of which self-edit to keep is done by reward filtering (rejection sampling: reinforce only positive-reward edits; for knowledge incorporation the single best-improving edit is rewarded).


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> holistic/outcome-level: the reward and self-edit operate at the level of whole-task downstream performance after the weight update (e.g., QA accuracy on a passage, solving an ARC task), not at the step/token level. There is no fine-grained error localization within a reasoning chain.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> inter-task / meta-learning: the RL outer loop learns a general policy for generating self-edits that transfers across task instances (and from single-passage to continued-pretraining and to new ARC tasks). Each adaptation also customizes weights for the specific new input, so it spans both, but the learned skill ('how to self-edit') is inter-task.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> avoidance-only / forward adaptation: SEAL adapts to incorporate new knowledge or new tasks rather than recovering from a specific failed trajectory mid-flight. It is not a mid-trajectory error-recovery method; improvement comes from selecting and reinforcing higher-reward self-edits in subsequent RL rounds.


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> knowledge incorporation (integrating new factual knowledge from text passages) and few-shot learning / abstract reasoning (few-shot generalization). Broadly: QA/reasoning and decision-making over how to adapt; tool-use is involved in the ARC setting (model invokes augmentation/optimization tools).

- **benchmarks**: SQuAD (no-passage-in-context QA variant, single-passage and continued-pretraining with 200 passages) for knowledge incorporation; a simplified subset of the ARC-AGI benchmark for few-shot learning.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> On SQuAD no-passage-in-context QA, SEAL improves accuracy from 32.7% (no adaptation; ~33.5% cited in intro) to 47.0% after two rounds of ReST-EM, outperforming finetuning on raw passages and on GPT-4.1-generated synthetic data. On the simplified ARC subset, SEAL reaches a 72.5% success rate vs 0% for ICL and 20% for test-time training with untrained self-edits.

- **baselines**:

> Knowledge incorporation: no adaptation (base model), finetuning on the raw passage text, finetuning on synthetic data generated by GPT-4.1, and 'Train on Passage + Synthetic' variants (implication-style self-edits without RL). Few-shot ARC: in-context learning (ICL), test-time training with self-edits but without RL training (untrained self-edits), and an oracle TTT upper bound.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> Knowledge incorporation single-passage: +14.3 points QA accuracy over no adaptation (32.7% -> 47.0%), and SEAL's self-generated data beats GPT-4.1-generated synthetic data (a much larger model). Continued-pretraining (200 passages): SEAL highest at 43.8%. Few-shot ARC: 72.5% vs 20% for untrained self-edits (+52.5 points) and vs 0% for ICL.

- **compute cost profile**:

> High training cost: the outer RL loop requires, per candidate self-edit, performing an inner SFT/TTT update and a full downstream evaluation to compute the reward, with M self-edits sampled per context across multiple ReST-EM rounds — i.e., many gradient updates + evaluations per RL step. The paper notes each reward computation involves finetuning and evaluating the model, making the loop expensive; small base models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B for knowledge incorporation, Llama-3.2-1B for ARC) and LoRA/efficient TTT are used to make it tractable. Inference-time adaptation also adds per-task finetuning cost vs a single forward pass. [exact wall-clock/FLOP multipliers not stated as a single number]


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> (1) Catastrophic forgetting: in the continual-learning experiment, repeated/sequential self-edits degrade performance on earlier tasks as new updates overwrite prior knowledge. (2) Reward computation is expensive (each evaluation requires an inner finetuning + evaluation pass). (3) Requires a paired downstream evaluation task tau with ground-truth labels to compute reward (context-dependent evaluation). (4) Self-edit formats are still human-templated per domain. (5) Demonstrated on relatively small models and a simplified ARC subset.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> oracle-label/ground-truth + env-reward: the RL reward is computed from the updated model's performance on a held-out evaluation set tau (QA answers / ARC ground-truth outputs), so it depends on access to ground-truth task labels (or a verifiable downstream signal). This external supervision is what makes the self-improvement reliable, in contrast to label-free self-consistency methods the authors explicitly critique as fundamentally limited.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive (with external/verifiable reward): SEAL reliably improves downstream performance because the self-edit policy is selected against a ground-truth-grounded reward, not pure self-judgment. The authors argue self-improvement through interaction with external data is more scalable than self-consistency-based self-improvement. The efficacy is therefore conditioned on having a verifiable downstream signal.

- **calibration effect**: not-measured: the paper does not report confidence-calibration or 'reasoning tax' metrics; it focuses on task accuracy after adaptation rather than on calibration.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**: n/a (SEAL is an adaptation/learning method, not a failure-attribution method; it does not produce a failure taxonomy or attribute errors to steps/agents).

- **failure mode addressed**:

> n/a as a direct target; however the paper itself exposes and discusses a key self-modification failure mode it suffers from: catastrophic forgetting / knowledge overwriting across sequential self-edits (a continual-learning failure), proposing replay, constrained updates, or representational superposition as future mitigations.

- **dataset or benchmark released**: No new reusable benchmark/dataset released; it uses existing resources (SQuAD, a simplified subset of ARC-AGI). Code is released at https://github.com/Continual-Intelligence/SEAL.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> ReST-EM (Singh et al., 2023, rejection sampling + SFT / EM-style RL); Test-Time Training (TTT) and TTT+ICL for ARC (Akyürek et al., 2024); implication-based knowledge incorporation / synthetic-data finetuning (Akyürek et al.; Lampinen et al.; Park et al.); RL-with-verifiable-reward for LLMs (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-style RLVR) and RLHF; meta-learning and self-referential / self-modifying networks (Schmidhuber line).

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Follow-up works building directly on SEAL include 'Search over Self-Edit Strategies for LLM Adaptation' (Cheong et al., arXiv:2601.14532, 2026, relaxes SEAL's fixed human self-edit template to let the model generate its own templates with an archive) and 'The Risks of Autonomy: Dynamic Auditing of Self-Editing Language Models in Critical Infrastructure' (DAF-SELM, Myakala et al., SoutheastCon 2026, addressing catastrophic forgetting / alignment drift / data poisoning audit for SEAL-style models).

- **citation count**: ~42 (Semantic Scholar, CorpusId 279318966, as of mid-2026)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> Not specifically targeting o1/R1-style reasoning models; SEAL is applied to standard instruction-tuned base models (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-1B). The framework is model-agnostic, and Future Work envisions models that 'reason about when and how to adapt' and distill chain-of-thought traces into weights, but native reasoning models are not the experimental subject.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Strong relevance: SEAL is explicitly on-policy (self-edits are sampled from, and rewards computed with, the current model to avoid stale off-policy triples), and it distills self-generated data into the model's own weights via SFT — effectively a self-distillation / on-policy data-generation loop. It can be viewed as on-policy distillation where the model distills its own RL-selected synthetic edits into parameters, and Future Work proposes distilling CoT traces into weights, closely echoing on-policy distillation / skill-internalization ideas.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Knowledge incorporation single-passage results are reported after two rounds of ReST-EM; the ARC few-shot setting adapts from a small number of demonstrations per task. SEAL is trained on single-example TTT episodes yet generalizes to the 200-passage continued-pretraining regime. Each ReST-EM round samples M candidate self-edits per context and reinforces positive-reward (or single best) edits. [exact total number of RL rollouts/gradient steps not reported as a single figure]

<a id="r036-gepa-reflective-prompt-evolution-can-outperform-reinforcement-learning"></a>
## GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning

**ID:** R036  **Category:** E (Parametric / learned reflection (training-based))  **Authors:** Agrawal et al.  **Venue:** arXiv 2025; ICLR 2026 (Oral)  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19457

### Basic info

- **name**: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**:

> Lakshya A Agrawal, Shangyin Tan, Dilara Soylu, Noah Ziems, Rishi Khare, Krista Opsahl-Ong, Arnav Singhvi, Herumb Shandilya, Michael J Ryan, Meng Jiang, Christopher Potts, Koushik Sen, Alexandros G. Dimakis, Ion Stoica, Dan Klein, Matei Zaharia, Omar Khattab et al. (lead affiliation: UC Berkeley; also Stanford, Databricks, MIT, Notre Dame, BespokeLabs.ai)

- **venue**: arXiv preprint (2507.19457); accepted to ICLR 2026 (Oral)

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19457

- **code url**: https://github.com/gepa-ai/gepa


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> verbal-self-critique (natural-language reflection over sampled execution/evaluation trajectories to diagnose problems and propose prompt edits); combined with population/evolutionary search and a Pareto-frontier candidate-merge (crossover) step

- **feedback source**:

> self-generated LLM reflection over rich textual traces, augmented by external-tool / environment feedback exposed in the evaluation metric mu_f (e.g., retrieval-relevant-document feedback, compiler/execution/profiling traces for code) plus the scalar task reward; uses train-set ground-truth labels/metric to score candidates

- **iteration structure**: population/evolutionary (genetic optimization loop maintaining a candidate pool with ancestry; iterative reflective mutation + system-aware crossover/merge, guided by Pareto-based stochastic candidate selection)

- **reflection object**:

> prompt/context — GEPA reflects on action trajectories (reasoning chains, tool calls, tool outputs, evaluation traces) and modifies the natural-language instructions/prompts of each module within a compound AI system; model weights are NOT updated


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal

- **requires training**: none (no weight updates; GEPA optimizes textual prompt parameters only. Its GRPO baseline uses RL with LoRA, but GEPA itself requires no training)

- **reward or critic model**:

> self-as-judge (an LLM performs reflective credit assignment over traces) combined with a verifiable/task evaluation metric (mu) and a feedback function (mu_f) that surfaces environment/tool textual feedback; no separately trained reward model

- **distillation target**: prompt — accumulated natural-language lessons are distilled into evolved high-level instructions/prompts for each module of the compound AI system (carried along the genetic/ancestry tree of candidates)

- **emergent vs engineered**: prompt/scaffold-engineered — reflection is an explicitly engineered optimizer step (reflective mutation meta-prompt + Pareto evolutionary search), not RL-emergent reasoning


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: playbook/cheatsheet (evolved instruction prompts accumulating high-level rules) backed by a population/candidate pool with ancestry tracking; lessons accumulate along the genetic tree

- **memory persistence**:

> cross-task (within a single optimization run over a task's training distribution); the resulting optimized prompt then transfers to held-out test instances of that task. Not designed as a cross-session production memory store

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> population-or-Pareto-selected — GEPA maintains an instance-wise Pareto frontier of candidates, prunes strictly dominated candidates, and stochastically samples promising ones; complementary lessons are combined via system-aware merge (crossover), preventing collapse to a single greedy line and escaping local optima


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> step-level / agent-level (multi-agent) — reflection performs implicit credit assignment that attributes success/failure to specific modules of the compound system (round-robin per-module updates), with module-level feedback when available (e.g., per-hop feedback in multi-hop systems)

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> inter-task — GEPA transfers experience across many training instances within a task to evolve a generalizable prompt for held-out instances (it is a task-level optimizer that learns high-level rules from trial and error, rather than refining a single output in-flight)

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**: avoidance-only — lessons from failed rollouts inform prompt mutations evaluated in subsequent optimization iterations; GEPA does not correct a trajectory mid-flight, it improves the prompt for future rollouts


### Application domain

- **task domains**: QA/reasoning (multi-hop), tool-use/retrieval (RAG), instruction-following, decision-making (privacy-aware delegation), math, and code (inference-time code/GPU-kernel optimization)

- **benchmarks**: HotpotQA, IFBench, HoVer, PUPA (the four core tasks); v2 adds AIME-2025 (math) and code optimization tasks (inference-time search, e.g., GPU/NPU kernel code), for six tasks total


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Across six tasks, GEPA outperforms GRPO (RLVR) by ~6% on average and by up to ~20% (up to 19pp on Qwen3-8B) while using up to 35x fewer rollouts; it also beats the SOTA prompt optimizer MIPROv2 by over 10% (e.g., +12pp accuracy on AIME-2025). In v1 Table 1, Qwen3-8B aggregate: Baseline 48.85, MIPROv2 55.11, GRPO 51.14, GEPA 61.28 (+12.44); GPT-4.1 mini aggregate: Baseline 52.67, MIPROv2 59.71, GEPA 66.97 (+14.29), GEPA+Merge 68.69 (+16.02)

- **baselines**:

> GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization, RL with verifiable rewards, 24,000 rollouts with LoRA), MIPROv2 (leading DSPy prompt optimizer), and the unoptimized base system; GEPA+Merge (with system-aware crossover) reported as an additional GEPA variant

- **gains vs baseline**:

> vs GRPO: +10% average gain (v1; v2 abstract states ~6pp average), up to 19-20pp (e.g., +19% on HotpotQA Qwen3-8B), with up to 35x fewer rollouts (and matching GRPO's best validation after as few as ~330-1179 rollouts, up to ~78x greater sample efficiency). vs MIPROv2: GEPA wins on every benchmark/model, aggregate +14% vs MIPROv2's +7% (more than double), e.g., +12pp on AIME-2025

- **compute cost profile**:

> Dramatically cheaper than RL: up to 35x fewer rollouts than GRPO (24,000-rollout LoRA baseline); GEPA reaches optimal test performance with ~678 (IFBench), 2,157 (PUPA), 6,438 (HotpotQA), 6,858 (HoVer) rollouts and matches GRPO validation with as few as ~330 rollouts (up to ~78x more sample-efficient). Most GEPA rollouts are spent on candidate validation on the Pareto set, not mutation. Each iteration also incurs extra LLM calls for reflective prompt generation


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> (1) The boundary between prompt-based and weight-based learning is not well understood; in data-abundant regimes or where large-scale rollouts are feasible, weight updates may outperform prompting. (2) GRPO baseline used LoRA (not full-parameter finetuning) and limited hyperparameter tuning. (3) GEPA optimizes instructions only, omitting few-shot/exemplar optimization. (4) Majority of rollouts spent on candidate validation; Pareto-validation set size and dynamic/subsampled validation under-explored. (5) Operates on fixed model weights (no weight-space adaptation). (6) Open direction: 'feedback engineering' — identifying which traces give the most useful learning signal

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> external-tool/verifier + oracle-label/ground-truth — GEPA depends on a task evaluation metric mu (with train-set labels/ground truth) to score candidates and on a feedback function mu_f surfacing environment/tool textual feedback (retrieval relevance, compiler/execution traces); reflection is not purely intrinsic. Improvement signal comes from real metric/reward, not unaided self-judgment

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive — using verifiable metric feedback plus reflective credit assignment, GEPA reliably improves over baselines, MIPROv2, and GRPO across all six tasks; gains are validated on held-out test sets, indicating genuine generalization rather than label leakage (test set held out during optimization)


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> attributes-failing-step — via reflective credit assignment, GEPA implicitly attributes final-outcome success/failure to specific modules/steps of the compound system to target prompt updates; not a dedicated failure-taxonomy classifier

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets sample inefficiency and sparse-scalar-reward credit-assignment limits of RLVR/GRPO, and the local-optima/premature-convergence failure of greedy prompt optimizers (addressed via Pareto-based illumination and system-aware merge to avoid getting stuck on one dominant strategy)

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new benchmark dataset released; benchmark suite (HotpotQA, IFBench, HoVer, PUPA, AIME-2025, code tasks) is largely drawn from prior work (Tan et al. 2025 / LangProBe). Open-source GEPA optimizer code and search-tree artifacts released at https://github.com/gepa-ai/gepa


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> GRPO (Shao et al. 2024) as the RL comparison; MIPROv2 (Opsahl-Ong et al. 2024) and DSPy as prior prompt optimizers; evolutionary/self-referential prompt evolution (PromptBreeder, Fernando et al. 2024; EvoPrompt, Guo et al. 2024); MAP-Elites/Pareto 'illumination' (Mouret & Clune 2015); compound-AI-system optimization (Optimas, Wu et al. 2025); LangProBe benchmark suite (Tan et al. 2025)

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Multi-module GRPO / 'Composing Policy Gradients and Prompt Optimization for Language Model Programs' (Ziems et al., arXiv:2508.04660; AI & Agentic Systems 2026); 'Automatically Learning Skills for Coding Agents' (Tan et al. 2026); optimize_anything: A Universal API for Optimizing any Text Parameter (Agrawal et al. 2026); Combee: Scaling Prompt Learning for Self-Improving Language Model Agents (Li et al. 2026); integration as the GEPA optimizer in DSPy and Meta's llama-prompt-ops

- **citation count**: 352 (Google Scholar, as of June 2026)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> partially — GEPA is model-agnostic and is evaluated with reasoning-capable models (Qwen3-8B with thinking, GPT-4.1 mini) and on reasoning tasks (AIME-2025), but it operates externally by evolving prompts rather than relying on a model's built-in o1/R1-style reflection; reflection is performed by an LLM as an optimizer step, not emergent within the target policy

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Related but distinct: GEPA distills lessons from on-policy sampled trajectories into prompts (textual policy improvement) rather than into weights; authors explicitly position it against on-policy RL (GRPO) and suggest future hybrid work using GEPA's language lessons to guide RL rollouts, unifying prompt- and weight-based adaptation (cf. Multi-module GRPO follow-up)

- **sample efficiency**:

> Very high: up to 35x fewer rollouts than GRPO (24,000-rollout LoRA baseline) to exceed it; matches GRPO's best validation with as few as ~330-1179 rollouts (up to ~78x greater sample efficiency); reaches optimal test performance with ~678 (IFBench) to ~6,858 (HoVer) rollouts


### Uncertain (not determined)

- calibration_effect

<a id="r063-trust-but-verify-a-self-verification-approach-to-reinforcement-learning-with-verifiable-rewards"></a>
## Trust, But Verify: A Self-Verification Approach to Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

**ID:** R063  **Category:** E (Parametric / learned reflection (training-based))  **Authors:** Xiaoyuan Liu et al. (Tencent)  **Venue:** NeurIPS 2025  **Learning locus:** gradient_weight_update  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13445

### Basic info

- **name**: Trust, But Verify: A Self-Verification Approach to Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Xiaoyuan Liu, Tian Liang, Zhiwei He, Jiahao Xu, Wenxuan Wang, Pinjia He, Zhaopeng Tu, Haitao Mi, Dong Yu (Tencent; CUHK-Shenzhen; SJTU). Lead affiliation: Tencent (AI Lab / corresponding author Zhaopeng Tu).

- **venue**: NeurIPS 2025 (accepted; OpenReview id gA3fFAEXNT). arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.13445.

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13445

- **code url**: https://github.com/xyliu-cs/RISE


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> learned-critic-model (self-verifier): the policy is RL-trained to critique and score its own on-policy solutions; verification is tool-verified against a rule-based outcome verifier that supplies ground-truth scores. So it combines verbal self-critique with verifiable-reward supervision rather than relying on a separate trained reward model.

- **feedback source**:

> verifiable reward from a deterministic rule-based outcome verifier (exact-match correctness of the final boxed answer against ground truth). The same outcome verifier supplies the ground-truth score that supervises the self-verification task, so feedback is environment/ground-truth-oracle based (label-supervised), not purely self-generated.

- **iteration structure**:

> online RL training loop (iterative across N PPO iterations). Within each iteration it is a two-stage rollout: (i) generate K solutions per problem, (ii) construct verification prompts from those on-policy solutions and generate K verification critiques; both trajectory types are mixed into one batch for the policy update. At inference it is single-shot (Pass@1) with optional test-time scaling via majority/verification-weighted voting (k=4, k=8).

- **reflection object**:

> Two coupled objects are reflected on and modified via weights: (1) the reasoning chain / solution output is improved through problem-solving reward, and (2) the model's own on-policy generated solution is the object of self-verification (the model critiques and scores its own solution). The learning ultimately updates model weights (parametric), so the persistent artifact modified is the policy parameters; no external prompt/skill/memory artifact is produced.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: gradient_weight_update

- **requires training**:

> RL (online PPO). Implemented with Proximal Policy Optimization (actor + critic, GAE, KL penalty, clipping) on top of Qwen2.5 base models; trained with the verl framework. No SFT or DPO stage in the main method (an SFT baseline is reported separately).

- **reward or critic model**:

> verifiable reward (rule-based deterministic outcome verifier giving binary/discrete correctness: +1 boxed-and-matched, -0.5 boxed-but-not-matched, -1 unboxed). The same verifier scores both solution generation and self-verification. PPO additionally uses a learned value/critic model for advantage estimation, but the improvement signal itself is a verifiable reward, not a learned reward model. The model also acts as self-as-judge for its own solutions, but that judgment is supervised by the verifiable reward.

- **distillation target**:

> model-weights. The self-verification skill is distilled into the policy parameters via the joint RL objective (verification trajectories contribute to the gradient update); there is no separate episodic memory, prompt, or skill-library artifact.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> Hybrid / engineered-objective with emergent behavior: the joint solve-and-verify RL objective and the verification prompt template are engineered, but the resulting more-frequent and more-accurate in-context self-verification behavior emerges from the RL optimization (verification phrase frequency rises +1.09 for 3B, +1.05 for 7B after training; not prompt-scaffolded at inference). It targets the 'superficial self-reflection' problem of plain RLVR-emergent reflection.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: short-term/scratchpad (the chain-of-thought reasoning and the verification critique within a response). No persistent long-term or episodic memory store; learned experience is held in model weights.

- **memory persistence**: within-episode for the scratchpad reasoning/verification; learned capability persists cross-task and cross-session only via the updated model weights (parametric), not via an explicit external memory.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> n/a — there is no external memory bank to curate. Online verification data is generated fresh each iteration from on-policy solutions and is not stored/accumulated (the ablation contrasts this with an offline/static verification set drawn from a distant policy).


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> holistic/outcome-level. The verifier judges only final-answer correctness (binary outcome), and the self-verification task asks for a single correctness score for the whole solution rather than localizing the failing step. The natural-language critique can discuss steps, but the reward signal is outcome-level (no step-level/process reward).

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> inter-task — learning transfers across the training distribution and to held-out benchmarks via weight updates; the model does not iteratively refine a single answer within one inference (no in-flight retry loop at test time). Each training problem is independent; the acquired solve+verify skill generalizes across tasks.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> avoidance-via-training plus internalized in-flight verification: at training time, errors shape the policy so future solutions/verifications improve (avoidance). The internalized verification can also recompute/recheck within a single reasoning trace (e.g. re-deriving constraints mid-solution), giving some mid-trajectory self-correction, but there is no explicit episodic retry-with-reset mechanism.


### Application domain

- **task domains**: math (mathematical reasoning). Future work mentions extension to code generation, physics, and other verifiable-reward domains, but experiments are math-only.

- **benchmarks**:

> Training: MATH-Hard (Level 3-5, 8,523 problems). Evaluation: MATH500, Minerva Math, OlympiadBench, AIME 2024, AMC 2023. Verification accuracy measured on the same benchmarks; off-the-shelf verifier comparison vs Math-Shepherd-7B and GPT-4o.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> On Qwen2.5 (1.5B/3B/7B) with PPO, RISE jointly improves reasoning Pass@1 and dramatically improves self-verification accuracy. Up to 2.8x increase in verification accuracy over a Zero-RL baseline; RISE-1.5B reaches 74.5% avg verification accuracy vs 26.8% for Zero-RL (+47.7 pts). RISE-3B: 33.5% avg reasoning (vs Zero-RL 32.5%) and 74.3% avg verification (vs 35.8%); reported +3.7% reasoning and +33.4% self-verification over Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. RISE-7B: 42.9% avg reasoning, 69.2% avg verification.

- **baselines**:

> Qwen2.5 Base, Qwen2.5 Instruct (instruction-tuned), SFT (on MATH-Hard), and Zero-RL (same RL setup as RISE but without the verification objective). For self-verification: off-the-shelf verifiers Math-Shepherd-7B (discriminative) and GPT-4o (generative). Reference point GPT-4o reported in the main table.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> Vs the strongest comparable baseline (Zero-RL, identical RL setup minus verification objective): reasoning avg gains are small (RISE-1.5B +0.4 pts to 24.4; RISE-3B +1.0 pts to 33.5; RISE-7B +1.2 pts to 42.9), while self-verification gains are large (1.5B +47.7 pts, 3B +38.5 pts, 7B +22.6 pts; up to 2.8x). Test-time: verification-weighted voting adds +0.2% (3B) and +1.9% (7B) over standard majority voting at k=4; RISE-7B 49.8% vs Zero-RL 48.3% at k=8 + self-verify. Self-verified reasoning accuracy gains over Zero-RL: +3.3% (1.5B), +1.7% (3B), +6.5% (7B).

- **compute cost profile**:

> Training: adds a verification rollout+update stage on top of standard RLVR. Default verification batch size 128 = 12.5% of the 1024 generation batch, so roughly +12.5% extra training rollouts/compute over Zero-RL; scaling verification ratio up to 100% further increases compute and keeps improving verification accuracy. Train batch 1024, mini-batch 128, K=8 rollouts/problem, temperature 1.0. Inference: base method is single-pass Pass@1 (no extra cost); optional test-time scaling uses k=4 or k=8 samples plus self-verification scoring (k-fold inference multiplier).


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Evaluated only on mathematical reasoning (no code/physics/general domains, left to future work). Only PPO is tested; GRPO/RLOO left to future work. Outcome-level (binary final-answer) verification only — no step-level/process verification, so error localization is coarse. Reasoning accuracy gains over Zero-RL are marginal (the main win is verification skill). Depends on a reliable rule-based outcome verifier and ground-truth answers for training, limiting applicability to non-verifiable domains. No dedicated limitations section in the paper; these are inferred from method scope and future-work discussion.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> external-tool/verifier + oracle-label/ground-truth at training time. Both the problem-solving reward and the self-verification ground-truth score come from a rule-based outcome verifier that requires the ground-truth answer. The learned self-verifier then operates intrinsically at inference (no oracle needed at test time), but the capability is acquired under ground-truth-supervised verifiable reward.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive (without test-time label leakage). The internalized self-verification improves self-verified reasoning accuracy (+3.3/+1.7/+6.5% over Zero-RL) and yields gains from verification-weighted voting at inference using only the model's own scores; RISE self-verifiers also outperform off-the-shelf verifiers (Math-Shepherd-7B, GPT-4o). Reasoning gains are modest but consistently positive, so self-correction is net-positive and does not require an oracle at test time.

- **calibration effect**:

> improves — the learned self-verification provides meaningful confidence signals: verification-weighted majority voting beats plain majority voting (+0.2% 3B, +1.9% 7B at k=4), indicating better answer calibration/confidence estimates. Explicit calibration metrics (e.g. ECE) are not reported, so this is improvement on a calibration-proxy rather than a direct calibration measurement.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> classifies-failure-mode (binary correctness judgment of its own solution) — the self-verifier outputs a critique plus a correct/incorrect score for a whole solution. It does not attribute a specific failing step (no step-level localization) or a responsible agent (single-agent setting).

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Directly targets 'superficial self-reflection' (models that nominally reflect/verify but do not robustly catch their own errors) — closely related to MAST-style superficial/ineffective self-verification and reflection failures. The case study shows RISE avoids a plausible-but-wrong verification (Zero-RL 'verifies' the wrong answer 222 by misapplying divisibility rules) by performing genuine multi-step re-derivation (validating 2220).

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new benchmark or trace dataset released. Code released at https://github.com/xyliu-cs/RISE; training uses existing MATH-Hard and evaluation uses existing public benchmarks (MATH500, Minerva, OlympiadBench, AIME24, AMC23).


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> RLVR / Zero-RL for reasoning (DeepSeek-R1, Open-Reasoner-Zero, Zeng et al. SimpleRL-Zoo), PPO (Schulman et al. 2017) with GAE; verifiable-reward training (Lambert et al. Tulu/RLVR); generation-verification gap and self-improvement (Song et al. 2024, Huang et al. sharpening); self-critique signals (Xi et al. 2024, Xie et al. 2025); generative/process verifiers (Math-Shepherd / Wang et al. 2023a, Lightman et al. process reward); self-rewarding / verification-for-self-improvement (Yuan et al. 2024, Xiong et al. 2025); self-play solve-and-test (Lin et al. 2025). Built on Qwen2.5 and the verl framework.

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Cited by and related to subsequent self-evolving/self-verification RL reasoning work, e.g. R-Zero: Self-Evolving Reasoning LLM from Zero Data (2025), and broader RLVR-with-self-verification follow-ups. (Specific downstream citations are limited given the recency; ~32 citing works as of mid-2026.)

- **citation count**: 32 (Semantic Scholar, as of 2026-06-08); influentialCitationCount 2.


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> Not specifically targeted at o1/R1-style reasoning models — RISE is the training method that *induces* reflective self-verification in standard Qwen2.5 base models, addressing the 'superficial self-reflection' that plain RLVR-emergent reflection (R1-style 'aha') exhibits. It is complementary to, rather than assuming, a built-in-reflection reasoning model.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Strongly on-policy: verification training data is constructed from the model's own on-policy generated solutions each iteration (ablation shows online/on-policy verification is crucial — an offline/distant-policy verification set sharply degrades verification accuracy). This is self-distillation of a verification skill into weights via on-policy RL rather than distillation from a separate teacher; conceptually aligned with on-policy distillation/self-improvement on the model's current output distribution.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Self-verification reward rises faster and to a higher level than the problem-solving reward during training (consistent with the generation-verification gap), so the verification skill is acquired sample-efficiently. Main runs trained ~96 PPO steps (offline-comparison policy taken at step 96, the final step); verification accuracy keeps scaling with more verification compute (12.5%->100% of generation batch). Exact total rollout/step counts to reach headline numbers are not fully specified.

<a id="r066-ledex-training-llms-to-better-self-debug-and-explain-code"></a>
## LeDex: Training LLMs to Better Self-Debug and Explain Code

**ID:** R066  **Category:** E (Parametric / learned reflection (training-based))  **Authors:** Jiang et al. (Purdue, AWS AI Labs, UVA)  **Venue:** NeurIPS 2024  **Learning locus:** gradient_weight_update  **URL:** https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/3ea832724870c700f0a03c665572e2a9-Abstract-Conference.html

### Basic info

- **name**: LeDex: Training LLMs to Better Self-Debug and Explain Code

- **year**: 2024

- **authors**: Nan Jiang et al. (Purdue University; AWS AI Labs; University of Virginia)

- **venue**: NeurIPS 2024 (Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37, pp. 35517-35543)

- **paper url**: https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/3ea832724870c700f0a03c665572e2a9-Abstract-Conference.html (arXiv:2405.18649)


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> learned-critic-model (trained reflective behavior via SFT+RL; the model learns to produce an explanation/critique of its own wrong code, with a trained reward signal for explanation quality). Feedback at training time is tool-verified (unit-test execution).

- **feedback source**:

> external-tool (Python interpreter / unit-test execution verification) used both to filter the training trajectories and as the unit-test passing-rate component of the RL reward; explanation quality measured via RoBERTa sentiment/embedding similarity. At inference, the model conditions on unit-test execution feedback (error message or failed test case).

- **iteration structure**:

> iterative-refine: code generation followed by self-debugging that explains the wrong code then refines it; can iterate for multiple rounds (evaluated up to 3 rounds of refinement) until a correct solution or max iterations is reached.

- **reflection object**:

> Primarily the output content (the generated wrong code) plus the reasoning chain: the model produces a natural-language explanation/diagnosis of the wrong code (CoT-style) and then a refinement. The corrective signal is baked into model weights (SFT + RL fine-tuning), so the durable change is to model weights, while the in-context object reflected upon is the buggy code + execution feedback.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: gradient_weight_update

- **requires training**: nested-RL+SFT: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on automatically collected and execution-verified explanation+refinement trajectories, followed by reinforcement learning (PPO) on both success and failure trajectories.

- **reward or critic model**:

> verifiable reward (unit-test passing rate S_ut and CodeBLEU similarity S_cb to verified correct refinements) combined with a learned-embedding explanation reward (RoBERTa cosine/sentiment similarity S_ex of the explanation to verified-correct explanations). Refinement reward R(r) and explanation reward R(e) are designed and applied separately within PPO.

- **distillation target**:

> model-weights: explanation+refinement capability is distilled (from a teacher LLM such as GPT-3.5-Turbo, CodeLlama-34B, or the model itself via self-bootstrap) into the student model's weights through SFT and then sharpened with RL.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> engineered: the reflective behavior (explain-then-refine chain) is scaffolded via prompt design and an explicitly engineered training pipeline (data collection, verification, SFT, and a hand-designed PPO reward), not RL-emergent in the R1 'aha-moment' sense.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: none (no external memory store at inference; experience is internalized into weights). Within an episode the chat history holds the buggy code and execution feedback as a short-term scratchpad/context.

- **memory persistence**: within-episode for the in-context buggy code/feedback; learned experience persists in weights cross-task (the fine-tuned model carries debugging ability across all test problems).

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> retrieval-gated / execution-verified filtering of training data: candidate explanations and refinements are kept only if the refinement passes all unit tests (execution verification); explanations are kept when paired with a correct refinement. There is no runtime episodic memory to curate.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> response-level / holistic: the model explains and refines the whole wrong solution conditioned on the failing test or error message, rather than localizing to a specific code block or token. (Unit-test passing rate gives outcome-level granularity in the reward.)

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> intra-task at inference (refine a single task's solution using its own execution feedback, optionally over multiple rounds); inter-task at training (debugging skill learned from many tasks transfers to new held-out tasks via weights).

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> post-hoc-revision: after an initial solution fails the unit tests, the model produces an explanation and a revised solution; supports iterative post-hoc refinement over multiple rounds rather than mid-trajectory in-flight correction.


### Application domain

- **task domains**: code (program synthesis / code generation and automated self-debugging/repair for Python programming tasks).

- **benchmarks**: Evaluation: MBPP, HumanEval, MBPP+, HumanEval+ (pass@k and success refinement rate). Training data sources: MBPP training set (374 problems), APPS training set (5,000 problems), and CodeContests.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> On three open-source backbones (StarCoder-15B, CodeLlama-7B, CodeLlama-13B), SFT improves pass@1 by up to 15.92% and pass@10 by up to 9.30% across four benchmarks; RL on top of SFT adds up to 3.54% pass@1 and 2.55% pass@10. Success refinement rate improves by up to ~10.15% (SFT) with up to a further 3.62% from RL.

- **baselines**:

> Prompting-based self-debugging on the same open-source backbones: 'Refine' (directly ask for a refinement) and 'Expl. + Refine' (ask for an explanation of the wrong code then refine, CoT-style); GPT-3.5-Turbo serves as a strong reference/teacher (e.g., on explanation quality and refinement rate). Prior training-based approaches discussed: ILF, CYCLE, Self-Edit, OpenCodeInterpreter, EURUS.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> vs prompting baseline: StarCoder-15B SFT (Expl.+Refine) +15.92% pass@1 and +6.30% pass@10 on MBPP&HumanEval (+14.13% pass@1, +9.30% pass@10 on MBPP+&HumanEval+); CodeLlama-7B SFT +14.41% pass@1; CodeLlama-13B SFT +12.23% pass@1. RL vs SFT: e.g., CodeLlama-13B +3.54% pass@1 on MBPP+&HumanEval+; StarCoder-15B +2.43% pass@1 / +2.55% pass@10 on MBPP&HumanEval. Success refinement rate (avg over 4 benchmarks): StarCoder-15B from 6.41-6.90% (prompting) to 16.27-16.56% (SFT, +9.37-10.15%) to 17.50-17.59% (RL); CodeLlama-13B up to 23.50% (RL).

- **compute cost profile**:

> Training cost: SFT for 2 epochs (batch size 128, lr 2e-5, AdamW, 500-step warmup, cosine decay) plus PPO RL (lr 2e-6, batch size 64, TRL library), all on 8x NVIDIA A100 40GB GPUs. Data-collection cost: sample 20 solutions per training problem (temperature 1.0) plus explanation+refinement generations from a teacher LLM, filtered by execution. Inference cost: roughly one extra generation per wrong solution per refinement round (multi-round iterative refinement multiplies calls by number of rounds, evaluated up to 3 rounds); explanation+refinement adds tokens vs direct refinement.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Reliance on specific teacher LLMs for data collection (GPT-3.5-Turbo, CodeLlama-34B, or self; other/smaller/mixed LLMs unexplored). Only two self-debug prompt types tested (direct refine; explain-then-refine); broader prompt strategies not explored. Requires unit tests / execution environment to verify training trajectories and supply RL reward, so depends on access to test cases. Demonstrated on relatively small Python benchmarks (MBPP/HumanEval and their + variants); not validated on repository-level or other languages.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> external-tool/verifier (and partially oracle-label at training): unit-test execution verifies refinements both for data filtering and as the RL reward; ground-truth correct refinements are used to compute the CodeBLEU similarity reward component. At inference, the model relies on provided unit-test execution feedback (error messages/failed test cases) to drive refinement, so it is not intrinsic-only.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive: training (SFT and RL) produces consistent pass@k and success-refinement-rate gains over prompting baselines on small open-source LLMs, including with execution-verified feedback. The gains are largely attributable to internalizing the explain-then-refine skill, but the method still depends on unit-test execution feedback rather than improving correction without any external signal.

- **calibration effect**: not-measured (the paper does not report confidence calibration; it focuses on pass@k, success refinement rate, and human/GPT-4-rated explanation quality).


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a (LeDex is a training method for self-debugging, not a failure-attribution/diagnosis benchmark; it does produce natural-language explanations of why code is wrong, but does not formally classify failure modes or attribute a responsible agent/step in a multi-agent taxonomy sense).

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets incorrect code generated by small open-source LLMs (logic/runtime/test-failing bugs) and the related failure mode of superficial or low-quality self-reflection: prompting-only self-debug on small LLMs barely refines wrong solutions (e.g., StarCoder-15B refines only 4.43% of MBPP wrong solutions vs 28.90% for GPT-3.5-Turbo); LeDex trains the model to produce useful explanations and effective refinements, mitigating ineffective/shallow self-correction.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug (Chen et al., 2024); Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023); Self-Edit and CYCLE (training-based code refinement); ILF / Imitation learning from Language Feedback (training with language feedback); OpenCodeInterpreter and EURUS (multi-turn interaction SFT datasets); PPO (Schulman et al.) via the TRL library; backbones StarCoder and CodeLlama; CodeBLEU and RoBERTa for reward components.

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Cited/contrasted as a training-based self-debug baseline by TGPR: Tree-Guided Policy Refinement for Robust Self-Debugging of LLMs (arXiv:2510.06878); ReflexiCoder (RL self-reflection/self-correction for code, contrasts LeDex's external-oracle dependence); Revisit Self-Debugging with Self-Generated Tests for Code Generation (ACL 2025); DePro: Understanding the Role of LLMs in Debugging Competitive Programming Code (arXiv:2603.19399).

- **citation count**: 49 (Semantic Scholar, mid-2025); ~49+


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> no: LeDex predates and does not target o1/R1-style reasoning models with built-in reflection; it explicitly trains explain-then-refine behavior into small non-reasoning code LLMs (StarCoder-15B, CodeLlama-7B/13B) via SFT+PPO rather than relying on emergent reflective reasoning.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Related to skill distillation: LeDex distills explanation+refinement skill from a teacher (GPT-3.5-Turbo / CodeLlama-34B) or self-bootstrapped data into the student via SFT, then does on-policy RL (PPO) on the model's own generated success/failure trajectories with execution-verified rewards. This SFT-distillation-then-on-policy-RL recipe is adjacent to on-policy distillation / skill-optimization, though the paper does not frame it using the on-policy-distillation terminology.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- code_url
