<a id="r053-first-try-matters-revisiting-the-role-of-reflection-in-reasoning-models"></a>
## First Try Matters: Revisiting the Role of Reflection in Reasoning Models

**ID:** R053  **Category:** F (Reasoning-model self-reflection (o1/R1-era) & its analysis)  **Authors:** Liwei Kang et al.  **Venue:** arXiv preprint (2025)  **Learning locus:** hybrid  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08308

### Basic info

- **name**: First Try Matters: Revisiting the Role of Reflection in Reasoning Models

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Liwei Kang, Yue Deng, Yao Xiao, Zhanfeng Mo, Wee Sun Lee, Lidong Bing (lead affiliation: MiroMind AI; with National University of Singapore and Singapore University of Technology and Design)

- **venue**: arXiv preprint (cs.AI); also indexed as DBLP CoRR abs/2510.08308. A version is under double-blind review on OpenReview (id g6xbW1FFXf), consistent with an ICLR-style submission.

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08308

- **code url**: https://github.com/Olafyii/first-try-matters


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**: calibration/probing

- **feedback source**: ground-truth-oracle

- **iteration structure**: single-shot

- **reflection object**:

> reasoning chain (the post-first-candidate portion of a long chain-of-thought is analyzed; the paper analyzes/categorizes the model's reflective reasoning trajectory rather than modifying output content, and for its proposed method it truncates the reasoning chain at inference time). It does not introduce a new corrective intervention; it is an analysis of native reflection plus an inference-time early-stopping controller over the reasoning chain.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: hybrid

- **requires training**:

> SFT (for the analysis experiments, SFT on Llama3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; the proposed early-stopping uses two small trained Qwen3-1.7B classifiers — a Candidate Answer Detector and a Question-aware Reflection Controller. The headline efficiency method itself applies no gradient update to the base reasoning model)

- **reward or critic model**:

> verifiable reward (correctness of candidate answers judged by the rule-based Math-Verify verifier during analysis; for the early-stopping method, two trained Qwen3-1.7B binary classifiers act as controllers rather than reward models)

- **distillation target**:

> none (the paper does not distill reflections into a reusable artifact; SFT experiments distill DeepSeek-R1/Qwen3-8B rollouts into student weights only to study the effect of reflection amount, and find gains come from first-answer correctness, not stored corrective skill)

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> Analysis of RL-emergent reflective behavior in o1/R1-style reasoning models (both RL-trained and SFT-distilled). The paper's own contribution (question-aware early-stopping via CAD+QRC controllers) is engineered/scaffolded on top of that emergent behavior.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: none

- **memory persistence**: within-episode

- **memory curation mechanism**: n/a


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> step-level (a long CoT is segmented into reasoning steps delimited by line breaks; an LLM-based extractor locates the positions of candidate answers, and reflections are defined as the content between two consecutive candidate answers; correctness transitions T->T, F->F, F->T, T->F are classified at the candidate-answer step level)

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> intra-task (the analysis concerns refinement/reflection within a single question's reasoning trajectory; the early-stopping intervention also operates within one task at inference time; there is no cross-task experience transfer)

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**: post-hoc-revision (the studied native reflections are post-first-answer revision attempts, found to be predominantly confirmatory and rarely corrective; the paper's intervention truncates rather than recovers)


### Application domain

- **task domains**: math

- **benchmarks**: AIME2024, AIME2025, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH500 (analysis over 3,427 rollouts per model; SFT evaluated on the combined set of these five)


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Question-aware adaptive early-stopping (CAD + QRC) on Qwen3-8B reduces reasoning tokens by 24.5% across five math datasets (15,125 -> 11,414 avg tokens) with only a 2.9% average accuracy drop (84.7% -> 81.8%); CAD alone gives 29.9% token reduction at a 3.8% drop.

- **baselines**:

> Native full-reflection generation of the reasoning models (e.g., Qwen3-8B with full reasoning); CAD-only early-stopping (terminate at first candidate) as an ablation vs CAD+QRC; for SFT studies, cut-at-i datasets (cut-at-1 through cut-at-6) and varying ratios (0%-100%) of corrective (F->T) reflections; before-vs-after RL comparison (MiroMind-M1-SFT vs MiroMind-M1-RL at 7B/32B).

- **gains vs baseline**:

> Efficiency: vs full Qwen3-8B reasoning, CAD+QRC cuts tokens 24.5% for a 2.9% accuracy drop (CAD-only: 29.9% tokens / 3.8% drop). Tunable trade-off: 1pp accuracy drop -> 12.0% token reduction; 8.12% accuracy drop -> 40.7% token reduction. Analysis findings: reflections after the first candidate consume 16.8%-47.8% of tokens but add only 1.4%-3.5% accuracy; >90% of reflections are confirmatory and corrective F->T reflections are mostly <2%. SFT: cut-at-6 beats cut-at-1 by 4.05% avg accuracy, of which +3.75% is from first-answer correctness and only +0.3% from reflections. RL gains come mainly from first-answer accuracy (+4.6% for 32B, +7.7% for 7B) with reflections contributing only +0.3%/+0.1%.

- **compute cost profile**:

> The proposed method REDUCES inference compute: ~24.5% fewer reasoning tokens (CAD+QRC) or ~29.9% (CAD only) vs single full-reflection pass, while staying within ~2.9-3.8% accuracy. It adds two lightweight Qwen3-1.7B classifiers (CAD scores each generated sentence; QRC scores the question once). Training-side cost in the analysis: six SFT datasets each fixed at 28M tokens (cut-at-1 has 6,754 questions, cut-at-6 has 3,405 questions); corrective-ratio study uses ~6K problems; SFT run on Llama3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Scope limited to mathematical reasoning (five math benchmarks) and to reflections occurring after a first candidate answer; the LLM-based candidate extractor is imperfect (94% human-judged correct on a 100-rollout/426-candidate sample); reflection-type analysis relies on Math-Verify rule-based checking; the early-stopping incurs a real accuracy cost (e.g., -5.8% on AIME2025); QRC/CAD are tuned with specific thresholds (0.05 / 0.5) and the trade-off is dataset-dependent; findings about reflection being confirmatory may not generalize beyond math or to non-reasoning-model LLMs.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> oracle-label/ground-truth — the analysis labels each candidate answer's correctness with the ground-truth-backed Math-Verify rule-based verifier to classify confirmatory vs corrective reflections. This is the discriminating variable: the paper SHOWS native reflections rarely flip wrong->right (corrective F->T mostly <2%), i.e., intrinsic self-correction is weak; the efficiency method does not require an oracle at inference (it relies on learned CAD/QRC classifiers).

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-negligible/confirmatory — native reflections are predominantly confirmatory (>90%) and rarely corrective (F->T mostly <2%); subsequent reflections add only 1.4%-3.5% accuracy while the first answer dominates final accuracy. Training to add corrective reflections does not increase the model's flip probability p(F->T) (best-vs-worst difference only 1.7%). Self-correction efficacy is therefore essentially marginal/task-dependent, with first-try correctness being the real driver.

- **calibration effect**:

> not-measured (the paper does not directly study confidence calibration; it studies answer-correctness transitions and token efficiency, finding reflections are mostly confirmatory rather than examining over/under-confidence)


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> classifies-failure-mode (taxonomy) — proposes a taxonomy of reflection transitions between consecutive candidate answers: T->T, F->F(same), F->F(diff), F->T (corrective), T->F (degradation), with T->T and F->F(same) defined as confirmatory and F->T as corrective.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets/exposes superficial or 'confirmatory' self-reflection (reflections that merely reaffirm an existing answer rather than correcting it) and the resulting overthinking/redundant-reflection token waste; relates to MAST-style superficial self-reflection and overthinking/redundant-reasoning modes. It also documents a counterintuitive mode: models reflect more on easy problems and less on hard ones (reflection budget misaligned with task difficulty).


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> DeepSeek-R1 (RLVR reasoning models), OpenAI o1, Chain-of-Thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022; Nye et al. 2021 scratchpads), inference-time scaling work (Snell et al. 2024; Muennighoff et al. 2025 s1; Brown et al. 2025); uses MiroMind-M1 (Li et al. 2025) SFT/RL data and models, Qwen3, gpt-oss, MiMo-7B-RL, Magistral, and the Math-Verify verifier; conceptually relates to critiques that self-reflection is superficial (Liu et al. 2025).

- **citation count**: 12 (Semantic Scholar, as of 2026-06; referenceCount 48)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> true — the paper specifically targets o1/R1-style reasoning models with built-in reflective reasoning (analyzes 8 such models: MiMo-7B-RL, gpt-oss-20b, Magistral-Small-2506, DeepSeek-R1-0528, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, Qwen3-8B, DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B) and argues their gains come from first-answer correctness rather than reflection.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Tangential. The SFT experiments distill DeepSeek-R1/Qwen3-8B rollouts into Llama3.1-8B/Qwen2.5-7B students and find more-reflection rollouts mainly raise first-answer accuracy (via diverse-path exposure), not corrective skill — implying that what gets distilled is improved first-try competence rather than a self-correction routine. Not framed as on-policy distillation, but informs OPD/skill-optimization debates about whether reflection is a transferable skill.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Analysis scale: 3,427 rollouts per model across 8 models (AIME2024/2025 32 rollouts per question, AMC 4, OlympiadBench and MATH500 1). SFT: six datasets fixed at 28M tokens each (cut-at-1 = 6,754 questions, cut-at-6 = 3,405 questions); corrective-ratio study ~6K problems. Early-stopping controllers (CAD, QRC) are Qwen3-1.7B trained on annotated MiroMind-M1-SFT rollouts. Human-eval robustness: 100 rollouts / 426 candidates, 94% correct.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- extended_by_or_inspired

<a id="r054-reasoning-about-uncertainty-do-reasoning-models-know-when-they-dont-know"></a>
## Reasoning about Uncertainty: Do Reasoning Models Know When They Don't Know?

**ID:** R054  **Category:** F (Reasoning-model self-reflection (o1/R1-era) & its analysis)  **Authors:** Zhiting Mei et al.  **Venue:** arXiv preprint (Princeton University)  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18183

### Basic info

- **name**: Reasoning about Uncertainty: Do Reasoning Models Know When They Don't Know?

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Zhiting Mei, Christina Zhang, Tenny Yin, Justin Lidard, Ola Shorinwa, Anirudha Majumdar (Princeton University)

- **venue**: arXiv preprint

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18183


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**: calibration/probing | verbal-self-critique (introspective UQ: a second-stage model verbally critiques the first model's chain-of-thought to recalibrate its confidence)

- **feedback source**:

> self-generated (the reasoning model introspects on its own chain-of-thought traces via self-verbalized prompting; ground-truth labels are used only externally by the authors to compute calibration metrics ECE/MCE, not fed back to the model). Black-box only — no logit/internal-state access.

- **iteration structure**:

> iterative-refine (two-stage introspective pipeline: stage 1 answers + verbalizes confidence; stage 2 reasons over the stage-1 trace to revise the confidence estimate; limited to two stages in this work, optimal stage count left to future work)

- **reflection object**:

> reasoning chain (the model reflects on its own chain-of-thought trace and final answer to identify flaws and re-estimate confidence). It does NOT modify the output answer itself — the second stage is restricted to reasoning about uncertainty/confidence, deliberately not updating the original answer to avoid hallucination/vacillation. So the modified artifact is the confidence/uncertainty estimate over the existing answer.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal

- **requires training**: none (all models evaluated zero-shot via API without any fine-tuning; introspection is purely prompt/inference-time)

- **reward or critic model**: self-as-judge (the reasoning model itself, in a second introspective stage, judges and re-scores the confidence of its own first-stage reasoning trace; no separate trained reward/critic model is used)

- **distillation target**: none (no reusable artifact is distilled; introspective UQ operates per-query at inference time and produces a recalibrated confidence estimate, not stored memory/skills/weights)

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> engineered (introspective UQ is a prompt/scaffold-engineered two-stage procedure layered on top of reasoning models; however the paper analyzes RL-emergent reasoning depth and finds that emergent deeper reasoning worsens calibration/overconfidence)


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: none (no persistent memory; the only state passed forward is the stage-1 chain-of-thought trace handed to the stage-2 introspection prompt within a single query)

- **memory persistence**: within-episode (the first-stage reasoning trace is provided to the second-stage introspection within the same query; nothing persists across questions/tasks/sessions)

- **memory curation mechanism**: n/a (no memory store is maintained)


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> holistic/outcome-level (introspection targets the overall correctness/confidence of the full response; the second stage identifies flaws in the chain-of-thought to adjust a single answer-level confidence score rather than localizing/correcting individual reasoning steps). The paper notes step-level/intermediate-step calibration benchmarks as future work.

- **intra task vs inter task**: intra-task (calibration and introspection are performed per question on a single task instance; no experience is transferred across tasks)

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**: post-hoc-revision (the second stage post-hoc revises the confidence estimate after the answer is produced; it explicitly does NOT correct the answer in-flight, so this is confidence revision rather than answer recovery)


### Application domain

- **task domains**: QA/reasoning (multiple-choice and open-ended question answering spanning arithmetic, science, humanities, professional knowledge, and factuality); analysis/UQ of reasoning models

- **benchmarks**:

> ARC-Challenge, GPQA, MMLU (abstract algebra, professional accounting, professional medicine, international law, sociology subsets), StrategyQA, SimpleQA. Calibration measured via Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Maximum Calibration Error (MCE) with reliability diagrams.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Reasoning models are systematically overconfident: self-verbalized confidence is often >85%, especially on incorrect responses; overconfidence grows with deeper reasoning (on consistently wrong-answered questions, o3-Mini shows a ~7% absolute ECE increase from low- to high-reasoning, Claude ~2%). Introspective UQ improves calibration for o3-Mini and DeepSeek R1 (largest gains on SimpleQA with the more conservative IUQ-Medium/IUQ-High prompts) but worsens it for Claude 3.7 Sonnet.

- **baselines**:

> Self-verbalized UQ prompt strategies without introspection: zero-shot basic prompting, chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, multi-step prompting, and Top-K prompting. Also contextualized against prior reported calibration of non-reasoning models (e.g., pre-RLHF GPT-4 had lower/better ECE on an MMLU subset).

- **gains vs baseline**:

> Introspection effect is model- and dataset-dependent rather than a uniform gain. Averaged over models, IUQ-Low marginally increases ECE while IUQ-Medium and IUQ-High decrease ECE (largest reductions on the hardest dataset, SimpleQA); MCE increases across datasets. For deeper reasoning on GPQA, low->high reasoning gives +10.8% accuracy and -5.5% ECE; but on saturated/hard datasets (e.g., SimpleQA) deeper reasoning increases ECE. Claude's accuracy/calibration trade-off: Claude is the best-calibrated model and ~2% more accurate than DeepSeek and >4% more accurate than o3-Mini, with weaker accuracy-ECE correlation (r=-0.69 vs near -1.0 for others).

- **compute cost profile**:

> Introspective UQ roughly doubles inference cost vs a single self-verbalized pass (two reasoning stages per query: one answer-generation pass plus one introspection pass over the trace). The reasoning-depth study additionally scales thinking-token budget across RE-Low/RE-Medium/RE-High levels, increasing inference time and energy with deeper reasoning. No training cost (zero-shot API evaluation).


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Analysis is restricted to black-box self-verbalized UQ (no access to closed-source logits/internal states); introspection limited to two stages (optimal stage count left to future work); Gemini excluded from reasoning-depth and introspection analyses due to insufficient support for reasoning-token budget / reasoning-trace analysis, and Grok 3 Beta not benchmarked (no access). Many existing benchmarks are saturated, making them uninformative for UQ; the work calls for new UQ benchmarks (including intermediate-step calibration). Introspection is not uniformly beneficial — it degrades Claude 3.7 Sonnet's calibration, possibly due to closed-source implementation details. Reasoning-depth tuning hurts format/completion compliance, especially in scientific domains (GPQA).

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> self-verify (the model recalibrates confidence purely by introspecting on its own chain-of-thought; no external tool/verifier, oracle label, or environment reward is given to the model. Ground-truth labels are used only by the authors offline to score calibration via ECE/MCE, not as feedback to the model.)

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent (introspective confidence recalibration is net-positive for o3-Mini and DeepSeek R1 — especially with conservative prompts on hard benchmarks like SimpleQA — but net-negative for Claude 3.7 Sonnet; IUQ-Low can even raise average ECE. This is confidence self-correction, not answer self-correction, since the answer is intentionally left unchanged.)

- **calibration effect**:

> mixed (a central, explicitly measured finding). Reasoning models are overconfident, and deeper RL-induced reasoning generally degrades calibration / worsens overconfidence — a 'reasoning tax' on calibration — particularly on incorrect responses where deeper reasoning reinforces a misguided thought process. Introspection improves calibration for some models (o3-Mini, DeepSeek R1) but worsens it for others (Claude 3.7 Sonnet).


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a (the paper is an analysis/UQ study of reasoning-model calibration and overconfidence, not a multi-agent failure-attribution method; introspection identifies flaws in a single model's own reasoning trace to adjust confidence but does not produce a failure-mode taxonomy or attribute responsibility across agents/steps)

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Overconfidence / poor calibration of reasoning models (confidently wrong responses / hallucinations). Closely related to the 'reasoning tax' and overthinking-style failure modes: deeper reasoning increases confidence on incorrect answers by reinforcing a flawed thought process. Also surfaces 'superficial self-reflection' risk — introspection does not uniformly help and can entrench overconfidence (e.g., Claude).


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Self-verbalized / black-box UQ for LLMs (e.g., Tian et al.; Xiong et al.; Lin et al.; verbalized confidence and Top-K prompting); calibration foundations (ECE/MCE, proper scoring rules, Guo et al.); chain-of-thought and multi-step prompting (Wei et al.; Kojima et al.); findings that RLHF degrades token-level calibration (OpenAI GPT-4 report). Targets RL-trained reasoning models: Claude 3.7, o3-Mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, DeepSeek R1.

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Cited by subsequent calibration/UQ-of-reasoning-models work, e.g., 'Process Supervision of Confidence Margin for Calibrated LLM Reasoning' (2026), 'Unsupervised Confidence Calibration for Reasoning LLMs from a Single Generation' (2026), 'How Uncertainty Estimation Scales with Sampling in Reasoning Models' (2026), 'Confidence Should Be Calibrated More Than One Turn Deep' (2026), 'Confidence Before Answering: A Paradigm Shift for Efficient LLM Uncertainty Estimation' (2026), and 'When Is Thinking Enough? Early Exit via Sufficiency Assessment for Efficient Reasoning' (2026).

- **citation count**: 32 (Semantic Scholar, as of 2026-06; influential citation count 3)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> Yes — the paper specifically targets o1/R1-era reasoning models with built-in RL-induced multi-step reasoning (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek R1, o3-Mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking) and analyzes how their native reasoning depth affects calibration; introspective UQ leverages the models' reasoning ability to reflect on their own chain-of-thought.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Weak/indirect. No distillation is performed; the method is purely inference-time. The authors propose (as future work) training reasoning models via reinforcement learning to explicitly reason about their own uncertainty/knowledge boundaries, which is conceptually adjacent to on-policy reflection optimization but is not implemented here.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Introspective UQ uses two inference passes per query (one answer pass + one introspection pass over the trace); the reasoning-depth study sweeps three reasoning-effort levels (RE-Low/Medium/High). No iterative trial budget beyond the two stages (stage count capped at two, with optimal depth left to future work).


### Uncertain (not determined)

- dataset_or_benchmark_released

<a id="r055-reasoning-models-better-express-their-confidence"></a>
## Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence

**ID:** R055  **Category:** F (Reasoning-model self-reflection (o1/R1-era) & its analysis)  **Authors:** Dongkeun Yoon et al.  **Venue:** arXiv preprint (KAIST, LG AI Research, CMU, UCL)  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14489

### Basic info

- **name**: Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**:

> Dongkeun Yoon, Seungone Kim, Sohee Yang, Sunkyoung Kim, Soyeon Kim, Yongil Kim, Eunbi Choi, Yireun Kim, Minjoon Seo et al. (KAIST; lead/first author Dongkeun Yoon, KAIST, work done during internship at LG AI Research; co-affiliations LG AI Research, CMU, UCL)

- **venue**: NeurIPS 2025 (accepted); originally arXiv preprint (arXiv:2505.14489, v1 May 2025, v2 Oct 2025)

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14489

- **code url**: https://github.com/MattYoon/reasoning-models-confidence


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> calibration/probing (verbalized confidence estimation analysis); the studied behavior is verbal self-critique via slow-thinking CoT (exploring alternatives, verifying, backtracking) used to adjust expressed confidence. The paper itself is an analysis/benchmarking study, not a new method.

- **feedback source**:

> self-generated (the model's own slow-thinking CoT dynamically adjusts verbalized confidence; no external tool/verifier/oracle is used to drive the confidence adjustment). For evaluation only, answer-correctness labels are matched against ground truth via GPT-4o mini to compute calibration metrics.

- **iteration structure**:

> single-shot (one CoT pass per question producing answer + verbalized confidence); analysis tracks confidence trajectory token-by-token within that single CoT. A discussion experiment (budget forcing, appending 'Wait,') tests extra inference rounds but does not reliably improve calibration.

- **reflection object**:

> output content (the verbalized/expressed confidence estimate) and the reasoning chain itself: the model reflects on its own chain-of-thought (via slow-thinking behaviors such as exploring alternatives, verifying, backtracking, epistemic markers) to dynamically refine the confidence it attaches to its answer. No prompt, skill, rules, code, or weights are modified.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal

- **requires training**:

> none (this is an inference-time analysis of existing reasoning vs non-reasoning models; the calibration gains require no weight update. Section 4.3 shows non-reasoning models gain calibration purely via in-context learning / few-shot slow-thinking exemplars). The reasoning models themselves were produced by prior RL/distillation, but no training is performed in this paper.

- **reward or critic model**:

> none (no reward model or external critic; confidence is self-expressed by the model through slow thinking. GPT-4o mini is used only as an answer-matching judge for scoring correctness, and GPT-4.1 is used only to edit CoTs in ablations — neither provides a learning/improvement signal).

- **distillation target**:

> none (reflection is not distilled into a persistent artifact in this paper). The closest related effect: in Section 4.3, R1-Distill-Qwen-32B slow-thinking traces are reused as few-shot in-context exemplars (prompt-level transfer) to elicit slow thinking in non-reasoning models, but this is in-context only, not a stored/optimized artifact.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> Primarily RL/distillation-emergent: the slow-thinking behaviors (exploring alternatives, backtracking, epistemic markers) that drive calibration emerge from how reasoning models (o1/R1-style) were trained, not from a hand-built reflection scaffold. The paper isolates this by showing Qwen3 (single checkpoint) is far better calibrated in Thinking vs Non-thinking mode, and that the behavior can also be elicited in non-reasoning models via engineered in-context demonstrations — i.e., the calibration gain is attributable to the slow-thinking process itself rather than to a specific training recipe.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> none (no persistent memory; analysis operates within a single CoT / scratchpad per question). For the in-context-learning experiment, a short-term in-context exemplar set (3 slow-thinking demonstrations) is used as prompt context, but nothing is stored across episodes.

- **memory persistence**: within-episode (confidence is adjusted only within a single chain-of-thought; no cross-episode/cross-task experience persistence).

- **memory curation mechanism**: n/a (no memory store is maintained or curated).


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> response-level for the headline calibration result (one confidence estimate per answer). The mechanistic analysis is finer-grained: token-level / step-level, since confidence is read out at each token position by appending '</think>\nAnswer:' to terminate reasoning early, revealing how confidence is refined across CoT steps (verification raises it, considering an alternative lowers it, rejecting the alternative raises it again).

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> intra-task: confidence is refined within a single question's reasoning process; there is no transfer of experience across tasks/episodes. (The in-context exemplars in 4.3 are static demonstrations, not accumulated cross-task experience.)

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> mid-trajectory-recovery (in-flight): the model dynamically corrects/refines its expressed confidence during the CoT as it explores and rejects alternatives, rather than retrying after a failed episode or revising post-hoc.


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> QA/reasoning (knowledge-focused factual QA and reasoning-intensive multiple-choice). Two task types: knowledge-focused (open-ended factual recall) and reasoning-intensive (math and non-math multiple-choice). Framed as foundational for trustworthy/reliable LLMs and uncertainty-aware LLM agents.

- **benchmarks**:

> Six datasets/subsets: TriviaQA and NonambigQA (knowledge-focused; NonambigQA derived from AmbigQA/Natural Questions), plus Math and Non-Math subsets of MMLU-Pro and of SuperGPQA (reasoning-intensive multiple-choice). 1,000 examples uniformly sampled per dataset/subset; bootstrapping over resampled subsets for robustness.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Six reasoning models (from four 32B-scale backbones) achieve strictly better verbalized confidence calibration than their non-reasoning counterparts in 33 out of 36 settings (6 model pairs x 6 datasets), measured by ECE (lower better), Brier Score (lower better), and AUROC (higher better). Gains hold even on knowledge-focused datasets where task accuracy is comparable, showing calibration gains are not merely a byproduct of better task accuracy.

- **baselines**:

> Non-reasoning, instruction-tuned counterparts of each reasoning model: Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (vs R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, QwQ-32B, Skywork-OR1-Preview-32B), GLM-4-32B-0414 (vs GLM-Z1-32B-0414), EXAONE-3.5-32B-Instruct (vs EXAONE-Deep-32B), and Qwen3-32B Non-thinking mode (vs Qwen3-32B Thinking mode). Also compared against advanced verbalized-confidence prompting baselines for non-reasoning models (Top-K, Multi-step) and an internal No-CoT lower bound.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> Large ECE reductions on knowledge-focused data. Example (TriviaQA, Qwen2.5-32B group): Qwen2.5-Instruct ECE 0.129 vs R1-Distill-Qwen 0.042 and QwQ 0.063; AUROC 0.769 vs 0.807 (QwQ). Qwen3-32B: Non-thinking ECE 0.207 / AUROC 0.650 vs Thinking ECE 0.063 / AUROC 0.807 on TriviaQA (and on NonambigQA ECE 0.403 / AUROC 0.572 vs 0.226 / 0.757) for the same checkpoint. In-context slow-thinking (Table 5) improves non-reasoning models too: e.g., GLM-4-32B on TriviaQA ECE 0.150->0.029, AUROC 0.631->0.796; on NonambigQA ECE 0.338->0.126, AUROC 0.573->0.715. Calibration gap also widens with model size.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Inference-time only; reasoning models incur the extra token cost of extended CoT (slow thinking) vs single-pass non-reasoning generation. Some reasoning models (R1-Distill, OR1-Preview, GLM-Z1) require a forced second inference round to elicit explicit Confidence Reasoning (regenerate up to </think> then re-prompt). Budget forcing (appending 'Wait,' for extra rounds) was tested but did not reliably improve calibration, indicating quality not quantity of slow thinking matters. No training compute (no gradient updates).


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Reasoning models still tend toward high confidence, rarely assigning values below ~55%; lower task accuracy (e.g., NonambigQA) yields notably higher ECE/Brier, so residual overconfidence remains. Main experiments are limited to 32B-scale open models; proprietary o1/R1 not directly benchmarked. Calibration is for verbalized confidence specifically. The forced-Confidence-Reasoning procedure for some models, GPT-based answer matching and GPT-4.1-based CoT editing in ablations, and 1,000-example subsampling are potential sources of noise (mitigated via bootstrapping and manual inspection of 100 examples per ablation setting).

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> intrinsic-only for the confidence-adjustment mechanism: the model improves its expressed confidence purely through its own slow-thinking CoT with no external verifier, tool, or oracle label feeding into the confidence. Ground-truth labels are used only for offline evaluation/scoring of calibration, not as a correction signal.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive: reasoning models become progressively better calibrated as the CoT unfolds (statistically significant improving slopes, p<0.05), while non-reasoning models show no such trend (sometimes worsening). This is a calibration (confidence) self-correction result rather than answer self-correction, and it improves without label leakage; removing slow-thinking (linearizing the CoT) significantly degrades calibration.

- **calibration effect**:

> improves: extended CoT / slow thinking strictly improves verbalized confidence calibration in 33/36 settings, directly contrasting the 'reasoning tax' / overconfidence concern. Ablations show non-linear reasoning (exploring alternatives, backtracking, refining) is the largest contributor; removing it degrades all three metrics, and removing epistemic markers causes overconfidence (worse ECE) though it can raise AUROC by collapsing predictions into two bins.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**: n/a (this work analyzes confidence calibration, not multi-agent failure attribution or a failure-mode taxonomy).

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets/exposes LLM overconfidence and miscalibration ('sounding confident even when wrong') in verbalized confidence. Shows that slow thinking mitigates overconfidence and that linearized/fast reasoning (removing exploration, backtracking, and epistemic uncertainty markers) produces overconfident, less-calibrated outputs. Relevant to reasoning-model failure modes like superficial self-reflection and overconfidence rather than MAST multi-agent modes.

- **dataset or benchmark released**: No new benchmark dataset released; evaluation reuses TriviaQA, NonambigQA, MMLU-Pro, and SuperGPQA. Code (and prompts/evaluation pipeline) released at https://github.com/MattYoon/reasoning-models-confidence.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Verbalized confidence estimation (Tian et al. 2023 'Just Ask for Calibration'; Xiong et al. 2024 'Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty'; Geng et al. 2024 survey); calibration metrics ECE (Naeini et al. 2015 / Guo et al. 2017), Brier Score, AUROC; reasoning models / inference-time scaling (OpenAI o1 (Jaech et al. 2024), DeepSeek-R1, QwQ-32B, Skywork-OR1, GLM-Z1, EXAONE-Deep, Qwen3); slow-thinking / cognitive-behavior characterization (Gandhi et al. 2025; Min et al. 2024 'imitate'); 'know what they know' calibration (Kadavath et al. 2022); budget forcing (Muennighoff et al. 2025, s1); in-context learning (Dong et al. 2022 survey).

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Cited by follow-up work on reasoning-model confidence/uncertainty, e.g. 'Thinking Out Loud: Do Reasoning Models Know When They're Right?' (Zeng, Xuan et al.) and 'Verbalized Confidence Triggers Self-...' (verbalized-confidence self-correction work) indexed on Semantic Scholar; broadly part of the 2025 line analyzing calibration of o1/R1-style reasoning models (concurrent work zhang2025reasoning trains a hidden-state probe over CoT, contrasted in the paper).

- **citation count**: 53 (Semantic Scholar, as of June 2026; influentialCitationCount 5)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> Yes — the paper specifically targets and holds for o1/R1-style reasoning models with extended-CoT slow thinking; its central thesis is that the built-in slow-thinking/reflective behavior of these models is what produces better verbalized confidence calibration, and that eliciting the same behavior (Qwen3 Thinking mode, or in-context slow-thinking in non-reasoning models) reproduces the benefit.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Indirect/weak: the studied reasoning models include distilled ones (R1-Distill-Qwen, derived from DeepSeek-R1 distillation), and Section 4.3 reuses R1-Distill-Qwen-32B's own slow-thinking traces as in-context exemplars (an on-policy-style transfer of reflective behavior into other models), but the paper does no on-policy distillation or skill-optimization itself; this is an analysis of inference-time behavior.

- **sample efficiency**:

> n/a — no training/iterative trials to reach the result; it is a single-pass inference benchmark. Calibration improves monotonically along a single CoT (the longer/slow-thinking the CoT, the better-calibrated), but forcing additional inference rounds (budget forcing) does not reliably improve calibration further.

<a id="r064-sets-leveraging-self-verification-and-self-correction-for-improved-test-time-scaling"></a>
## SETS: Leveraging Self-Verification and Self-Correction for Improved Test-Time Scaling

**ID:** R064  **Category:** F (Reasoning-model self-reflection (o1/R1-era) & its analysis)  **Authors:** Jiefeng Chen et al. (Google)  **Venue:** TMLR 2025  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://openreview.net/forum?id=Wv9NMJoKww

### Basic info

- **name**: SETS: Leveraging Self-Verification and Self-Correction for Improved Test-Time Scaling

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Jiefeng Chen et al. (Google Cloud AI Research / Google DeepMind); co-authors Jie Ren, Xinyun Chen, Chengrun Yang, Ruoxi Sun, Jinsung Yoon, Sercan O. Arik

- **venue**: TMLR 2025 (arXiv preprint 2501.19306, first submitted 2025-01-31)

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19306 (OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=Wv9NMJoKww)


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**: verbal-self-critique (LLM's own zero-shot Self-Verify produces natural-language feedback that drives Self-Correct); no learned critic model and no external tool/oracle

- **feedback source**:

> self-generated (the same LLM verifies its own proposed solution and emits a correct/incorrect judgement plus rationale; rule-based parsing of the verification string sets J(r)); final answer selected by majority voting via exact match

- **iteration structure**:

> Hybrid of parallel + sequential: m initial responses are sampled in parallel, then each is iteratively refined via Self-Verify -> Self-Correct up to n rounds (early-stop once self-verified correct), then majority voting aggregates the m refined responses. SELF-REFINE is the special case m=1.

- **reflection object**:

> output content / answer (the proposed solution y_k is revised). Operates on the response text rather than on a persistent reasoning chain, action trajectory, prompt, skill, or weights; the self-verification feedback r_k targets the candidate answer to be corrected.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal (no weight update; SETS is a training-free, test-time/inference-time scaling framework that uses only the LLM's existing capabilities)

- **requires training**: none (explicitly 'without any model training'; no fine-tuned reward or revision models, unlike snell2024scaling which trained task-specific verifiers/revision models)

- **reward or critic model**:

> self-as-judge: the LLM's own zero-shot self-verification provides the improvement signal (J(r) judgement function), combined with majority voting for final selection. No trained reward model, no verifiable/external reward.

- **distillation target**: none (reflection is not distilled into any reusable artifact; each query is solved fresh at test time with no episodic memory, skill, rule, or weight update persisted)

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> prompt/scaffold-engineered: SETS is a hand-designed inference algorithm with tailored Sampling/Self-Verify/Self-Correct prompts orchestrated by Algorithm 1. However, it explicitly relies on and is enabled by the (RL-trained) self-verification/self-correction abilities that have emerged in recent advanced LLMs, and is also applied to RL-trained 'thinking' models.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: short-term/scratchpad (within a single query: the running set of {y_k, r_k} solution-feedback pairs is carried in the Self-Correct prompt context); no long-term memory

- **memory persistence**: within-episode (per-query only; nothing is carried across queries, tasks, or sessions)

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> n/a / append-only within an episode (the Self-Correct prompt accumulates the prior solutions and verification feedback {y_k, r_k}_{k=0..j}; bounded by the max number of rounds n, default n=4); no cross-episode memory to curate


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> holistic/outcome-level (response-level): Self-Verify emits a single correct/incorrect judgement on the whole proposed solution (J(r) in {0,1}) and Self-Correct revises the full answer; it does not localize errors to individual reasoning steps, code blocks, or tokens

- **intra task vs inter task**: intra-task: refinement happens within a single query (Self-Verify/Self-Correct rounds on the same problem); there is no transfer of experience across tasks or queries

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> post-hoc-revision: after a complete candidate answer is produced, it is self-verified and, if judged incorrect, revised by Self-Correct over up to n rounds; this is iterative post-hoc correction of completed answers (not mid-trajectory in-flight recovery, not next-episode avoidance)


### Application domain

- **task domains**: planning, QA/reasoning, math, coding (broadly: complex reasoning tasks with objectively verifiable, well-structured answers)

- **benchmarks**: NATURAL PLAN (Trip Planning, Meeting Planning), LiveBench Reasoning (spatial, zebra_puzzle, web_of_lies_v2), MATH 500, AIME 2024-2025, LiveCodeBench TestOutputPred (six datasets total)


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Up to 10.9% absolute accuracy improvement over the strongest comparable training-free baselines across planning/reasoning/math/coding, with both non-thinking and thinking models; SETS shows more advantageous (less-saturating, higher) test-time scaling curves than repeated sampling (BoN+Majority Vote) and SELF-REFINE.

- **baselines**:

> SELF-REFINE (madaan2024self; sequential, m=1); BoN+Majority Vote (a.k.a. Self-Consistency, wangself); BoN+Self-Eval (LLM picks best answer via multi-choice QA prompt, ren2023self); BoN+Self-Verify (sample m, self-verify each, majority vote over verified-correct). All baselines are training-free with no external reward models, for fair comparison.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> Reported up to +10.9% accuracy over the strongest training-free baseline. SETS adds Self-Correct on top of BoN+Self-Verify (the strongest single-component baseline) and adds parallel sampling on top of SELF-REFINE. Diagnostic Self-Correction deltas (SELF-REFINE-style, Table 2): e.g., GEMINI-1.5-Pro Trip Planning +10.94 by round 2 and LiveCodeBench TestOutputPred +22.17 by round 2; GEMINI-2.5-Flash Meeting Planning +12.10 and LiveBench Reasoning +14.67 by round 2. Gains are largest when the model's own self-verification/self-correction is strong, and small/absent when it is weak (e.g., Claude-3.5-Sonnet on LiveBench Reasoning).

- **compute cost profile**:

> Test-time-only (no training cost). Inference cost is many-fold a single pass: SETS samples m initial responses (search space m in [1,50] non-thinking, [1,25] thinking) and applies up to n rounds (n in [1,10], default n=4) of Self-Verify + Self-Correct per sample, each operation being a separate LLM call; recommended practical setting m=50, n=4. Cost measured primarily by average number of output tokens (also API calls and financial cost in appendices). Claimed to be more compute-optimal than baselines: reaches higher accuracy at equal token budget and saturates less, but is strictly more expensive than a single forward pass.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Efficacy is directly tied to (and bottlenecked by) the base LLM's intrinsic self-verification and self-correction quality; weak self-verification/self-correction (or weak instruction-following, e.g. GEMINI-2.5-Flash-Lite-Thinking on Trip Planning yielding 'None' parses) yields little/no gain. Self-correction can even degrade accuracy on some model/task pairs (e.g., GEMINI-2.5-Flash on MATH 500: round-1 delta -3.80, round-2 -1.80; GEMINI-1.5-Pro AIME round-1 -5.00). Restricted to tasks with objectively verifiable, well-structured (exact-match/rule-checkable) answers; majority voting limits it to such answer formats. Text-only evaluation; needs better aggregation (e.g., Universal Self-Consistency) and prompt optimization to extend to open-ended domains like summarization/tool-use and to multimodal.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> self-verify (intrinsic): the framework uses ONLY the LLM's own self-verification feedback, with no external tool, verifier, ground-truth oracle, or environment reward at inference. Authors note an upper-bound analysis with oracle selection (BoN+Oracle) for reference, but the deployed method is oracle-free; on LiveCodeBench TestOutputPred SETS even surpassed BoN+Oracle, indicating self-verify+self-correct can beat label-based selection when the model is strong.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent / capability-dependent and explicitly net-positive only when the base model has strong self-verification and self-correction; can be net-negative on some model/dataset pairs (correction degrades accuracy, e.g., GEMINI-2.5-Flash on MATH 500, GEMINI-1.5-Pro on AIME). Improves WITHOUT label leakage (no oracle/ground-truth used at inference), which directly counters the huanglarge (Huang et al.) critique that LLMs cannot self-correct intrinsically; SETS argues advanced LLMs now can, when correction is guided by self-verification and aggregated by voting.

- **calibration effect**:

> not-measured directly as a calibration metric, though related signals are reported: self-verification precision/recall/F1 per model-task (Table 2) and a Confidence-weighted Voting variant (Appendix D.11) that 'generally outperforms standard majority voting' but is task-dependent (the simpler method is sometimes superior, indicating the confidence heuristic's reliability varies). No explicit over/under-confidence ('reasoning tax') quantification.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a (SETS is a test-time scaling method, not a failure-attribution/diagnosis system; it does not classify failure modes or attribute responsible agents/steps). It does include a qualitative analysis of self-verification's own failure modes in Appendix D.12.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets answer-level reasoning errors via post-hoc self-verification + self-correction, addressing the saturation of repeated sampling and the premature early-stopping/limited-scaling of SELF-REFINE. Relevant to MAST-style 'superficial self-reflection' / ineffective verification: SETS exposes that gains require genuine self-verification capability and that weak self-verification (low recall, or false-positive corrections on already-correct answers) can cause net-negative correction.

- **dataset or benchmark released**: No new dataset/benchmark released; the work evaluates on existing public benchmarks (NATURAL PLAN, LiveBench Reasoning, MATH 500, AIME 2024-2025, LiveCodeBench TestOutputPred).


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> SELF-REFINE (Madaan et al. 2024; SETS generalizes it as the m=1 special case); repeated sampling / Best-of-N (Brown et al. 2024); Self-Consistency majority voting (Wang et al.); LLM self-verification (Weng et al. 2023; Zhao et al. 2025 sample-then-verify); BoN+Self-Eval (Ren et al. 2023); compute-optimal test-time scaling with trained verifiers/revision models (Snell et al. 2024, which SETS replaces with training-free self-operations); responds to Huang et al. (huanglarge) on the limits of intrinsic self-correction.

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Cited by follow-up test-time-scaling / self-verification work including: 'S2R: Teaching LLMs to Self-verify and Self-correct via Reinforcement Learning'; 'Efficient Test-Time Scaling via Self-Calibration'; 'Solve-Detect-Verify: Inference-Time Scaling with Flexible Generative Verifier'; 'When To Solve, When To Verify: Compute-Optimal Problem Solving and Generative Verification for LLM Reasoning'; 'Putting the Value Back in RL: Better Test-Time Scaling by Unifying LLM Reasoners With Verifiers'; 'SELF-REDRAFT'; 'DynScaling: verifier-free inference scaling'; and surveys on test-time scaling (e.g., 'A Survey on Test-Time Scaling in Large Language Models').

- **citation count**: 55 (Semantic Scholar, as of 2026-06; CorpusId 276079888)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> Partially: SETS is model-agnostic and applies to both 'non-thinking' models (GEMINI-1.5-Pro, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Qwen3-235B-A22B, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct) and 'thinking'/reasoning models (GEMINI-2.5-Flash-Lite-Thinking, GEMINI-2.5-Flash-Preview). Authors frame SETS as a 'capability amplifier, not a creator of reasoning': it leverages but does not require built-in reflection, and yields substantial additional gains even on thinking models.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Weak/none: SETS does no distillation and no weight update; it is a training-free inference procedure. Conceptual contrast to on-policy distillation/self-training (e.g., qu2024recursive's iterative fine-tuning to teach self-correction): SETS instead exploits already-trained self-verification/self-correction at test time without distilling reflections into weights or a reusable artifact.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Hyperparameter-controlled rather than learned: practical recommended setting m=50 samples with n=4 max self-verify/self-correct rounds; self-correction returns generally diminish after n~4 (Trip/Meeting Planning), and refinement typically stops before 10 iterations. Search ranges: m in [1,50] (non-thinking) / [1,25] (thinking), n in [1,10].


### Uncertain (not determined)

- code_url

<a id="r065-thoughts-are-all-over-the-place-on-the-underthinking-of-o1-like-llms"></a>
## Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs

**ID:** R065  **Category:** F (Reasoning-model self-reflection (o1/R1-era) & its analysis)  **Authors:** Yue Wang et al.  **Venue:** arXiv 2025 (submitted to ICML 2025)  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.18585

### Basic info

- **name**: Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**:

> Yue Wang, Qiuzhi Liu, Jiahao Xu, Tian Liang, Xingyu Chen, Zhiwei He, Linfeng Song, Dian Yu, Juntao Li, Zhuosheng Zhang, Rui Wang, Zhaopeng Tu, Haitao Mi, Dong Yu et al.; lead affiliation Tencent AI Lab (with Soochow University and Shanghai Jiao Tong University)

- **venue**: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2501.18585, Jan 2025); subsequently accepted at NeurIPS 2025 (poster, title 'On the Underthinking of Long Reasoning Models'). Semantic Scholar indexes venue as arXiv.org.

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.18585

- **code url**: https://github.com/wangyuenlp/underthinking


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> calibration/probing (analysis of the model's own self-reflective thought-switching behavior); the proposed fix is a decoding-time intervention (Thought Switching Penalty, TIP) rather than a verbal self-critique loop. Reflection here is the o1-like model's native strategy-switching/reflective CoT, which the paper analyzes and constrains.

- **feedback source**:

> self-generated (the model's own long chain-of-thought is analyzed); ground-truth-oracle is used offline only for the analysis/metric (LLM-as-judge with DeepSeek-R1-Distill models assesses thought correctness, and known answers label correct/incorrect responses). The TIP intervention itself uses no external feedback at decode time.

- **iteration structure**: single-shot (TIP is a single-pass decoding modification; no iterative refine or retry). Analysis additionally combines TIP with best-of-N sampling (Self-Consistency, Laconic Decoding) for evaluation.

- **reflection object**:

> reasoning chain (the intermediate 'thoughts' / reasoning strategies within a single long CoT). TIP modifies the decoding distribution over thought-switching tokens to keep the model elaborating the current reasoning thought instead of prematurely switching to a new one; it does not modify weights, prompt, or stored skills.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal

- **requires training**: none

- **reward or critic model**:

> none for the deployed TIP method (training-free decoding penalty). For the offline analysis only, an LLM-as-judge (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B) is used to assess whether each thought can lead to the correct answer (achieving 82.9% / 81.8% agreement accuracy on correct/incorrect examples).

- **distillation target**: none (no reflection artifact is distilled or persisted; TIP is an inference-time logit adjustment with no stored memory, skill, rule, prompt, or weight update).

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> Analyzes RL-emergent reflective behavior (the native strategy-switching/reflection of RL-trained o1-like models such as QwQ-32B-Preview and DeepSeek-R1), and proposes an engineered decoding-time scaffold (TIP) to constrain that emergent behavior. So: emergent behavior studied, engineered fix applied (no fine-tuning).


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: none

- **memory persistence**: within-episode

- **memory curation mechanism**: n/a


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> step-level (per reasoning 'thought' / strategy segment). Underthinking is localized to the thought index where a correct-but-abandoned thought occurs; the underthinking metric measures the token position of the first correct thought within an incorrect response.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> intra-task (the analysis and the TIP penalty operate within a single problem's reasoning trace; no experience is transferred across tasks). Hyperparameters (alpha=3, beta=600) are tuned on AIME2022/23 and applied unchanged to other test sets, but no per-task learning occurs.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> mid-trajectory-recovery (TIP intervenes in-flight during decoding to discourage premature thought switching and keep the model on a promising path before it abandons it); it is not retry-based avoidance or post-hoc revision.


### Application domain

- **task domains**: math; QA/reasoning (graduate-level science). Specifically competition math (MATH, AIME) and graduate-level multiple-choice science (GPQA).

- **benchmarks**: MATH500 (esp. Level 5 / MATH500-Hard), GPQA Diamond (198 questions), AIME2024 (30 problems); AIME2022 and AIME2023 used as a development/tuning set (90 instances total for assessment).


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Identifies 'underthinking': on AIME2024, o1-like LLMs consume on average 225% more tokens in incorrect responses than in correct ones, due to 418% more frequent thought switching, without improved accuracy. The training-free TIP decoding penalty consistently improves QwQ-32B-Preview Pass@1 accuracy while lowering the underthinking (UT) score: AIME2024 41.7 -> 45.8 (UT 72.4 -> 68.2), MATH500-Hard/Level5 82.8 -> 84.3 (UT 71.1 -> 69.7), GPQA Diamond 57.1 -> 59.3 (UT 59.1 -> 56.5), with no model fine-tuning.

- **baselines**:

> Vanilla (standard) decoding of QwQ-32B-Preview; prompt engineering (DeepSeek-R1 + Prompt) as an alternative intervention; best-of-N selection baselines Self-Consistency and Laconic Decoding (shortest-of-N), each evaluated with and without TIP; also descriptive comparison against conventional LLMs (Qwen-Math-72B, Llama3.3-70B) that do not show the underthinking length gap.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> TIP over vanilla QwQ-32B-Preview (Pass@1, same alpha=3/beta=600 hyperparameters): +4.1 points on AIME2024 (41.7 -> 45.8), +1.5 on MATH500-Hard (82.8 -> 84.3), +2.2 on GPQA Diamond (57.1 -> 59.3). When combined with best-of-N: with Self-Consistency, QwQ Pass@4 AIME2024 rises 43.7 -> 51.4 (+7.7); with Laconic Decoding, R1-Distill-Qwen-32B Pass@8 AIME2024 rises 74.4 -> 78.0 (+3.6) and UT 8.7 -> 7.3. Prompt engineering gives only modest changes vs TIP. UT scores consistently decrease, indicating more thorough reasoning.

- **compute cost profile**:

> TIP itself adds negligible cost: it is a single-pass decoding-time logit adjustment on thought-switching tokens (alpha penalty for beta positions from each thought start), no fine-tuning, no extra forward passes vs standard decoding. The underlying problem it targets is wasted compute: incorrect responses use ~225% more tokens (e.g., AIME2024 incorrect 16,108 vs correct 5,549 tokens for QwQ; 26.4 vs 7.0 thoughts). Best-of-N variants (Self-Consistency / Laconic with N=4/8/16) multiply inference cost by N as expected.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Requires logit access (TIP could not be applied to DeepSeek-R1-671B via API, which forbids logit modification), so it is limited to open-weight models. Thought-switching tokens are heuristically identified (e.g., 'alternatively'), relying on LLM segmentation (Llama-3.3-70B) that is imperfect. Hyperparameters (alpha, beta) are tuned on AIME2022/23 and may need re-tuning. Gains on easier benchmarks (MATH500-Hard, GPQA) are modest (~1.5-2.2 points). The thought-correctness assessment uses LLM-as-judge (~82% agreement), introducing noise. The work analyzes only two/three open o1-like models on math/science.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> intrinsic-only for the deployed TIP method (training-free, no labels at decode time). For the offline diagnostic analysis and the underthinking metric, oracle-label/ground-truth (known correct answers) plus an LLM-judge are used to identify correct-but-abandoned thoughts; this oracle is only used to characterize the phenomenon, not by TIP at inference.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive (task-dependent magnitude). TIP improves accuracy across all three challenging test sets without label leakage at inference and reduces underthinking scores; gains are largest on the hardest set (AIME2024, +4.1) and modest elsewhere. The paper frames the issue as the o1-like models' native reflective thought-switching being net-negative when excessive; TIP corrects this by penalizing premature switching.

- **calibration effect**:

> not-measured (no explicit confidence-calibration / ECE analysis). The paper instead measures token-efficiency (the underthinking UT score) and accuracy. It documents that more capable models (DeepSeek-R1-671B) can paradoxically have higher UT scores on some sets, i.e. more elaborate but inefficient reasoning when uncertain.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> classifies-failure-mode (taxonomy): formally defines and characterizes 'underthinking' as a distinct failure mode (premature abandonment of promising reasoning paths via excessive thought switching), distinguishing it from 'overthinking' (Chen et al. 2024) and from genuine lack of understanding; attributes failing steps via the first-correct-thought index and quantifies it with the UT metric.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> underthinking: frequent thought-switching without sufficiently deep exploration of promising reasoning paths, leading to inadequate reasoning depth, wasted tokens, and lower accuracy on hard problems. Explicitly contrasted with overthinking. Maps to MAST-style reasoning failures such as superficial/inefficient self-reflection and premature termination of a line of reasoning (the paper also cites 'I give up' mid-reasoning as a form of underthinking).

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new dataset/benchmark; introduces a reusable metric (the underthinking score xi_UT measuring token efficiency in incorrect responses) and releases code at https://github.com/wangyuenlp/underthinking. Uses existing benchmarks (MATH500, GPQA Diamond, AIME).


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Overthinking analysis of o1-like LLMs (Chen et al. 2024, 'Do Not Think That Much for 2+3=?', arXiv:2412.21187) as a direct companion/counterpart; o1 and its replicas QwQ (Qwen 2024), DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek 2025), Kimi-1.5 (Kimi 2025); coverage/length penalties in neural machine translation (Tu et al. 2016; Wu et al. 2016) that inspire TIP; Self-Consistency (Wang et al. 2023) and Chain-of-Thought (Wei et al. 2022); Laconic Decoding (Raoof & Dimakis).

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Cited by subsequent efficient-reasoning / reasoning-length-control and reasoning-failure-analysis work, e.g. 'When More is Less: Understanding Chain-of-Thought Length in LLMs' (Wu et al. 2025), s1: Simple Test-Time Scaling (Muennighoff et al. 2025), 'Training Language Models to Reason Efficiently' (Arora & Zanette 2025); and later 2025-2026 works such as PathCal (state-aware reflection-marker calibration for efficient reasoning), STOP (structured on-policy pruning of long-form reasoning), TRIAGE (metacognitive control under resource constraints), EntroCut (entropy-guided adaptive CoT truncation), and surveys on mechanistic understanding of large reasoning models and their failures.

- **citation count**: 154 (Semantic Scholar, as of June 2026; influentialCitationCount 11)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> true. The paper specifically targets o1/R1-style reasoning models with built-in long-CoT reflection (QwQ-32B-Preview, DeepSeek-R1-671B, DeepSeek-R1-Preview, R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, R1-Distill-Llama-70B); the underthinking phenomenon and the TIP fix are defined relative to their native thought-switching/reflective behavior, and explicitly do NOT manifest the same way in conventional LLMs (Qwen-Math-72B, Llama3.3-70B).

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Weak/indirect. TIP is a training-free, on-policy decoding-time steering of the model's own generation (no distillation, no weight update). It relates to on-policy distillation only insofar as it shapes on-policy reasoning trajectories at inference; some citing works (e.g. Self-Verified Distillation, STOP on-policy pruning) build on the underthinking lens within distillation/RL pipelines, but this paper itself performs no distillation.

- **sample efficiency**:

> TIP is applied with a single set of hyperparameters (alpha=3, beta=600) tuned via grid search over alpha in {3,5,10,20,30} and beta in {300,400,500,600,700} on the AIME2022/23 development set, then transferred unchanged. Pass@1 results are reported over 4 samples. Best-of-N analyses average over 10,000 random-sampling trials drawn from 32 generated responses per setting.

<a id="r073-thinking-out-loud-do-reasoning-models-know-when-theyre-right"></a>
## Thinking Out Loud: Do Reasoning Models Know When They're Right?

**ID:** R073  **Category:** F (Reasoning-model self-reflection (o1/R1-era) & its analysis)  **Authors:** Qingcheng Zeng et al.  **Venue:** EMNLP 2025 (Main)  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.73/

### Basic info

- **name**: Thinking Out Loud: Do Reasoning Models Know When They're Right?

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Qingcheng Zeng, Weihao Xuan (co-first), Leyang Cui, Rob Voigt; lead affiliation Northwestern University (with University of Tokyo / RIKEN AIP, Westlake University, UC Davis)

- **venue**: EMNLP 2025 (Main), Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, pp. 1394-1407 (arXiv:2504.06564, submitted Apr 2025)

- **paper url**: https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.73/


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> calibration/probing — analysis of verbalized confidence (verbalized uncertainty) as a lens onto the self-reflective behavior of large reasoning models; it is an empirical analysis paper, not a self-correction method. It also tests a self-reflection prompting strategy (two-round dialogue eliciting an answer then a confidence self-assessment) as one of three prompting conditions.

- **feedback source**:

> self-generated (models verbalize their own confidence / 'I don't know' decisions); calibration is then scored against ground-truth correctness as an evaluation oracle (the model receives no feedback signal — this is measurement, not training).

- **iteration structure**:

> single-shot (the analysis itself is one-pass evaluation per prompt). One of the three prompting strategies (self-reflection / SR) uses a two-round dialogue: round one elicits the answer, round two elicits a confidence self-evaluation.

- **reflection object**:

> reasoning chain and output content — the study reflects on the model's verbalized confidence about its own answer and on the long chain-of-thought reasoning trace (analyzing how chain length relates to confidence, accuracy, and calibration). No artifact (prompt, skill, weights) is modified by the paper itself; it analyzes models produced by SFT-distillation and RL.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal

- **requires training**:

> none (the paper performs no training; it analyzes off-the-shelf models). The analysis contrasts three training pipelines of the studied models: instruct models (SFT + general/alignment RL), SFT reasoning models (distillation on long CoT traces), and RL reasoning models (reasoning RL on top of the distilled models).

- **reward or critic model**: self-as-judge (models verbalize their own confidence); ground-truth correctness is used only to score calibration, not as a reward. No trained reward or critic model is introduced.

- **distillation target**:

> none — the paper does not distill reflection into a reusable artifact. It studies models whose reasoning was created via distillation (R1-Distill-Qwen on 800k traces) and reasoning RL, but produces no new artifact itself.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> Analyzes RL-emergent self-reflective behavior in large reasoning models (o1/R1-style 'Wait, but...' introspection) rather than prompt/scaffold-engineered reflection like Reflexion; the finding is that distillation + RL progressively shape (and in factuality settings erode) calibration. The self-reflection prompting strategy it also tests is prompt-engineered, but the paper's central object is the emergent reflective behavior.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: none (no memory mechanism; single-pass evaluation study)

- **memory persistence**: within-episode (no cross-episode/cross-task memory used)

- **memory curation mechanism**: n/a


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> holistic/outcome-level — calibration (ECE/ACE) and failure prediction (AUROC, AUPRC) are computed at the whole-response/answer level; confidence is verbalized for the final answer, not per reasoning step. The chain-length analysis associates accuracy/confidence with overall trace length (response-level), not token-level attribution.

- **intra task vs inter task**: n/a (analysis paper, not a learning method); the closest framing is cross-domain generalization — RL-trained calibration gains transfer across domains (e.g., math-RL improving science-reasoning calibration).

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> n/a — the paper studies whether models recognize their knowledge boundaries and abstain ('I don't know' / 'not attempted'); it finds LRMs abstain less (avoidance failure), but it is an analysis, not a recovery/avoidance method.


### Application domain

- **task domains**: QA/reasoning (math, scientific reasoning, general logical reasoning) and factuality QA. Code reasoning was excluded because most models could not emit code and a confidence score simultaneously.

- **benchmarks**:

> AIME 2024 & AIME 2025 (math, 30 questions each, 5 runs); GPQA-Diamond (198 graduate-level science MCQs) and SuperGPQA (1500 sampled questions); LiveBench-Reasoning (150 reasoning problems); SimpleQA and FreshQA (FreshQA-2025-04-28) for factuality.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Reasoning-oriented training laddered up calibration on reasoning-heavy tasks but eroded knowledge-boundary awareness on factuality. Example: R1-Distill-Qwen-32B vs Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct on AIME — accuracy 9.67% -> 65.7%, ECE 0.752 -> 0.240, AUROC 0.695 -> 0.813 (vanilla CoT). On factuality, LRMs gave far fewer 'not attempted'/'I don't know' answers (32B: instruct 2492 vs SFT-reasoning 76 vs RL-reasoning 63 over SimpleQA+FreshQA) without commensurate accuracy gains except DeepSeek-R1 — a 'reasoning tax.'

- **baselines**:

> Within-architecture comparison across three model types: instruct models (Qwen2.5-14B/32B-Instruct, DeepSeek-V3) vs SFT reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B/32B) vs RL reasoning models (DeepCoder-14B-Preview, Skywork-OR1-32B-Preview, DeepSeek-R1). Three prompting strategies compared: vanilla CoT, vanilla CoT with probability mass, and self-reflection.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> On reasoning benchmarks, RL reasoning models beat SFT-only counterparts: e.g., Skywork-32B vs R1-Distill-Qwen-32B on AIME ECE 0.183 vs 0.240, AUROC 0.928 vs 0.813; on LiveBench-Reasoning Skywork ECE 0.074 vs 0.152. SFT over instruct gave the largest jump (32B AIME ECE 0.752->0.240). On factuality the pattern reverses for small models — a U-shaped calibration trajectory (instruct -> SFT-reasoning worsens -> RL-reasoning partially recovers): e.g., 32B SimpleQA+FreshQA shared-question ECE 0.591 (instruct) -> 0.640 (SFT) -> 0.600 (RL); DeepSeek-R1 shared ECE 0.496 -> 0.317 vs DeepSeek-V3.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Inference allows up to 32,000 new tokens per generation at temperature 0.6; reasoning models emit long CoT chains so token cost is much higher than single-pass instruct answers. The self-reflection prompting strategy doubles the dialogue (two rounds). No training conducted by the authors. Chain-length analysis: longer chains (>10,000 tokens) correlate with lower accuracy and increased ECE for small-scale models.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Code reasoning excluded (most models could not output a code snippet plus a confidence score together). Factuality outputs were auto-graded following Wei et al. (SimpleQA protocol) without human verification. Findings about reduced knowledge-boundary awareness ('reasoning tax') are strongest for small-scale (14B/32B) open-source LRMs; large-scale DeepSeek-R1 mostly avoids the degradation. Studies open-source LRMs only on the reasoning RL side; calibration is sensitive to prompt design.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> intrinsic-only for the model behavior studied (verbalized confidence is fully self-generated); ground-truth labels are used only as an evaluation oracle to compute calibration/failure-prediction metrics, not as feedback to the model.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent — reasoning-oriented training improves calibration (self-assessment) on reasoning-heavy tasks but degrades knowledge-boundary recognition on factuality for small-scale models (the 'reasoning tax'); large-scale RL models (DeepSeek-R1) recover. Not a self-correction method per se, so framed as a calibration/awareness effect.

- **calibration effect**:

> mixed — improves on reasoning-heavy benchmarks (math/science/general reasoning), in a progressive laddered fashion instruct < SFT-reasoning < RL-reasoning; degrades/overconfident on factuality for small-scale models ('reasoning tax', far fewer 'I don't know' responses), with partial U-shaped recovery under RL and full recovery at large scale (DeepSeek-R1).


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**: n/a (not a failure-attribution study; it diagnoses a calibration/knowledge-boundary failure mode rather than attributing responsibility to agents or steps)

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Diminished awareness of knowledge boundaries / over-attempting (very low 'I don't know'/'not attempted' rates) leading to confident hallucination on factuality tasks — a 'reasoning tax' (related to the 'hallucination tax' discussed in Song et al. and Kirichenko et al. AbstentionBench). Also documents overconfidence with shorter/less-elaborate reasoning, and a length-vs-accuracy degradation (overthinking) where longer chains correlate with lower accuracy.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI 2025) and o1 (OpenAI 2024) reasoning-model paradigm; R1-Distill-Qwen, DeepCoder-14B, Skywork-OR1 as evaluated models; verbalized confidence / calibration literature (Tian et al. 2023; Xiong et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2024); SimpleQA (Wei et al. 2024) and FreshQA (Vu et al. 2023) factuality protocols; ECE (Guo et al. 2017) and ACE (Nixon et al. 2019); DeepSeek-R1 Thoughtology (Marjanović et al. 2025) for the chain-length analysis; Chu et al. 2025 ('SFT memorizes, RL generalizes').

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Connects to concurrent and follow-on work on the 'hallucination tax' / abstention failures of RL reasoning models: Song et al. (2025), Kirichenko et al. (2025, AbstentionBench), Kalai et al. (2025, 'Why Language Models Hallucinate'), Mei et al. (2025), Yoon et al. (2025), and Tu et al. (2025) on reward design for uncertainty. (Specific named successors citing this paper not individually confirmed; cited 12 times per Semantic Scholar.)

- **citation count**: 12 (Semantic Scholar, as of mid-2026; CorpusId 277633781)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> true — the paper specifically targets large reasoning models (o1/R1-era) with built-in long-CoT self-reflective behavior, contrasting them against instruct models to isolate the effect of reasoning-oriented distillation and RL on verbalized calibration.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Indirectly relevant: the SFT reasoning models studied (R1-Distill-Qwen-14B/32B) are off-policy distillation on 800k R1-generated traces (600k long reasoning chains + 200k non-reasoning), and the RL reasoning models add reasoning RL on top. The paper frames distillation as 'memorize' (in-domain calibration gains, factuality calibration loss) vs RL as 'generalize' (domain-agnostic calibration recovery), echoing Chu et al. (2025). No explicit on-policy-distillation method is used.

- **sample efficiency**: n/a (analysis paper, no learning trials). Evaluation protocol: AIME and LiveBench-Reasoning run 5 times and aggregated; GPQA-Diamond 198 items, SuperGPQA 1500 sampled items, M=10 calibration bins.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- code_url
- dataset_or_benchmark_released
