<a id="r074-reasoning-models-know-when-theyre-right-probing-hidden-states-for-self-verification"></a>
## Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification

**ID:** R074  **Category:** F (Reasoning-model self-reflection (o1/R1-era) & its analysis)  **Authors:** Anqi Zhang et al.  **Venue:** arXiv preprint (New York University / NYU Shanghai)  **Learning locus:** gradient_weight_update  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05419

### Basic info

- **name**: Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Anqi Zhang, Yulin Chen, Jane Pan, Chen Zhao, Aurojit Panda, Jinyang Li, He He; lead affiliation New York University (with NYU Shanghai)

- **venue**: COLM 2025 (Conference on Language Modeling); originally arXiv preprint 2504.05419 (April 2025)

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05419


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> calibration/probing — a trained linear/MLP probe over the reasoning model's hidden states classifies the correctness of intermediate answers and is used as a learned verifier (self-verification via internal representations, not verbal self-critique)

- **feedback source**:

> hidden-state-probe: a binary classifier reads the model's last-layer hidden states at intermediate-answer positions. Probe supervision (training labels) comes from Gemini 2.0 Flash extracting/judging intermediate answers against ground-truth answers (ground-truth-oracle used only to label probe training data, not at inference)

- **iteration structure**:

> single-shot probing of a fixed reasoning trace; at inference the probe drives a confidence-thresholded early-exit that sequentially scores each intermediate answer chunk and truncates the chain-of-thought once confidence exceeds the threshold (no re-sampling or retry)

- **reflection object**:

> reasoning chain — specifically the intermediate answers within a long Chain-of-Thought (CoT). The probe reflects on the correctness of each intermediate answer encoded in the model's hidden states; the actionable use modifies the reasoning trace length (early exit). The probe itself is a separately trained artifact (gradient weight update on the small classifier, not the base model).


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**:

> gradient_weight_update — a lightweight MLP/linear probe is trained (Adam, weighted BCE, grid search) on hidden-state representations; the base reasoning model's weights are frozen. The learned-signal lives in the trained probe rather than in-context.

- **requires training**:

> SFT-style supervised training of the probe only: a two-layer MLP (often degenerating to a linear probe, hidden size d=0) trained with weighted binary cross-entropy via Adam. No RL; the base reasoning model is not updated.

- **reward or critic model**:

> trained reward/critic model — the probe is a trained correctness classifier (verifier) over hidden states; it functions as a separate learned verifier of intermediate-answer correctness rather than self-as-judge or a verbal critic

- **distillation target**:

> model-weights (of the auxiliary probe): correctness information latent in the reasoning model's hidden states is distilled into a small trained classifier (probe) that is reused at inference as a verifier; no episodic-memory, skill library, or prompt artifact is produced

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> Hybrid framing: the self-verification SIGNAL is RL/long-CoT-emergent — correctness information is found to be inherently (often linearly) encoded in reasoning models' hidden states and is far weaker in non-reasoning instruct models, suggesting it is acquired during long-CoT training. EXPLOITING it (the probe + early-exit) is engineered. Key finding: models encode correctness yet fail to exploit it during inference.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: none — no episodic memory, scratchpad reuse, or skill library; the only persistent learned artifact is the trained probe (a verifier), and analysis is over fixed reasoning traces

- **memory persistence**:

> n/a — the probe is trained once per (model, dataset) and applied at inference; there is no cross-episode experience accumulation. (Probe generalizes across some datasets, e.g. GSM8K<->MATH transfer, but this is OOD generalization, not memory.)

- **memory curation mechanism**: n/a — no memory store to curate. Probe training data is down-sampled to <=1000 examples per dataset (pilot showed no performance loss); class imbalance is handled with a weighted BCE loss rather than memory curation.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> step-level / intermediate-answer-level — the probe scores correctness at each intermediate-answer chunk within the long CoT (a chunk being one reasoning path delimited by 'wait'/'double-check'/'alternatively' keywords). It also predicts future-answer correctness from earlier paragraph positions mid-chunk (look-ahead), i.e. before the intermediate answer is fully generated.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> intra-task — operates within a single problem's reasoning trace (verifying intermediate answers and deciding when to stop reasoning on that same problem). Cross-dataset probe transfer is studied as OOD generalization but the corrective mechanism is intra-task, not experience transfer across tasks.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> neither recovery nor avoidance in the trajectory-correction sense — the probe does not correct or re-route reasoning; it performs confidence-based early termination (exit when a correct intermediate answer is detected with high confidence), i.e. an efficiency/overthinking-mitigation intervention rather than mid-trajectory error correction or next-episode avoidance


### Application domain

- **task domains**: math reasoning and logical (QA/reasoning) tasks — verifiable-answer domains used to enable automatic correctness labeling

- **benchmarks**:

> GSM8K, MATH, AIME (mathematical reasoning), and KnowLogic (a 5.4k multiple-choice knowledge-driven logical-reasoning benchmark). Reasoning models probed: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B/70B, R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B/32B, and QwQ-32B; non-reasoning baseline Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> A simple probe over hidden states verifies intermediate-answer correctness with ROC-AUC >0.7 (>0.9 for R1-Distill-Qwen-32B on AIME) and ECE <0.1 (well-calibrated). Used as a verifier for confidence-based early-exit on R1-Distill-Llama-8B / MATH: ~24% reduction in inference tokens at threshold 0.85 with maintained accuracy (88.2% vs no-exit), and 19% token reduction at threshold 0.9 with identical accuracy (88.6%).

- **baselines**:

> (1) No early-exit (full reasoning) baseline accuracy on R1-Distill-Llama-8B/MATH; (2) static early-exit (terminate after a fixed number m of intermediate-answer chunks) as the comparison early-exit strategy; (3) probes trained on non-reasoning Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct representations (to show correctness encoding is much weaker without long-CoT training); plus ECE/Brier/ROC-AUC reported per model and dataset.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> vs no-early-exit: ~24% fewer tokens at ~equal accuracy (88.2% vs full reasoning at threshold 0.85), 19% fewer tokens at identical 88.6% accuracy at threshold 0.9. vs static early-exit at equal token budget: up to +5% accuracy (confidence-based 87.4% at Thr=0.8 vs static ~82.5%); at matched accuracy (>85%) the confidence-based exit uses significantly fewer tokens than static (m=6). Probe on reasoning models markedly outperforms probe on non-reasoning Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (lower classification + higher calibration error for the latter).

- **compute cost profile**:

> Reduces inference compute relative to full reasoning: ~19-24% fewer generated tokens via early-exit (max generation cap 10K tokens). The probe is extremely cheap to train (two-layer MLP, often a linear probe, batch size 64, <=200 epochs with early stopping, training sets down-sampled to <=1000 examples) and cheap to run (single forward read of last-layer hidden states per chunk). Labeling step uses Gemini 2.0 Flash to extract/judge intermediate answers during probing-data construction.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Probe does not stably generalize out-of-domain (e.g. logical-reasoning KnowLogic <-> math probes transfer poorly), and calibration degrades on harder OOD data such as AIME. Correctness encoding is weak in non-reasoning models, and the precise training origin of the self-verification ability remains unclear. The early-exit study is demonstrated on a single model/dataset (R1-Distill-Llama-8B on MATH). Probe training labels depend on a Gemini-based judge plus ground-truth answers (requires verifiable-answer tasks). Core caveat: models encode correctness but do not exploit it natively, so overthinking persists without the external probe-based intervention.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> At inference: self-verify via the model's own hidden states (no ground-truth label needed once the probe is trained). For probe TRAINING: oracle-label/ground-truth dependency — Gemini 2.0 Flash extracts intermediate answers and judges them against ground-truth answers to create the supervised probe labels. So the verifier is learned from oracle labels but applied label-free at test time.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive (efficiency, not accuracy uplift): early-exit maintains accuracy while cutting tokens, and beats static exit at matched budgets. It does not raise final accuracy beyond the model's full-reasoning ceiling; its value is mitigating overthinking. The probe's verification is reliable in-distribution but task-dependent OOD.

- **calibration effect**:

> improves / strongly positive on the calibration axis — trained probes are highly calibrated (ECE <0.1, e.g. as low as 0.01-0.03 in-distribution; Brier scores reported). Calibration can degrade on harder OOD data (e.g. AIME ECE up to ~0.25-0.31 for transferred probes). The central message is that reasoning models internally hold well-calibrated correctness signals they fail to use.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> attributes-failing-step (in a soft sense) — the probe localizes correctness to specific intermediate-answer chunks/steps in the CoT and can flag a correct answer early; it is a correctness classifier rather than a multi-agent failure-attribution or counterfactual-localization method

- **failure mode addressed**:

> overthinking — the paper directly targets and empirically demonstrates the overthinking failure mode of reasoning models (continuing to generate reasoning/re-checks even after a correct, high-confidence intermediate answer). Relates to underthinking/overthinking discussions and to superficial self-verification (models encode correctness but do not act on it).


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Internal-representation correctness probing (Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Burns et al. 2024 CCS-style linear probes), white-box uncertainty estimation outperforming black-box verbalized confidence (Xiong et al. 2024; Kapoor et al. 2024), learned verifiers / process reward models (Cobbe et al. 2021; Lightman et al. 2023), and overthinking/efficient-reasoning analyses of reasoning models (Chen et al. 2025; Sui et al. 2025); reasoning models DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI et al. 2025), OpenAI o1, and QwQ-32B.

- **citation count**: 136 (Semantic Scholar, as of mid-2026); reference count 42


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> Yes — the method specifically targets o1/R1-era long-CoT reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill series, QwQ-32B). The probed self-verification signal is shown to be a property of reasoning models, substantially weaker in the non-reasoning Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct counterpart, indicating it emerges from long-CoT training.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Indirect — correctness information that is implicitly present in the reasoning model's on-policy long-CoT hidden states is distilled into an explicit lightweight probe/verifier. Not on-policy distillation in the policy-update sense (base model frozen), but it can be seen as distilling a latent self-verification skill into a reusable verifier that could inform training-time concision/overthinking objectives.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Very high for the probe: training sets down-sampled to <=1000 examples per (model, dataset) with no observed performance loss; probe often reduces to a linear probe (hidden size d=0). Trained <=200 epochs with early stopping, batch size 64, 8:2 train/val split. At inference the early-exit yields its token savings (~19-24%) without additional sampling.

# G. Memory, experience-distillation & lifelong agents

<a id="r014-expel-llm-agents-are-experiential-learners"></a>
## ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners

**ID:** R014  **Category:** G (Memory, experience-distillation & lifelong agents)  **Authors:** Zhao et al.  **Venue:** AAAI 2024  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10144

### Basic info

- **name**: ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners

- **year**: 2023

- **authors**: Andrew Zhao, Daniel Huang, Quentin Xu, Matthieu Lin, Yong-Jin Liu, Gao Huang (lead: Gao Huang, Tsinghua University / LeapLab; with HKUST collaborators)

- **venue**: AAAI 2024 (38th AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence); first submitted to arXiv Aug 2023 (2308.10144)

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10144

- **code url**: https://github.com/LeapLabTHU/ExpeL (project page: https://andrewzh112.github.io/expel)


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> verbal-self-critique (Reflexion-style natural-language self-reflection used only during the training/experience-gathering phase) combined with cross-task insight extraction (an LLM compares success/failure trajectory pairs and lists of successes to distill natural-language rules); no learned critic model and no separate reward model.

- **feedback source**:

> environment-reward / task success signal during experience gathering (deterministic environments give a binary success/fail outcome that triggers self-reflection and retries) plus self-generated comparison (the LLM contrasts its own successful vs. failed trajectories). At evaluation there is no external feedback — the agent runs single-shot.

- **iteration structure**:

> Two-phase: (1) training/experience-gathering uses episodic-retry-with-reset via Reflexion (retry each training task up to Z times, self-reflecting between trials); (2) evaluation is single-shot (one attempt per unseen task, no retries). Insight extraction iterates over the experience pool with ADD/EDIT/UPVOTE/DOWNVOTE operations. (An optional 'ExpeL+Reflexion' setting adds retries at eval time.)

- **reflection object**:

> Multiple objects: (a) action trajectories (collected and stored), and (b) the prompt/context — specifically a curated list of natural-language 'insights' (structured rules/best-practices/failure-patterns) plus retrieved successful trajectories used as in-context examples. The base LLM weights are never modified. So the reflected-on/modified artifacts are reusable cross-task insights (structured rules) and the in-context demonstration set (prompt/context), distilled from action trajectories.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal (no weight update; learning lives in extracted natural-language insights and a retrievable pool of successful trajectories injected into the prompt)

- **requires training**:

> none (no gradient updates to the policy LLM; uses closed-source API models like gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 for actions and gpt-4-0613 for insight extraction). The 'experience-gathering' is environment interaction, not parameter training.

- **reward or critic model**:

> self-as-judge / verifiable task-success signal: improvement signal comes from the environment's binary task-success outcome (used to label trajectories success/fail) and from the LLM itself acting as the insight-extractor/judge over success-failure comparisons. No trained reward model, no separate retrospective model.

- **distillation target**:

> Reflection/experience is distilled into two reusable artifacts injected at inference: (1) structured-rules/constitution — a curated list of natural-language insights (with importance counts, edited via ADD/EDIT/UPVOTE/DOWNVOTE); and (2) episodic-memory — a Faiss vectorstore of successful trajectories retrieved by task similarity as few-shot examples. No model-weights distillation.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> prompt/scaffold-engineered: the reflective and experiential-learning behavior is hand-designed (Reflexion-style retries + an explicit insight-extraction prompt with discrete edit operators + kNN trajectory retrieval). The paper additionally reports qualitatively 'emergent abilities' (e.g., world-model belief updates, self-correction) arising from the extracted insights, but these emerge from engineered scaffolding rather than RL training.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> Combination of skill/insight library (a curated list of cross-task natural-language insights, i.e., a playbook/cheatsheet of rules) and long-term-episodic memory (a Faiss vectorstore of successful trajectories retrieved via kNN / all-mpnet-base-v2 embeddings).

- **memory persistence**:

> cross-task: experiences and insights are accumulated from a pool of training tasks and reused on unseen evaluation tasks within the same distribution; insights can also be transferred cross-domain (HotpotQA -> FEVER). Memory is built in training and frozen for evaluation (not continuously updated online during deployment).

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> overwrite/evolution (self-relinking) for insights: an importance count (init 2) increments on UPVOTE/EDIT and decrements on DOWNVOTE; insights at count zero are removed; LLM can ADD/EDIT, keeping the rule list compact and self-curated. For the trajectory pool: append-only success trajectories with retrieval-gated access (only top-k task-similar successes are injected at inference, bounding context).


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> Mixed: holistic/outcome-level for the success/fail labeling, and response-/trajectory-level for reflection and insight extraction (the agent contrasts whole failed vs. successful trajectories for the same task and abstracts patterns). It does not perform fine-grained step-level or token-level error attribution.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> inter-task: ExpeL's core contribution is transferring experience across tasks (and across domains in the transfer-learning experiment), explicitly contrasted with Reflexion which only does intra-task refinement via repeated attempts on the same task.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> avoidance-only at evaluation (single-shot; learned insights help avoid past mistakes proactively rather than recover in-flight). During training it uses retry-with-reset (Reflexion). Qualitatively the paper notes emergent mid-trajectory self-correction (e.g., putting back a wrongly taken object in ALFWorld), but the designed mechanism is failure avoidance via distilled insights, not a built-in recovery loop.


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> decision-making / interactive agent tasks: knowledge-intensive QA/reasoning (HotpotQA), embodied household task completion (ALFWorld), web-navigation/online-shopping (WebShop), and fact verification (FEVER, transfer target). All text-based, deterministic environments.

- **benchmarks**: HotpotQA, ALFWorld, WebShop, FEVER (transfer target). Baselines/IL results imported from the ReAct paper.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Without any parameter updates, ExpeL (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 actor, gpt-4-0613 insight extractor) consistently outperforms ReAct/Act across all three domains: HotpotQA 39.0% vs ReAct 28.0% success rate (+11 pts); ALFWorld 59.0% vs ReAct 40.0% (+19 pts); and it matches/exceeds Reflexion without test-time retries (HotpotQA 39% vs Reflexion ~40% at R3; ALFWorld 59% vs Reflexion 54.4% at R3). Transfer: HotpotQA->FEVER insights raise FEVER from ReAct 63% to ExpeL Transfer 70%.

- **baselines**:

> ReAct and Act (no-reasoning variant) as primary planning-agent baselines (all using gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 at eval); Reflexion (intra-task self-improvement) for comparison; Imitation Learning (IL) numbers taken from the ReAct paper; plus internal ablations: ExpeL (insights-only), ExpeL (retrieve-only), hand-crafted insights, gpt-3.5 insights, reason-similarity retrieval, random-sampled retrieval.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> vs ReAct (strongest comparable single-shot baseline): HotpotQA +11.0 pts (28.0% -> 39.0%), ALFWorld +19.0 pts (40.0% -> 59.0%), WebShop improved (full ExpeL > insights-only 37%/retrieve-only 38%). vs Reflexion (which uses test-time retries): ExpeL is roughly on par on HotpotQA (39% vs ~40% at R3) and better on ALFWorld (59% vs 54.4% at R3) using only a single attempt. Transfer to FEVER: +7 pts over ReAct (63% -> 70%); +5 pts over the no-task-demo transfer variant (65% -> 70%). Ablations confirm insights and retrieval are synergistic (each alone underperforms full ExpeL).

- **compute cost profile**:

> Inference cost is higher than a single-pass ReAct because the prompt is augmented with extracted insights plus top-k retrieved successful trajectories (longer context, more tokens; the paper reports token/step statistics in Appendix Tab. 6). One-time training/experience-gathering cost: Reflexion-style retries (up to Z attempts) over a pool of training tasks, plus iterative gpt-4 insight-extraction passes — but no gradient steps and no large interaction budget required. At evaluation it is single-shot (one rollout per task), avoiding Reflexion's multiplicative retry cost.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Stated limitations: (1) only text-based observations (no images/vision); (2) demonstrated mainly with closed-source API LLMs (open-source LLM agents left to future work); (3) insights currently fit in the context window, but truly lifelong learning would need a retrieval step over insights to manage context size; (4) prompting techniques lack the theoretical underpinnings of RL, which may affect policy optimality/efficiency; (5) only deterministic environments are studied (WebShop was modified to be deterministic). Implicitly, gains depend on having a useful, diverse training-task pool and on the insight-extraction LLM (gpt-4) quality.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> env-reward / verifiable-success during training: experience gathering relies on the environment's binary task-success signal (and Reflexion self-reflection on failures) to label and curate experiences. It does NOT use ground-truth labels at evaluation (single-shot, no oracle). So it is between 'env-reward' (training-time) and 'intrinsic/self-verify' (eval-time): no test-time oracle, but training-time success signals from the environment are required.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive (and task-dependent in which sub-mechanism dominates): adding distilled insights + retrieved successes improves over ReAct on all three domains without label leakage at evaluation. Insights help most on HotpotQA (reasoning-heavy), retrieval helps most on ALFWorld (action-heavy), and they are synergistic. One negative finding: adding raw Reflexion reflections into the insight-extraction step hurt performance (reflections sometimes hallucinate), so the curated success/failure-comparison insights are what work.

- **calibration effect**:

> not-measured (the paper does not quantify confidence calibration or a 'reasoning tax'; it predates the reasoning-model calibration literature and reports only task success rates and qualitative behavior, e.g., the agent learning to commit to a probable answer rather than saying 'Unknown').


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a (ExpeL is an experiential-learning agent, not a failure-attribution method). It does informally classify/abstract recurring failure patterns into natural-language insights during insight extraction (comparing failed vs. successful trajectories), but it does not attribute blame to specific agents or pinpoint failing steps as a taxonomy.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets/mitigates generic single-agent failure modes via distilled best-practices and failure-pattern insights: e.g., inefficient/exploratory actions and wrong priors (belief updates, e.g., where to find a pan in ALFWorld), premature giving-up ('Unknown'/'information not available' instead of committing to a probable answer in HotpotQA), and inability to reassess/recover after a misstep. Relative to MAST-style taxonomies these map loosely to 'superficial self-reflection' and unproductive action loops, but the paper does not use MAST's 14-mode framework.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new benchmark/dataset released; evaluation reuses existing benchmarks (HotpotQA, ALFWorld, WebShop, FEVER). The authors released code (https://github.com/LeapLabTHU/ExpeL) and a project page with trajectory/insight demos.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023) for self-reflective retry-based experience gathering; ReAct (Yao et al. 2023) as the base planning algorithm (reason+act); in-context/prompt-based learning and retrieval-augmented generation (semantically-similar in-context examples, Liu et al. 2022); experience replay / off-policy RL framing (Lin 1992; Watkins & Dayan 1992); Faiss (Johnson et al. 2019) and all-mpnet-base-v2 (Song et al. 2020) for retrieval.

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Widely cited as a foundational experience-distillation / memory-agent method and grouped with follow-ups such as Agent Workflow Memory (AWM, Wang et al., ICML 2025) which induces reusable workflows from experience; broader lines on self-evolving / lifelong LLM-agent memory, skill libraries, and procedural-memory / playbook approaches (e.g., Voyager-style skill libraries, A-MEM, agent memory surveys). [Specific direct-successor list beyond AWM is partly inferred from citation context.]

- **citation count**: 596 (Semantic Scholar, as of June 2026; influential citations 69)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> No / not targeted: ExpeL (2023) predates o1/R1-style reasoning models with built-in reflection and was built around non-reasoning API models (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 actor, gpt-4-0613 insight extractor). Its scaffolded insight-extraction is conceptually orthogonal to and could complement built-in-reflection reasoning models, but the paper does not target or evaluate them.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Conceptually relevant but distinct: the paper frames experience gathering as off-policy learning (a behavior policy using Reflexion provides trajectories; 'policy improvement' is done via insight extraction and similar-task retrieval rather than gradient on-policy distillation). It distills behavior into natural-language artifacts (insights + retrievable demos) instead of into model weights, so it is a verbal/in-context analogue of skill/experience distillation rather than gradient-based on-policy distillation.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Relatively sample-efficient and improves with more experience: the paper shows a monotonic correlation between the number of diverse autonomously-gathered experiences and final performance (Fig. 6), and emphasizes it needs no large interaction budget or human labels. Concretely it gathers experiences over a pool of training tasks with up to Z Reflexion retries per task (exact task counts and Z value are in Appendix Tab. 4; not extracted here), then evaluates single-shot. [Exact #trials-to-gain not pinpointed.]

<a id="r018-generative-agents-interactive-simulacra-of-human-behavior"></a>
## Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior

**ID:** R018  **Category:** G (Memory, experience-distillation & lifelong agents)  **Authors:** Park et al.  **Venue:** UIST 2023  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03442

### Basic info

- **name**: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior

- **year**: 2023

- **authors**: Joon Sung Park, Joseph C. O'Brien, Carrie J. Cai, Meredith Ringel Morris, Percy Liang, Michael S. Bernstein; lead affiliation: Stanford University (with Google Research / Google DeepMind co-authors)

- **venue**: UIST 2023 (Proceedings of the 36th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology); DOI 10.1145/3586183.3606763

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03442

- **code url**: https://github.com/joonspk-research/generative_agents


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> verbal-self-critique (self-generated higher-level abstraction/synthesis of memories rather than error-driven self-criticism). The agent periodically queries the LLM to generate salient questions about its recent experiences, retrieves relevant memories, and prompts the LLM to extract higher-level 'insights' (reflections) that cite the supporting records, building a recursive reflection tree.

- **feedback source**: self-generated: reflections are produced entirely by the LLM from the agent's own observational memory stream; no external tool, unit test, ground-truth oracle, or environment reward is used to verify reflections.

- **iteration structure**:

> iterative-refine / continual: reflections are generated periodically during the ongoing simulation (triggered when the summed importance of recently perceived events exceeds a threshold of 150, roughly two-to-three times per simulated day), and reflections recursively build on prior reflections and observations to form a tree.

- **reflection object**:

> reasoning chain / abstracted beliefs derived from the action+observation trajectory: the agent reflects on its raw observational memory (and prior reflections) to synthesize higher-level abstract thoughts ('insights') about itself and others, which are stored back into the memory stream as a new memory type and later retrieved to guide planning and behavior. It does not modify model weights, the agent's own code, or a separate skill library.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**:

> in_context_verbal (no weight update): all learning/adaptation happens via natural-language memory accumulation, periodic reflection synthesis, and retrieval into the prompt; the underlying gpt3.5-turbo model is never fine-tuned.

- **requires training**: none (uses a frozen gpt3.5-turbo/ChatGPT via prompting; no SFT, RL, or preference tuning).

- **reward or critic model**:

> none / self-as-judge: there is no trained reward model or external critic. The LLM itself assigns importance scores to memories (1-10 poignancy) and generates reflections; relevance is computed via embedding cosine similarity. No verifiable reward signal is used.

- **distillation target**:

> episodic-memory: reflections are distilled into natural-language memory objects (reflections) stored in the long-term memory stream, persisting within the simulation and reused via retrieval. They are not distilled into reusable skills/workflows, structured rules/constitutions, prompts, or model weights.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> prompt/scaffold-engineered: reflection is an explicitly engineered architectural component (a designed prompting pipeline that triggers on an importance threshold and synthesizes insights), not an RL-emergent behavior. Emergent *social* behaviors (information diffusion, relationship formation, coordination) arise at the population level, but the reflection mechanism itself is hand-designed.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> long-term-episodic memory stream of natural-language observations, augmented with synthesized higher-level reflections and plans; effectively a structured experience log (with importance scores and embedding vectors per record).

- **memory persistence**:

> cross-episode within a single long-running simulation / cross-session within the simulated world: the memory stream is a complete, append-only record persisting across the agent's simulated days; not evaluated as a cross-task or production cross-session lifelong memory beyond the sandbox.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> retrieval-gated + append-only: the full memory stream is retained append-only (raw observations, reflections, plans), and ballooning is managed at read time by a retrieval function that scores candidate memories on recency (exponential decay, factor 0.995), importance (LLM-assigned poignancy), and relevance (embedding cosine similarity), surfacing only the top-scoring memories that fit the context window. Reflection also acts as a form of self-summarization into higher-level abstractions.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> holistic/outcome-level: reflection synthesizes general high-level abstractions about the agent's experiences rather than localizing or correcting specific erroneous steps, tokens, or actions; there is no fine-grained error attribution.

- **intra task vs inter task**: inter-task / cross-experience: reflections generalize across many accumulated observations over time and inform future planning and behavior, rather than refining a single bounded task output within one episode.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> neither classic recovery nor avoidance in the error-correction sense: there is no retry/reset loop and no mid-trajectory error correction; reflection continuously updates the agent's beliefs which shape subsequent planning, but the framework does not target task-failure recovery.


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> decision-making / social simulation / dialogue: believable open-ended human-behavior simulation in an interactive sandbox ('Smallville', inspired by The Sims) with 25 agents that plan daily routines, converse, form relationships, and coordinate emergent social events.

- **benchmarks**:

> No standard reasoning/code benchmark. Evaluation uses a custom controlled human study: 'agent interview' questions across five categories (self-knowledge, memory, plans, reactions, reflections) scored by 100 Prolific crowd evaluators and aggregated via TrueSkill ranking; plus end-to-end emergent-behavior case studies (information diffusion, relationship formation, Valentine's Day party coordination).


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> In the controlled human evaluation (believability ranking via TrueSkill), the full generative-agent architecture (observation + planning + reflection + memory) was rated most believable (mu=29.89, sigma=0.72), outperforming all ablations and even human crowdworker-authored responses (mu=22.95); ablation removing reflection dropped it to the next-best mu=26.88.

- **baselines**:

> Ablated versions of the architecture: (1) no reflection; (2) no reflection and no planning; (3) no memory, planning, or reflection (this 'fully ablated' condition represents prior work, e.g. Park et al. 2022, Binz & Schulz 2023, Horton 2023); plus a human crowdworker condition where workers watched an agent's replay/memory and authored responses in the agent's voice.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> Full architecture mu=29.89 vs no-reflection mu=26.88 (reflection adds ~3.0 TrueSkill mu), vs no-reflection/no-planning mu=25.64, vs crowdworker mu=22.95, vs fully-ablated prior-work baseline mu=21.21. Full vs fully-ablated baseline yields Cohen's d=8.16 (~8 standard deviations). Differences confirmed significant by Kruskal-Wallis (H(4)=150.29, p<0.001) and Dunn post-hoc (all pairwise p<0.001 except the two worst conditions, crowdworker vs fully-ablated).

- **compute cost profile**:

> High: simulating 25 agents for two simulated days required substantial time and resources, costing 'thousands of dollars in token credits' and taking multiple days to complete, due to heavy per-step LLM prompting for perception, planning, reflection, and dialogue. No single-pass token multiplier is reported; the authors explicitly flag cost-effectiveness and real-time interactivity (parallelization, purpose-built models) as future work.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Reported failure/erratic modes: (1) growing memory makes relevant retrieval and appropriate action-location selection harder, leading some agents to choose atypical locations over time; (2) misclassification of physical/social norms not conveyed in natural language (e.g. single-occupancy dorm bathroom, stores closed after hours); (3) inheriting overly formal/instruction-tuned speech and behavior from the LLM. Agents also hallucinate embellishments to memory and may fail to retrieve relevant memories. Broader limits: short simulation timescale, weak (non-gold-standard) human baseline, very high cost/non-real-time, and unknown robustness to prompt hacking, memory hacking, and hallucination.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> intrinsic-only / self-verify: reflection and all memory scoring rely solely on the agent's own LLM outputs over its self-generated observation memory; there is no external tool, verifier, environment reward, or ground-truth label feeding the reflection process.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent / net-positive for the studied objective (believability): the ablation shows reflection causally improves believability (mu 26.88 -> 29.89). However, this is not error-correction on a verifiable task; reflection synthesizes beliefs without any oracle, and the paper documents hallucinated 'embellishments' showing the unverified abstractions can introduce inaccuracies.

- **calibration effect**:

> not-measured: the paper does not report confidence calibration or any 'reasoning tax' analysis; it measures believability rankings, not probabilistic calibration. It does note qualitative overconfidence/embellishment (agents fabricate knowledge embellishments), but no calibration metric is computed.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a: this is not a failure-attribution/diagnosis method. It does not classify failure modes of other systems, attribute responsible agents, or localize failing steps; its reflection is for belief synthesis, not error attribution.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> n/a (not a failure-attribution paper). The mechanism targets the inability of raw observational memory to generalize/make inferences (addressed via reflection). Its own documented failure modes loosely relate to MAST-style 'superficial reflection' and information-handling errors (hallucinated memory embellishment, retrieval failures, norm misclassification), but the paper predates and does not use the MAST taxonomy.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No reusable benchmark/trace dataset released as such; the authors open-sourced the full simulation code and architecture (https://github.com/joonspk-research/generative_agents) and the interactive Smallville sandbox, which became a widely reused experimental platform.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Extends large language models (gpt3.5-turbo/ChatGPT, OpenAI 2022) with a memory-stream + retrieval (recency/importance/relevance, embedding similarity) + planning + reflection architecture. Builds on prior social-simulacra and LLM-agent work cited as the ablated 'prior work' baseline (Park et al. 2022 'Social Simulacra'; Binz & Schulz 2023; Horton 2023 'homo silicus'), and on cognitive/architectural ideas of memory and reflection.

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Seminal for the LLM-agent memory+reflection line. Inspired/anticipates and is widely cited by works such as Reflexion, Voyager, ExpeL, MemGPT, AgentSims/AgentVerse, CAMEL, generative-agent social-simulation follow-ups (e.g. Concordia, Smallville-derived sandboxes), and large-scale agent-society / market/economic simulations; broadly cited across memory-augmented and self-reflective LLM-agent research.

- **citation count**: ~4322 (Semantic Scholar, as of 2026; rapidly growing — one of the most-cited LLM-agent papers).


### Other / reserved fields

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Not applicable / no link: the method performs no policy/weight distillation; experience is accumulated and 'distilled' only into natural-language episodic memory and reflections used in-context, with no on-policy distillation or weight-space skill optimization.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Not framed in trials-to-gain terms. Reflections are triggered when accumulated event importance exceeds 150 (about 2-3 reflections per simulated agent-day); the full architecture's believability gain is achieved without any training trials, but at high per-step LLM-call cost (thousands of dollars for a 25-agent, 2-day simulation).


### Uncertain (not determined)

- reasoning_model_native

<a id="r037-agentic-context-engineering-evolving-contexts-for-self-improving-language-models"></a>
## Agentic Context Engineering: Evolving Contexts for Self-Improving Language Models

**ID:** R037  **Category:** G (Memory, experience-distillation & lifelong agents)  **Authors:** Zhang et al.  **Venue:** arXiv 2025  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04618

### Basic info

- **name**: Agentic Context Engineering: Evolving Contexts for Self-Improving Language Models

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Qizheng Zhang, Changran Hu, Shubhangi Upasani, et al. (Stanford University; SambaNova Systems; UC Berkeley). Equal contribution: Qizheng Zhang (Stanford), Changran Hu (SambaNova).

- **venue**: ICLR 2026 (arXiv preprint arXiv:2510.04618, submitted Oct 2025); also appears on OpenReview (forum eC4ygDs02R).

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04618


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> verbal-self-critique (a dedicated LLM 'Reflector' role critiques Generator trajectories to distill insights from successes and errors); feedback can be tool-verified (code execution success/failure) or ground-truth-label-guided depending on availability.

- **feedback source**:

> Mixed: self-generated natural-language reflection plus external execution feedback (code execution success/failure in agent tasks, formula correctness). Can optionally use ground-truth-oracle labels (offline/with-GT-labels setting); notably ACE also works WITHOUT labeled supervision by leveraging natural execution feedback.

- **iteration structure**:

> iterative-refine: Generator produces trajectories, Reflector iteratively critiques (up to 5 refinement rounds), Curator merges delta updates; offline adaptation runs over multiple epochs (up to 5); online adaptation updates context sequentially per test sample. Incremental delta updates rather than monolithic rewrite.

- **reflection object**:

> prompt/context (the evolving 'playbook' context made of itemized bullets). ACE reflects on the agent's action trajectory and reasoning to extract reusable strategies, domain concepts, and failure modes, which are then written as structured context entries. It modifies the input context, not model weights.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal

- **requires training**: none (no weight updates; pure context/prompt adaptation at inference/adaptation time).

- **reward or critic model**:

> self-as-judge: a Reflector LLM (same base model, DeepSeek-V3.1 non-thinking, for fairness) serves as the critic that judges trajectories and extracts lessons; improvement signal can also come from verifiable execution feedback (code success/failure) and optionally ground-truth labels. No separately trained reward model.

- **distillation target**:

> prompt / playbook-cheatsheet: reflection is distilled into a structured, evolving context (a 'playbook' of itemized bullets with metadata and helpful/harmful counters). This functions as a curated prompt/agent-memory artifact rather than model weights.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> prompt/scaffold-engineered: ACE is an engineered modular agentic scaffold (Generator/Reflector/Curator with delta updates and grow-and-refine), in the lineage of Reflexion and Dynamic Cheatsheet; reflective behavior is built into the framework, not RL-emergent.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> playbook/cheatsheet (structured context of itemized 'bullets'); used both as offline system prompt and online agent memory. Each bullet has metadata (unique id, helpful/harmful counters) and content (reusable strategy, domain concept, or failure mode).

- **memory persistence**:

> cross-task (and cross-episode): context accumulates and is reused across samples/tasks. Offline adaptation builds a context on the training split reused at test; online adaptation evolves memory sequentially across the test stream.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> overwrite/evolution via incremental delta updates plus a grow-and-refine principle: new bullets are appended with new ids while existing bullets are updated in place (e.g., incrementing helpful/harmful counters); periodic de-duplication (semantic-embedding-based) and pruning control redundancy, performed by lightweight non-LLM merging logic. Explicitly designed to avoid 'context collapse' from monolithic rewriting.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> step-level / itemized: insights and corrections are localized to individual context 'bullets' (delta entries) rather than rewriting the whole context; the Reflector attributes which specific bullets/strategies were helpful or misleading within a trajectory.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> inter-task: ACE transfers accumulated experience (reusable strategies, domain concepts, failure modes) across tasks/samples via the evolving context, in the spirit of Reflexion/ExpeL/Dynamic Cheatsheet; it also supports within-stream online refinement.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> avoidance-oriented: lessons (including recorded failure modes) are written into the context so future tasks avoid past pitfalls; updates happen per-sample (online) or per-epoch (offline) rather than as mid-trajectory in-flight correction.


### Application domain

- **task domains**: tool-use / agentic (LLM agents interacting with apps and APIs) and domain-specific reasoning (financial analysis with XBRL).

- **benchmarks**:

> AppWorld (autonomous agent tasks: API understanding, code generation, environment interaction; test-normal and test-challenge splits; metrics TGC/SGC); FiNER (XBRL token labeling, 139 entity types); Formula (XBRL numerical-reasoning extraction). HotpotQA and Game of 24 discussed as cases where ACE is less beneficial.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> On AppWorld (DeepSeek-V3.1 base), ReAct+ACE reaches 59.4% average (offline, +17.0 over 42.4 ReAct baseline) and matches top-ranked IBM CUGA (GPT-4.1-based, 60.3%) on the leaderboard while surpassing it on the harder test-challenge split, despite using a smaller open-source model. Overall +10.6% average over baselines on agents and +8.6% on finance.

- **baselines**:

> Base LLM (ReAct for AppWorld); In-Context Learning (ICL, few/many-shot); MIPROv2 (DSPy prompt optimizer, auto='heavy'); GEPA (reflective Genetic-Pareto prompt optimizer); Dynamic Cheatsheet (DC, online adaptive memory); top-ranked production agent IBM CUGA (GPT-4.1) for leaderboard comparison.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> Agents (AppWorld): +10.6% average over baselines; offline ReAct+ACE beats ReAct+ICL by 12.3% and ReAct+GEPA by 11.9%; online beats Dynamic Cheatsheet by 7.6%; up to +17.1% over ReAct without ground-truth labels. Finance (FiNER+Formula): +8.6% average with GT labels; offline beats ICL/MIPROv2/GEPA by 10.9% avg; online beats DC by 6.2%; e.g. Formula offline 67.5->85.5 (+18.0).

- **compute cost profile**:

> Substantially cheaper than monolithic-rewrite optimizers due to incremental delta updates and non-LLM merge/de-dup. Offline AppWorld: 82.3% lower adaptation latency and 75.1% fewer rollouts vs GEPA. Online FiNER: 91.5% lower adaptation latency and 83.6% lower token dollar cost vs Dynamic Cheatsheet. Produces longer contexts than GEPA but without linear inference-cost/GPU-memory increase.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Relies on a reasonably strong Reflector; if it fails to extract meaningful insights, the context can become noisy or harmful. Effectiveness depends critically on feedback quality: without reliable signals (GT labels or execution outcomes) both ACE and DC can degrade and the context may be polluted by spurious signals (e.g., FiNER without labels: -3.4). Not all tasks need rich contexts (HotpotQA, Game of 24 benefit from concise instructions); ACE is most useful where detailed domain knowledge, complex tool use, or env-specific strategies are required.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> task-dependent: in agent tasks works with external-tool/execution feedback (intrinsic, no oracle labels needed, +14.8% without GT); in domain-specific (finance) tasks it largely requires oracle-label/ground-truth or reliable signals, degrading without them. So it spans self-verify -> external-tool/verifier -> oracle-label depending on domain; feedback reliability is the discriminating variable.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent / requires reliable feedback: net-positive under rich feedback (agent execution signals, formula correctness), but can be net-negative when feedback is absent or unreliable (e.g., online FiNER without labels -3.4, DC without labels -3.7). Does not require ground-truth labels for agent tasks but does benefit from them for finance.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> classifies-failure-mode (qualitatively): the Reflector identifies recurring pitfalls/common failure modes and records them as context bullets; bullets carry helpful/harmful counters tracking which strategies misled the agent. Not a formal failure-attribution benchmark method.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets brevity bias (optimization collapsing to short generic prompts that drop domain insights) and context collapse (monolithic LLM rewriting abruptly erasing accumulated knowledge, e.g. AppWorld context dropping from 18,282 tokens/66.7% acc to 122 tokens/57.1% acc in one step). Records domain-specific failure modes and tool-use pitfalls; addresses superficial/lossy self-reflection by separating reflection from curation.

- **dataset or benchmark released**: No new dataset/benchmark released; uses existing AppWorld, FiNER, Formula. Authors release the LLM prompts used for ACE and baselines for reproducibility (Appendix D). Code release not confirmed.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Dynamic Cheatsheet (Suzgun et al. — adaptive test-time memory, the agentic architecture ACE builds on); Reflexion (verbal reflection on failures); GEPA (reflective Genetic-Pareto prompt evolution); TextGrad (textual 'gradient' prompt optimization); MIPROv2/DSPy (prompt optimization); A-MEM (agentic memory entries); ReAct (agent scaffold/base implementation); ICL (in-context learning).

- **citation count**: approximately 181 (Google Scholar, 'Cited by 181' for the main arXiv entry, as of June 2026; a separate Scholar citation cluster lists 23). Semantic Scholar count not retrievable (API rate-limited).


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> No / not-native: ACE is an external scaffold applied around a base model (DeepSeek-V3.1 in non-thinking mode); it does not target o1/R1-style built-in reflection. It is complementary to reasoning models but its reflection comes from the engineered Reflector role, not the model's internal reasoning.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Related conceptually: ACE distills the model's own on-policy execution trajectories (Generator outputs) and their natural execution feedback into a reusable context/playbook artifact (a form of experience/skill distillation), but uses no weight updates or policy gradients; it is a context-level analogue to on-policy skill distillation rather than parameter-space distillation.

- **sample efficiency**:

> High relative to optimizers: achieves gains with up to 5 epochs / max 5 Reflector refinement rounds and batch size 1, using 75.1% fewer rollouts than GEPA on offline AppWorld; GEPA itself is noted as needing up to 35x fewer rollouts than RL. Exact minimal-sample threshold not isolated.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- calibration_effect
- code_url
- extended_by_or_inspired

<a id="r038-dynamic-cheatsheet-test-time-learning-with-adaptive-memory"></a>
## Dynamic Cheatsheet: Test-Time Learning with Adaptive Memory

**ID:** R038  **Category:** G (Memory, experience-distillation & lifelong agents)  **Authors:** Suzgun et al.  **Venue:** EACL 2026 (arXiv preprint 2025)  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07952

### Basic info

- **name**: Dynamic Cheatsheet: Test-Time Learning with Adaptive Memory

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Mirac Suzgun, Mert Yuksekgonul, Federico Bianchi, Dan Jurafsky, James Zou (Stanford University)

- **venue**: EACL 2026 (Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics); arXiv preprint posted April 2025

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07952

- **code url**: https://github.com/suzgunmirac/dynamic-cheatsheet


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> verbal-self-critique (the same black-box LM acts as a 'curator' that judges the usefulness/correctness of its own generated solutions and distills/prunes them into memory, prompted via task-agnostic instructions; no external verifier or learned critic). For code-heavy tasks the model can also self-validate via a Python interpreter, but the core curation signal is self-generated.

- **feedback source**:

> self-generated (the curator assesses correctness and generalizability of its own outputs without ground-truth labels or human feedback). Optionally augmented by an external Python interpreter for code-based tasks (Game of 24, Math Equation Balancer), but no ground-truth oracle is used.

- **iteration structure**:

> iterative-refine across a sequence of test queries (online-learning style): for each new query the generator answers conditioned on current memory, then the curator updates memory; this repeats query-by-query (inter-task accumulation rather than within-query retry). DC-RS additionally retrieves before answering.

- **reflection object**:

> reusable skill/workflow plus prompt/context: DC reflects on and curates a compact external text memory ('cheatsheet') of transferable strategies, problem-solving insights, heuristics, and reusable code snippets (e.g., a Python brute-force solver). It modifies the in-context memory artifact, not the model's reasoning chain in-place and not the model weights.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal

- **requires training**: none (no gradient updates; works on black-box LLM APIs such as GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet without modifying parameters)

- **reward or critic model**:

> self-as-judge (the same LM, prompted as a curator, decides what to store/refine/prune; no trained reward model, no verifiable reward, no ground-truth labels). For code tasks an interpreter can provide an execution-based check.

- **distillation target**:

> reusable-skill/workflow (and prompt): reflection is distilled into a self-curated, evolving cheatsheet of concise strategies, insights, and code snippets that persists in context and is reused across queries; explicitly NOT model-weights and NOT raw episodic transcripts.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> prompt/scaffold-engineered: the reflective/curation behavior is induced by task-agnostic prompts that define the Gen (generator) and Cur (curator) roles plus a retrieval mechanism; it is an external scaffold, not an RL-emergent capability. The behavior depends on the base model already having strong generative competence.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: playbook/cheatsheet (a self-curated, evolving external text memory of strategies, insights, and reusable code snippets); DC-RS additionally maintains a retrievable store of past input-output pairs

- **memory persistence**:

> cross-task (persists and accumulates across a sequence of distinct test queries within a benchmark / test-time stream). It is a test-time, online-learning memory rather than a productionized cross-session store, though it is designed to bridge isolated inference events.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> self-summarized/curated with overwrite/evolution: the LM curator (Cur) selectively (i) distills useful/generalizable solutions into compact entries, (ii) refines or removes incorrect/superseded entries, and (iii) consolidates for clarity and compactness to avoid context ballooning. DC-RS adds a retrieval-gated step (top-k=3 cosine-similarity retrieval over past input-output pairs via text-embedding-3-small) feeding the curator before generation.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> holistic/outcome-level (the curator judges whole candidate solutions as useful/correct or flawed and decides whether to store, refine, or prune the corresponding memory entry; errors are addressed at the level of strategies/solutions, not at step or token granularity).

- **intra task vs inter task**: inter-task: DC transfers distilled experience (strategies, code snippets, heuristics) across different test queries/problems; it does not iteratively refine a single answer within one query the way Self-Refine does.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> avoidance-only: corrections influence future queries (the curator prunes/refines faulty heuristics so later problems benefit); DC does not perform mid-trajectory in-flight recovery of the current answer, and there is no episodic retry-with-reset of the same query.


### Application domain

- **task domains**: math/competition reasoning, QA/reasoning (knowledge-intensive multiple-choice), heuristic-search arithmetic puzzles, tool-use (Python code generation/execution)

- **benchmarks**: AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AIME 2020-2024, GPQA-Diamond, Game of 24, Math Equation Balancer, MMLU-Pro (Engineering and Physics)


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> GPT-4o's Game of 24 accuracy jumped from 10% (baseline) to 99% under DC-RS after discovering and reusing a Python brute-force solver; Claude 3.5 Sonnet's AIME 2024 accuracy more than doubled from 23.3% to 50.0% (DC-Cu), with +30% on AIME 2025 (6.7% to 36.7%), all at inference time without weight updates or labels.

- **baselines**:

> Baseline prompting (BL, vanilla minimal-instruction one-off inference); DC-empty (DC-no-memory, structured problem-solving + tool-use instructions but no retained memory, a strong baseline); Full-History appending (FH, raw uncurated transcript); Dynamic Retrieval (DR, retrieval of verbatim past pairs without curation); and Majority Voting (MV) over 3 samples.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> vs strongest comparable baseline (DC-empty / DR, isolating the memory-curation effect): Game of 24 GPT-4o DC-RS 99% vs DC-empty 19% (+80); Claude Sonnet AIME 2024 DC-Cu 50.0% vs DC-empty 36.7% (+13.3, and +26.7 vs BL 23.3%); AIME 2025 Sonnet 36.7% (DC-Cu) vs 23.3% (DC-empty); GPQA-Diamond Sonnet 68.7% (DC-RS) vs 63.6% (DR) and 60.1% (DC-empty), +9.1 over BL; MMLU-Pro Physics Sonnet 82.0% vs 74.0% BL (+8); Math Equation Balancer Sonnet 44.8% BL to 98-100%. DC also beats FH (Sonnet AIME 2024: 50.0% DC vs 26.7% FH; GPT-4o FH degraded to 13.3% vs 40.0% DC-RS) and beats majority voting (MV gave no gain over BL on AIME).

- **compute cost profile**:

> No gradient/training cost (black-box, no weight updates). Inference adds a curator call (and a retrieval step in DC-RS) after each query, so it is sequential and not trivially batchable. Output-token overhead grows but stays modest due to curation: on AIME 2024, Claude Sonnet averaged ~370 tokens (BL), 494 (DC-empty), 1035 (DC-RS), 1831 (DC-Cu) per query; over time it reduces redundant re-derivation (e.g., reusing a stored Python snippet), so curation becomes a net efficiency gain versus uncurated FH which blows up context length and cost.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Not a panacea: DC amplifies strong models but cannot fix foundational reasoning gaps. Smaller/weaker models (GPT-4o-mini, Claude 3.5 Haiku) gain little or even degrade because they produce too few correct solutions to seed memory and struggle to retrieve/refine entries (generative-competence and long-context-generation limits). Reasoning/'R1' models (DeepSeek R1, o1) showed minimal/inconsistent gains (outputs too verbose to curate). Faulty heuristics can be amplified if they enter memory; retrieval can introduce noise/confusion (GPT-4o dipped on GPQA-Diamond with bad retrieval); models sometimes abbreviate memory ('Previous content [...] preserved') degrading stored heuristics; sequential structure hampers large-scale parallel/batch inference; benefits are larger when test queries are structurally similar (curriculum/ordering matters).

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> intrinsic-only / self-verify: the curator has NO access to ground-truth labels or human feedback and must assess correctness/usefulness by itself. For code-amenable tasks (Game of 24, Math Equation Balancer) an external Python interpreter can verify execution, providing a quasi-verifiable signal, but DC's headline claim is that it works without ground-truth oracle labels.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent (and capacity-dependent): strongly net-positive for capable base models on tasks with structural regularity and code-amenable solutions (Game of 24, Math Equation Balancer, AIME, GPQA-Diamond for Claude), but net-neutral or slightly net-negative for GPT-4o on MMLU-Pro and GPQA-Diamond and for smaller/reasoning models, where curated memory can be noisy or misapplied. Improves without explicit label leakage.

- **calibration effect**:

> not-measured (the paper does not report calibration/confidence metrics; it reports task accuracy. It does note risk of amplifying faulty heuristics and of overconfident-looking abbreviated memory updates, but no calibration analysis is given).


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**: n/a (Dynamic Cheatsheet is a memory/test-time-learning method, not a failure-attribution or failure-mode-classification method; it does not produce a failure taxonomy or attribute responsible steps/agents).

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets repetitive re-derivation and re-committing of the same mistakes (e.g., recurring arithmetic errors) by reusing validated strategies/code; mitigates context ballooning from uncurated history. Self-acknowledged failure modes it can suffer: amplification of faulty heuristics (error propagation/loops), superficial/abbreviated self-reflection during curation, and retrieval noise; loosely maps to MAST-style issues such as error propagation and ineffective self-reflection, though the paper does not use MAST terminology.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new benchmark released, but the authors release all original input-output pairs and curated-memory artifacts in their codebase (github.com/suzgunmirac/dynamic-cheatsheet) for the evaluated tasks (AIME subsets, Game of 24 100-example set, Math Equation Balancer 250 expressions, GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Pro samples).


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Retrieval-augmented generation (Guu et al. REALM; Borgeaud et al. RETRO); in-context / online learning and test-time adaptation; self-reflection and self-refinement scaffolds (Reflexion, Self-Refine, Self-RAG); Tree/Graph-of-Thoughts style search (Yao et al. Game of 24, Besta et al.); STaR/self-taught reasoning and curriculum learning; Suzgun & Kalai (meta-prompting / 2024) for the Game of 24 setup.

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Agentic Context Engineering (ACE, Evolving Contexts for Self-Improving Language Models, Stanford/SambaNova 2025, OpenReview eC4ygDs02R) explicitly builds on Dynamic Cheatsheet's adaptive memory; Evo-Memory / ReMem (arXiv 2511.20857, benchmarking LLM-agent test-time learning with self-evolving memory) directly extends and benchmarks DC alongside Agent Workflow Memory; surveys on LLM agent memory (e.g., 'From Storage to Experience') and curated lists (Awesome-AI-Memory) cite it as a key memory-modules / experience-distillation method.

- **citation count**: 72 (Semantic Scholar API, fetched 2026-06; ~50-72 across sources)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> No / negative result: DC is designed for black-box non-reasoning LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet). The authors explicitly tested reasoning/'R1' models (DeepSeek R1, o1) and found minimal or inconsistent gains because their outputs were too verbose to curate effectively, so DC does not hold well for o1/R1-style models with built-in reflection.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Conceptually related to on-policy skill distillation but label-free: DC distills the model's own (on-policy) successful solutions/strategies into a reusable in-context skill library (cheatsheet) that conditions future generations, analogous to self-improvement via self-generated experience, but with NO gradient/weight distillation and NO ground-truth reward; it is verbal/in-context self-distillation into prompt-space rather than into model weights.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Online, no separate training phase: improvement accrues query-by-query over a single pass through the test stream (e.g., 30-250 examples per benchmark). Game of 24 shows a sharp jump early once the Python solver snippet is discovered and stored (then reused for the remaining ~100 examples); GPQA-Diamond improves gradually as snippets accumulate. No multi-trial retry per query is required.

<a id="r039-self-generated-in-context-examples-improve-llm-agents-for-sequential-decision-making-tasks"></a>
## Self-Generated In-Context Examples Improve LLM Agents for Sequential Decision-Making Tasks

**ID:** R039  **Category:** G (Memory, experience-distillation & lifelong agents)  **Authors:** Sarukkai et al.  **Venue:** NeurIPS 2025  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://openreview.net/forum?id=WdL3O58gde

### Basic info

- **name**: Self-Generated In-Context Examples Improve LLM Agents for Sequential Decision-Making Tasks

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Vishnu Sarukkai, Zhiqiang Xie, Kayvon Fatahalian (Stanford University)

- **venue**: NeurIPS 2025 (poster); prior version at ICML 2025 Workshop (PUT)

- **paper url**: https://openreview.net/forum?id=WdL3O58gde (arXiv:2505.00234)

- **code url**: https://github.com/VSAnimator/llm_self_improvement


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> none (no verbal self-critique); self-improvement is via accumulating/curating self-generated successful trajectories as retrieved in-context examples, analogous to reward-weighted regression. Reflection in the verbal-critique sense is explicitly NOT used: failed trajectories are discarded to avoid step-level attribution ambiguity.

- **feedback source**:

> environment-reward (binary task success/failure signal); a trajectory is retained only if the episode succeeds. No external tool verifier beyond the environment's own success check, no human, no ground-truth label per step.

- **iteration structure**:

> episodic-retry-with-reset across many tasks: agent runs ReAct episodes, appends successful trajectories to a database, and that database serves as in-context examples for future tasks. Database curation uses a population/evolutionary mechanism (population-based training: M parallel agent-database pairs, periodically copying the best DB into the worst).

- **reflection object**:

> action trajectory (full reasoning+action traces) stored and reused as in-context examples; equivalently the prompt/context is modified at inference via the retrieved exemplar database. No weight update; the agent's policy is shaped purely through which trajectories populate and are retrieved from the database (a reusable experience/skill store).


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal

- **requires training**:

> none (no gradient updates to the agent; 'training' = growing and curating an in-context example database). The paper also shows in an appendix that the self-generated trajectories can additionally be used for SFT, but the core method requires no fine-tuning.

- **reward or critic model**:

> verifiable reward (binary environment success signal selects which trajectories are stored); exemplar utility scores Q(tau) are computed from downstream retrieval-conditioned success rates (a value-estimation-style self-as-judge over trajectory usefulness). No trained reward model or separate critic network.

- **distillation target**:

> episodic-memory / reusable-skill: self-generated successful trajectories distilled into a curated retrievable database of in-context examples. (Appendix also demonstrates the same self-generated data can be distilled into model-weights via SFT, but that is secondary.)

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> engineered (scaffold/algorithmic): a ReAct-style agent with an external trajectory database and explicit accumulation + population-based curation + utility-based exemplar selection. The improvement is from the data-curation loop, not RL-emergent reflective behavior in the model.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: long-term-episodic / skill-library: a database of self-generated successful trajectories used as in-context examples (with multi-key retrieval over reasoning).

- **memory persistence**: cross-task (and cross-episode): the trajectory database accumulates across many tasks during deployment, enabling continual learning and expanding coverage to new tasks without retraining.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> population-or-Pareto-selected + retrieval-gated utility pruning: (1) Trajectory Bootstrapping appends successful trajectories (append-only base); (2) Database-level curation (DB-Cur) runs M parallel databases and copies the best-performing DB into the worst (population-based training, K doubling: 10,20,40,...); (3) Exemplar-level curation (EX-Cur) scores each trajectory by retrieval-conditioned success Q(tau) and retains only the top-1 trajectory per unique task goal, yielding a compact distilled DB.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> holistic/outcome-level: trajectories are kept or discarded based on whole-episode success; the method deliberately avoids step-level error attribution (failed trajectories are dropped to sidestep which-step-caused-failure ambiguity). Retrieval, however, operates at step level (re-retrieval at each step).

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> inter-task: experience is transferred across tasks by reusing prior successful trajectories as in-context examples for new tasks (akin to Reflexion/ExpeL/AWM-style cross-task transfer), not within-a-single-task refinement.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> avoidance-only: improvement comes from steering future episodes toward patterns resembling past successes; there is no mid-trajectory self-correction or post-hoc revision of a failed run (failed trajectories are discarded).


### Application domain

- **task domains**: decision-making / embodied-text (household navigation & object manipulation), code (interactive SQL/tool-use), and a crafting/reasoning game

- **benchmarks**: ALFWorld, InterCode-SQL, Wordcraft


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> On ALFWorld, success rises from 73% (Fixed-DB baseline) to 93% with the full method (Traj-BS + DB-Cur + EX-Cur), a +20pp gain using GPT-4o-mini; surpasses approaches using more powerful LLMs and hand-crafted components. Naive trajectory accumulation alone lifts ALFWorld 73%->89%, Wordcraft 55%->64%, InterCode-SQL 75%->79%.

- **baselines**:

> Fixed-DB (fixed in-context example database / ReAct with static exemplars); upgrading model GPT-4o-mini -> GPT-4o; multiple test-time attempts (1->5 retries); task-specific human engineering (AutoManual, Chen et al. 2024); hierarchical approaches (Fu et al. 2024); ReAct-Finetune (SFT comparison in appendix).

- **gains vs baseline**:

> ALFWorld +20pp over Fixed-DB (73%->93%); Traj-BS alone adds +16/+4/+9 pp on ALFWorld/InterCode-SQL/Wordcraft. The +20pp self-curation gain on ALFWorld exceeds the +15pp from upgrading GPT-4o-mini to GPT-4o and the +18pp from AutoManual's human engineering, and nearly matches the +23pp from 5 test-time retries while using only a single inference pass. DB-Cur raises ALFWorld 0.89->0.91; EX-Cur gives the largest Wordcraft boost (+8pp to 0.72) and +2pp InterCode-SQL; combined curation reaches 0.93 ALFWorld and 0.82 InterCode-SQL.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Test-time: ~1x single inference pass (no extra test-time retries or success verification needed), the key efficiency claim vs test-time scaling. Training/build-time overhead: maintaining M parallel databases (up to 2x when combining both curation methods) and retrieval at every step over hundreds/thousands of accumulated trajectories; reviewers noted total build + per-step retrieval costs are not exhaustively analyzed. During DB construction, build-time success rates were ~81.3% (ALFWorld), 76.9% (InterCode), 58.6% (Wordcraft), so 18.7/23.1/41.4% of attempts are discarded.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> (1) Failed trajectories are discarded -> potential inefficiency of wasted LLM calls (left as future work). (2) Gains may partly reflect accumulating a critical mass of exemplars covering the relatively small test distribution (e.g., ALFWorld test = 134 tasks across 6 types; retrieved exemplars may be very similar to test tasks). (3) Results limited to GPT-4o-mini, limiting generalizability across model families. (4) Build-time/retrieval compute not fully analyzed; DB-Cur adds variance-reduction but extra compute. (5) Avoidance-only — no mechanism to correct in-flight failures.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> env-reward: the method depends on the environment providing a binary success/failure signal to decide which trajectories to store; no per-step ground-truth labels and no self-verification of intermediate steps. Improvement is driven by environment-verified successes, not intrinsic self-critique.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive (task-dependent magnitude): consistent gains across all three benchmarks (largest on ALFWorld +20pp, smaller on InterCode-SQL). Because retention is gated by environment success rather than self-judgment, it avoids the label-leakage / intrinsic-self-correction failure mode; gains scale with accumulated experience.

- **calibration effect**: not-measured (no analysis of model confidence/calibration; the method targets task success rate, not calibration of a reasoning model).


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**: n/a — the method explicitly avoids failure attribution; failed trajectories are discarded precisely to sidestep step-level which-step-caused-failure attribution ambiguity.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets weak/under-specified task policies by injecting environment-verified successful exemplars; mitigates run-to-run variability via population-based DB curation and low-utility/redundant exemplar accumulation via utility-based pruning. Does not address self-reflection-specific failure modes (superficial self-reflection, error-loops) since it does not perform verbal reflection.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new benchmark released; code and starter databases (ALFWorld, Wordcraft) released at github.com/VSAnimator/llm_self_improvement. Self-generated trajectory databases are produced by the method rather than published as a fixed dataset.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> ReAct (Yao et al.); Reflexion / ExpeL (verbal experience reuse, in-context cross-task transfer); reward-weighted regression (RL); population-based training (Jaderberg et al.); in-context RL / algorithm distillation (Laskin et al. 2023, Lee et al. 2023); retrieval-augmented in-context learning. Benchmarks: ALFWorld (Shridhar et al. 2020), InterCode-SQL (Yang et al. 2023), Wordcraft.

- **citation count**: ~25 (Google Scholar / arXiv 'Cited by 25' as of mid-2026)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**: no — evaluated only with GPT-4o-mini (a non-reasoning model); the mechanism is model-agnostic scaffolding and is not specific to o1/R1-style reasoning models with built-in reflection.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Strong conceptual link: trajectory bootstrapping is described as analogous to reward-weighted regression and learns only from the agent's own (on-policy) successful rollouts. The self-generated, environment-verified trajectories form an on-policy experience corpus that improves the policy in-context, and the paper shows the same data can be distilled into weights via SFT (an on-policy-distillation-style use of self-generated data).

- **sample efficiency**:

> Gains accrue as the database grows over hundreds-to-thousands of task attempts; performance scales with accumulated experience. DB-Cur uses K-doubling evaluation windows (10,20,40,...). Exact #trials to reach 93% on ALFWorld not pinned to a single number, but build-time used 5 training runs; the method matches a 5-attempt test-time-retry baseline using only 1 test-time pass.
