<a id="r047-in-prospect-and-retrospect-reflective-memory-management-for-long-term-personalized-dialogue-agents"></a>
## In Prospect and Retrospect: Reflective Memory Management for Long-term Personalized Dialogue Agents

**ID:** R047  **Category:** G (Memory, experience-distillation & lifelong agents)  **Authors:** Tan et al.  **Venue:** ACL 2025 (Long Papers), Vienna  **Learning locus:** hybrid  **URL:** https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.413/

### Basic info

- **name**: In Prospect and Retrospect: Reflective Memory Management for Long-term Personalized Dialogue Agents

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**:

> Zhen Tan, Jun Yan, I-Hung Hsu, Rujun Han, Zifeng Wang, Long T. Le, Yiwen Song, Yanfei Chen, Hamid Palangi, George Lee, Anand Iyer, Tianlong Chen, Huan Liu, Chen-Yu Lee, Tomas Pfister (Tan et al.). Lead affiliation: Arizona State University; work done during an internship at Google Cloud AI Research (Google Cloud AI; UNC Chapel Hill).

- **venue**: ACL 2025 (Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Volume 1: Long Papers), Vienna, Austria, pp. 8416-8439. arXiv preprint 2503.08026 (Mar 2025).

- **paper url**: https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.413/ (arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.08026)


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> Hybrid of two reflective loops: (1) Prospective Reflection is verbal self-critique style summarization (an LLM decomposes/merges dialogue sessions into topic-based memory entries); (2) Retrospective Reflection is a learned-critic / RL-reranking signal where the LLM's own citation behavior serves as a self-as-judge feedback source to train a lightweight reranker online. Overall: verbal-self-critique (memory writing) + self-generated-attribution-as-reward (retrieval refinement).

- **feedback source**:

> self-generated: the generator LLM produces a response together with citations to individual retrieved memory entries; cited memories receive reward +1 (Useful), uncited memories -1 (Not Useful). No human labels or ground-truth retrieval labels are required (unsupervised / self-supervised online feedback). Prospective summarization is also LLM-self-generated.

- **iteration structure**:

> iterative-refine in an online, streaming fashion across a multi-session conversation: at each turn the reranker is updated via REINFORCE from citation rewards (Retrospective Reflection); at the end of each session memory is extracted and merged/added into the memory bank (Prospective Reflection). Not single-shot; not tree/MCTS search.

- **reflection object**:

> Two objects: (a) the external memory bank content/organization (topic summaries paired with raw dialogue segments) is created and consolidated (Prospective Reflection), and (b) the retrieval/reranking policy parameters (a lightweight MLP reranker with residual connections, phi) are updated via RL (Retrospective Reflection). It does NOT modify the LLM generator weights, the underlying dense retriever, the reasoning chain, or agent code; it modifies stored memory and a small auxiliary reranker.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: hybrid

- **requires training**:

> RL (online): the reranker is trained with REINFORCE/policy gradient from citation-based rewards. No SFT/DPO of the LLM; the base dense retriever and generator LLM are frozen. Optional offline supervised contrastive pretraining of the retriever is explored as an add-on (Section 8.6) but is not required.

- **reward or critic model**:

> self-as-judge / verifiable-style self-generated reward: the generator LLM's citation of a memory in its final response acts as a binary reward signal (+1 cited / -1 not cited) used as a REINFORCE reward; no separately trained reward model. Citation reliability validated (Precision 87.6 / Recall 85.8 / F1 86.7 overall against a Gemini-1.5-Pro judge).

- **distillation target**:

> episodic-memory (a per-user topic-organized memory bank of (topic summary, raw dialogue) entries) PLUS model-weights of a small auxiliary reranker (the RL signal is distilled into the reranker's parameters phi). The LLM's reflections are persisted both as curated memory entries and as a learned retrieval policy, rather than as reusable skills/prompts.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> Engineered/scaffold-based: both Prospective Reflection (prompted summarization/merge) and Retrospective Reflection (citation-prompting + REINFORCE reranker update) are explicitly designed pipeline components with hand-written prompts and a Gumbel-softmax differentiable ranking module. The reflective behavior is not RL-emergent (no 'aha'-style emergent reflection in the base model).


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> long-term-episodic external memory bank, organized as structured topic-based notes: each entry is a (topic summary, raw dialogue segment) pair, with the summary used as the retrieval key. Spans utterance/turn/session granularities via adaptive topic decomposition.

- **memory persistence**: cross-session (multi-session personalized dialogue): memory persists across distinct user sessions and is the sole repository for information from previous sessions; designed for long-term per-user personalization.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> self-summarized/curated with overwrite/evolution: at session end Prospective Reflection extracts topic memories, then UpdateMemory either Adds a new topic or Merges the new summary into an existing relevant entry (consolidating/overwriting it), keeping the bank coherent and reducing redundancy/fragmentation. Retrieval is additionally retrieval-gated by a learned reranker that selects Top-M from Top-K.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> Two levels: response-level/topic-level for memory organization (topics span one or more turns), and entry-level (per-memory) for the corrective signal: each individual retrieved memory entry is independently rewarded +1/-1 based on whether it was cited, giving fine-grained per-item retrieval credit assignment rather than a single holistic outcome reward.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> inter-task / cross-session transfer: experience (citation signal and consolidated memory) accumulated from past sessions is used to improve retrieval and personalization in future sessions/queries; the reranker adapts online across the conversation, and memory transfers user knowledge across sessions.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> avoidance-style retrieval improvement: retrospective reflection corrects future retrieval (next-turn/next-query memory selection) based on past citation feedback rather than recovering an in-flight reasoning trajectory; prospective reflection improves future retrievability. It is post-hoc with respect to retrieval (refines subsequent retrievals), not mid-trajectory generation recovery.


### Application domain

- **task domains**: dialogue (long-term personalized multi-session conversation); QA over conversational memory (personal-knowledge question answering).

- **benchmarks**:

> MSC (Multi-Session Chat, Xu et al. 2022) and LongMemEval (Wu et al. 2024). Metrics: METEOR and BERTScore (MSC response quality), Recall@K (LongMemEval retrieval), and LLM-judge Accuracy (LongMemEval, judge = Gemini-1.5-Pro); also LLM-as-judge on MSC and a human evaluation with Cohen's kappa.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> RMM with the GTE retriever (Gemini-1.5-Flash generator) reaches 33.4% METEOR / 57.1% BERTScore on MSC and 69.8% Recall@5 / 70.4% Accuracy on LongMemEval; vs No-memory-management baseline this is >10% absolute accuracy gain on LongMemEval (e.g., 70.4% vs 57.4% Long-Context), and >5% over the strongest comparable baseline (GTE-RAG: 27.5 METEOR / 52.1 BERT / 62.4 Recall@5 / 63.6 Acc).

- **baselines**:

> No History; Long Context (stuff history into context window, truncate older turns); RAG with frozen dense retrievers (Contriever, Stella, GTE); MemoryBank (Zhong et al. 2024, Ebbinghaus forgetting-curve retrieval); LD-Agent (Li et al. 2024, long/short-term memory banks with keyword-matching heuristics); and an Oracle retriever (ground-truth annotated turns) as an upper bound on LongMemEval.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> Vs strongest comparable baseline GTE-RAG: MSC +5.9 METEOR (33.4 vs 27.5) and +5.0 BERTScore (57.1 vs 52.1); LongMemEval +7.4 Recall@5 (69.8 vs 62.4) and +6.8 Accuracy (70.4 vs 63.6). Vs Long-Context (no memory mgmt) on LongMemEval: +13.0 Accuracy (70.4 vs 57.4). Robust across retrievers (gains hold even with weaker Contriever: 30.8 METEOR / 55.4 BERT MSC, 60.4 Recall@5 / 61.2 Acc LongMemEval). Oracle upper bound: 100.0 Recall / 90.2 Acc.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Response + citations generated in a single LLM call (citations conditioned on the response), so no extra generation pass for the reward; thus inference cost is comparable to RAG (retrieve+rerank+generate) plus a session-end summarization/merge LLM call for Prospective Reflection. Training overhead is the online REINFORCE reranker (a small MLP: batch size 4, lr 1e-3, Gumbel temperature 0.5, baseline b=0.5); experiments used 16 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. RL is noted as the main computational cost. Citation usefulness score converges by ~step 1000.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Stated by authors: (1) the RL-based memory reranking can be computationally expensive, especially at large scale or for real-time applications; (2) the framework is text-only and does not handle multi-modal (image/audio/video) dialogue; (3) the memory updating mechanism may need further optimization for dynamically evolving long-term user interactions. Empirically: stronger generator Gemini-1.5-Pro UNDERperforms Gemini-1.5-Flash within RMM (e.g., 24.6 vs 30.8 METEOR on MSC; 58.6 vs 61.2 Acc on LongMemEval), attributed to stronger alignment-tuned models abstaining on personal-information queries; RR without a reranker (full retriever fine-tuning via RL) degrades badly (20.3 METEOR / 31.0 Acc) due to needing large data and catastrophic forgetting. Also privacy/ethical concerns flagged for deployment.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> self-verify (intrinsic, no oracle labels): the improvement signal is the generator LLM's own citation behavior, not ground-truth labels or environment reward. An Oracle retriever is reported only as an upper-bound reference (100 Recall / 90.2 Acc), not used to train RMM. Citation-as-reward reliability is itself validated (~86.7 overall F1). So self-correction here does NOT depend on label leakage, though it inherits the generator's citation accuracy as a ceiling.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive in the studied setting: ablations show full RMM (PR+RR+reranker) is best, and adding RR with the reranker improves over RAG on retrieval (e.g., 58.8 Recall@5 vs 54.3); the online citation reward steadily raises the useful-citation ratio (~0.2 -> ~0.4 over 1000 steps). Caveat: the corrective RL is only net-positive when applied to the lightweight reranker; applying RL to fine-tune the full retriever (no reranker) is net-negative due to data-hunger and catastrophic forgetting.

- **calibration effect**:

> not-measured: the paper does not report confidence-calibration metrics. It indirectly observes that a more strongly aligned model (Gemini-1.5-Pro) abstains more on personal queries (a behavioral effect), but does not quantify calibration/overconfidence.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a: RMM is a memory-management method, not a failure-attribution method; it does not classify failure modes or attribute responsible agents/steps. (It does implicitly localize unhelpful retrieved memories via the per-entry citation signal, but this is retrieval credit assignment, not a failure-attribution taxonomy.)

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets long-term memory failure modes: (a) fragmented/incomplete memory from rigid fixed-granularity chunking (turn/session boundaries misaligned with topic structure), and (b) poor/static retrieval that distracts the LLM with irrelevant context ('lost in the middle' / noisy retrieval degrading responses). Loosely maps to memory/retrieval-grounding errors rather than MAST multi-agent failure modes.

- **dataset or benchmark released**: No new dataset/benchmark released; evaluation reuses existing public datasets MSC (Xu et al. 2022) and LongMemEval (Wu et al. 2024). MemoryBank/LD-Agent baselines implemented on the LongMemEval codebase.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> RAG with dense retrievers (Contriever, Stella, GTE); prior memory-augmented personalized dialogue agents: LD-Agent (Li et al. 2024a), MemoryBank (Zhong et al. 2024, Ebbinghaus forgetting curve), Theanine (Kim et al. 2024, timeline memory), CoMemNN (Pei et al. 2021); LongMemEval (Wu et al. 2024) and MSC (Xu et al. 2022) benchmarks; LoCoMo (Maharana et al. 2024); LLM attribution/citation methods (Kenthapadi et al. 2024; Buchmann et al. 2024); Gumbel-softmax / Categorical reparameterization (Gumbel 1954; Jang et al. 2017; Maddison et al. 2014); REINFORCE policy gradient. Generator: Gemini-1.5-Flash/Pro.


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> No / not-native: RMM targets general dialogue LLMs (Gemini-1.5-Flash/Pro) and engineers reflection externally via prompting + an RL reranker; it does not rely on or specifically target o1/R1-style models with built-in reflective reasoning. Notably a more aligned model did not help.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Weak/indirect: the RL reranker is updated on-policy (REINFORCE on the policy's own Top-M selections with a baseline), and the reward is generated by the same on-policy generator's citations, giving an on-policy self-improvement flavor for retrieval. However it is not on-policy distillation into the LLM's weights or a skill library; the distillation target is an auxiliary reranker plus curated episodic memory.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Online REINFORCE on the reranker converges relatively quickly: the useful-citation ratio rises from ~0.2 and converges to ~0.4 by ~1000 RL training steps (batch size 4). It is designed to be sample-efficient/unsupervised (no labeled retrieval data needed); optional offline supervised pretraining with a handful of labels further boosts the retriever.

<a id="r069-agent-workflow-memory"></a>
## Agent Workflow Memory

**ID:** R069  **Category:** G (Memory, experience-distillation & lifelong agents)  **Authors:** Wang et al.  **Venue:** ICML 2025 (arXiv preprint Sep 2024)  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07429

### Basic info

- **name**: Agent Workflow Memory

- **year**: 2024

- **authors**: Zora Zhiruo Wang, Jiayuan Mao, Daniel Fried, Graham Neubig (Carnegie Mellon University; MIT)

- **venue**: ICML 2025 (PMLR v267, pp. 63897-63911); arXiv preprint (submitted Sep 2024)

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07429

- **code url**: https://github.com/zorazrw/agent-workflow-memory


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**: search-guided

- **feedback source**:

> self-generated; in the online setting an LM-based evaluator (AutoEval-style binary success judge from Pan et al. 2024) gates which self-generated trajectories are kept; in the offline setting canonical human-annotated training trajectories are used as the source of experiences

- **iteration structure**: iterative-refine (streaming continual learning: induce-integrate-utilize loop over a stream of tasks; offline variant is a single up-front induction pass over training examples)

- **reflection object**:

> reusable skill/workflow (also prompt/context): AWM reflects on past action trajectories to abstract commonly reused routines ('workflows') and injects them into the agent's text memory/context to guide future actions; it does not modify the model's reasoning chain in-flight nor update weights


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal

- **requires training**: none

- **reward or critic model**:

> self-as-judge / separate retrospective LM evaluator (online setting uses an LM-based binary success evaluator following Pan et al. 2024 / AutoEval to filter trajectories before inducing workflows); no trained reward model and no verifiable execution reward is used to gate induction

- **distillation target**:

> reusable-skill/workflow: successful experiences are distilled by an LM induction module into abstracted, parameterized workflows (NL description + sequence of observation/reasoning/action steps with example-specific values replaced by placeholders), stored in a textual workflow memory

- **emergent vs engineered**: prompt/scaffold-engineered: the workflow-induction and integration behavior is built via prompting an LM to extract abstract sub-routines and by appending them to memory; it is not an RL-emergent reflective behavior


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: skill-library (a workflow memory / library of induced reusable routines appended to the agent's textual memory; base memory holds documentation of built-in actions like CLICK and TYPE)

- **memory persistence**:

> cross-task (online: workflows accumulate across the stream of test tasks within a website group; offline: workflows induced from training examples are reused across all test examples). Run on a per-website basis to keep the workflow collection small and relevant

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> self-summarized/curated plus retrieval-gated relevance: an LM abstracts and segments trajectories into fine-grained workflows (deduplicated in the rule-based variant); memory is kept small by grouping/running AWM on a per-website basis so only relevant workflows accumulate. Online induction is gated by an LM success evaluator (only success-judged trajectories are distilled). Effectively append-only with abstraction; new complex workflows are built on top of previously induced ones (snowball effect)


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> step-level / block-level: workflows are induced at the granularity of reusable multi-step sub-routines (action blocks), and abstraction operates over step sequences; success/failure judgment in the online setting is holistic/outcome-level (binary task success)

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> inter-task: AWM transfers distilled experience (workflows) across tasks, websites, and domains; explicitly demonstrated cross-template, cross-website, and cross-domain generalization (contrasted with intra-task refinement methods like Self-Refine)

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> avoidance-only: AWM does not correct a trajectory mid-flight; it improves performance on subsequent tasks by providing better workflow guidance. In the online setting only success-judged trajectories are distilled, so failed trajectories are simply not turned into workflows rather than recovered


### Application domain

- **task domains**: web-navigation (digital agents); domains covered include travel, shopping/e-commerce, social media/forum discussions, collaborative software development, content management

- **benchmarks**: WebArena (812 tasks, 5 websites/4 domains, execution-based) and Mind2Web (cross-task, cross-website, cross-domain splits; 1000+ tasks from 200+ domains combined)


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> On WebArena (online AWM, GPT-4 gpt-4-0613), 35.5% total success rate vs 23.5% for the BrowserGym baseline (+12.0 absolute, +51.1% relative), also beating SteP (33.0%, uses 14 human-written workflows) by +7.6% relative while using ~2.0 fewer steps/task. On Mind2Web cross-task offline (GPT-4), step success rate 45.1% vs MindAct 36.2% (+8.9 abs), and +24.6% relative step-wise success rate gain reported overall

- **baselines**:

> WebArena: WebArena base agent (Zhou et al. 2024, 14.9%), AutoEval (Pan et al. 2024, 20.2%), BrowserGym (Drouin et al. 2024, 23.5%; ax-tree variant 15.0%), SteP (Sodhi et al. 2023, 33.0%, human-engineered workflows). Mind2Web: MindAct (Deng et al. 2023), Synapse (Zheng et al. 2024, retrieves concrete examples), CogAgent

- **gains vs baseline**:

> WebArena: +12.0 absolute / +51.1% relative SR over BrowserGym (strongest autonomous baseline); +11.8 to +30.7 absolute points across the five website splits; also +7.6% relative over the human-workflow SteP baseline. Mind2Web cross-task: +8.9 step-SR over MindAct (GPT-4, 45.1 vs 36.2); generalization gains of +7.4-8.9 (cross-task), +3.6-3.8 (cross-website), +14.0-16.9 (cross-domain) absolute step-SR over MindAct; online AWM surpasses baselines by 8.9-14.0 absolute points as train-test gap widens

- **compute cost profile**:

> Reduces, rather than increases, inference cost vs comparable methods: AWM uses ~2.0 fewer steps/task than BrowserGym on WebArena (5.9 vs 7.9 steps) and ~40.8 fewer steps on average than AutoEval (5.9 vs 46.7). Extra cost is one LM induction call per (group of) successful trajectory plus an LM evaluator call per task in the online setting; no training/gradient cost (training-free). Workflows add tokens to the context but the per-website grouping keeps memory small


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Online induction can distill incorrect workflows from model-predicted trajectories that are wrongly judged successful, degrading performance; AWM follows workflows somewhat rigidly and agents struggle to identify when to diverge from workflow guidelines (lower action F1 vs MindAct); workflow-as-action variant (AWM_AS) is used by agents only ~18.5% of the time (resistance to new actions) and pre-determined action sequences fail under dynamic environment changes (e.g., flight-booking pop-up airports) because intermediate states are not observed; evaluated only on text-based web navigation (GPT-3.5/GPT-4), not embodied/visual or weight-update settings; offline relies on availability of distribution-matched annotated examples

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> self-verify (online) / partially oracle-dependent (offline): online AWM relies on a self-/LM-based success evaluator (no ground-truth labels) to gate which trajectories become workflows; offline AWM relies on canonical human-annotated training trajectories (a form of ground-truth/oracle supervision). No execution-based verifiable reward gates induction. The authors note imperfect online evaluation can introduce noisy/incorrect workflows

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive (and task-dependent): induced workflows consistently improve success on subsequent tasks across WebArena and Mind2Web; gains widen as the train-test distribution gap grows. However, the online setting can be net-negative on a per-workflow basis when the evaluator mislabels failed trajectories as successes, and AWM_text/AWM_AS variants sometimes trade higher step-SR for lower task-SR

- **calibration effect**: not-measured (paper does not report confidence calibration; it measures task/step success rate and step counts, not model calibration or a 'reasoning tax')


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**: n/a (AWM is an experience-distillation/memory method, not a failure-attribution method; it does not classify failure modes or attribute responsibility to steps/agents)

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets lack of cross-task reuse and inability to adapt over time (agents solving each task in isolation, not learning from past successes); related to MAST-style 'no/superficial reflection' and poor reuse of prior experience. The online variant's risk of distilling wrong workflows relates to error-propagation/noisy-memory failure modes; workflow rigidity relates to inability to recover from dynamic state changes

- **dataset or benchmark released**: No new dataset/benchmark released; evaluates on existing WebArena and Mind2Web. Releases code (and induced workflows) at https://github.com/zorazrw/agent-workflow-memory


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Reflexion-style learning-from-experience and skill/library-induction lineage: Voyager (Guanzhi Wang et al. 2024, skill library), LATM/Cai et al. 2023 and CRAFT/ASL-style LM tool/skill creation (Wang et al. 2024b/c), Synapse (Zheng et al. 2024, retrieved exemplars), MindAct/Mind2Web (Deng et al. 2023), WebArena (Zhou et al. 2024), BrowserGym (Drouin et al. 2024), SteP (Sodhi et al. 2023), AutoEval LM evaluator (Pan et al. 2024); program-synthesis library learning (DreamCoder/Ellis et al., Stitch/Bowers et al.)

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Cited by and related to subsequent agent-memory / workflow-induction and self-evolving agent work, e.g., Benchmarking Agentic Workflow Generation (WorfBench, arXiv:2410.07869), AgentGen / automatic agentic workflow generation, and broader 'experience-following' / skill-library memory agents (e.g., AWM appears as a baseline in later agent-memory and self-improving-agent surveys and papers). Specific successors include workflow-generation benchmarks and LLM-agent memory frameworks published 2024-2025

- **citation count**: 174 (Semantic Scholar, as of 2026-06; influential citations 16)


### Other / reserved fields

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Conceptually adjacent to on-policy distillation/skill-optimization: in the online setting AWM distills the agent's own (on-policy) successful trajectories into reusable workflows that are then re-injected to improve subsequent behavior, but the distillation is into in-context textual skills rather than model weights, and there is no gradient/policy update

- **sample efficiency**:

> Highly sample-efficient: on WebArena (map split) AWM_online reaches near-peak success after only ~40 streamed examples (fast early learning curve, gap over baseline rising as high as 22.5 points after rolling over tens of examples); requires no training data in the online setting and only the existing training set in the offline setting

# H. Self-evolving / self-modifying agents

<a id="r019-voyager-an-open-ended-embodied-agent-with-large-language-models"></a>
## Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models

**ID:** R019  **Category:** H (Self-evolving / self-modifying agents)  **Authors:** Wang et al.  **Venue:** TMLR 2024  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16291

### Basic info

- **name**: Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models

- **year**: 2023

- **authors**: Guanzhi Wang, Yuqi Xie, Yunfan Jiang, Ajay Mandlekar, Chaowei Xiao, Yuke Zhu, Linxi 'Jim' Fan, Anima Anandkumar et al. (NVIDIA; Caltech; UT Austin; Stanford; UW-Madison)

- **venue**: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR) 2024; also certified at ICLR 2025 Journal Track. First arXiv preprint May 2023 (arXiv:2305.16291).

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16291

- **code url**: https://github.com/MineDojo/Voyager (project page: https://voyager.minedojo.org/)


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> tool-verified + verbal-self-critique. Iterative prompting with three feedback channels: (1) environment feedback (e.g. 'I need 7 more iron ingots'), (2) execution errors from the code interpreter, and (3) a separate self-verification GPT-4 'critic' agent that checks task success and, on failure, produces a textual critique on how to complete the task. The authors argue this is more comprehensive than Reflexion's self-reflection because it both checks success and reflects on mistakes.

- **feedback source**:

> external-tool (Minecraft/Mineflayer environment feedback + program-interpreter execution errors) combined with self-generated signal (a separate GPT-4 instance acting as a self-verification critic). No human-labeled ground truth in the main loop (humans only used optionally for 3D-building multimodal feedback).

- **iteration structure**:

> iterative-refine within a task (regenerate/refine code each round incorporating environment feedback, execution errors, and critique) with episodic-retry-with-reset across tasks: if the agent is stuck after 4 rounds of code generation, the automatic curriculum is queried for another task and the failed task can be re-attempted later. Lifelong loop: curriculum -> code generation/refinement -> self-verification -> add skill to library.

- **reflection object**:

> Primarily the agent's own code/skill (executable JavaScript program for a task) which is iteratively refined and then stored. Also the action trajectory/plan and the curriculum context (completed/failed task list). The most distinctive object is the reusable skill (executable code) added to an ever-growing skill library, plus reasoning chains (chain-of-thought before code generation).


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal

- **requires training**: none (no model parameter fine-tuning; GPT-4 accessed via blackbox API queries). Learning is purely in-context via prompting and an external skill library + curriculum.

- **reward or critic model**:

> self-as-judge: a separate instantiated GPT-4 agent acts as a self-verification critic that decides task success/failure and gives a critique. No trained reward model; partial verifiable signal comes from the environment/interpreter (execution errors, environment state).

- **distillation target**:

> reusable-skill/workflow. Successful refined behaviors are distilled into executable code skills stored in a vector-database skill library, indexed by the GPT-3.5-generated embedding of each skill's description; retrieved (top-5) and composed for new tasks, compounding capability and alleviating catastrophic forgetting.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> prompt/scaffold-engineered. The reflective/self-improving behavior is produced by an engineered multi-prompt scaffold (automatic curriculum + skill library + iterative prompting with self-verification critic) wrapped around a frozen GPT-4, not by RL-emergent reflection in the model weights.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> skill-library (vector database of executable code skills, key = embedding of program description, value = program) plus short-term scratchpad context (current state, last-round code, feedback) and a curriculum-level record of completed/failed tasks.

- **memory persistence**:

> cross-task and cross-episode within a lifelong run; the skill library is also shown to transfer cross-world (zero-shot generalization in a new Minecraft world, and even plug-and-play into AutoGPT). Not framed as a cross-session production deployment.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> append-only with refinement before insertion: a new skill is only added after self-verification confirms task success, and skills are iteratively refined before storage; skills can be overwritten/updated when a function with the same task is regenerated. Growth is bounded by retrieval-gating (top-5 relevant skills retrieved by embedding similarity rather than dumping the whole library into context).


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> holistic/outcome-level for self-verification (did the task succeed?) combined with block-level/line-level for code (execution errors and environment feedback localize the failing operation, e.g. missing ingredients or invalid item, enabling targeted code fixes). Effectively step/block-level within a code skill.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> both. Intra-task: iterative refinement of a single skill's code within up to 4 rounds. Inter-task: experience transfer across tasks via the persistent skill library and the curriculum's record of past successes/failures, enabling compositional reuse and generalization to new tasks/worlds.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> mix of mid-trajectory-recovery and avoidance: within a task it recovers in-flight by fixing code using environment/error/critique feedback (post-hoc revision of the generated program each round); across tasks, if stuck after 4 rounds it avoids by moving to a new curriculum task and may re-attempt the failed task later.


### Application domain

- **task domains**: embodied/games (open-ended Minecraft lifelong learning), with code generation (executable JavaScript skills) and tool-use/decision-making as the underlying mechanism.

- **benchmarks**:

> MineDojo / Minecraft (via Mineflayer JavaScript API). Custom evaluation axes rather than a standard NLP benchmark: number of unique items discovered, Minecraft tech-tree mastery (wooden->stone->iron->diamond tools), map traversal distance, and zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks (Diamond Pickaxe, Golden Sword, Lava Bucket, Compass) in a new world.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Using a frozen GPT-4 (gpt-4-0314) with no fine-tuning, Voyager obtains 3.3x more unique items (63 unique items within 160 prompting iterations; the TMLR camera-ready states 3.1x), travels 2.3x longer distances, and unlocks key tech-tree milestones up to 15.3x faster than prior SOTA, and is the only method to unlock the diamond tier (1/3 trials). It also generalizes its learned skill library zero-shot to a new world, solving novel tasks that all baselines fail.

- **baselines**:

> ReAct (Yao et al. 2022), Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023), and AutoGPT — all re-interpreted/re-implemented to run in MineDojo with the same environment feedback and agent-state observations. Internal ablation baselines: Voyager w/o Skill Library, random/manual curriculum, removing each feedback type (environment feedback, execution errors, self-verification), and GPT-3.5 vs GPT-4 for code generation.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> Tech tree (avg prompting iterations over 3 trials, fewer is better): Voyager reaches wooden in 6+/-2, stone 11+/-2, iron 21+/-7, diamond 102 (1/3); AutoGPT reaches wooden 92+/-72, stone 94+/-72, iron 135+/-103, never diamond; ReAct and Reflexion fail all tiers (0/3). => ~15.3x faster wooden, 8.5x stone, 6.4x iron vs strongest baseline. Exploration: 63 unique items, 3.3x AutoGPT (the next best). Zero-shot generalization: Voyager solves all 4 unseen tasks (3/3 each, e.g. Diamond Pickaxe 19+/-3 iters), while ReAct/Reflexion/AutoGPT solve none within 50 iters; adding Voyager's skill library to AutoGPT lets it solve some tasks (plug-and-play boost).

- **compute cost profile**:

> No gradient training (zero training cost; GPT-4 used only via API). Inference cost is the dominant cost: multi-agent, multi-round prompting (curriculum + code-gen with up to 4 refinement rounds + a separate self-verification GPT-4 agent + GPT-3.5 for self-ask/embeddings), so many GPT-4 calls per skill. Authors explicitly flag GPT-4 cost as a limitation: GPT-4 is ~15x more expensive than GPT-3.5, but GPT-3.5/open-source LLMs cannot provide the required code-generation quality (GPT-4 yields 5.7x more unique items than GPT-3.5 in ablation).


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Cost: GPT-4 API is expensive (~15x GPT-3.5) and the quality jump is required. Inaccuracies: agent can get stuck and fail to generate a correct skill; the self-verification module occasionally fails (e.g. not recognizing spider string as a success signal for beating a spider). Hallucinations: the automatic curriculum sometimes proposes non-existent/unachievable tasks (e.g. craft a 'copper sword'), and code generation hallucinates invalid game facts (e.g. using cobblestone as fuel) or calls non-existent control-primitive APIs, causing execution errors. No visual/multimodal perception in the main system (GPT-4 was text-only at the time).

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> external-tool/verifier plus self-verify, but NOT ground-truth-oracle. Success is judged by a self-verification GPT-4 critic (self-verify) augmented by deterministic environment feedback and interpreter execution errors (external tool/verifier). No human-labeled oracle in the loop; the environment provides partially verifiable state but final task-success judgement is LLM-self-judged, so it can err.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive in this setting: ablations show self-verification is the single most important feedback type (removing it drops discovered item count by 73%), and the iterative environment/error feedback meaningfully improves program synthesis. Efficacy is supported by the strong verifiable/environment signal; the self-judged success check is imperfect and occasionally wrong.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a (Voyager is a self-evolving agent, not a failure-attribution method). Within itself it does classify task success/failure and produce a corrective critique, and execution errors localize the failing code operation, but it does not formally attribute failures across agents or steps as a taxonomy.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets catastrophic forgetting (via compositional skill library), inability to recover from execution errors (via interpreter-error feedback), and poor open-ended exploration / getting stuck (via automatic curriculum and self-verification deciding when to move on or retry). Relative to MAST-style modes, it mitigates 'premature termination' and aims past 'superficial self-reflection' by combining success-checking with reflective critique; it itself can still suffer from hallucination and superficial/incorrect self-verification.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new benchmark dataset; built on the existing MineDojo/Mineflayer Minecraft environment. The team open-sourced the full codebase and all prompts (https://github.com/MineDojo/Voyager), and the learned skill library is reusable/plug-and-play.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023) and ReAct (Yao et al. 2022) for verbal self-reflection/reasoning+acting; MineDojo (Fan et al. 2022) and Mineflayer for the Minecraft environment/API; DreamCoder (Ellis et al. 2020) for the program-as-skill / library-learning idea; chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022); GPT-4 (OpenAI 2023). Contrasts with RL/imitation Minecraft agents (VPT, DreamerV3, MineDojo) and LLM planners (GITM, DEPS/Describe-Explain-Plan-Select, Plan4MC).

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Inspired and is frequently compared against later open-world / lifelong-agent and skill/workflow-memory works, e.g. JARVIS-1 (memory-augmented multimodal Minecraft agent, 2023), GITM (Ghost in the Minecraft), ExpeL (experiential learning), and Agent Workflow Memory (AWM) and other 'skill library / reusable workflow' agent methods; widely cited as the canonical executable-skill-library self-evolving agent.

- **citation count**: ~1,406 (Semantic Scholar, as fetched 2026-06-08); Google Scholar reports ~1,914.


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> no. Voyager wraps a frozen non-reasoning GPT-4 (gpt-4-0314) with an external scaffold; reflection is engineered via prompting, not native to an o1/R1-style reasoning model. The approach is in principle model-agnostic given a capable code-generating backbone.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Conceptually related to skill/experience distillation: refined on-policy rollouts (successful, self-verified executable skills) are distilled into a retrievable skill library that improves future behavior. However, it is in-context only (no weight updates / no on-policy gradient distillation), so it is an in-context analogue rather than true on-policy distillation.

- **sample efficiency**:

> High in trials-to-milestone terms vs baselines: reaches wooden tool in ~6 prompting iterations, stone ~11, iron ~21 (vs AutoGPT 92/94/135), and solves unseen tasks in ~18-21 iterations (3/3) where baselines fail within 50. Each 'iteration' is a multi-call GPT-4 round (up to 4 code-gen rounds per task), so API-call cost per skill is non-trivial.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- calibration_effect

<a id="r035-se-agent-self-evolution-trajectory-optimization-in-multi-step-reasoning-with-llm-based-agents"></a>
## SE-Agent: Self-Evolution Trajectory Optimization in Multi-Step Reasoning with LLM-Based Agents

**ID:** R035  **Category:** H (Self-evolving / self-modifying agents)  **Authors:** Lin et al.  **Venue:** NeurIPS 2025  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/a911e543a95493ae5004fdc01909043e-Abstract-Conference.html

### Basic info

- **name**: SE-Agent: Self-Evolution Trajectory Optimization in Multi-Step Reasoning with LLM-Based Agents

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Jiaye Lin, Yifu Guo, et al. (14 authors); lead affiliations Tsinghua University (THU) and StepFun, with PKU/UCAS/UofT/UCR/USYD/UMN collaborators

- **venue**: NeurIPS 2025 (poster); arXiv preprint arXiv:2508.02085 (first submitted Aug 2025)

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02085 (NeurIPS proceedings: https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/a911e543a95493ae5004fdc01909043e-Abstract-Conference.html)

- **code url**: https://github.com/JARVIS-Xs/SE-Agent


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> verbal-self-critique + search-guided + population/evolutionary. The agent verbally reflects on each pilot trajectory (Reflect/Revise), then runs an evolutionary search over a pool of trajectories using three operators (revision, recombination, refinement). Conceptually a genetic-algorithm / expert-iteration style search rather than plain single-trajectory MCTS.

- **feedback source**:

> Mixed: (1) self-generated LLM critique (Reflect, ExpertEval) and (2) external-tool / rule-based structural validation (AutoEval: non-empty patch files, sufficient code-editing steps, reasonable trajectory length). Final reported success on SWE-bench Verified is measured by developer-written unit tests, but the in-loop trajectory selection reward is a weighted combination of AutoEval (rule-based) + LLM ExpertEval, not the held-out test oracle.

- **iteration structure**:

> population/evolutionary: starts from a pool of diverse initial 'pilot' trajectories (Gamma_0) and iteratively evolves generations Gamma_k via revision, recombination (crossover/transfer/restructuring) and refinement (multi-dimensional reward + elite selection), until convergence (max-reward improvement < epsilon) or a max iteration budget. Default 10 candidate trajectories, 5 distinct planning strategies for seeding.

- **reflection object**:

> action trajectory (the full multi-step reasoning/interaction trajectory). SE-Agent reflects on and manipulates entire pilot trajectories at the trajectory level (revising, recombining segments via crossover, and refining) rather than editing isolated output tokens or model weights. The underlying base LLM is frozen; only the trajectories/search are optimized.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal

- **requires training**: none — base LLMs are frozen and used as-is (plug-and-play wrapper around SWE-Agent / CodeAct). No SFT/RL/DPO weight updates; improvement comes entirely from inference-time evolutionary trajectory optimization.

- **reward or critic model**:

> self-as-judge + verifiable-structural reward (no separately trained reward model). The multi-dimensional Reward(tau,t) = w1*TaskCompletion + w2*ReasoningQuality + w3*Efficiency, where TaskCompletion = AutoEval (rule-based structural checks) + lambda*ExpertEval (the LLM itself acting as judge). ReasoningQuality is LLM-judged.

- **distillation target**:

> none — reflections are not distilled into a persisted reusable artifact (no skill library, no weight update, no cross-task memory). Cross-trajectory insight lives only inside the current task's evolving trajectory pool and is discarded after the task; the final output is the single highest-reward trajectory tau*.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> engineered / scaffold-engineered. The reflective and evolutionary behavior is explicitly prompt- and operator-engineered (revision, recombination, refinement operators with hand-designed prompts and a hand-designed reward), not RL-emergent like an R1-style 'aha' moment.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: short-term/scratchpad — the evolving trajectory pool (population of candidate trajectories for the current task) acts as working memory. No long-term episodic memory or persistent skill library.

- **memory persistence**: within-episode (per-task). The trajectory pool and cross-trajectory inspiration are confined to solving a single task; nothing is carried across tasks or sessions.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> population-or-Pareto-selected: each generation applies Select(Gamma_k ∪ Gamma_k' ∪ Gamma_k^new, o) to retain o elite trajectories by reward score while preserving diversity via trajectory-dissimilarity metrics, preventing the pool from ballooning and avoiding homogeneous collapse.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> holistic/trajectory-level (action-trajectory level). SE-Agent reflects on and operates over whole trajectories (and trajectory segments via crossover), identifying logical inconsistencies and under-developed reasoning steps across the trajectory rather than at token level. The case study frames the win as escaping step-local 'tunnel vision' to find a root-cause fix in a different file.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> intra-task: experience is reused across multiple trajectories of the SAME task (cross-trajectory inspiration within one task's evolution), not transferred across different tasks. No inter-task experience transfer like Reflexion/ExpeL.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> post-hoc-revision combined with avoidance via population search: suboptimal pilot trajectories are revised/recombined into improved ones and low-reward paths are pruned by selection, rather than correcting a single trajectory mid-flight.


### Application domain

- **task domains**: code (real-world software engineering / GitHub issue resolution). Framework is presented as general for multi-step reasoning (math, planning, creative tasks mentioned), but evaluated only on code/SWE.

- **benchmarks**: SWE-bench Verified (500 curated real-world GitHub issues).


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> On SWE-bench Verified, integrating SE-Agent yields up to 55% relative improvement and achieves SOTA among open-source agents. With Claude-3.7-Sonnet it reaches 61.2% Pass@1 (63.6% Pass@5) vs SWE-Agent 40.6% / SWE-Search 47.4%. A footnote reports 80.0% with Claude-4-Sonnet using the latest SWE-Agent (vs 66.6% baseline on the 2025-05-22 SWE-bench Verified leaderboard).

- **baselines**:

> SWE-Agent (CodeAct-based) and SWE-Search (MCTS-based) — both strong open-source SWE frameworks. Evaluated across 5 LLMs: DeepSeek-V3-0324, Qwen-2.5-72b-Instruct, Llama-3.1-70b-Instruct (open-source), GPT-4o, Claude-3.7-Sonnet (closed-source).

- **gains vs baseline**:

> Pass@1 vs SWE-Agent: +112% relative (Llama-3.1-70b: 15.4%->32.6%), +80% (GPT-4o: 22.4%->40.4%), +51% (Claude-3.7: 40.6%->61.2%); DeepSeek-V3 31.6%->54.8%, Qwen-2.5-72b 18.8%->38.8%. Vs the stronger MCTS-based SWE-Search: roughly +30% relative on average (e.g., Claude-3.7 47.4%->61.2%, DeepSeek-V3 39.4%->54.8%). SE-Agent also uniquely resolves 12 issues that no baseline solves.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Inference-time multiplier: generates a pool of ~10 candidate trajectories per task (default), seeded by 5 planning strategies, plus revision/recombination/refinement passes — i.e., a multi-trajectory (population) search rather than a single pass. Authors report near-optimal performance at just 10 candidate trajectories and claim that, under matched maximum-API-cost budgets, SE-Agent still beats baselines on Pass@1; positioned as more efficient than open-ended Test-Time-Scaling. No exact token-count multiplier is given. No training cost (base models frozen).


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> No explicit Limitations section in the paper body. Practical limits inferable from the design/scope: (1) evaluated only on SWE-bench Verified (code), so generality to math/embodied/other domains is asserted but unverified (left to future work, e.g., DeepSearch, embodied intelligence); (2) inference cost scales with the trajectory-pool size and multiple operator passes; (3) the in-loop reward relies on LLM self-judgment (ExpertEval) plus hand-tuned weights (w1,w2,w3,lambda) and rule-based structural checks, which may be gamed or miscalibrated; (4) improvements are within-task only — no persistent learning/transfer across tasks.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> external-tool/verifier (partial). The in-loop signal blends self-verification (LLM ExpertEval/ReasoningQuality) with rule-based structural validation (AutoEval: non-empty patch, sufficient edit steps, trajectory length) — NOT the held-out unit-test oracle, which is used only for final scoring. So selection does not directly leak the ground-truth test labels; structural validators provide the external grounding.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive on the evaluated benchmark: consistent Pass@1/Pass@5 gains across all 5 LLMs over both CodeAct and MCTS baselines, with ablations showing each operator (revision, recombination, refinement) contributes and removing any one lowers Pass@1. Efficacy demonstrated only on SWE-bench Verified (code).


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a — SE-Agent is a self-improvement / search method, not a failure-attribution method. It implicitly localizes weaknesses during the per-trajectory Reflect step (identifying logical inconsistencies / underdeveloped steps) but does not produce a failure taxonomy or attribute responsibility across agents.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets homogeneous/redundant search and local-optima 'tunnel vision' (near-identical rollouts that only tweak surface expressions), i.e., a diversity-collapse / underthinking-style failure where probabilistic LLMs gravitate to high-probability solution patterns. Loosely maps to MAST-style 'superficial self-reflection' and lack-of-exploration error loops; cross-trajectory recombination is the proposed remedy.

- **dataset or benchmark released**: No new dataset/benchmark released. Code and demonstration materials released at https://github.com/JARVIS-Xs/SE-Agent (uses existing SWE-bench Verified).


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> SWE-Agent / agent-computer interface (Yang et al.) and CodeAct as the underlying code-agent scaffold; ReAct (Yao et al.) as the multi-turn reasoning paradigm; MCTS-based search (SWE-Search) as the primary search baseline it critiques and extends; Reflexion and CRITIC as self-improvement predecessors; conceptual roots in genetic/evolutionary algorithms and self-play / expert iteration.

- **citation count**: ~31 (Semantic Scholar, mid-2026; ~43 per Google Scholar via arXiv listing)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> No — SE-Agent is model-agnostic and was evaluated on standard instruction-tuned chat/code LLMs (DeepSeek-V3, Qwen-2.5-72b, Llama-3.1-70b, GPT-4o, Claude-3.7/4-Sonnet), not o1/R1-style built-in-reflection reasoning models. It adds reflection externally via scaffolding, but is claimed to remain effective regardless of base-model improvements as long as tasks need multi-step reasoning.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Weak/none. SE-Agent does not perform on-policy distillation or weight-level skill optimization; it is an inference-time evolutionary trajectory search with frozen models. Conceptually adjacent to expert-iteration / self-play (each trajectory-optimization step acts as an 'improvement operator'), but no policy is distilled into weights or a reusable skill artifact.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Reaches near-optimal performance with ~10 candidate trajectories per task (5 planning seeds + revision/recombination/refinement); authors emphasize 'remarkably fewer evolutionary cycles' than a classic genetic algorithm. Exact iteration counts per task not reported.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- calibration_effect

<a id="r040-memento-skills-let-agents-design-agents"></a>
## Memento-Skills: Let Agents Design Agents

**ID:** R040  **Category:** H (Self-evolving / self-modifying agents)  **Authors:** Huichi Zhou et al. (incl. Jun Wang)  **Venue:** arXiv preprint  **Learning locus:** hybrid  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.18743

### Basic info

- **name**: Memento-Skills: Let Agents Design Agents

- **year**: 2026

- **authors**: Huichi Zhou et al. (Memento-Team), lead affiliation University College London (UCL); 17 authors including Jun Wang (UCL); other contributors from Jilin University, HKUST(GZ), and the AI Lab of the Yangtze River Delta.

- **venue**: arXiv preprint

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.18743

- **code url**: https://github.com/Memento-Teams/Memento-Skills (skill dataset/market at https://skills.memento.run/market/)


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**: verbal-self-critique

- **feedback source**:

> self-generated (LLM-as-judge verdict + diagnostic execution traces); a synthetic unit-test gate verifies rewritten skills; in benchmark training the judge is scored against ground-truth answers (GAIA/HLE have verifiable answers)

- **iteration structure**:

> iterative-refine (closed-loop Read-Write loop: Observe -> Read -> Act -> Feedback -> Write, with up to K=3 reflective retries per task and multiple training rounds R0-R3); population-like skill-library growth across episodes

- **reflection object**:

> Primarily reusable skill/workflow artefacts ('skill folders' = SKILL.md declarative spec + helper scripts + prompts), plus the prompt/context (stateful prompt and a 'tip memory'). Adaptation also targets the agent's own code (executable skill code) and the routing policy, but never the LLM weights.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**:

> in_context_verbal (no weight update) — described by the authors as 'continual learning without updating LLM parameters'; the only gradient training is on the small external skill-router embedding model, not the policy LLM, so it is effectively non-parametric for the agent policy

- **requires training**: none for the policy LLM (frozen). The skill router is trained with single-step offline RL (multi-positive InfoNCE contrastive fine-tuning) on top of a Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B model; no RL/SFT on the generative LLM.

- **reward or critic model**:

> self-as-judge (LLM-as-a-judge, MT-bench style) provides the CORRECT/INCORRECT signal driving reflection; for the router, a verifiable reward r(q,d) (whether retrieved skill is the right tool) defines a one-step soft Q-function

- **distillation target**: reusable-skill/workflow — reflection is consolidated into executable, multi-artefact skills (markdown spec + code + prompts) stored as persistent external memory; also accumulates a prompt-level 'tip memory'

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> prompt/scaffold-engineered — the reflective behaviour is an explicitly designed Read-Write loop (failure-attribution selector, skill rewriter, skill-discovery escalation, unit-test gate). It is not RL-emergent 'aha' reasoning; the only learned-by-gradient component is the external router embedding.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: skill-library (external, writable; SKILL.md + helper scripts + prompts), augmented by a short prompt-level tip memory

- **memory persistence**: cross-task and cross-session (production) — skills persist in an external library that grows over time and is reused across tasks and deployments without retraining

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> overwrite/evolution (self-relinking) — Write actively mutates skills: failure attribution selects the responsible skill, skill rewriter applies targeted in-place edits, and when a skill's running utility drops below threshold delta the system escalates to skill discovery (restructure or synthesize new skill); a utility table tracks empirical success rate, and an automatic unit-test gate validates and rolls back regressive mutations (retrieval-gated read via behaviour-aligned router)


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> agent-level / skill-level — an LLM-based failure attribution selector inspects the full execution trace and judge rationale to identify the single skill most responsible for the error (skill-level credit assignment), then patches that skill

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> inter-task — refined skills transfer across tasks; the paper shows cross-task transfer is strongest when the skill library aligns with the benchmark's domain structure (e.g., a skill refined on one Biology question is reused for unseen Biology questions on HLE; weaker on diverse GAIA)

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> mixed: post-hoc-revision plus within-task mid-trajectory recovery — after a failed attempt the agent rewrites the skill and retries (up to K reflective rounds 5b-5d) on the same task, and the revised skills also avoid the failure mode on future tasks


### Application domain

- **task domains**: general (general AI assistant tasks), QA/reasoning across academic subjects, tool-use, web-navigation/search, multi-modality, terminal/code operations; agent-designing (meta-agent that builds task-specific agents)

- **benchmarks**:

> GAIA (General AI Assistants; 165 validation questions split 100 train / 65 test) and HLE (Humanity's Last Exam; subset of 788 train / 342 test from 2,500 questions across 8 subjects); router evaluated on 140 synthetic routing queries


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> On GAIA test set, full Memento-Skills reaches 66.0% accuracy vs 52.3% for the static Read-Write baseline (+13.7 pp, 26.2% relative); on HLE test set, 38.7% vs 17.9% (+20.8 pp, 116.2% relative, more than doubling the baseline). Base LLM: Gemini-3.1-Flash.

- **baselines**:

> A 'Read-Write' ablation that keeps the same read-write loop (skill retrieval + LLM execution + feedback) but disables all skill-level optimisation (no failure attribution, no skill rewriting, no skill discovery). Router baselines: BM25 (sparse) and Qwen3-Embedding (dense semantic).

- **gains vs baseline**:

> GAIA test +13.7 pp (66.0% vs 52.3%, 26.2% relative); HLE test +20.8 pp (38.7% vs 17.9%, 116.2% relative). Training-time gains: GAIA 65.1% -> 91.6% over 3 retry rounds; HLE 30.8% (R0) -> 54.5% (R3). Router: Recall@1 0.60 vs 0.54 (Qwen3) and 0.32 (BM25); route hit rate 0.58 vs 0.53/0.29; judge success rate 0.80 vs 0.79 (Qwen3) and 0.50 (BM25).

- **compute cost profile**:

> Zero retraining / zero gradient updates to the policy LLM; adaptation cost is the external skill memory plus router fine-tuning. Inference cost includes up to K=3 reflective retries per training question (extra LLM calls + judge + unit-test execution) plus retrieval over a growing skill library; router training uses ~5k crawled skills with ~3k sampled as seed for synthetic query generation. Authors emphasise '$400 in compute to learn nothing' from fine-tuning vs near-zero retraining cost; reported production figures (illustrative dialogue) ~195ms p99 latency, 93.5% accuracy.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Limited cross-task transfer when tasks are highly diverse (on GAIA most training-optimised skills were never triggered at test time because no similar test question existed); transfer depends on domain alignment. Diminishing returns as the skill library saturates (memory coverage radius shrinks). Some domains saturate early/low (HLE Engineering plateaus at ~42.1%) suggesting skill-level abstraction is insufficient for certain domains. Sandbox safety / isolation (whether skills run without breaking the environment) is explicitly left to future work. Embedding similarity is a poor proxy for behavioural utility (motivating the trained router).

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> external-tool/verifier plus oracle-label on benchmarks: improvement relies on an LLM-as-judge verdict and a synthetic unit-test gate; on GAIA/HLE the judge effectively uses the benchmark's unambiguous ground-truth answers during training rounds, so reported training gains depend on verifiable-answer feedback. The router uses a verifiable reward (correct-skill label).

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive (task-dependent) — skill optimisation adds +13.7 pp (GAIA) and +20.8 pp (HLE) over the no-optimisation baseline; ablation removing skill optimisation drops accuracy (~8% in the reported case) and removing the trained router causes retrieval collapse. Gains are largest where domain-aligned skill reuse is possible.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> attributes-responsible-agent / attributes-failing-step — an LLM-based failure attribution selector examines the full execution trace and judge rationale to identify the single skill most responsible for the error and performs skill-level credit assignment before targeted rewriting

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets task-execution failures via skill-level credit assignment and patching: superficial/insufficient skill specifications, brittle narrowly-scoped skills, and routing errors where semantically-similar-but-behaviourally-wrong skills are retrieved (curse of embedding similarity). Adds guardrails / alternative strategies for observed failure modes while preserving generality; escalates to new-skill discovery when in-place patching is insufficient.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> Yes — an open-sourced curated skill dataset/marketplace (https://skills.memento.run/market/) built from public GitHub skills (filtered to >500 stars, SHA-256 dedup), plus code at https://github.com/Memento-Teams/Memento-Skills. No new evaluation benchmark released (uses existing GAIA and HLE).


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Memento 2 (Stateful Reflective Decision Process / Read-Write Reflective Learning, Reflected MDP and KL-regularised soft policy iteration convergence theorem) [wang2025memento2]; Memento: Fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs (Zhou et al. 2025); case-based-reasoning LLM agents DS-Agent and functional test-script generation (Guo et al.); LLM-as-a-judge (MT-Bench, Zheng et al.); Qwen3-Embedding; BM25. Conceptually related to GEPA (reflective prompt evolution) and Letta skill learning, which it contrasts itself against.

- **citation count**: 23 (Semantic Scholar, as of June 2026; influentialCitationCount 2)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**: no — the method is model-agnostic and applied to a frozen general LLM (Gemini-3.1-Flash); reflection is externalised in skills/prompts rather than relying on a built-in reasoning/'aha' mechanism of an o1/R1-style model

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Strong conceptual link: routing is cast as single-step OFFLINE RL (one-step soft Q-learning / KL-regularised Boltzmann policy) deliberately because the on-policy exploration space is too sparse (~8k skills, few hundred tasks). Reflection distills experience into reusable executable skills (skill optimisation) rather than into model weights, an alternative to on-policy distillation that updates externalised behaviour instead of parameters.

- **sample efficiency**:

> High in episode terms: substantial gains within 3-4 training rounds (GAIA 65.1%->91.6% over 3 retries; HLE 30.8%->54.5% over R0-R3) using only 100 (GAIA) / 788 (HLE) training questions and 5 atomic seed skills, with zero policy-LLM gradient steps. Library grows from 5 seed skills to 41 (GAIA) / 235 (HLE). Authors note diminishing returns ~O(n^{-1/d}) as coverage saturates.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- calibration_effect
- extended_by_or_inspired

<a id="r048-gödel-agent-a-self-referential-agent-framework-for-recursively-self-improvement"></a>
## Gödel Agent: A Self-Referential Agent Framework for Recursively Self-Improvement

**ID:** R048  **Category:** H (Self-evolving / self-modifying agents)  **Authors:** Yin et al.  **Venue:** ACL 2025 (Long Papers); arXiv Oct 2024  **Learning locus:** gradient_weight_update  **URL:** https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.1354/

### Basic info

- **name**: Gödel Agent: A Self-Referential Agent Framework for Recursively Self-Improvement

- **year**: 2024

- **authors**: Xunjian Yin, Xinyi Wang, Liangming Pan, Li Lin, Xiaojun Wan, William Yang Wang (lead affiliation: Peking University; also UC Santa Barbara and University of Arizona)

- **venue**: ACL 2025 (Long Papers), ACL Anthology 2025.acl-long.1354; first released as arXiv preprint 2410.04444 (Oct 2024)

- **paper url**: https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.1354/ (arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.04444)

- **code url**: https://github.com/Arvid-pku/Godel_Agent


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> verbal-self-critique over its own source code: the LLM introspects/reads its current runtime code and reasons ('thinking before acting') about whether and how to rewrite itself; the meta-optimization loop itself (not just task outputs) is the object of critique. Closest to a search-guided / self-referential code-rewriting variant of verbal self-critique rather than learned-critic or debate

- **feedback source**:

> environment-reward — a task utility function U(E, pi) computed on a validation set provides a real-valued performance score after each self-modification; supplemented by execution error traces/feedback (error-handling mechanism) and self-generated reasoning. No trained critic; feedback is the held-out validation accuracy/F1 signal

- **iteration structure**:

> iterative-refine via recursive self-improvement: the main loop is implemented as a recursive function (continue_improve) rather than a fixed iteration loop; each recursive depth the agent inspects/modifies its code and re-evaluates. Runs are organized as multiple independent self-improvement cycles (6 cycles, up to 30 iterations each) with reversion to a previous best when performance declines

- **reflection object**:

> agent's own code/architecture — Gödel Agent reads and rewrites its own runtime Python code via monkey patching, modifying both the task policy pi and the self-referential learning algorithm I (the meta-optimizer), including the code responsible for analysis and modification itself. It does NOT update model weights; the underlying LLM is fixed (though the paper proposes future fine-tuning of its own LLM as a direction)


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal

- **requires training**:

> none — no gradient updates to the LLM; 'learning' is realized entirely by the (fixed) LLM rewriting its own runtime code/prompts guided by validation feedback. Despite the task's metadata tag of gradient_weight_update, the implemented method performs no weight updates (the paper lists self-LLM-finetuning only as future work)

- **reward or critic model**:

> verifiable reward — a task utility/evaluation function on a validation set (e.g., MGSM accuracy, DROP F1) supplies the scalar improvement signal; the LLM also acts as self-as-judge when deciding which code modifications to keep. No separately trained reward or retrospective model

- **distillation target**:

> model-weights — N/A; reflection is distilled into the agent's own rewritten code (its policy pi and meta-optimizer I) held in runtime memory, i.e., a self-modifying code artifact rather than episodic memory, a skill library, or model weights. The closest fitting categorical label is none-of-the-fixed-options; the persisted artifact is the evolved agent source code itself

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> prompt/scaffold-engineered — the self-referential rewriting behavior is engineered via a goal prompt that grants the agent privileges to self-modify plus an initial scaffold (self_inspect, interact, self_update, continue_improve actions, thinking, error-handling, code/LLM-calling tools). It is not RL-emergent (no R1-style 'aha'); the LLM's reasoning drives the engineered self-modification loop


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> short-term/scratchpad — the agent operates on its own runtime memory (Python local/global variables, classes, functions) which it inspects and overwrites; carried error information across steps acts as a working scratchpad. No dedicated long-term episodic store or skill library; the 'memory' is the live mutable code/state of the agent itself

- **memory persistence**:

> within-episode / cross-episode — state and code changes persist across recursive iterations within a self-improvement cycle (cross-iteration within an optimization run) and the optimized agent is saved and reused at test time; it is not a cross-session production memory system

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> overwrite/evolution (self-relinking) — the agent dynamically rewrites its own code in runtime memory (add/replace/remove logic via monkey patching); when a modification degrades performance it can revert to a previous optimal algorithm, and error traces are carried forward. Curation is the agent's own self-modification rather than an external append/summarize policy


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> block-level (code) / holistic — feedback is primarily outcome-level (validation score after a modification), but the agent localizes changes to specific code blocks/modules of its own logic that it chooses to rewrite; execution errors are localized via error traces (and, in case studies, an error-trace library) to the failing code segment

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> inter-task — Gödel Agent transfers/optimizes its agent design over many validation instances within a task to produce an optimized agent for held-out test instances (a task-level self-optimizer), analogous to Reflexion/ExpeL-style inter-task improvement rather than refining a single answer in-flight

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> avoidance-only with reversion — failed or performance-degrading self-modifications are detected via validation feedback and the agent reverts to a prior best or adjusts its optimization direction in subsequent iterations; it does not correct an in-flight task trajectory (mid-trajectory recovery is not the mechanism). Error-handling lets it skip a crashing modification and carry the error forward


### Application domain

- **task domains**: QA/reasoning, math, science, and reading comprehension (described by authors as coding, science, math, and reasoning / multitasking); plus a Game of 24 reasoning case study

- **benchmarks**: DROP (reading comprehension, F1), MGSM (multilingual math, accuracy), MMLU (multi-task, accuracy), GPQA (graduate-level science, accuracy); Game of 24 used as a case study


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> With GPT-3.5 under matched constraints (Gödel-base, closed-book), Gödel Agent meets or beats the SOTA automated-design baseline Meta Agent Search on all four benchmarks, most notably +~11% on MGSM (64.2% vs 53.4%). Scores: DROP F1 80.9, MGSM 64.2%, MMLU 70.9%, GPQA 34.9%. The unconstrained Gödel-free variant (allowed to call stronger models e.g. GPT-4o) reaches DROP 90.5, MGSM 90.6%, MMLU 87.9%, GPQA 55.7%

- **baselines**:

> Hand-designed: Chain-of-Thought, CoT-SC (Self-Consistency), Self-Refine, LLM-Debate, Step-back Abstraction, Quality-Diversity, Role Assignment. Automated agent design (main comparison): Meta Agent Search (Hu et al. 2024, ADAS). Also compared against a random-sampling baseline (Appendix F)

- **gains vs baseline**:

> vs the strongest baseline Meta Agent Search (GPT-3.5, matched setting): MGSM +10.8pp (64.2 vs 53.4), DROP F1 +1.5 (80.9 vs 79.4), MMLU +1.3pp (70.9 vs 69.6), GPQA +0.3pp (34.9 vs 34.6) — large gain on math/reasoning, comparable elsewhere. Authors also report faster convergence and lower compute than Meta Agent Search (Appendix D). The unconstrained Gödel-free version far exceeds all baselines (e.g., MGSM 90.6%) largely by spontaneously calling stronger models

- **compute cost profile**:

> Inference/test-time-compute method (no training/gradient cost). Optimization budget: 6 independent self-improvement cycles per task, up to 30 self-improvement iterations per cycle on the validation set, each iteration involving LLM calls for reasoning + code rewriting + a validation evaluation; authors report fewer iterations and lower computational cost than Meta Agent Search (Appendix D). Exact API-call/token multiplier not stated numerically


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> (1) As the first self-referential agent it must build all task code autonomously, so it is not compared to heavily-engineered systems like OpenDevin and is not expected to beat them; experiments only demonstrate feasibility. (2) As the self-modified system grows complex it may need exponentially more intelligence to understand itself, so a fully self-referential system can lose self-referential capability as it evolves (Yampolskiy 2015); the breakdown point is unstudied. (3) Cannot reliably innovate beyond SOTA algorithms given current LLM limits (e.g., does not surpass Tree-of-Thought on Game of 24). (4) Robustness: in 100 MGSM trials it occasionally makes erroneous changes — 4% unexpected terminations, 92% temporary performance drops, and 14% of trials ultimately fail (worse than the initial policy). (5) Safety concerns from unconstrained self-modification (proposed mitigations: sandboxing, constrained modifications)

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> env-reward — improvement depends on a task utility/validation-set evaluation function (and execution error feedback), i.e., environment reward signal from a held-out validation set rather than unaided intrinsic self-judgment. It is not pure intrinsic self-verification (validation labels/metric provide the signal), but it is not full per-instance ground-truth oracle access during test either

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive but task-dependent — under matched settings it improves over hand-designed agents and matches/beats Meta Agent Search, with the largest gains on reasoning/math; however 14% of MGSM optimization trials end worse than the initial policy and it cannot exceed strong existing algorithms (e.g., ToT) on Game of 24. Final task performance usually exceeds the initial baseline thanks to reversion to prior best when performance declines


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a — not a failure-attribution method; it uses execution error traces and validation-score drops to decide which self-modifications to keep or revert, but does not classify failure modes via a taxonomy or attribute responsibility across agents/steps

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets the design-space limitation of static hand-designed and fixed meta-learning agents (inability to search the whole agent design space). Its own observed failure modes (cross-link to error-loop / self-modification instability): error-loop / crash from modifying the recursive-improvement module (4% terminations), temporary performance regressions (92%), and net-negative optimization runs (14%); mitigated by error handling and reversion rather than eliminated

- **dataset or benchmark released**: No new dataset/benchmark released; evaluation reuses existing benchmarks (DROP, MGSM, MMLU, GPQA, Game of 24) following the setup of Hu et al. (2024). Open-source code released at https://github.com/Arvid-pku/Godel_Agent


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Gödel machine (Schmidhuber 2003) and recursive self-improvement theory (Good 1966; Schmidhuber 1987; Wang 2018; Yampolskiy 2015; Steunebrink & Schmidhuber 2012); Meta Agent Search / ADAS (Hu et al. 2024) as the automated-agent-design predecessor and main baseline; self-taught optimizer / STOP (Zelikman et al. 2023); fine-tuning-based self-improvement (Havrilla et al. 2024; Qu et al. 2024 RISE; Kumar et al. 2024); reflection/self-refine agent methods (Shinn et al. 2024 Reflexion; Madaan et al. 2024 Self-Refine); monkey patching (Bimal 2012)

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Huxley-Gödel Machine (Wang, Piekos, ... Schmidhuber 2025); Polaris: A Gödel Agent Framework for Small Language Models through Experience-Abstracted Policy Repair (Kakade et al. 2026, Highly Influenced); CLMC: Code-Level Metacognition for LLM Agents (Jian et al. 2025, ICDM); AgentBreeder (Rosser & Foerster 2025); SwarmAgentic (Zhang et al. 2025, EMNLP); Agentic Neural Networks (Ma et al. 2025); Weak-for-Strong / W4S (Nie et al. 2025); JudgeFlow (Ma et al. 2026); also discussed alongside A Self-Improving Coding Agent (Robeyns et al.) and Live-SWE-agent (Xia et al.)

- **citation count**: 18 (Semantic Scholar, as of June 2026; Google Scholar count is likely higher)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> no — evaluated with GPT-3.5 (and optionally GPT-4o calls in the unconstrained variant); it engineers a self-modification scaffold around a standard (non-reasoning-specialized) LLM rather than relying on o1/R1-style built-in reflection. The authors note future LLM capability gains would unlock more innovative self-optimization

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Weak link — Gödel Agent does not distill on-policy rollouts into weights; its analogue of policy improvement is on-policy code/prompt rewriting evaluated against a validation utility (a non-gradient, test-time-compute form of self-improvement). The paper frames self-code-modification as an executable, more diverse form of test-time computing rather than on-policy distillation into model weights

- **sample efficiency**:

> Per-task optimization uses 6 self-improvement cycles with up to 30 iterations each (so a few hundred LLM-reasoning + validation evaluations per task); authors report it converges in fewer iterations and at lower compute than Meta Agent Search (Appendix D), though no precise sample-efficiency multiplier is given


### Uncertain (not determined)

- calibration_effect
