<a id="r049-darwin-gödel-machine-open-ended-evolution-of-self-improving-agents"></a>
## Darwin Gödel Machine: Open-Ended Evolution of Self-Improving Agents

**ID:** R049  **Category:** H (Self-evolving / self-modifying agents)  **Authors:** Zhang, Hu et al.  **Venue:** arXiv preprint (2025); Sakana AI / UBC  **Learning locus:** gradient_weight_update  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22954

### Basic info

- **name**: Darwin Gödel Machine: Open-Ended Evolution of Self-Improving Agents

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Jenny Zhang, Shengran Hu, Cong Lu, Robert Lange, Jeff Clune (co-first: Zhang & Hu; co-senior: Lange & Clune); lead affiliations: University of British Columbia / Vector Institute / Sakana AI / Canada CIFAR AI Chair

- **venue**: Accepted as ICLR 2026 Poster (OpenReview id pUpzQZTvGY); first released as arXiv preprint (arXiv:2505.22954, submitted 29 May 2025, latest v3 12 Mar 2026)

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22954

- **code url**: https://github.com/jennyzzt/dgm


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> search-guided | tool-verified — population/evolutionary open-ended search over self-generated code modifications, where each candidate is empirically validated on coding benchmarks; agents also analyze their own benchmark evaluation logs to propose the next self-improvement (a form of log-based self-diagnosis), and discovered workflow improvements include using another FM as a peer-reviewer/judge to select among multiple attempts

- **feedback source**:

> external-tool / benchmark evaluation: each self-modified agent is empirically validated on coding benchmark subsets (SWE-bench Verified and Polyglot), with success measured by passing the tasks' tests; a foundation model proposes the modification from the agent's own evaluation logs (self-generated proposal grounded in empirical benchmark scores). No ground-truth test results are revealed to the agent during evaluation (pass@1 setting on Polyglot).

- **iteration structure**:

> population/evolutionary — open-ended archive-based search (Darwinian). Starting from one base agent, 80 iterations generate one new agent per iteration; parents are sampled from a growing archive (selection roughly proportional to performance score and inversely to number of children), self-modify, are evaluated, and surviving agents (compile + retain codebase-editing ability) are added back to the archive, forming a branching tree of agents (parallel exploration of many lineages).

- **reflection object**:

> agent's own code/architecture — the DGM reflects on and rewrites its own Python codebase (the coding agent's tools, prompts, and workflows, e.g., finer-grained edit tools, long-context/history summarization, multiple solution attempts with FM-based peer-review selection). Self-improvement is framed as a coding task that modifies the agent's own components. The underlying foundation-model weights are NOT modified (frozen FMs), and the open-ended exploration / archive-maintenance process itself is fixed and not modifiable.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**:

> in_context_verbal (no weight update) — despite the item metadata labeling it gradient_weight_update, the actual mechanism modifies the agent's source code (prompts, tools, workflows) on top of FROZEN pretrained foundation models; no gradient/weight updates are performed in this version. The paper explicitly lists rewriting its own training script to update the FM weights as future work, not implemented here.

- **requires training**: none — no SFT/RL/DPO; foundation models are frozen. Improvement comes from evolutionary search over self-written code, not from parameter updates.

- **reward or critic model**:

> verifiable reward (empirical benchmark pass-rate on coding tasks) drives parent selection/survival; additionally a discovered workflow uses a separate FM as a self-judge/peer-reviewer to pick the best among multiple solution attempts (self-as-judge at the task-solving level). No trained reward model.

- **distillation target**:

> reusable-skill/workflow + agent code — improvements are distilled into the agent's own code repository (better edit tools, context-window management, multi-attempt + peer-review workflow), persisted as archived agents (a population of code artifacts). Not distilled into model weights.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> engineered scaffold/search with emergent discoveries — the open-ended evolutionary scaffold, archive, and parent-selection are human-designed and fixed, but the specific tool/workflow innovations (granular editing, history summarization, peer-review selection, considering prior attempts) are autonomously discovered/emergent within that search, not hand-coded by the authors.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> skill-library / archive — a growing Darwinian archive (tree) of all discovered coding agents serves as the long-term store of reusable code-based skills/workflows; each agent also has short-term scratchpad context and discovered long-context history summarization within a task.

- **memory persistence**:

> cross-task / cross-iteration — the archive persists across all 80 iterations of a run; archived agents act as stepping stones that can be branched from much later than their discovery. Discovered improvements also transfer cross-benchmark and cross-model (held-out evaluations).

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> population-or-Pareto-selected (archive growth gated by validity) — every newly generated agent that compiles AND retains codebase-editing functionality is added to the archive (append to population); agents that lose editing ability or fail to compile are discarded. The archive itself is append-only over a run; parent selection (score-proportional, child-count-inverse) curates which lineages get explored rather than pruning the archive.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> agent-level / block-level (code) — modifications target whole functional components of the agent's codebase (specific tools, workflow blocks); the agent diagnoses weaknesses from its own evaluation logs and proposes a single next feature/fix, operating at the level of code blocks/components rather than token-level or single-response level.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> inter-task (cross-generation) — the core learning is transferring improvements across iterations/generations of agents and across tasks/benchmarks (self-improvement of the agent design), not refining a single task answer. (A discovered intra-task workflow does make multiple attempts within one task and picks the best.)

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> avoidance / escape via open-ended search — failed or degraded self-modifications are discarded (avoidance); because branching can occur from any archived agent with non-zero probability, the DGM can escape deceptive performance dips (e.g., recovered after dips at iterations 4 and 56 on SWE-bench) by branching from earlier stepping-stones rather than only from the latest best.


### Application domain

- **task domains**: code (software engineering / automated program repair + multi-language coding); the method is a self-improving coding agent. Preliminary safety-oriented extension explores FM hallucination countermeasures (Appendix H).

- **benchmarks**: SWE-bench (SWE-bench Verified subset; also SWE-bench-verified-mini for staged eval) and Polyglot (Aider Polyglot, multi-language: C++, Rust, Python, etc.)


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> On SWE-bench Verified, the DGM autonomously improved the coding agent from 20.0% to 50.0% over 80 iterations; on the full Polyglot benchmark it improved from 14.2% to 30.7% (38.0% on the 50-task Polyglot eval subset). Base/best agents both use frozen FMs (Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) for SWE-bench self-mod and eval; Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) self-mod + o3-mini eval for Polyglot).

- **baselines**:

> Two ablation baselines: 'DGM w/o self-improve' (fixed base meta-agent, replicating ADAS in this setting) and 'DGM w/o open-ended exploration' (no archive; always self-modifies the latest valid version). Also compared to handcrafted open-source agents: checked SoTA open-source SWE-bench solution, and Aider (representative Polyglot agent).

- **gains vs baseline**:

> DGM outperforms both ablation baselines on SWE-bench and Polyglot: removing self-improvement causes gains to taper off quickly after early iterations; removing open-ended exploration makes recovery from poor self-modifications hard. Final DGM agent (+30.0 pts on SWE-bench, 20.0%->50.0%) is comparable to the checked human-designed open-source SoTA on SWE-bench, and on Polyglot the discovered agent far surpasses Aider. Transfer: best SWE-bench agent reaches 28.9% on held-out Polyglot (vs 14.2% base); best Polyglot agent reaches 24.5% on held-out SWE-bench (vs 20.0% base). Model transfer: with o3-mini, base 23.0% -> DGM 33.0%; with Claude 3.7 Sonnet, base 19.0% -> DGM 59.5% (SWE-bench, 200 tasks).

- **compute cost profile**:

> Very high training/search cost: a single DGM run on SWE-bench takes ~2 weeks and ~USD 22,000 in API costs (vs ~USD 10,000 for either ablation baseline). 80 iterations with staged evaluation (10 -> 50/60 -> 200 tasks). Per-evaluation cost estimates: ~USD 350 for 60 SWE-bench tasks (Claude 3.5 Sonnet New); ~USD 5 for 60 Polyglot tasks (o3-mini). Higher-performing discovered agents also incur greater inference cost than the base agent, though cost and performance are not strictly correlated.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Requires extensive compute (~2 weeks, ~$22k per SWE-bench run); still falls short of closed-source SoTA SWE-bench solutions. Inherently bounded by the frozen FM's capabilities (esp. reasoning); does not yet modify FM weights. The open-ended exploration/archive process is itself fixed and not self-modifiable. Assumes coding-benchmark performance is a good proxy for self-improvement ability (alignment that may not hold beyond coding). Safety risks: optimizing solely for a benchmark could amplify misalignment over generations and produce increasingly uninterpretable code; mitigated via sandboxing, time limits, traceable archive lineage, and human oversight. Single-objective tie of self-improvement to one benchmark (co-evolving tasks left as future work).

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> external-tool/verifier (benchmark test execution) — improvement signal comes from empirical pass-rates on coding benchmark tests, i.e., verifiable execution-grounded feedback. Notably, on Polyglot it uses pass@1 where the agent NEVER sees ground-truth test results (unlike the leaderboard's pass@2), so it is not oracle-label leakage; survival/selection depends on this external test-based evaluation rather than intrinsic self-verification alone.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive (in the coding-self-improvement domain) — sustained performance gains across iterations on both benchmarks; ablations show that BOTH self-improvement and open-ended exploration are required for continued gains (removing either causes stagnation or brittle recovery). Gains generalize across models, benchmarks, and languages (held-out tests), indicating real skill acquisition rather than benchmark overfitting. Efficacy is contingent on a meaningful empirical evaluation signal.

- **calibration effect**: not-measured — the paper does not report a confidence-calibration analysis; its 'reflection' is at the agent-design/search level, not reasoning-confidence calibration.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> classifies/diagnoses-from-logs (lightweight) — each agent analyzes its own benchmark evaluation logs to identify weaknesses and propose the next improvement, a form of self-diagnosis of failing behavior; however the paper does not present a formal failure-mode taxonomy or per-step counterfactual attribution. Not a dedicated failure-attribution method.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets and self-fixes coding-agent capability gaps: imprecise/coarse file editing (improved to line-level viewing and string-replacement editing), context-window overflow on long trajectories (added history summarization / long-context management), and single-shot brittleness (added multiple attempts plus FM peer-review selection and consideration of prior attempts). Broadly addresses stagnation/local-optima in agent self-design via open-ended archive search. Not mapped to MAST's multi-agent failure taxonomy.

- **dataset or benchmark released**: No new benchmark released; uses existing SWE-bench Verified (and SWE-bench-verified-mini) and Aider Polyglot. The DGM system code and discovered agent archive are open-sourced at https://github.com/jennyzzt/dgm.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Gödel machine (Schmidhuber, 2007/1987); Darwinian evolution & open-endedness / quality-diversity research (Stanley & Lehman; Clune 2019 AI-Generating Algorithms; Zhang et al. 2024 OMNI-EPIC; Faldor et al. 2025); ADAS — Automated Design of Agentic Systems (Hu et al., 2025, the 'DGM w/o self-improve' baseline); Gödel Agent (Yin et al., 2024) and STOP / Self-Taught Optimizer (Zelikman et al., 2024) self-modifying scaffolds; FM tool-use agents (Schick et al. 2023 Toolformer; Anthropic Claude). Benchmarks: SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024), Polyglot/Aider (Gauthier, 2024).

- **extended by or inspired**:

> HyperAgents / DGM-Hyperagents (DGM-H, arXiv:2603.19461) — extends DGM to make the meta-level self-modification procedure itself editable and generalizes beyond coding (paper review, robotics reward design, Olympiad-math grading); Huxley-Gödel Machine (HGM, arXiv:2510.21614, OpenReview T0EiEuhOOL) — guides self-modification by an estimated Clade Metaproductivity (CMP) and outperforms DGM and SICA on SWE-bench Verified and Polyglot; Self-Improving Coding Agent (SICA, Robeyns et al., 2025); POLARIS Gödel-agent framework for small LMs (arXiv:2603.23129); GODEGEN / 'The Living Agent' production evolutionary self-improvement.


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> Partially / model-agnostic — the DGM uses frozen FMs and is not specific to reasoning models, but it was run with and transfers across both standard and reasoning-style models (Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet, OpenAI o3-mini used for Polyglot eval and SWE-bench transfer). Its reflection is at the code/scaffold level, not reliant on a model's built-in reflection.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Indirect — the DGM distills self-discovered improvements into reusable code/workflows (a skill-library/scaffold-optimization analogue) rather than into weights; it is related to skill/workflow optimization and agent self-design, but does not perform on-policy distillation into model parameters (FMs are frozen). Updating the FM via self-rewritten training scripts is named as future work.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Low / compute-heavy: ~80 search iterations (one new agent per iteration) over ~2 weeks and ~USD 22,000 to raise SWE-bench from 20.0% to 50.0%; staged evaluation (10 -> 50/60 -> up to 200 tasks per agent) is used to limit cost. The authors explicitly cite low efficiency as a limitation and call for more compute-efficient variants.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- citation_count

<a id="r050-live-swe-agent-can-software-engineering-agents-self-evolve-on-the-fly"></a>
## Live-SWE-agent: Can Software Engineering Agents Self-Evolve on the Fly?

**ID:** R050  **Category:** H (Self-evolving / self-modifying agents)  **Authors:** Xia et al.  **Venue:** arXiv preprint (Nov 2025); UIUC  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13646

### Basic info

- **name**: Live-SWE-agent: Can Software Engineering Agents Self-Evolve on the Fly?

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Chunqiu Steven Xia, Zhe Wang, Yan Yang, Yuxiang Wei, Lingming Zhang (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; Yan Yang as a research intern). First author Chunqiu Steven Xia; senior/lead author Lingming Zhang.

- **venue**: arXiv preprint (cs.SE; also cross-listed cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.LG). arXiv:2511.13646, submitted 17 Nov 2025, last revised 24 Nov 2025 (v3). No peer-reviewed venue at time of writing.

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13646

- **code url**:

> https://github.com/OpenAutoCoder/live-swe-agent (MIT license; built on top of mini-SWE-agent; trajectories/patches/results released in v1.0.0 release and on HuggingFace at livesweagent/datasets; leaderboard at https://live-swe-agent.github.io/).


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> verbal-self-critique used to drive scaffold self-modification (tool synthesis). After every environment step, a lightweight 'step-reflection' prompt is appended asking the agent to reflect on its past trajectory and decide whether creating/revising a custom tool would accelerate progress. The reflection is self-generated natural language; the resulting tool creation is empirically validated by running it (tool-verified execution feedback).

- **feedback source**:

> Mixed but primarily self-generated reflection plus external-tool/execution feedback. The agent receives the environment/bash command output (return code + stdout/stderr) and a reflection prompt; tools it creates are executed and their outputs (including informative success/error messages) provide grounding. No ground-truth oracle labels or hidden test cases are used to guide solving (single patch sampled per issue, no test-time scaling).

- **iteration structure**:

> iterative-refine within a single episode (per issue): a standard agentic issue-solving loop (mini-SWE-agent) where at each step the agent emits ONE bash command and is then prompted to reflect on whether to synthesize/modify a custom tool. Tool creation is a continuous, interleaved process (not one-shot preprocessing). No tree/MCTS search, no population/evolutionary search, no test-time scaling (one patch per issue; temperature 0.0 for Claude, 1.0 for OpenAI; max 250 steps, max $3/issue).

- **reflection object**:

> agent's own code/architecture (its scaffold) — specifically the agent's action space via custom tool creation. The agent reflects on its action trajectory and synthesizes/modifies executable Python scripts (custom tools such as edit tools, code-search utilities, file analyzers, e.g. a MARC-file analyzer or a Go static analyzer) that become first-class actions. Conceptually the framework targets the whole scaffold (system prompt, environment interaction, workflow), but this paper instantiates self-evolution on the tool-creation subspace. The base agentic loop itself is left unchanged.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal

- **requires training**:

> none. No offline training, fine-tuning, RL, DPO, or weight updates of any kind. Self-evolution is purely runtime/in-context via prompt-driven tool synthesis; the approach is LLM-agnostic and applied as a lightweight modification on top of an existing agent (mini-SWE-agent).

- **reward or critic model**:

> none / self-as-judge: there is no trained reward model or separate critic. The improvement signal is the agent's own reflection (self-as-judge over its trajectory) grounded by execution feedback from the tools and bash commands it runs (verifiable execution outcomes such as a tool's success/error message). Unlike prior self-evolving agents (DGM/HGM/SICA), it does NOT use offline benchmark scores as an evolution fitness signal.

- **distillation target**:

> reusable-skill/workflow (within an episode): reflection is distilled into executable custom tools (Python scripts) that the agent reuses across steps of the current task. These tools are NOT persisted across tasks in the current implementation (each evolved agent/tool set is discarded after the task); the authors explicitly propose, as future work, serializing useful tools and insights via 'Skills' to enable cross-task continuous self-evolution. So in the released system the distillation artifact is per-episode reusable tools rather than persistent skills or weights.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> prompt/scaffold-engineered: the reflective tool-creation behavior is engineered via two minimal prompt modifications to mini-SWE-agent — (1) initial-prompt instructions/examples on how to create and use custom Python tools (and an instruction that tools need not be general), and (2) a reflection message appended after each step. It leverages the LLM's intrinsic tool-creation ability but the trigger is engineered, not RL-emergent. Ablation shows both the tool-creation prompt and the reflection step are individually load-bearing.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> skill-library (per-task) / short-term-scratchpad: the synthesized custom tools form a small task-local library of executable scripts the agent accumulates and reuses within the episode (avg ~3.28 tools/issue with full Live-SWE-agent). Beyond that, only the standard agent conversation/context scratchpad. No long-term episodic store or external memory database in the current implementation.

- **memory persistence**:

> within-episode (within-task): tools and accumulated context live only for the duration of solving a single issue and are not carried over to future tasks. Cross-task persistence (saving tools/insights via 'Skills') is proposed only as future work.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> overwrite/evolution (self-relinking) within the episode: the agent iteratively creates and then modifies/refines its own tools as its understanding of the failure mode evolves (tools are not a fixed one-shot set). There is no formal cross-episode curation/summarization/Pareto-selection because memory does not persist across tasks; redundancy/context bloat is managed by the agent's own design choices (e.g., a search tool that caps results to top-20 matches to avoid inflating the context window).


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> step-level / action-level: reflection occurs after each agent step on the trajectory so far, deciding whether a new/revised tool would help. Errors are addressed at the level of individual actions/steps (e.g., recognizing that a bash 'sed' edit silently failed and synthesizing an edit tool that reports success/failure). It is not token-level or holistic-outcome-only; granularity is the action/step and the tool subcomponent of the scaffold.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> intra-task: experience (custom tools, insights) is exploited only within the current task to refine the agent's own capabilities while solving that issue. It does NOT transfer experience across tasks in the released system (each task starts from the same minimal bash-only scaffold). Cross-task (inter-task) transfer is explicitly left to future work via Skills serialization.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> mid-trajectory-recovery (in-flight): because reflection and tool synthesis happen continuously during the episode, the agent corrects its approach in-flight (e.g., after observing an ineffective bash workflow it builds a better custom tool and continues). It is not avoidance-only-across-episodes (no episodic reset/retry) and not purely post-hoc revision.


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> code / software engineering — autonomous real-world GitHub issue resolution (repository navigation, running tests, editing source, submitting patches). Multilingual code (Python, Go, TypeScript, JavaScript, and on SWE-bench Multilingual also Rust, Ruby, C/C++, PHP, Java). Authors note applicability to other SE tasks (test generation, vulnerability detection/patching, from-scratch software synthesis) as future directions.

- **benchmarks**:

> SWE-bench Verified (500 problems); SWE-Bench Pro (731 public problems across 11 repositories and 4 languages, Scale AI); SWE-bench Multilingual (50-problem subset, 9 languages); SWE-bench Verified-60 subset (used by HGM to compare self-improving agents); 50-problem random SWE-bench Verified subset for ablations.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> On SWE-bench Verified, Live-SWE-agent reaches 77.4% solve rate (with Gemini 3 Pro, v3 headline) without test-time scaling, outperforming all existing software agents including the best proprietary solution; with Claude 4.5 Sonnet it scores 75.4% (best open-source at submission). On the harder SWE-Bench Pro it achieves the best-known solve rate of 45.8% (Claude 4.5 Sonnet). GitHub leaderboard later reports Claude Opus 4.5 + Live-SWE-agent at 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified. All gains come with no offline training (zero offline cost).

- **baselines**:

> mini-SWE-agent (the bash-only base scaffold it builds on, across GPT-5-Mini / GPT-5 / Claude 4.5 Sonnet / Gemini 3 Pro); SWE-agent (~7,000 LOC, top of SWE-Bench Pro leaderboard); and prior offline self-evolving agents on the Verified-60 subset: SICA (Self-Improving Coding Agent), DGM (Darwin-Godel Machine), HGM (Huxley-Godel Machine). Figure 1 also compares against top open-source and proprietary commercial scaffolds on the public leaderboards.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> vs base mini-SWE-agent on SWE-bench Verified: Claude 4.5 Sonnet 75.4% vs 70.6% (+4.8 pts), GPT-5 68.4% vs 65.0% (+3.4), GPT-5-Mini 63.0% vs 59.8% (+3.2), Gemini 3 Pro 77.4% vs 74.2% (+3.2). On SWE-Bench Pro: 45.8% vs SWE-agent 43.6% (+2.2 pts), new SOTA. vs offline self-evolving agents on Verified-60: Live-SWE-agent 65.0% vs HGM 56.7% (+8.3 pts, the strongest baseline), DGM 53.3%, SICA 50.0% (all run with GPT-5-Mini). On SWE-bench Multilingual subset: 46.0% vs 40.0% (+6.0 pts). Ablation (50-problem Verified subset, Claude 4.5 Sonnet): full 76.0% vs w/o reflection 64.0% (+12) vs w/o tool creation 62.0% (+14).

- **compute cost profile**:

> Inference cost roughly comparable to the base agent — negligible overhead. SWE-bench Verified avg cost: Live-SWE-agent (Claude 4.5 Sonnet) $0.68 vs mini-SWE-agent $0.56; for GPT-5 it was even slightly cheaper ($0.27 vs $0.28) because custom tools replace multi-step bash sequences; SWE-Bench Pro $0.73/issue; Multilingual $0.66 vs $0.59. Crucially, ZERO offline/training cost, versus offline self-evolving baselines requiring 500+ GPU/agent hours (DGM 1231 hrs, HGM 512 hrs; SICA an infinite loop) and DGM's reported ~$22,000 per SWE-bench run. No test-time scaling (single patch per issue), so no inference-multiplier from sampling.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> (1) Depends on a sufficiently strong base LLM: weaker models fail to synthesize useful tools — GPT-5-Nano DROPS from 44.0% (mini) to 14.0% (Live, -68.2% relative) because it misunderstands tool creation and gets stuck in loops; GPT-5-Mini is roughly flat/slightly negative (60.0% -> 58.0%, -3.3%). So benefits accrue mainly to stronger models. (2) Self-evolution is limited to tool creation (not yet the full scaffold/system-prompt/workflow). (3) No cross-task persistence — tools are discarded after each task. (4) Evaluated only on SE issue-resolution benchmarks; broader-domain claims are aspirational. (5) Single-patch, no test-time scaling, so the absolute ceiling is not explored.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> external-tool/verifier (no oracle labels). The method relies only on intrinsic reflection plus execution feedback from the bash environment and the agent's own synthesized tools (return codes, informative tool success/error messages). It does NOT use ground-truth patches, hidden test outcomes, or benchmark labels to steer solving or to drive evolution — distinguishing it from offline self-evolving agents (DGM/HGM/SICA) that use benchmark solve-rate as the evolution fitness signal. Self-correction here is grounded in real execution signals, not label leakage.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent / model-dependent net-positive: on strong models it is net-positive (e.g., Claude 4.5 Sonnet +14 pts on the ablation subset; consistent gains across GPT-5, Claude 4/4.5, Gemini 3 Pro). On weak models it is net-negative (GPT-5-Nano -30 pts absolute; GPT-5-Mini slightly negative). The reflection step is necessary: removing it loses 12 pts (76.0% -> 64.0%). Improvement is achieved without any oracle/label leakage, grounded in execution feedback.

- **calibration effect**: not-measured (the paper reports solve rates, costs, and tool statistics but does not study confidence calibration, overconfidence, or a 'reasoning tax').


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a — Live-SWE-agent is a self-evolving solver, not a failure-attribution/diagnosis method. It does not classify failure modes into a taxonomy or attribute blame to specific agents/steps. (Implicitly, its step-reflection diagnoses local inefficiencies — e.g., silent 'sed' edit failures or costly multi-step searches — and responds by synthesizing better tools, but this is not framed as failure attribution.)

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets agent inefficiency/ineffectiveness arising from a fixed, generic tool set: (a) silent/uninformative tool errors (e.g., bash 'sed' replacing a non-existent string returns success with no warning, misleading the agent into thinking an edit succeeded) — addressed by edit tools that report success/failure; (b) context-window bloat and wasted steps from chained bash commands (grep/find/cat) for routine tasks like code search — addressed by custom search tools that exclude irrelevant folders and cap output; (c) inability to handle specialized inputs (e.g., binary MARC files, Go static analysis) with generic tools. Relates loosely to MAST modes of inefficient tool use / wasted steps, though MAST is not referenced.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new benchmark/dataset is introduced (uses existing SWE-bench Verified, SWE-Bench Pro, SWE-bench Multilingual). However, the authors release reusable artifacts: complete trajectories, patches, and results on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-Bench Pro (GitHub v1.0.0 release and HuggingFace livesweagent/datasets), plus the open-source Live-SWE-agent code/config and a public model leaderboard (live-swe-agent.github.io) for fair, apples-to-apples model comparison under a common open scaffold.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> mini-SWE-agent (the ~100-LOC bash-only base scaffold it directly extends; from the SWE-agent line, Yang et al.); SWE-agent / OpenHands / AutoCoderRover / Agentless / Moatless (SE agent and agentless lineage); ChatRepair (interactive feedback-driven repair); the offline self-improving / Godel-machine line it contrasts with and improves on: Darwin-Godel Machine (DGM, Zhang et al. 2025), Huxley-Godel Machine (HGM, Wang et al. 2025), Self-Improving Coding Agent (SICA, Robeyns et al. 2025); general LLM tool-creation work (Voyager, CREATOR, TROVE, Alita, LLMs-as-tool-makers); SWE-bench / SWE-bench Verified / SWE-Bench Pro / SWE-bench Multilingual benchmarks; references the 'Skills' concept for future cross-task persistence.

- **citation count**: 48 (Semantic Scholar, fields=citationCount via Graph API for arXiv:2511.13646, as of June 2026; influentialCitationCount = 7, referenceCount = 40).


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> Not-native but synergistic with strong/reasoning models: Live-SWE-agent is an external prompt-level scaffold, not a property baked into o1/R1-style models. However, its efficacy scales with model strength/reasoning capability — strong models (GPT-5, Claude 4/4.5, Gemini 3 Pro, Opus 4.5) gain the most, while weak models (GPT-5-Nano) regress. It targets frontier models' intrinsic tool-synthesis/reasoning ability rather than relying on built-in chain-of-thought reflection.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Related at the in-context level: Live-SWE-agent distills the model's own on-policy reflections/trajectories into reusable executable tools within an episode (experience -> reusable skill artifact), a context/action-space analogue of on-policy skill distillation, but with NO weight updates or policy gradients. The authors separately note that the on-the-fly self-evolution idea could be folded into LLM training to provide additional learning signals (a forward link toward training-time/on-policy self-evolution), but this is left as future work.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Single-attempt and highly sample-efficient at solve time: one patch sampled per issue, no test-time scaling, temperature 0.0 (Claude), max 250 steps and $3 budget per issue. The 'evolution' costs no extra training trials — gains require zero offline rollouts/gradient steps (vs DGM 1231 hrs / HGM 512 hrs offline). Within an episode it synthesizes on average ~3.28 custom tools (full Live-SWE-agent) vs 2.92 without the reflection step.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- extended_by_or_inspired

<a id="r070-a-self-improving-coding-agent"></a>
## A Self-Improving Coding Agent

**ID:** R070  **Category:** H (Self-evolving / self-modifying agents)  **Authors:** Robeyns et al.  **Venue:** ICLR 2025 Workshop (SSI-FM); arXiv Apr 2025  **Learning locus:** gradient_weight_update  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15228

### Basic info

- **name**: A Self-Improving Coding Agent

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Maxime Robeyns, Martin Szummer, Laurence Aitchison (University of Bristol / iGent AI)

- **venue**: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2504.15228, Apr 2025; v2 May 2025). Associated with ICLR 2025 Workshop on Scaling Self-Improving Foundation Models (SSI-FM); arXiv comment notes it was submitted as a preprint to NeurIPS 2025.

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15228

- **code url**: https://github.com/MaximeRobeyns/self_improving_coding_agent


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**: verbal-self-critique (LLM reflection over an archive of prior agent versions and their benchmark results, used to propose and implement code edits to the agent itself)

- **feedback source**:

> environment-reward (a scalar utility computed from benchmark accuracy, wall-clock time and dollar cost over a fixed benchmark set; benchmark scoring uses unit-tests for SWE-Bench/LiveCodeBench and closeness/location checks for the two synthetic benchmarks). Also uses an asynchronous LLM overseer as a self-generated supervisory signal.

- **iteration structure**:

> population/evolutionary-style archive loop: maintains an archive of previous agents with their utility scores; each iteration the best-performing prior agent is selected as the meta-agent and instructed to inspect the archive, identify and implement an improvement, then the new agent is re-benchmarked and added to the archive (run for 15 iterations).

- **reflection object**:

> agent's own code/architecture: the agent edits its full Python codebase, including tools, sub-agents, prompts, oversight mechanisms, context-management / KV-cache schemes, and editing tools. It eliminates the meta-agent/target-agent distinction (self-referential), modifying output content, action trajectory scaffolding, prompts and reusable tools all at once.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**:

> in_context_verbal (no weight update). Despite the source one_line tagging 'gradient_weight_update', the paper explicitly states it is a 'data-efficient, non gradient-based learning mechanism driven by LLM reflection and code updates' — improvement is encoded in the agent's source code, not in model weights.

- **requires training**: none (no model fine-tuning; learning is realized purely through code/prompt self-edits selected by a utility function)

- **reward or critic model**:

> self-as-judge plus verifiable reward: a hand-defined utility function U = 0.5*p_score + 0.25*(cost term) + 0.25*(time term) over benchmark results selects the next meta/base agent; an asynchronous LLM overseer acts as a critic that can intervene or cancel pathological runs. No trained reward model.

- **distillation target**:

> model-weights: none. The reflection is distilled into the agent's own source code / architecture (reusable tools, sub-agents, prompts, editing and context-management code) — i.e. into reusable-skill/workflow and prompt artifacts persisted in the codebase and archive, not into weights.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> scaffold-engineered: improvements are prompt/scaffold/code edits proposed by an LLM reflecting on an explicit archive; the self-improvement loop and utility function are hand-designed. Reflective behavior is not RL-emergent.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> structured-notes/archive plus skill-library: an archive of all prior agent versions with their benchmark/utility results (queryable via an 'archive analysis' tool); accumulated agent code itself functions as a growing library of reusable tools and sub-agents. Within a run, sub-agents and a scratchpad-style appended context manage short-term state.

- **memory persistence**: cross-task / cross-iteration: the agent archive and the evolving codebase persist across all meta-improvement iterations and across the different benchmark tasks within a run.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> population-or-Pareto-selected: all iterations (including failures) are kept append-only in the archive, but the next meta-agent and base agent are selected by argmax of the utility score, so low-utility variants are not propagated as the working agent. Within an agent run, context is curated via sub-agent summarization and periodic diff re-consolidation.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> agent-level / block-level (code): reflection identifies which component of the agent system (a tool, sub-agent, prompt, or code module) to add or modify; concrete improvements (e.g. a diff-based 'smart edit' tool, AST symbol locator) are block-level code edits rather than token- or step-level corrections of a single output.

- **intra task vs inter task**: inter-task: experience (utility over a benchmark suite) is aggregated across tasks and across iterations to drive code changes that transfer to all future tasks, rather than refining a single task's output in place.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> avoidance-only: failed agent variants persist in the archive as examples of what not to do and the next iteration selects a better base agent; there is no mid-trajectory weight-level correction. (Within a run the asynchronous overseer can intervene mid-trajectory to cancel/redirect stuck agents, a form of in-flight recovery at the scaffolding level.)


### Application domain

- **task domains**: code (software engineering, file editing, codebase navigation), competitive programming, and math/QA reasoning (tool-use and decision-making throughout)

- **benchmarks**:

> SWE-Bench Verified (random 50-question subset), LiveCodeBench (50 random questions), two synthetic agent-curated benchmarks (a file-editing benchmark and a symbol-location / codebase-navigation benchmark), plus a separate reasoning run on AIME 2024 and GPQA Diamond


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> On a random 50-question subset of SWE-Bench Verified, accuracy improved from 17% (initial agent, iteration 0) to 53% (peak, iteration 14) over 15 self-improvement iterations using Claude Sonnet 3.5 (v2) as the main model (with an o3-mini reasoning sub-agent). The full 15-iteration run cost ~$7,000 in API usage.

- **baselines**:

> Primarily a within-run self-comparison: the initial hand-built agent (iteration 0) versus successive self-improved iterations. Conceptually positioned against ADAS (separate meta-agent/target-agent), Goedel Agent, and the STOP self-taught optimizer (Zelikman et al.) as related prior self-/auto-design systems; for reasoning, against the raw o3-mini-high model.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> SWE-Bench Verified subset: +36 points (17% -> 53% peak; 51% at final iteration 15). Synthetic file-editing benchmark: ~0.82 -> ~0.96 (peak iter 6). Symbol-location benchmark: ~0.35 -> ~0.43. LiveCodeBench: modest, ~0.65 -> ~0.71. Average per-problem time and cost also fell (e.g. mean time ~130s -> ~114s). On reasoning tasks (AIME 2024 + GPQA Diamond) there was little to no improvement: the agent system averaged ~76% while o3-mini-high alone scored 87% (AIME) and 79% (GPQA Diamond), i.e. the scaffolding hurt for strong reasoning models.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Training/search cost: ~$7,000 in API calls for a single 15-iteration self-improvement run; each meta-improvement iteration can take ~1 hour of agent runtime plus a full benchmark sweep. Inference per benchmark problem: roughly $1.6-2.7 cost, ~104-151s wall time, ~0.22-0.30M tokens, ~30-41% cache hit rate (Table 1). Per-problem hard caps: $10 max cost and 300s (5-minute) timeout with a 0.5 timeout penalty.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> 1) Hard for the LLM meta-agent to autonomously generate genuinely novel, feasible, high-'taste' improvement ideas each step; bad ideas waste a full edit-plus-benchmark cycle. 2) Strong path dependency / fixation: early feature suggestions (e.g. fixating on caching open files) bias and lower the quality of later suggestions, giving high-variance runs. 3) Short 300s timeouts and per-problem cost caps depress initial scores, so much early 'improvement' is just speed/cost optimization not traditionally captured by SWE-Bench. 4) Agent-system saturation on reasoning tasks: with already-strong reasoning models the scaffolding adds little or can interrupt the model's native chain-of-thought, degrading performance. 5) Risk of running out of signal from a static benchmark set; no weight updates.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> external-tool/verifier plus env-reward: improvement requires running the agent on a benchmark suite with automated scoring (unit tests for SWE-Bench/LiveCodeBench, closeness/location checks for synthetic tasks) aggregated into a utility function. It is not intrinsic-only — selection of which self-edits to keep is driven entirely by external benchmark/environment feedback (no ground-truth labels leaked into the agent's reasoning, but objective verifiable scores are required).

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent: net-positive on longer-horizon agentic/coding tasks (notably SWE-Bench Verified 17%->53%, file editing, navigation, and reduced cost/time), but net-negative-to-flat on reasoning-heavy tasks (AIME/GPQA), where the scaffolding underperformed the bare reasoning model (76% vs 87%/79%). Gains depend on having external benchmark feedback.

- **calibration effect**:

> not-measured (the paper does not report calibration/confidence metrics; the closest observation is a 'scaffolding interrupts reasoning models' effect on AIME/GPQA, suggesting added components can degrade strong reasoning-model performance).


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a (the system is not a failure-attribution method; however, its asynchronous overseer classifies pathological/off-task behaviors and can attribute and cancel a stuck agent or sub-agent at the agent level, and the archive records which iterations failed).

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets agent-scaffolding inefficiencies: slow/token-inefficient file editing, poor code/symbol navigation, and getting stuck in loops or off-task behavior (handled by the asynchronous overseer). Relevant MAST-style modes include error-loops / being stuck, premature termination, and superficial/path-dependent self-reflection (fixation). It also surfaces an overthinking-style failure: scaffolding interrupting a reasoning model's chain-of-thought.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> Code released (SICA reference framework on GitHub). Two agent-curated synthetic benchmarks are defined within the released codebase: a file-editing benchmark (built from SWE-bench repos using consecutive-commit edits) and a symbol-location/codebase-navigation benchmark. No standalone labeled failure-trace dataset is released.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> ADAS (Automated Design of Agentic Systems; Hu et al. 2024) for the archive + meta-improvement loop; Goedel Agent (self-modifying agent) and STOP / self-taught optimizer for recursively self-improving code generation (Zelikman et al.); self-refinement (Self-Refine, Madaan et al.) and self-reflection (Reflexion, Shinn et al.); prompt-optimization work OPRO and Promptbreeder; open-endedness / autotelic and intrinsically-motivated RL work; AlphaEvolve and AgentSquare as related automated agent-design systems.

- **citation count**: 23 (Semantic Scholar, retrieved 2026-06; influentialCitationCount 0)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> no / partial: the method itself is scaffold-based and not native to o1/R1-style reasoning models. Empirically the authors find that with strong reasoning models (o3-mini, and they discuss o1/R1) the scaffolding tends to interrupt the native reasoning chain-of-thought and yields little or negative benefit, so it does not hold well for reasoning-model-native settings.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> No direct link to on-policy distillation: there is no weight update or policy distillation. The authors characterize the code/prompt self-editing as 'in some sense very sample-efficient' and explicitly flag jointly fine-tuning the foundation model with the agent system (citing AlphaEvolve) as future work, which is the closest conceptual bridge to weight-level / distillation approaches.

- **sample efficiency**:

> High in the authors' framing: substantial gains (SWE-Bench subset 17%->53%) achieved in only 15 meta-improvement iterations by inspecting the archive of outcomes, described as 'very sample-efficient' since each iteration's detailed archive inspection informs large code modifications. However each iteration is expensive (~1 hour runtime + full benchmark sweep; ~$7,000 total for the run).

<a id="r071-huxley-gödel-machine-human-level-coding-agent-development-by-an-approximation-of-the-optimal-self-improving-machine"></a>
## Huxley-Gödel Machine: Human-Level Coding Agent Development by an Approximation of the Optimal Self-Improving Machine

**ID:** R071  **Category:** H (Self-evolving / self-modifying agents)  **Authors:** Wang, Piękos et al.  **Venue:** arXiv preprint (Oct 2025)  **Learning locus:** gradient_weight_update  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.21614

### Basic info

- **name**: Huxley-Gödel Machine: Human-Level Coding Agent Development by an Approximation of the Optimal Self-Improving Machine

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**:

> Wenyi Wang, Piotr Piękos (equal contribution), Li Nanbo, Firas Laakom, Yimeng Chen, Mateusz Ostaszewski, Mingchen Zhuge, Jürgen Schmidhuber; lead affiliation King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), Thuwal, Saudi Arabia

- **venue**: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2510.21614, cs.AI, submitted 24 Oct 2025, v3 29 Oct 2025); also under review (OpenReview id T0EiEuhOOL, likely ICLR 2026 submission)

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.21614

- **code url**: https://github.com/metauto-ai/HGM


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**: search-guided

- **feedback source**:

> external-tool (execution-grounded software-engineering benchmark evaluation: agent-task pass/fail outcomes on SWE-bench and Polyglot tasks). The self-modification proposals are produced by an LLM coding agent editing its own codebase; the improvement signal comes from benchmark task success indicators aggregated over a clade, not from a learned critic or human feedback.

- **iteration structure**:

> population/evolutionary tree-search. Self-improvement is formalized as an iterative tree-search problem: from an initial root agent, a tree (archive) of self-modified agents is grown. A compound policy decides at each step whether to expand (generate a self-modified child agent) or evaluate (run an existing agent on one more task). Expansion is guided by Thompson Sampling over clade-metaproductivity (CMP) estimates with an exploration-exploitation scheduler; expansion vs. evaluation timing follows a UCB-Air-style infinite-armed-bandit rule (expand when N_t^alpha >= |T_t|, alpha=0.6). Decoupled, asynchronous (HGM-Async) execution across CPUs.

- **reflection object**:

> agent's own code/architecture. Each node is a coding agent (a full software-engineering project / scaffolding) that edits its own codebase to produce a self-modified child agent. The thing being reflected on/modified is the agent's own code and tool/scaffold architecture (self-referential self-modification). The underlying LLM backbone weights are NOT updated.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**:

> in_context_verbal (no weight update). Despite the item-level 'gradient_weight_update' tag, the method itself performs NO gradient/weight updates: it is a non-gradient, search-based self-improvement that mutates agent code via LLM-driven edits and selects via clade-aggregated benchmark outcomes. The LLM weights (GPT-5/GPT-5-mini, Qwen3-Coder) are frozen throughout; learning is encoded entirely in the evolved agent code/scaffold and the search archive.

- **requires training**: none. No SFT, RL, or preference training of the model is performed. Improvement is achieved purely through LLM-driven code self-modification guided by a bandit search; the LLM backbones remain frozen.

- **reward or critic model**:

> verifiable reward. The improvement signal is the binary success/failure of an agent on benchmark coding tasks (execution-grounded, repeatable trials), aggregated into the Clade-Metaproductivity (CMP) estimator CMP_hat(a) = n_success^C(a) / (n_success^C(a) + n_failure^C(a)). No trained reward model, no LLM-as-judge, no separate retrospective model.

- **distillation target**:

> agent code/scaffold (reusable artifact). The improvements are distilled into the evolved coding-agent's own source code / scaffolding (the discovered best-belief agent), which is a reusable, transferable artifact (it transfers across datasets SWE-Verified->SWE-Lite and across LLMs GPT-5-mini->GPT-5). It is not distilled into model-weights, episodic memory, or a constitution. The persistent search archive (tree of agents with success/failure counts) is an additional artifact guiding selection.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> engineered. The self-improvement loop, CMP estimator, Thompson-sampling expansion policy, and asynchronous scheduler are an explicitly engineered search scaffold/algorithm wrapped around frozen LLMs. The reflective self-modification behavior is produced by prompting an LLM coding agent to edit its own code; it is not an RL-emergent reasoning behavior of the base model.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> structured-notes/graph (a tree/archive of evolved agents). The archive T_t is a tree of self-modified agents, each annotated with the number of passed/failed task evaluations (n_success, n_failure); this serves as the population memory that the search policy reads to compute clade-metaproductivity and to select agents to expand/evaluate.

- **memory persistence**:

> cross-task. Within a single self-improvement run, the agent archive (tree) persists and accumulates evaluation evidence across many tasks and across iterations of self-modification. The discovered agent then transfers cross-task/cross-model at deployment (SWE-Verified->SWE-Lite, GPT-5-mini->GPT-5), but there is no production cross-session online memory described.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> population-or-Pareto-selected (clade-aggregated, append-only tree with bandit-guided selection). The tree of agents is grown append-only, but selection of which nodes to expand/evaluate is governed by Thompson sampling over clade-metaproductivity, so unpromising lineages are deprioritized and early-stopped; the final returned agent is the 'best-belief' agent (highest epsilon-percentile of the utility posterior). This concentrates compute on promising clades rather than retaining/exploring all uniformly.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> agent-level (node/clade-level in the search tree). The corrective/selection signal operates at the granularity of whole agents and their clades (lineages): an agent's promise is judged by aggregating descendant outcomes (CMP), and evaluation is done at the single agent-task-pair granularity. There is no step-level or token-level error localization; the self-modification edits to code are proposed holistically by the LLM coding agent.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> inter-task. Experience (benchmark outcomes) is aggregated across many tasks and across the lineage of self-modifications to guide which agent to evolve next; the goal is to discover an agent that generalizes across downstream tasks, not to refine a single task's output in place.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> avoidance-only. Improvement happens across generations of self-modified agents (a better child agent replaces/outperforms its parent in expectation); there is no in-flight mid-trajectory recovery within a single task episode. The mechanism is to seed/select more productive lineages and prune stagnant ones, and to early-stop unpromising agents.


### Application domain

- **task domains**: code (autonomous software-engineering / coding-agent development). Self-improving coding agents that fix real-world GitHub issues and solve programming challenges.

- **benchmarks**:

> SWE-bench Verified (SWE-Verified, 500 tasks; 60-task subset SWE-Verified-60), SWE-bench Lite (SWE-Lite, 300 tasks), and Polyglot (Aider Polyglot coding problems). Comparison also references the swebench.com SWE-Lite leaderboard.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Optimized on SWE-bench Verified (500 tasks, 8000 evaluations) with GPT-5-mini, HGM discovers an agent solving 61.4% of SWE-Verified tasks (up from a 53.2% initial agent), the top GPT-5-mini-based system and top-10 overall on the leaderboard. The HGM-discovered agent transferred to SWE-bench Lite with GPT-5 reaches 57.0% (standard) / 47.8% (filtered), matching the best officially checked human-engineered coding agent (SWE-agent: 56.7% standard / 48.3% filtered) i.e. human-level coding-agent performance.

- **baselines**:

> Prior self-improving coding-agent development methods: Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM, Zhang et al. 2025a) and Self-Improving Coding Agent (SICA, Robeyns et al. 2025); shared identical initial agent (from DGM's official implementation). For human comparison: best officially checked human-engineered coding agents on the SWE-bench leaderboards, notably SWE-agent (Yang et al. 2024), and SWE-agent+GPT-5-mini / SWE-agent+Claude-4-Sonnet adaptations.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> Self-improving capability (best-belief agent, same 800-evaluation budget, same initial agent at 40% SWE-Verified-60 / 20.3% Polyglot): SWE-Verified-60 HGM 56.7% (+16.7) vs DGM 53.3% (+13.3) vs SICA 50.0% (+10); Polyglot HGM 30.5% (+10.2) vs DGM 27.1% (+6.8) vs SICA 25.4% (+5.1). Generalization to SWE-Lite (filtered/standard): HGM agent 40.1%/49.0% vs initial ancestor 34.8%/44.0% and vs SWE-agent+GPT-5-mini 39.6%/47.6%. With GPT-5 transfer, HGM agent 47.8%/57.0% vs best leaderboard SWE-agent 48.3%/56.7%. CMP-estimator fidelity (Pearson, weighted/unweighted): SWE-Verified-60 HGM 0.778/0.512 vs DGM 0.285/0.406 vs SICA 0.444/0.444; Polyglot HGM 0.626/0.873 vs DGM 0.383/0.357 vs SICA 0.274/0.274.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Training/search cost is measured in allocated CPU-hours for a fixed budget of 800 task evaluations (with the same initial agent and backbones). HGM is markedly more efficient than baselines: SWE-Verified-60 HGM 517 hours vs DGM 1231 hours (2.38x faster; SICA entered an infinite loop / context-window errors after ~360 evaluations); Polyglot HGM 347 hours vs DGM 2385 hours (6.86x faster) and vs SICA 572 hours (1.65x faster). Efficiency comes from asynchronous decoupling of expansion and evaluation and single-agent-task-pair evaluations enabling early stopping. Backbones: GPT-5 (expansion) + GPT-5-mini (evaluation) for SWE; Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct (expansion) + Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct (evaluation) for Polyglot. The full-scale run used 8000 evaluations on 500 SWE-Verified tasks. No per-token inference multiplier is reported.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Stated limitations and caveats: (1) Theoretical equivalence to the Gödel Machine holds only under Assumption 1 (objective is a function of only the final agent; repeatable trials with time/event-independent outcomes; each self-modification costs exactly one budget unit; only self-modification incurs time cost) — a much more restricted setting than the original single-life Gödel Machine. (2) HGM only approximates CMP via a clade-aggregated empirical estimator; it does not have the true CMP oracle. (3) Authors caution that higher leaderboard scores do not necessarily indicate superior general coding ability, since both human- and machine-designed agents may overfit to the benchmark. (4) Results are confined to coding-agent/software-engineering tasks and to specific LLM backbones (GPT-5 family, Qwen3-Coder). (5) No model-weight learning — improvement is bounded by what the frozen LLMs can express via code edits.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> external-tool/verifier. The method depends fundamentally on execution-grounded, repeatable benchmark evaluations (task pass/fail) as the improvement signal — it is not intrinsic self-verification. It does NOT use ground-truth output labels or hidden test results for the agent under test in the Polyglot setting (following DGM, agents have no access to private test cases/results there), but it does rely on benchmark task-success outcomes as a verifiable external reward to estimate metaproductivity.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive (task-dependent on benchmark feedback). Using clade-metaproductivity guidance, HGM reliably produces agents that improve over their initial ancestor and over DGM/SICA on every reported benchmark, and these gains transfer to unseen tasks and larger models (evidence against mere overfitting). The improvement requires external benchmark (verifiable) feedback; the paper's central contribution is precisely that immediate benchmark performance is an unreliable selection signal (the Metaproductivity-Performance Mismatch), which clade-level aggregation corrects.

- **calibration effect**: not-measured. The paper does not study reasoning-model confidence calibration or a 'reasoning tax'; it concerns selection-criterion fidelity (CMP estimation correlation), not probabilistic calibration of model outputs.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a. HGM is a self-improvement/agent-design method, not a failure-attribution method; it does not produce a failure-mode taxonomy or attribute responsibility to agents/steps. It does, however, diagnose a meta-level pathology — the Metaproductivity-Performance Mismatch (MPM) — i.e., that benchmark score is a misleading proxy for self-improvement potential.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> The core failure mode targeted is the Metaproductivity-Performance Mismatch (MPM): greedy selection by immediate benchmark performance can pick high-scoring agents that seed stagnating lineages while overlooking lower-scoring agents that seed productive self-improvement lineages. Related inefficiency addressed: baselines (DGM/SICA) conflate expansion and evaluation so a newly created agent monopolizes evaluations (e.g., an agent failing nine tasks keeps consuming evaluations) — HGM fixes this via decoupled, single-agent-task-pair evaluation with early stopping. No mapping to MAST's multi-agent failure taxonomy is provided.

- **dataset or benchmark released**: No new dataset/benchmark released. The paper releases code at https://github.com/metauto-ai/HGM and the discovered/optimized coding agents; evaluation uses existing benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified/Lite, Polyglot).


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Gödel Machine (Schmidhuber 2003) and self-referential learning (Schmidhuber 1987); Success-Story Algorithm (Schmidhuber & Zhao 1996); Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM, Zhang et al. 2025a); Self-Improving Coding Agent (SICA, Robeyns et al. 2025); Self-Taught Optimizer / STOP (Zelikman et al. 2024) and Gödel Agent (Yin et al. 2024); Huxley's (1957) notion of clade; SWE-agent (Yang et al. 2024) and SWE-bench (Jimenez et al. 2024); bandit/search foundations: Thompson Sampling (Agrawal & Goyal 2012; Chapelle & Li 2011), UCB-Air infinite-armed bandits (Wang et al. 2008), fixed-budget BAI and MCTS/UCT.

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Cited by (Semantic Scholar, ~16 citing papers): Live-SWE-agent (Xia et al., self-evolving SWE agent on the fly), MemEvolve: Meta-Evolution of Agent Memory Systems (Zhang et al.), AEvo / Harnessing Agentic Evolution (Zhang et al.), EvoFSM: Controllable Self-Evolution for Deep Research with Finite State Machines, Evolutionary Ensemble of Agents (EvE), Search over Self-Edit Strategies for LLM Adaptation (Cheong et al.), AutoEnv (Zhang et al.), Pioneer Agent (Atreja et al.), SE-Bench and SWE-EVO (benchmarks for self-evolution / long-horizon software evolution).

- **citation count**: 16 (Semantic Scholar, as of June 2026; 2 highly-influential citations)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> false. HGM does not require or rely on built-in-reflection reasoning models (o1/R1-style); it wraps frozen general LLMs (GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, Qwen3-Coder) in an external code-self-modification + bandit-search scaffold. Reflection/improvement is engineered at the agent-code/search level, not native to the model.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> No on-policy distillation. HGM performs no policy distillation or weight updates; improvements are distilled into evolved agent code/scaffolds via search rather than into model weights. Conceptually adjacent to skill/scaffold optimization (the discovered agent is a reusable skill artifact) and to population-based search, but it is explicitly a non-gradient, LLM-reflection-and-code-update learning mechanism (as characterized for its predecessor SICA).

- **sample efficiency**:

> Reported in number of benchmark task evaluations (and allocated CPU-hours) rather than gradient steps. Self-improving-capability comparison used a budget of 800 evaluations; the full SWE-Verified optimization used 8000 evaluations to reach 61.4%. HGM is substantially more sample/compute efficient than DGM and SICA at fixed budget (2.38x faster than DGM on SWE-Verified-60; 6.86x faster than DGM and 1.65x faster than SICA on Polyglot), attributed to clade-aggregated estimates (more samples per decision), decoupled single-agent-task-pair evaluation with early stopping, and asynchronous parallelism.

# I. Failure analysis & attribution

<a id="r020-why-do-multi-agent-llm-systems-fail-mast"></a>
## Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)

**ID:** R020  **Category:** I (Failure analysis & attribution)  **Authors:** Cemri et al.  **Venue:** arXiv 2025 (UC Berkeley)  **Learning locus:** n/a  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657

### Basic info

- **name**: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Mert Cemri, Melissa Z. Pan, Shuyi Yang, et al. (13 authors incl. Dan Klein, Matei Zaharia, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Ion Stoica); lead affiliation UC Berkeley (with Intesa Sanpaolo).

- **venue**: NeurIPS 2025 (poster); originally arXiv preprint (arXiv:2503.13657, submitted Mar 2025, last revised v3 Oct 2025).

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657

- **code url**:

> Open-sourced: MAST-Data traces/annotations + LLM-as-a-Judge annotator released; MAST usable as a Python library via `pip install agentdash` (GitHub: multi-agent-systems-failure-taxonomy / mast-related repos by the authors).


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> none — this is a failure-analysis/diagnosis work, not a self-correction method. It builds an empirical failure taxonomy (MAST) and an LLM-as-a-Judge annotator; reflection/correction is the object of study, not a mechanism the paper proposes. (One studied failure mode, FM-2.6 / superficial self-reflection-style errors, concerns reasoning-action mismatch in agents.)

- **feedback source**:

> human (expert annotators with kappa=0.88 inter-annotator agreement) for taxonomy construction; LLM-as-a-Judge (GPT-4o-based) for scalable annotation, validated against human ground-truth labels. Diagnostic interventions use task-success-rate (environment/oracle) signals.

- **iteration structure**: single-shot (analysis/taxonomy work). Methodology iterates over traces via Grounded Theory open-coding rounds, but the artifact is a static taxonomy + dataset + judge, not an iterative agent loop.

- **reflection object**:

> n/a as a self-improvement target. As an object of analysis, MAST characterizes failures in the agents' action trajectory, inter-agent communication/coordination, system design/prompt specification, and verification stages of multi-agent LLM systems.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: n/a (failure-analysis / dataset / taxonomy work; no learning signal or weight update in the contribution itself).

- **requires training**: none for the core contribution (taxonomy + dataset + LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline use prompting/in-context judging). Diagnostic interventions are prompt/workflow edits, not training.

- **reward or critic model**: self-as-judge / meta-judge in the analysis sense: an LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline annotates failure modes (94% accuracy, Cohen's kappa 0.77 vs human experts). No trained reward model; ground-truth comes from human annotation.

- **distillation target**:

> none — the reusable artifacts are the MAST taxonomy, the MAST-Data trace dataset, and the LLM annotator, not a distilled reflection/skill/weights. (Closest analogue: a structured rules/taxonomy framework for diagnosing failures.)

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> n/a — the paper does not propose reflective behavior. The failures it catalogs arise in scaffold-engineered MAS (e.g., ChatDev, MetaGPT, AG2); one insight is that some failures (e.g., inter-agent misalignment / 'theory of mind' collapse) are not fixable by scaffolding alone and may require model-level training.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: none (analysis work). The released MAST-Data is a static annotated-trace corpus, not an agent memory module.

- **memory persistence**: n/a (no agent memory mechanism proposed; MAST-Data is a persistent released dataset/resource).

- **memory curation mechanism**: n/a — no memory curation mechanism. Dataset curation used Grounded Theory open coding over traces and theoretical sampling, but this is research methodology, not runtime memory curation.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> agent-level (multi-agent) and step-level: MAST attributes failures to specific failure modes occurring at specific stages/agents within a trace (e.g., a particular agent disobeying role spec, a step repetition, a verification step). The taxonomy spans holistic system-design issues down to step-level coordination/verification errors.

- **intra task vs inter task**: n/a as a learning method. As analysis, it studies failures within individual task traces across many tasks/benchmarks to extract generalizable failure modes.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> n/a — diagnostic, not corrective at runtime. The paper's MAST-guided interventions are post-hoc system-design fixes (e.g., adding a verification step, fixing role specification) applied between runs, i.e., closer to post-hoc-revision / avoidance via redesign rather than mid-trajectory recovery.


### Application domain

- **task domains**: code (software development), math, general agent / tool-use & web tasks (general agentic problem-solving). Spans coding, math problem-solving, and general agent benchmarks.

- **benchmarks**:

> ProgramDev / ProgramDev-v2 (ChatDev, MetaGPT, OpenManus), SWE-Bench Lite (HyperAgent), AppWorld Test-C, GSM-Plus / GSMPlus (AG2 MathChat), OlympiadBench, MMLU, GAIA (Magentic-One). 7 MAS frameworks: ChatDev, MetaGPT, HyperAgent, AppWorld, AG2 (MathChat), Magentic-One, OpenManus.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Built MAST: 14 fine-grained failure modes in 3 categories (System Design, Inter-Agent Misalignment, Task Verification) from analysis of 150 traces with kappa=0.88 inter-annotator agreement; MAST-Data = 1600+ annotated traces across 7 MAS frameworks and 4 model families; LLM-as-a-Judge annotator reaches 94% accuracy / Cohen's kappa 0.77 vs human experts. MAST-guided interventions yield up to +15.6% task-success improvement (e.g., adding a high-level objective-verification step to ChatDev on ProgramDev; +9.4% from fixing CEO role specification) with the same underlying LLM.

- **baselines**:

> Not a method-vs-baseline paper. Comparisons are: human annotation vs LLM-as-a-Judge annotation (agreement); and baseline (unmodified) MAS configurations vs MAST-guided intervention variants. Contrasted conceptually with prior work like the Who&When dataset (Zhang et al.) for failure attribution.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> Intervention case studies on the SAME base LLM: +9.4% overall task success (ChatDev, ensuring the CEO/leader agent has final say / improved role specification), and a maximum +15.6% improvement (ChatDev on ProgramDev, adding a high-level task-objective verification step). The paper stresses these isolated fixes are insufficient and full reliability needs structural MAS redesign.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Annotation cost: LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline replaces expensive human annotation (humans spent many hours per disagreement-resolution round). No inference-multiplier claim for a proposed agent method (there is none). Interventions add an extra verification/role step (modest extra agent calls) but no training cost.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Failures often stem from fundamental system-design and model-level limitations (e.g., 'theory of mind' / social-reasoning gaps in inter-agent misalignment) that scaffolding fixes (e.g., MCP/A2A communication protocols, prompt tweaks) cannot fully resolve; MAST-guided fixes give partial gains only. Failure distributions are illustrative and depend on specific MAS/benchmark/model configurations; LLM-as-a-Judge agreement (kappa 0.77) is lower than human IAA (0.88). Taxonomy/dataset are descriptive, not a solution.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> For diagnosis: relies on human expert labels (oracle ground-truth) to build/validate the taxonomy and the LLM judge. For intervention evaluation: env-reward / task-success-rate (and human-evaluated completion). The LLM-as-a-Judge itself performs intrinsic LLM judgment validated against oracle labels.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent (and a cautionary finding). The paper documents that current MAS self-verification and inter-agent self-correction are often inadequate (FC3 task-verification failures; FM-3.2 no/incomplete verification, FM-3.3 incorrect verification), and that agents frequently fail to detect/correct their own errors; multi-level verification is needed rather than sole reliance on final-stage low-level checks.

- **calibration effect**: not-measured (no calibration / confidence study; out of scope).


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> classifies-failure-mode (taxonomy) AND attributes-responsible-agent / attributes-failing-step: MAST is a 14-mode/3-category taxonomy and the annotation pipeline localizes which failure mode occurs (often tied to a specific agent and stage) within a trace.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Defines/exposes 14 failure modes in 3 categories. FC1 System Design: FM-1.1 disobey task specification (11.8%), FM-1.2 disobey role specification (1.5%), FM-1.3 step repetition (15.7%), FM-1.4 loss of conversation history / context loss (2.8%), FM-1.5 unaware of termination conditions / not recognizing completion (12.4%). FC2 Inter-Agent Misalignment: FM-2.1 conversation reset (2.2%), FM-2.2 fail to ask for clarification / proceed on wrong assumptions (6.8%), FM-2.3 task derailment (7.4%), FM-2.4 information withholding (0.85%), FM-2.5 ignored other agent's input (1.9%), FM-2.6 reasoning-action mismatch (13.2%). FC3 Task Verification: FM-3.1 premature termination (6.2%), FM-3.2 no or incomplete verification (8.2%), FM-3.3 incorrect verification (9.1%). Cross-links to MAST's own canonical 14 modes (this paper IS MAST); relevant to inter-agent misalignment, premature termination, superficial verification/self-reflection, and error-loop (step repetition) modes.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> Yes — MAST-Data: 1600+ annotated traces across 7 MAS frameworks and 4 model families (GPT-4/GPT-4o/GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, CodeLlama-7B); plus MAST-Data-human (inter-annotator study with human labels); the MAST taxonomy itself; and the open-sourced LLM-as-a-Judge annotator pipeline (Python library `agentdash`).


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Grounded Theory / open-coding qualitative methodology (Glaser & Strauss; Khandkar); prior MAS frameworks it analyzes (ChatDev, MetaGPT, AG2/AutoGen MathChat, HyperAgent, AppWorld, Magentic-One, OpenManus); LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm; concurrent failure-attribution work (Zhang et al. 'Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When?' / Who&When dataset).

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Widely cited as the anchor MAS-failure taxonomy. Follow-ups include AgenTracer (Who Is Inducing Failure...), FAMAS (spectrum-based failure attribution), CORRECT (condensed error recognition / knowledge transfer), DoVer (intervention-driven auto debugging), Aegis (automated error generation & attribution), AgentAsk (edge-level error taxonomy + clarification module), SupervisorAgent (runtime supervision), and various MAS-reliability/uncertainty works (e.g., Entropy Judger, HiddenBench collective-reasoning failures).

- **citation count**: 260 (Semantic Scholar, as of June 2026)


### Other / reserved fields

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Not applicable — no distillation/skill-optimization mechanism. Relevant to OPD-style synthesis only indirectly: the paper argues some failures need model-level training (e.g., for inter-agent 'social reasoning'), motivating training-based rather than purely in-context fixes.

- **sample efficiency**: n/a (no iterative trial-to-gain metric). Taxonomy was developed from ~150 traces; full MAST-Data spans 1600+ traces.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- reasoning_model_native
