<a id="r051-agentracer-who-is-inducing-failure-in-the-llm-agentic-systems"></a>
## AgenTracer: Who Is Inducing Failure in the LLM Agentic Systems?

**ID:** R051  **Category:** I (Failure analysis & attribution)  **Authors:** Guibin Zhang et al.  **Venue:** arXiv preprint (2025)  **Learning locus:** gradient_weight_update  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.03312

### Basic info

- **name**: AgenTracer: Who Is Inducing Failure in the LLM Agentic Systems?

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Guibin Zhang, Junhao Wang, Junjie Chen (equal contribution), Wangchunshu Zhou, Kun Wang, Shuicheng Yan. Lead affiliation: National University of Singapore (NUS); also CUHK, OPPO, NTU.

- **venue**: arXiv preprint (2025); also under review (OpenReview submission, id l05DseqvuD)

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.03312

- **code url**: https://github.com/bingreeky/AgenTracer (project page: https://bingreeky.github.io/atracer/)


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**: learned-critic-model

- **feedback source**:

> external-tool/oracle during data construction (counterfactual replay uses an oracle rectification operator with ground-truth solution G and environmental feedback F; programmatic fault injection uses an attacker/perturbation operator); the deployed AgenTracer-8B tracer itself acts as a learned retrospective critic that emits attribution + reasoning feedback to the failing multi-agent system.

- **iteration structure**:

> Data construction: episodic counterfactual replay (sequential per-step oracle rectification with re-simulation until the earliest decisive error is found) plus single-shot programmatic fault injection. Deployment for self-improvement: episodic-retry, iterated for 3 rounds where the tracer's feedback is injected into the next problem-solving episode.

- **reflection object**:

> action trajectory / agent-level credit assignment: AgenTracer reflects on a full multi-agent execution trajectory (logs + environmental feedback) and localizes the decisive error step and the failure-responsible agent; the learning that produces the tracer modifies model weights (QWEN3-8B fine-tuned via RL). The feedback delivered downstream targets the failing agent's action/reasoning for the next episode.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: gradient_weight_update

- **requires training**: RL (online GRPO-style policy optimization with dynamic clipping on QWEN3-8B); the curated TracerTraj-2.5K dataset is built by an oracle-driven annotation pipeline rather than human SFT labels.

- **reward or critic model**:

> verifiable reward / separate retrospective model. Training uses a programmatic multi-granular reward (binary agent-level indicator + Gaussian step-level proximity reward, gated by a strict binary format reward); the resulting AgenTracer-8B is itself a separate trained failure-tracer (retrospective critic) for downstream multi-agent systems.

- **distillation target**: model-weights: the oracle-annotated failure-attribution knowledge (TracerTraj-2.5K) is distilled into the weights of the lightweight AgenTracer-8B tracer via RL.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> engineered: the failure-attribution capability is explicitly trained via a designed multi-granular RL reward over an automatically-annotated dataset, not RL-emergent self-reflection. The tracer does emit a <think>...</think> reasoning trace, but the attribution behavior is deliberately optimized rather than spontaneously emergent.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> none (no persistent memory store for the tracer); it operates over the full provided trajectory log in an 'all-at-once' single-pass setting. The reusable artifact is the released TracerTraj-2.5K dataset, not a runtime memory.

- **memory persistence**: within-episode (the tracer consumes a single trajectory per inference; in the self-improvement loop, feedback is passed cross-episode within the same task across 3 rounds).

- **memory curation mechanism**: n/a (no runtime memory curation; for the training dataset, curation is done by counterfactual-replay annotation selecting the earliest decisive error and a 9:1 train/test split).


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**: step-level and agent-level (multi-agent): AgenTracer outputs both the decisive error step t* and the failure-responsible agent i*, supervised by a multi-granular reward at both granularities.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> inter-task: the tracer is trained on trajectories from six frameworks and six datasets and generalizes to unseen Who&When trajectories; the diagnostic feedback transfers experience across episodes/tasks to improve downstream systems.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> avoidance-only / post-hoc-revision: AgenTracer performs post-hoc failure attribution on a completed failed trajectory, then supplies feedback used to avoid the error in subsequent retry rounds (it does not correct mid-trajectory in-flight).


### Application domain

- **task domains**: code, math (mathematical reasoning), general agentic tasks (tool-use / QA / decision-making); applied to multi-agent system debugging and self-evolution.

- **benchmarks**:

> Who&When (handcraft subset from Magnetic-One and automated subset from AG2); TracerTraj-Code, TracerTraj-Math, TracerTraj-Agentic held-out test sets. Underlying task datasets: MBPP+, KodCode, Blackjack, GAIA, HotpotQA, MATH, GSM8K. Downstream systems boosted: MetaGPT and MaAS (Multi-agent Architecture Search / agentic supernet).


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> AgenTracer-8B outperforms giant proprietary LLMs on Who&When by up to 18.18% (vs Gemini-2.5-Pro) and ~12.21% (vs DeepSeek-R1) in attribution accuracy; on Who&When (handcraft) it reaches 69.10/63.82 agent-level (w/ G / w/o G) and 20.68/20.68 step-level, beating the best baselines (Claude-Sonnet-4 56.90/50.00 agent, 17.24/18.97 step). As actionable feedback it boosts off-the-shelf multi-agent systems (MetaGPT, MaAS) by 4.8-14.2%.

- **baselines**:

> Attribution baselines: DeepSeek-R1, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Sonnet-4, GPT-4.1, Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-Coder, Qwen3-8B (untrained backbone), Llama-3.2-3B. Self-improvement baselines: Self-Refine and CRITIC (both instantiated with GPT-4.1).

- **gains vs baseline**:

> On Who&When vs the strongest comparable reasoning LLMs: +18.18% over Gemini-2.5-Pro and +12.21% over DeepSeek-R1 (headline deltas). Per-table examples: on Who&When (handcraft) agent-level w/ G, AgenTracer 69.10 vs DeepSeek-R1/Claude-Sonnet-4 56.90 (+12.2); on TracerTraj-Math step-level w/o G, AgenTracer 57.63 vs Claude-Sonnet-4 46.03 (+11.6). For downstream self-improvement, AgenTracer-8B feedback yields 4.8-14.2% gains over the failing system and outperforms Self-Refine/CRITIC over 3 iterative rounds.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Tracer is a lightweight 8B model (QWEN3-8B backbone), explicitly positioned as cheaper than calling giant proprietary LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Sonnet-4, DeepSeek-R1) for attribution. Inference uses a single 'all-at-once' pass over the trajectory. Training: RL on the verl platform on one server with 8x NVIDIA H100 (80GB), batch size 32, rollout number 8, learning rate 1e-6. Data construction incurs extra cost from oracle counterfactual replay (per-step re-simulation) and DeepSeek-R1-based analyzer/perturbation. Self-improvement adds ~3 extra rollout rounds per task.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Failure attribution is intrinsically hard: errors are subtle, originate early, and stay hidden behind seemingly correct later outputs. Absolute step-level accuracy remains modest on the hardest sets (e.g. ~20.68% on Who&When handcraft step-level). Providing ground truth G does not consistently help and can mislead attribution. The decisive-error formalization assumes a single earliest pivotal error and an oracle rectification operator, which may not capture compound/interacting failures. Reliance on DeepSeek-R1 as analyzer/perturbation for data generation introduces dependence on a strong external model.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> Training data construction is oracle-dependent (uses ground-truth solution G + environmental feedback F + oracle rectification for counterfactual replay, and known-by-construction labels for fault injection). At deployment, the tracer is evaluated both w/ G (oracle access) and w/o G (no ground truth); the harder, more practical w/o-G setting is emphasized and AgenTracer-8B remains strong there, indicating it does not require oracle labels at inference time.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> net-positive: AgenTracer-8B's feedback delivers consistent 4.8-14.2% downstream gains to MetaGPT/MaAS and beats Self-Refine and CRITIC; attribution remains robust in the w/o-G setting (e.g. maintains 57.63% step-level on TracerTraj-Math while DeepSeek-R1 drops ~9.21% without G), suggesting improvement without label leakage.

- **calibration effect**: not-measured (the paper does not report confidence calibration of the tracer; it focuses on attribution accuracy and downstream task gains).


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> attributes-responsible-agent + attributes-failing-step + counterfactual-localization: AgenTracer identifies both the failure-responsible agent i* and the decisive error step t*, localized via counterfactual replay (oracle rectification with re-simulation to find the earliest step whose correction flips failure to success).

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets the general space of multi-agent system failures characterized by MAST (14 failure patterns ranging from task/role disobedience to reasoning-action mismatches) and the high failure rates (up to 86.7%) reported by the UC Berkeley study; specifically localizes the single decisive error (root cause) within long traces, including early hidden errors that propagate (e.g. a Web-Surfer agent retrieving the wrong file early, only revealed many steps later). Relevant MAST-style modes: improper task decomposition, role disobedience, premature/incorrect intermediate results, error propagation across agents.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> Yes: TracerTraj (TracerTraj-2.5K) released - 2,000+ high-fidelity annotated trajectory-error pairs (Coding 1288, Mathematical Reasoning 630, General Agentic 558; curated trajectories 2170/1185/1300 respectively), spanning six multi-agent frameworks (MetaGPT, AutoGen, Smolagents, AgentPrune, AFlow, OWL-Workforce) and benchmarks (MBPP+, KodCode, Blackjack, MATH, GSM8K, GAIA, HotpotQA). Code and model released at https://github.com/bingreeky/AgenTracer.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Who&When / 'Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When?' (Zhang et al. 2025, arXiv:2505.00212) for the failure-attribution task formulation and benchmark; MAST 'Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?' (Cemri et al. 2025, arXiv:2503.13657) for failure taxonomy and 'all-at-once' evaluation; QWEN3-8B backbone (Yang et al. 2025); DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al. 2025) as analyzer/perturbation model; verl RL training platform; GRPO-style RL; multi-agent frameworks MetaGPT, AutoGen, Smolagents, AgentPrune, AFlow, OWL-Workforce. Conceptually related to Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023) and CRITIC (Gou et al. 2024).

- **citation count**: 48 (Semantic Scholar, as of June 2026); influential citation count 5


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> partial: the tracer is trained from a reasoning model (QWEN3-8B) and emits a <think>...</think> reasoning trace used as feedback, and it is evaluated against reasoning-LLM baselines (o1/R1/Gemini-2.5-Pro/Claude-Sonnet-4). It is not specifically designed to require o1/R1-style built-in reflection; rather it demonstrates that small RL-trained tracers beat large reasoning models at attribution.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Related but distinct: AgenTracer uses online (on-policy) GRPO-style RL with a programmatic verifiable reward rather than distillation from a teacher model. It can be viewed as distilling oracle-derived counterfactual attribution labels into an 8B policy via RL; no explicit on-policy distillation from a teacher is used.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Trained on TracerTraj-2.5K (~2,000+ annotated trajectory-error pairs, 9:1 train/test split) with RL (batch size 32, rollout number 8) on 8x H100; the resulting 8B model outperforms far larger LLMs, indicating strong data/parameter efficiency. Self-improvement loop reaches gains within 3 iterative rounds. Exact gradient-step count not reported.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- extended_by_or_inspired

<a id="r052-mas-fire-fault-injection-and-reliability-evaluation-for-llm-based-multi-agent-systems"></a>
## MAS-FIRE: Fault Injection and Reliability Evaluation for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems

**ID:** R052  **Category:** I (Failure analysis & attribution)  **Authors:** Jin Jia et al.  **Venue:** arXiv preprint (Feb 2026)  **Learning locus:** n/a  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19843

### Basic info

- **name**: MAS-FIRE: Fault Injection and Reliability Evaluation for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems

- **year**: 2026

- **authors**: Jin Jia, Zhiling Deng, Zhuangbin Chen (corresponding), Yingqi Wang, Zibin Zheng — Sun Yat-sen University, Zhuhai, Guangdong, China

- **venue**: arXiv preprint (cs.SE / cs.AI); BibTeX lists it as @inproceedings, but no peer-reviewed venue confirmed as of mid-2026

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19843

- **code url**: https://github.com/wxhhxn/MASFIRE (experimental data and fault-injection artifacts)


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> none (this is a failure-analysis / fault-injection evaluation framework, not a reflection method). It does, however, empirically characterize the self-correction / fault-tolerant behaviors of existing MAS, including iterative critique-refine loops (Table-Critic) and reasoning-level self-detection of semantic faults.

- **feedback source**:

> n/a for the framework itself (it injects faults rather than learning from them). The MAS it evaluates use mixed feedback sources: environment error feedback / automatic retry (tool errors), critic-agent judge signals (Table-Critic), and shared-context retrieval (MetaGPT message pool). Ground truth is used only for scoring task success (HumanEval, WikiTQ, WebShop).

- **iteration structure**:

> n/a for the framework (single-pass fault injection per task, single-trial Pass@1 evaluation). The evaluated MAS span single-shot linear pipelines (MetaGPT, Camel) and iterative-refine closed loops (Table-Critic critic-refiner).

- **reflection object**:

> n/a — the paper does not modify a reflection target. What MAS-FIRE manipulates (to expose fault tolerance) is: prompts/context (system + user prompts), agent runtime outputs (reasoning chains, planning outputs, tool calls), and message routing. The fault-tolerant behaviors it observes act on action trajectory, reasoning chain, and inter-agent messages.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: n/a (analysis/evaluation framework — no learning signal; no weight update and no in-context experience accumulation in the framework itself)

- **requires training**: none (no training; the framework runs and perturbs off-the-shelf MAS with GPT-5 and DeepSeek-V3 backbones; GPT-5-mini is used as a semantic-fault injector and GPT-5 as an LLM-as-a-judge annotator, neither is fine-tuned)

- **reward or critic model**:

> none for the framework. Evaluation uses an LLM-as-a-judge (GPT-5) to label fault-tolerant behaviors in execution logs, validated against human annotation at Cohen's Kappa = 0.94. Task success is scored against ground-truth benchmark answers.

- **distillation target**:

> none (no reusable learned artifact is distilled). The reusable outputs are conceptual: a 15-type fault taxonomy, a four-tier fault-tolerance behavioral taxonomy, and process-level robustness metrics (RS, Occurrence, Local Success, Success).

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> n/a — neither. MAS-FIRE engineers fault injectors (scaffold-engineered perturbations via prompt modification, response rewriting, message routing) and then observes whether the target MAS's fault tolerance is architecture/rule-engineered (mechanism/rule tiers) or model-reasoning-driven (prompt/reasoning tiers). It explicitly decouples engineered structural resilience from emergent model-reasoning resilience.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> n/a for the framework. Among evaluated systems: MetaGPT uses a shared message pool (long-term, globally accessible scratchpad/context) that the paper finds buffers Memory Faults; Camel uses sequential bilateral dialogue (short-term context only); Table-Critic uses an iterative critique loop.

- **memory persistence**: n/a (no cross-episode memory in the framework). Evaluated MAS persist context within-episode (within a task run); MetaGPT's shared message pool keeps globally accessible context across agents within a task.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> n/a for the framework. The paper notes MetaGPT performs rule-based message deduplication / role-based subscription filtering (retrieval-gated / rule-filtered context), and that aggressive context compression (a 'Context Length Violation' fault) is itself an injected failure mode.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> Multi-granularity by design: agent-level (multi-agent; intra-agent vs inter-agent fault split), step-level (faults injected at specific execution points — planning output, tool call, message), and response-level (response rewriting). Diagnosis is process-level via the (Occurrence, Local-Success, Success) triplet plus a four-tier (mechanism/rule/prompt/reasoning) attribution of where resilience originates.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> intra-task (faults are injected and recovery is observed within a single task run; single-trial Pass@1). No cross-task experience transfer is studied. 'Intra-agent vs inter-agent' in the paper refers to fault location, not learning transfer.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> Studies mid-trajectory recovery (in-flight): the framework measures whether MAS detect injected faults and correct them during execution (e.g., automatic retry on tool errors, Table-Critic's closed-loop critique-refinement, downstream agents compensating). Local Success Rate (L_f) vs Success Rate (S_f) explicitly captures whether in-flight recovery translates to end-to-end success.


### Application domain

- **task domains**: code generation (MetaGPT), table QA / multi-step table reasoning (Table-Critic), web navigation / decision-making in simulated e-commerce (Camel); broadly software-engineering reliability of LLM multi-agent systems

- **benchmarks**: HumanEval (164 tasks, MetaGPT code gen); WikiTableQuestions / WikiTQ (400 sampled from 4,344, Table-Critic); WebShop (251 tasks, AgentBoard-annotated version, Camel)


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Iterative, closed-loop topologies neutralize over 40% of faults that cause catastrophic collapse in linear workflows. Concretely, for Planning Faults Table-Critic's critique loop keeps RS > 89% while MetaGPT's linear pipeline drops to 43.84% (Delta RS ~ +45%); for Memory/Critical-Info-Loss faults MetaGPT's shared message pool keeps RS > 90% vs Camel's ~67% (Delta RS ~ +25%). Configuration/Instruction faults collapse linear MAS to RS as low as 0.0%.

- **baselines**:

> Compared across three representative MAS architectures (MetaGPT hierarchical/linear pipeline; Table-Critic iterative critic-refiner closed loop; Camel bilateral role-play) and two foundation models (GPT-5 vs DeepSeek-V3). Fault-free baseline success rates: MetaGPT 99.0%/89.0%, Table-Critic 87.0%/78.3%, Camel 37.8%/33.0% (GPT-5/DeepSeek-V3). No prior fault-injection framework baseline; positioned against outcome-only evaluation (AgentBench, AgentBoard, AppWorld, ScienceAgentBench, OpenJudge) and prior injection work (AutoInject).

- **gains vs baseline**:

> Architectural deltas (vs strongest comparable architecture under same fault): iterative critique loop +~45% RS over linear pipeline on Planning Faults; shared message pool +~25% RS on Critical Information Loss; +~17% average RS for stronger model (GPT-5) on semantic faults with shared-pool architectures (Hallucination +22.05%: 45.34% vs 23.29%; Inexecutable Plan +12.06%: 55.90% vs 43.84%). Counterintuitive reversal: under Blind Trust, weaker DeepSeek-V3 beats GPT-5 by 64.29% (70.61% vs 6.32%) because GPT-5's strict instruction-following obeys the corrupted directive.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Single-trial (Pass@1) evaluation despite non-deterministic agents (no variance/repeated-run reporting); only three MAS and two backbone models; Communication Faults injectable only into MetaGPT (others lack a communication module); some tool-faults inapplicable to tasks without tool calls; ~1% injection failures re-executed; fault-tolerant behavior taxonomy derived via Grounded Theory by the authors (potential subjectivity, mitigated by kappa=0.94 LLM-judge agreement); WikiTQ sub-sampled to 400 of 4,344. Findings are correlational/diagnostic, not a remediation method.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> For the framework: ground-truth-oracle is used to score whether tasks remain successful (RS), and an LLM-judge (with human-validated labels) to attribute behaviors. The fault-tolerance the framework observes in MAS spans intrinsic self-verify (reasoning-level), external-tool/verifier (environment retry, critic agent), and rule-based filters; the key finding is that semantically-valid-but-incorrect faults bypass mechanism/rule filters and rely solely on model reasoning (Reasoning-Level FT, O_f = 100%).

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent and architecture-dependent. Mechanism/rule-tier defenses give near-certain recovery for structural faults (Communication Faults RS > 93%, tool-format L_f = 100%). Reasoning-tier self-correction is the sole defense for semantic faults but has low detection in linear pipelines. Crucially, stronger instruction-following can be net-negative: under Blind Trust, GPT-5's compliance collapses RS to 6.32% while non-compliant DeepSeek-V3 recovers to 70.61% (correction degrades with model strength when recovery requires disobeying a corrupted directive).

- **calibration effect**:

> not-measured (the paper does not study probabilistic calibration / confidence). It does document an analogous 'reasoning tax'-style failure: superior models' strict instruction adherence makes them MORE vulnerable to prompt-level corruption (Blind Trust), an over-compliance liability rather than a calibration metric.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> classifies-failure-mode (15-type fault taxonomy across 7 categories: intra-agent Planning/Memory/Reasoning/Action; inter-agent Configuration/Instruction/Communication) AND attributes-failing-step / source-of-resilience via the four-tier (mechanism/rule/prompt/reasoning) fault-tolerance attribution, plus attributes-responsible-agent through intra- vs inter-agent localization and process-level (O_f, L_f, S_f) diagnosis. It does not perform counterfactual localization of an organic failure (faults are injected, not attributed post-hoc to an unknown cause).

- **failure mode addressed**:

> 15 injected fault types: Role Ambiguity, Blind Trust (Configuration); Instruction Logic Conflict, Instruction Ambiguity (Instruction); Inexecutable Plan, Critical Information Loss (Planning); Memory Loss, Context Length Violation (Memory); Hallucination (Reasoning); Tool Selection Error, Parameter Filling Error, Parameter Format Error (Action); Message Cycle, Message Storm, Message Broadcast Amplification (Communication). Cross-links to MAST-style modes: inter-agent misalignment (Blind Trust, Role Ambiguity), information withholding / context loss (Critical Info Loss, Memory Loss), reasoning drift / hallucination, error loops / no termination (Message Cycle), and superficial self-reflection (Judge accepts erroneous reasoning ~93.68% of failed Blind-Trust cases).

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> Yes — experimental data and fault-injection artifacts released at https://github.com/wxhhxn/MASFIRE (execution-log corpus spanning 15 fault types x 3 MAS architectures x 2 foundation models, with the fault taxonomy, behavior definitions, and metrics). Not a fixed held-out benchmark like Who&When; it is a reusable injection framework + log corpus.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Fault injection / chaos engineering and mutation testing (Meiklejohn ServiceLevel FI, MicroFI, IntelliFT); MAS failure studies (Cemri et al. 'Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail?' / MAST; AutoInject — Huang et al. 'On the Resilience of LLM-Based Multi-Agent Collaboration with Faulty Agents', ICML 2025; TRAIL); the evaluated MAS frameworks themselves (MetaGPT, Table-Critic, CAMEL); outcome-oriented MAS evaluation (AgentBench, AgentBoard, AppWorld, ScienceAgentBench, OpenJudge); LLM self-correction limits (Huang et al. 'LLMs cannot self-correct reasoning yet').

- **citation count**: 0 (Semantic Scholar Corpus ID 285973197 shows 62 outbound references and no indexed inbound citations; very recent preprint, Feb 2026)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> Partially relevant: GPT-5 is one of the two evaluated backbones and the paper's most distinctive finding concerns strong, instruction-following ('reasoning-capable') models being MORE fragile under prompt corruption (Blind Trust). However, the framework is model-agnostic and not specifically designed for o1/R1-style built-in reflection.

- **on policy distillation link**: n/a — no distillation or on-policy skill optimization; this is an evaluation/diagnostic framework, not a training method.

- **sample efficiency**: n/a (no learning iterations). Evaluation scale: single-trial Pass@1 over 164 (HumanEval) + 400 (WikiTQ sampled) + 251 (WebShop) tasks x 15 fault types x 3 MAS x 2 models; ~99% injection success rate.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- compute_cost_profile
- extended_by_or_inspired

<a id="r072-which-agent-causes-task-failures-and-when-on-automated-failure-attribution-of-llm-multi-agent-systems"></a>
## Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? On Automated Failure Attribution of LLM Multi-Agent Systems

**ID:** R072  **Category:** I (Failure analysis & attribution)  **Authors:** Shaokun Zhang et al.  **Venue:** ICML 2025 (Spotlight)  **Learning locus:** hybrid  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00212

### Basic info

- **name**: Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? On Automated Failure Attribution of LLM Multi-Agent Systems

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**:

> Shaokun Zhang, Ming Yin, Jieyu Zhang, Jiale Liu, Zhiguang Han, Jingyang Zhang, Beibin Li, Chi Wang, Huazheng Wang, Yiran Chen, Qingyun Wu (lead affiliations: Pennsylvania State University; co-authors from University of Washington, Duke University, Microsoft Research / AG2, Oregon State University)

- **venue**: ICML 2025 (Forty-second International Conference on Machine Learning), Spotlight; also arXiv:2505.00212

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00212

- **code url**: https://github.com/ag2ai/Agents_Failure_Attribution (dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Kevin355/Who_and_When)


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> learned-critic-model | multi-agent-debate (LLM-as-judge for failure attribution). The work uses LLM-as-judge methods that critique a completed multi-agent failure trace to attribute the responsible agent and decisive error step; it is an analysis/benchmark of attribution (a form of post-hoc self-reflection / critic) rather than an in-loop self-correction method.

- **feedback source**:

> self-generated (LLM judge reasoning over the failure log) plus an optional ground-truth-oracle signal: experiments are run under a 'With Ground Truth' setting (final query answer available to the judge) and a 'Without Ground Truth' setting; human expert annotations provide the evaluation ground truth.

- **iteration structure**:

> single-shot (All-at-Once: judge sees full log once) and iterative (Step-by-Step: incremental step-wise judging until first error; Binary Search: halving the log iteratively to localize the step). A Hybrid method runs All-at-Once then Step-by-Step sequentially.

- **reflection object**:

> action trajectory / conversation log of an LLM multi-agent system. The methods reflect on a completed multi-agent failure log to localize (1) the failure-responsible agent and (2) the decisive error step; nothing in the multi-agent system's content, prompts, weights, or skills is modified by the attribution itself.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: hybrid

- **requires training**:

> none for the three evaluated attribution methods (all are prompting-based LLM-as-judge with frozen models, GPT-4o primary; open models Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B/72B-Instruct are also used as judges without fine-tuning in the main experiments). The released repo/benchmark is positioned to support future training (e.g., reward models / fine-tuned attributors), but the paper itself reports no weight updates.

- **reward or critic model**:

> self-as-judge (an LLM is the attribution critic). No trained reward model is used; the work explicitly notes that the resulting decisive-error signal could later serve as a reward for RL or as feedback for agent self-improvement, and contrasts with process reward models (Math-Shepherd, ProcessBench) which target single-LLM reasoning rather than multi-agent attribution.

- **distillation target**:

> none. The reflection (failure attribution) is not distilled into a reusable artifact within the paper; the reusable output is the Who&When benchmark and the attribution method recipes, not a learned skill/memory/weight artifact.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> prompt/scaffold-engineered. The three attribution strategies (All-at-Once, Step-by-Step, Binary Search) and the Hybrid combination are hand-designed prompting scaffolds; the paper finds that engineering a reasoning mechanism into the prompt helps more than swapping to RL-emergent reasoning models (o1/R1).


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: none (the attribution methods are stateless judges over a single failure log per instance; no persistent memory/skill library is built). The Who&When dataset itself is a static corpus of annotated failure logs.

- **memory persistence**: within-episode (judgment is performed per failure log / per task instance; no cross-episode or cross-session memory is maintained by the methods).

- **memory curation mechanism**: n/a


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> agent-level (multi-agent) and step-level. The task is defined as jointly identifying the failure-responsible agent (Who) and the decisive error step (When); evaluation uses Agent-Level Accuracy, Step-Level Accuracy, and Step-Level Accuracy with Tolerance (+/-1 to +/-5 steps).

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> intra-task analysis at the single-data-instance level (localize the failure within one task's trace). The paper also notes the three methods are more effective at extracting statistical (dataset-level) conclusions than precise single-instance attribution, but it does not transfer learned experience across tasks.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> post-hoc-revision / diagnosis. Attribution is performed after the multi-agent system has already failed; it produces a debugging signal rather than recovering mid-trajectory or avoiding future failures within the studied pipeline.


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> general agentic problem-solving / multi-agent systems debugging; underlying queries are real-world web/tool-use and reasoning tasks (web navigation, file handling, information seeking, QA/reasoning) drawn from GAIA and AssistantBench.

- **benchmarks**:

> Who&When (the introduced benchmark: 127 LLM multi-agent systems, 184 annotated failure tasks; Algorithm-Generated subset via CaptainAgent/AG2 and Hand-Crafted subset via Magnetic-One). Source queries: GAIA and AssistantBench. Related/contrast benchmarks discussed: ProcessBench, DevAI.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> On Who&When, the best automated failure-attribution method reaches 53.5% accuracy at identifying the failure-responsible agent (All-at-Once, averaged across the with/without-ground-truth settings) but only 14.2% accuracy at pinpointing the decisive failure step (Step-by-Step); some methods (e.g., All-at-Once on step-level) fall below the random baseline. SOTA reasoning models (OpenAI o1, DeepSeek R1) do not reach practical usability.

- **baselines**:

> Random baseline (Agent-Level 29.10% algorithm-generated / 12.00% hand-crafted; Step-Level 19.06% / 4.16%); the three attribution methods compared against each other (All-at-Once vs Step-by-Step vs Binary Search) and against a Hybrid combination; judge-model ablations across GPT-4o, GPT-4, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B/72B-Instruct, and reasoning models OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek R1.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> All-at-Once beats Step-by-Step on agent-level accuracy by ~19.13% and ~20.69% (with ground truth) and ~25.1% and ~20.69% (without ground truth); all three methods exceed the random baseline on agent-level accuracy, confirming the task is nontrivial. Conversely on step-level accuracy Step-by-Step is best (top in 3 of 4 cases) while All-at-Once can fall below random. The Hybrid (Step-by-Step & All-at-Once) achieves the best of both: 57.02% agent-level and 12.28% step-level on hand-crafted systems, vs Binary Search 43.97%/6.90%, All-at-Once 57.02%/4.39%, Step-by-Step 35.96%/7.90%. Providing ground truth improves all methods on all metrics over the no-ground-truth setting.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Inference-only (no training). Token cost varies sharply by method on hand-crafted systems: All-at-Once ~17,106 tokens (cheapest, single pass), Binary Search ~34,659 tokens, Step-by-Step ~87,720 tokens, and the Hybrid method ~149,177 tokens (highest, since it runs two algorithms sequentially). Whole-dataset evaluation across many models was limited to hand-crafted systems due to high token/compute cost.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> (1) Even the best method is far from practically usable, especially at step-level (best ~14.2%, near 0% when logs are longest). (2) Performance degrades sharply as failure-log/context length increases (Levels 1-5: 5-17 up to 93-130 steps), converging toward 0% at the maximum length due to a long-context 'space-in-the-needle' retrieval problem. (3) Methods trade off: large-receptive-field (All-at-Once) is good for Who but bad for When; incremental (Step-by-Step) is the reverse. (4) Stronger reasoning models (o1, R1) do not reliably beat GPT-4o (R1 underperforms GPT-4o in 3 of 4 cases). (5) The formulation assumes a single deterministic failure-responsible agent and one decisive error step, which later work (e.g., 'Rethinking Failure Attribution', 2026) critiques as too rigid and not capturing cascading/multi-cause failures or attribution reasoning. (6) Study is single-data-instance level; dataset-level statistical attribution is more reliable than per-instance.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> task-dependent on oracle access: in the 'With Ground Truth' setting the final query answer (a partial oracle) is available and measurably boosts all methods on all metrics; in the 'Without Ground Truth' setting only the running log is used (intrinsic self-verify), and accuracy drops. The headline 53.5%/14.2% numbers are averaged over both settings, so the method is not purely intrinsic.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent / requires-oracle. As a debugging signal the methods are net-positive over random for agent identification, but for step localization the strongest single method (All-at-Once) can be net-negative (below random); reliable use benefits from ground-truth labels and from combining methods (Hybrid). The paper frames attribution as a feedback signal for downstream self-improvement rather than demonstrating closed-loop self-correction gains.

- **calibration effect**: not-measured (the paper reports accuracy of attribution, not confidence calibration of the judged systems).


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> attributes-responsible-agent and attributes-failing-step. The work formalizes joint Who (failure-responsible agent) and When (decisive error step) attribution over LLM multi-agent traces, with a causal/counterfactual notion of the 'decisive error' step that, if corrected, would change the outcome.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets localization of the single decisive error in multi-agent cooperation that causes system-level task failure (the agent and step whose error propagates to failure). It exposes attribution-side failure modes such as long-context retrieval failure ('space-in-the-needle'), inability to localize within long traces, and the difficulty of disambiguating multiple erring agents. It is complementary to MAST-style taxonomies (Cemri et al. 2025) but does not itself classify the 14 MAST failure modes; it provides agent/step localization rather than a failure-mode taxonomy.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> Yes. Who&When benchmark: failure logs from 127 LLM multi-agent systems with 184 fine-grained annotated failure tasks (each labeled with failure-responsible agent, decisive error step, and a natural-language explanation), split into Algorithm-Generated (CaptainAgent/AG2) and Hand-Crafted (Magnetic-One) subsets, built on GAIA and AssistantBench queries. Released on GitHub (ag2ai/Agents_Failure_Attribution) and Hugging Face (Kevin355/Who_and_When), MIT-licensed.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> CaptainAgent / AG2 (AutoGen) for algorithm-generated systems (Song et al. 2024); Magnetic-One generalist multi-agent system (Fourney et al. 2024); GAIA (Mialon et al. 2023) and AssistantBench (Yoran et al. 2024) for source queries; LLM-as-judge / LLM-as-evaluator line (Zhuge et al. 2024 DevAI; van Schaik & Pugh 2024); Reflexion-style self-reflection (Shinn et al. 2024); process reward / step-error-localization work (Math-Shepherd Wang et al. 2023; ProcessBench; Lightman et al. 2023).

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Subsequent automated failure-attribution work that adopts or critiques the Who&When formulation, e.g., 'Rethinking Failure Attribution in Multi-Agent Systems: A Multi-Perspective Benchmark and Evaluation' (2026, arXiv:2603.25001), 'Intention-behavior consistency-based automated failure attribution for LLM-driven multi-agent systems' (ScienceDirect 2026), and follow-ups by Zhang et al. 2025a/b, Kong et al. 2025, Ma et al. 2025, and West et al. 2025; complements MAST (Cemri et al. 2025).

- **citation count**: 90 (Semantic Scholar, as of June 2026; 22 influential citations)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> Partially evaluated, not native. The method is model-agnostic prompting; the paper explicitly tests reasoning models OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek R1 as judges and finds they do NOT reliably outperform GPT-4o (R1 underperforms GPT-4o in 3 of 4 cases; o1 not consistently better), concluding that built-in reasoning models alone do not solve failure attribution.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Not a training method, so no trials-to-gain measure; cost is per-instance inference. Token-cost ranking per hand-crafted instance: All-at-Once ~17.1K (1 pass), Binary Search ~34.7K, Step-by-Step ~87.7K, Hybrid ~149.2K tokens.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- on_policy_distillation_link

# J. Surveys & roadmaps

<a id="r022-when-can-llms-actually-correct-their-own-mistakes-a-critical-survey-of-self-correction-of-llms"></a>
## When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs

**ID:** R022  **Category:** J (Surveys & roadmaps)  **Authors:** Kamoi et al.  **Venue:** TACL 2024  **Learning locus:** n/a  **URL:** https://aclanthology.org/2024.tacl-1.78/

### Basic info

- **name**: When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs

- **year**: 2024

- **authors**: Ryo Kamoi, Yusen Zhang, Nan Zhang, Jiawei Han, Rui Zhang (Penn State University; University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign). First author Ryo Kamoi et al.

- **venue**: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics (TACL), Volume 12, pp. 1417-1440, MIT Press, 2024 (arXiv 2406.01297, June 2024)

- **paper url**: https://aclanthology.org/2024.tacl-1.78/ (arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01297 ; DOI: 10.1162/tacl_a_00713)

- **code url**: No executable code (this is a survey). Author maintains a companion paper list: https://github.com/ryokamoi/llm-self-correction-papers


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> none (analysis/survey). The survey itself proposes no new method; it categorizes and critically analyzes verbal-self-critique (intrinsic self-correction), tool-verified self-correction, and fine-tuned/learned-critic self-correction across the surveyed literature.

- **feedback source**:

> n/a as a method. As an analysis, it categorizes feedback sources used by surveyed work: self-generated (prompted LLM self-evaluation), external-tool (code interpreter, search engine, proof assistant, Wikipedia API), ground-truth-oracle (unrealistic settings), human assessment, and fine-tuned feedback/critic models. Its central finding is that the feedback-generation stage is the bottleneck.

- **iteration structure**: n/a (survey). It frames self-correction as a 3-stage pipeline (initial response generation -> feedback -> refinement), typically iterative-refine in the surveyed methods, but proposes no iteration scheme of its own.

- **reflection object**:

> Survey analysis, not a method. The object of self-correction in the surveyed literature is the LLM's output content / response (e.g., refining a generated answer, code, or text), optionally via reflecting on the reasoning chain. The survey's own 'object' is the research-question taxonomy and experimental methodology of the self-correction field, plus model weights when discussing fine-tuning-based self-correction.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**:

> n/a (analysis/survey). The survey spans both in_context_verbal (intrinsic/prompted self-correction) and gradient_weight_update (fine-tuning-enabled self-correction) paradigms; it concludes intrinsic in-context self-correction is unreliable in general tasks while large-scale fine-tuning enables self-correction.

- **requires training**:

> n/a (survey). It analyzes methods spanning none (prompted intrinsic), SFT (large-scale fine-tuning on reference feedback, e.g., SelFee, Self-Critique, Baldur), RL (RL4F, and emerging o1-style RL post-survey), and cross-model critic training (REFINER, RL4F). Key finding: large-scale fine-tuning enables self-correction.

- **reward or critic model**:

> n/a (survey). Categorizes the improvement signals used by surveyed work: self-as-judge (prompted LLM, found unreliable), trained reward/critic model (cross-model: REFINER T5, RL4F T5, Self-Correction GPT-Neo), verifiable reward / reliable external feedback (code interpreter, proof assistant), and unrealistic ground-truth oracle.

- **distillation target**:

> n/a as a method. In the surveyed fine-tuning line, reflection/feedback is distilled into model-weights (large-scale fine-tuning on reference feedback); the survey identifies this as the main reliable route besides external tools.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> Survey covers both. It primarily analyzes prompt/scaffold-engineered self-correction (e.g., Self-Refine, Reflexion, RCI, CRITIC) and finds it unreliable; in Section 12 it notes the emerging RL-trained/emergent reflection trend (OpenAI o1, Kumar et al. 2024, Qu et al. 2024) as a promising post-survey direction.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**: n/a (survey). Surveyed intrinsic methods mostly use short-term/scratchpad-style within-pass refinement; some (e.g., Reflexion) use episodic memory of past attempts, but the survey itself proposes no memory mechanism.

- **memory persistence**: n/a (survey). Surveyed methods range from within-episode refinement to cross-episode retry memory (Reflexion); not a property of the survey itself.

- **memory curation mechanism**: n/a (survey).


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> Survey analysis. It discusses self-correction mostly at the response/outcome level, and highlights that decomposable responses (where verification can be done per-component / step-level) are exceptionally suited to self-correction; recognizing errors is only easier than generating answers for tasks whose verification is exceptionally easy.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> Primarily intra-task: the survey defines self-correction as inference-time refinement of a response within a single task (initial response -> feedback -> refinement). It explicitly scopes out broader self-training/self-improvement that transfers across tasks (Section 9 distinguishes it from Pan et al. 2024).

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**: post-hoc-revision. The survey's notion of self-correction is post-hoc refinement of an initial response (mid-inference), not mid-trajectory recovery or next-episode avoidance.


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> Survey spans: reasoning/math, code, closed-book knowledge QA, open-book/context-based QA, open-ended text generation (dialogue, summarization, detoxification), decision-making/planning (computer tasks, games), and general alignment. Findings differ by domain: external-tool tasks (code) work well; general reasoning/knowledge intrinsic self-correction does not.

- **benchmarks**:

> Aggregated across surveyed papers: GSM8K, SVAMP, MATH-style math reasoning, HumanEval/MBPP-style and text-to-code coding, HotpotQA, CommonsenseQA (CSQA), Natural Questions (NQ), Strategy/SQA, QReCC, MiniWoB++/computer tasks, ALFWorld-style game environments, MT-Bench, topic-based summarization, detoxification (RealToxicityPrompts-style), proof generation (Baldur). No single benchmark is the survey's own.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Three headline conclusions (qualitative meta-findings, not a single number): (1) no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except in tasks exceptionally suited for it; (2) self-correction works well in tasks with reliable external feedback (e.g., code via interpreters); (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables self-correction. The bottleneck is feedback generation, not refinement.

- **baselines**:

> Methodological critique: the survey argues many self-correction studies are not compared against sufficiently strong baselines (RQ3). It re-categorizes prior frameworks as Realistic (Fair / Unfair) vs Unrealistic (oracle), exposing over-evaluation. It compares against negative-results papers (Huang et al. 2024a 'LLMs cannot self-correct reasoning yet'; CRITIC-without-tool; RCI without oracle).

- **gains vs baseline**:

> No own quantitative delta (survey). Its comparative finding: intrinsic prompted self-correction shows no reliable net gain over best-possible initial responses in general tasks; reported gains in prior work often stem from weak initial-response prompts (unfair) or oracle stopping/feedback (unrealistic), which over-evaluate self-correction.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Survey notes self-correction adds inference-time cost (extra generation + feedback + refinement passes, i.e., a multiplier over single-pass generation) and that fine-tuning-based self-correction requires large-scale human-annotated training data; it argues this cost is often not justified versus stronger single-pass baselines (RQ3 under-examined).


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> (1) LLMs struggle to generate reliable feedback on their own responses via in-context learning (feedback-generation bottleneck). (2) Many prior studies do not define research questions precisely (conflate RQ1/RQ2/RQ3). (3) Common over-evaluation via oracle information (ground-truth stop/feedback = unrealistic) and weak initial-response prompts (unfair). (4) Survey scope: inference-time self-correction only, primarily papers up to May 2024; cross-model setups cannot test RQ1/RQ2.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> THE central thesis: self-correction's success is determined by the feedback source. intrinsic-only (prompted self-verify) generally fails in general tasks; external-tool/verifier (reliable feedback, e.g., code interpreter, proof assistant, search-derived info) works; oracle-label/ground-truth settings are unrealistic and over-evaluate; fine-tuned feedback (env/reward-trained) works at scale. Reliable external feedback or large-scale fine-tuning is required.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent / requires-oracle-or-external-feedback. Net-positive only when (a) the task is exceptionally suited (decomposable / verification much easier than generation), (b) reliable external feedback is available, or (c) large-scale fine-tuning is used. Intrinsic prompted self-correction is not shown to be net-positive in general tasks without label leakage.

- **calibration effect**:

> not-measured (survey predates the reasoning-model 'reasoning tax' framing). It documents that prompted LLMs frequently fail to detect their own mistakes (poor self-verification), implying weak self-assessment, but does not quantify a calibration/overconfidence effect.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> classifies-failure-mode (taxonomy). It provides a taxonomy of self-correction research questions (RQ1/RQ2/RQ3) and frameworks (Realistic: Fair/Unfair vs Unrealistic/oracle), and catalogs failure/over-evaluation modes in prior work (oracle stopping, oracle feedback, weak initial-response prompts, insufficient baselines, conflated RQs).

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets methodological/evaluation failure modes of the self-correction literature: superficial/unreliable self-reflection (LLMs cannot generate good feedback on their own outputs), over-evaluation via oracle information, unfair weak initial-response prompts, conflation of distinct research questions, and missing strong baselines. It exposes 'self-correction does not actually work intrinsically' as the core illusory result.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new dataset/benchmark. Releases a checklist for designing appropriate self-correction experiments (Section 8) and a companion curated paper list (github.com/ryokamoi/llm-self-correction-papers) as reusable community resources.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Motivated by negative-results analyses, esp. Huang et al. 2024a 'Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet' (ICLR 2024). Complements Pan et al. 2024 survey on self-correction (broader, includes training). Surveys foundational methods: Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023), Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023), RCI (Kim et al. 2023), CRITIC (Gou et al. 2024), Constitutional AI (Bai et al. 2022), Self-Debug, RARR, SelFee, Baldur, REFINER, RL4F, Self-Correction (Welleck et al. 2023).

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Frequently cited as the authoritative critical reference on when LLM self-correction works; cited by subsequent self-correction / self-verification analyses (e.g., 'Understanding the Dark Side of LLMs' Intrinsic Self-Correction') and by RL-trained self-correction work (SCoRe/Kumar et al. 2024, Qu et al. 2024) and o1-style reasoning-model discussions. The same group's 'Evaluating LLMs at Detecting Errors in LLM Responses' (COLM 2024) is a closely related follow-up.

- **citation count**: 288 (Google Scholar, as of 2026-06; confirmed via Ryo Kamoi's verified Scholar profile)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> Partially. The survey predates wide reasoning-model deployment but Section 12 explicitly discusses OpenAI o1 (RL-trained to recognize and refine its own mistakes) and RL-based self-correction (Kumar et al. 2024, Qu et al. 2024) as the emerging trend; it does not yet hold conclusions specific to o1/R1-class models, noting they are not comprehensively analyzed.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Indirect. The survey's finding that large-scale fine-tuning (SFT on reference feedback) and RL/self-corrective learning (Welleck et al. 2023) are the reliable routes to self-correction connects to distilling correction ability into weights; it does not discuss on-policy distillation by name.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Not applicable as a single number (survey). It notes fine-tuning-based self-correction typically relies on large training data / large-scale human annotation and flags self-correction with small training data as an unexplored, sample-efficiency-relevant future direction.

<a id="r056-a-survey-on-self-evolution-of-large-language-models"></a>
## A Survey on Self-Evolution of Large Language Models

**ID:** R056  **Category:** J (Surveys & roadmaps)  **Authors:** Zhengwei Tao et al.  **Venue:** arXiv preprint (Alibaba Group + Peking University + NTU)  **Learning locus:** hybrid  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.14387

### Basic info

- **name**: A Survey on Self-Evolution of Large Language Models

- **year**: 2024

- **authors**:

> Zhengwei Tao, Ting-En Lin, Xiancai Chen, Hangyu Li, Yuchuan Wu, Yongbin Li, Zhi Jin, Fei Huang, Dacheng Tao, Jingren Zhou et al. — lead affiliations: Peking University (Key Lab of HCST, School of Computer Science), Alibaba Group (Tongyi Lab / Conversation AI), and Nanyang Technological University. Work done while Zhengwei Tao was interning at Alibaba.

- **venue**: arXiv preprint (cs.CL / cs.AI); not peer-reviewed at time of writing (v1 22 Apr 2024, v2 3 Jun 2024)

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.14387

- **code url**: https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI/tree/main/Awesome-Self-Evolution-of-LLM (curated reading list / awesome-list of self-evolution papers; no single method implementation)


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> survey/none (this is an analysis paper, not a method). It taxonomizes reflection-bearing approaches it reviews, spanning verbal-self-critique (Self-Refine, Reflexion, RCI, CRITIC), critique-free correction (STaR, Self-Debugging), learned/self-reward critics (Self-Reward, SIRLC, DLMA), tool/environment-verified feedback (Self-Debugging, CRITIC, SelfEvolve), and multi-agent debate (ChatEval, Debates). The survey's own contribution is the conceptual framework, not a new reflection mechanism.

- **feedback source**:

> Survey-level: catalogs all sources. Its 'Feedback' axis (Sec 4.3) splits feedback into (1) Model feedback — self-generated, e.g. self-as-judge / self-reward (Self-Reward, SIRLC, CAI, Self-Refine, Self-Alignment) and (2) Environment feedback — external tool/interpreter/compiler, search, simulated or real environments, unit tests, and reward signals (SelfEvolve, Self-Debugging, Reflexion, CRITIC, RoboCat, SOTOPIA-pi). Ground-truth/human supervision is framed as the costly status quo that self-evolution aims to reduce.

- **iteration structure**:

> Defines self-evolution as iterative cycles: at iteration t the model picks an evolution objective E^t, acquires experience (tasks, solutions, feedback), refines it, updates itself, and evaluates — feeding the next objective E^{t+1}. So the canonical structure is iterative-refine / episodic loops; the surveyed literature also includes single-shot refine, tree/search, and population/evolutionary (model-merging) methods. Notes that current methods empirically struggle to improve beyond ~3 self-evolution rounds.

- **reflection object**:

> Survey spans the full spectrum and explicitly factors 'Updating' into In-Weight vs In-Context. Objects reflected on / modified include: output content and reasoning chains/rationales (refinement, STaR), action trajectories (agent methods), prompt/context and external memory notes/rules (working & external memory: Reflexion, TRAN, MoT, IML, ICE, MemGPT), structured rules/constitutions (CAI, TRAN), model weights (replay/regularization/architecture updates: ReST, InstructGPT, LoRA, model soups, EvoLLM), and even model architecture/merging (Model Soups, UltraFuser, EvoLLM model merging).


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: hybrid

- **requires training**:

> Survey covers the full range. Its 'Updating' taxonomy explicitly contrasts In-Weight updating (SFT via replay e.g. ReST/ReSTEM/SOTOPIA-pi/LLM2LLM; RL/preference e.g. InstructGPT-style RLHF, WARM, DLMA; regularization e.g. Elastic Reset, FuseLLM; architecture e.g. LoRA/ConPET/Model Soups/EvoLLM) against In-Context updating (external + working memory, no weight change). Thus: none | SFT | RL | DPO/preference | continual/regularized updates are all in scope.

- **reward or critic model**:

> All variants surveyed: none, self-as-judge (LLM-as-a-judge), trained reward models (reward-score selection / best-checkpoint selection per InstructGPT, WARM), verifiable/environment reward (tool, interpreter, env), and self-reward (Self-Reward, SIRLC, DLMA). The survey notes self-critics that have NOT co-evolved with the objective as a key reason self-evolution stalls after a few rounds.

- **distillation target**:

> Survey identifies multiple distillation/persistence forms under Updating: episodic-memory and reflected rationales/rules stored in external memory (MoT, MemoryBank, TiM, IML, ICE, TRAN, MemGPT); working-memory context (Reflexion, Agent-Pro, ProAgent); structured rules/constitutions (CAI, TRAN); prompts (PromptBreeder); and model-weights (replay/regularization/architecture-based in-weight updating, including model merging). It is the only survey field where 'all of the above' applies.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> Predominantly engineered/scaffolded — the surveyed pipeline (acquire-refine-update-evaluate with human-designed modules) is overwhelmingly prompt/framework-engineered. The survey's autonomy taxonomy (Low/Medium/High) frames current work as Low-level (humans design every module f); Medium/High autonomy (model designs its own evolution pipeline; emergent self-diagnosis) is posed as an open problem and the ultimate goal, not yet achieved. Predates o1/R1, so RL-emergent reflection ('aha') is not a central theme.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> Survey covers all: none, short-term/scratchpad (working memory), long-term-episodic and structured-notes/rules (external memory), skill/experience repositories, and playbook/rule cheatsheets. Updating Sec 6.2 splits memory into External Memory (collect/update/retrieve past experiences & reflected rationales) and Working Memory (in-context state used within the agent loop, e.g. Reflexion).

- **memory persistence**:

> Spans within-episode (working memory), cross-episode and cross-task (external memory of experiences/rationales, e.g. MemoryBank, MemGPT, IML, TRAN), up to longer-lived stores. The iterative cycle is inherently cross-episode/cross-task since refined experience is carried into subsequent iterations.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> Survey catalogs operations on external memory in a table (Table 2): Insert, Reflect, and Forget. MoT/TiM are insert-only (append-like); TRAN/IML/ICE/AesopAgent add Reflect (curate/summarize rules from experience); MemoryBank and MemGPT add Forget (eviction / FIFO rolling history) to keep memory bounded. So mechanisms surveyed include append-only, self-summarized/curated (reflect), and overwrite/forget (eviction).


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> Survey-level (covers all granularities). Its Experience Refinement axis includes instance-level filtering/correcting and the Evaluation section contrasts instance-level critic/reflection with coarser task-/model-level qualitative evaluation, noting task/model-level critique is still underdeveloped. Methods reviewed range from holistic/outcome-level (filtering, self-consistency) to response-level (Self-Refine), step/trajectory-level (agent trajectory methods), and code block-level (Self-Debugging, LDB).

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> Both. Intra-task refinement (refine a single task's solution, e.g. Self-Refine, Self-Debugging, iterative refinement) and inter-task transfer of distilled experience across tasks/iterations (Reflexion, IML, TRAN, ExpeL-style memory, ReST replay into weights) are both within the 'experience acquisition -> refinement -> updating' cycle, which is explicitly designed to carry experience forward across iterations and tasks.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> Survey covers all modes. Negative-experience methods (RLCD, DLMA, contrastive/perturbative solutions, COTERRORSET) and rule-from-mistakes memory (TRAN) emphasize avoidance of repeated errors in future episodes; iterative/critique-based correcting (Self-Refine, Reflexion, Self-Debugging) covers post-hoc and mid-trajectory revision. Not framed as a single method's choice; presented across the taxonomy.


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> General/cross-domain survey: code, math, QA/reasoning, tool-use, web/embodied agents, dialogue (diagnostic dialogue, social skills, role-playing), decision-making, and general alignment/safety. Evolution directions enumerated: Improving Performance, Adaptation to Feedback, Expansion of Knowledge Base, and Safety/Ethics/Bias reduction.

- **benchmarks**:

> As a survey it does not run a unified benchmark; it references representative tasks/benchmarks used by surveyed methods (e.g. reasoning GSM8K/MATH-style, code HumanEval/MBPP-style, agent/social environments such as ALFWorld, SOTOPIA, and instruction/tool-use benchmarks like UltraTool, T-Eval). For Evaluation it discusses dynamic LLM-based benchmarks (e.g. Sotopia) as a future direction over static benchmarks. No single headline benchmark table of its own.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> No empirical headline result — this is a conceptual/analysis survey, not an evaluated method. Its primary contribution is a unified conceptual framework defining self-evolution as iterative cycles of four phases (experience acquisition, experience refinement, updating, evaluation), plus a taxonomy of evolution objectives/abilities and per-module method taxonomies, and an identification of open problems (objective diversity/hierarchy, levels of autonomy, theoretical grounding, stability-plasticity, evaluation, safety/superalignment).

- **baselines**:

> n/a (survey; no experimental baselines). Conceptually positions self-evolution against the prevailing paradigm of learning from costly human/external-model supervision, arguing the latter faces performance ceilings and cost limits as task complexity/diversity grows.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> n/a — no quantitative delta reported by the survey itself. The argued qualitative 'gain' is scalability: self-generated-experience learning reduces dependence on human/teacher supervision and offers a potential path to scale LLMs toward superintelligence, though the survey cautions this is unproven and theoretically under-grounded.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Not quantified as a single number. The survey argues a key motivation for self-evolution is reducing the cost of human/external-model supervision, and explicitly notes In-Context updating (memory) enables 'fast adaptive updates without expensive training costs' versus In-Weight updating which requires gradient/training compute. No inference-multiplier or rollout-count figures are given.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Survey's own Open Problems (Sec 8): (1) Objectives are narrow vs the vast space of human needs and lack hierarchical structure; (2) Most frameworks are Low-autonomy (every module hand-designed), needing human effort and not deployment-efficient — Medium/High autonomy is unsolved; (3) Lack of theoretical grounding — self-improvement mechanisms unclear, mixed evidence on whether LLMs self-correct without external feedback, risk of reduced diversity / 'model collapse' / self-consuming training loops, and methods empirically stall after ~3 rounds; (4) Updating faces the stability-plasticity dilemma (catastrophic forgetting vs adaptation); (5) Static benchmarks become unreliable, need dynamic/evolving evaluation; (6) Safety & superalignment of increasingly autonomous, self-evolving systems.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> Survey treats external/environment feedback vs intrinsic self-feedback as a central, contested axis. It explicitly cites the mixed evidence: Huang et al. observed self-corrective behavior in models >22B parameters, while Ganguli et al. found LLMs struggle to self-correct reasoning errors WITHOUT external feedback. The 'Feedback' module separates Model (self) feedback from Environment (external/verifiable) feedback, acknowledging external/verifiable signals are often what makes self-evolution work.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent / contested (per the survey). It reports mixed results in the literature: self-correction/self-improvement can be net-positive in some settings (e.g. large models, with feedback) but unreliable without external feedback; further, repeated self-evolution tends to plateau or degrade after a few rounds (hypothesized: self-critic has not co-evolved with the objective), and training on self-generated data risks diversity loss and model collapse.

- **calibration effect**:

> not-measured. The survey predates the o1/R1 reasoning-model 'reasoning tax' calibration discourse and does not analyze calibration/overconfidence of reflective self-correction; it instead frames reliability via the external-feedback dependency and model-collapse risks.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a — this is a self-evolution survey, not a failure-attribution method. It does discuss failure-relevant phenomena (self-correction failure without external feedback, model collapse, self-evolution plateau after ~3 rounds, stability-plasticity/catastrophic forgetting) but does not classify or attribute failures via a taxonomy of multi-agent failure modes.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Failure modes discussed (not in MAST's 14-mode taxonomy terms): superficial/ineffective self-reflection and inability to self-correct reasoning errors without external feedback; error accumulation in self-consuming training loops / model collapse; reduced output diversity from self-generated data; self-evolution stagnation after limited iterations (self-critic not co-evolving with objective); catastrophic forgetting (stability-plasticity dilemma); and safety/alignment failures (bias, superalignment) of autonomous systems.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new dataset or benchmark released. The artifact is a curated GitHub reading list (Awesome-Self-Evolution-of-LLM) of surveyed papers; the survey advocates for future dynamic/evolving benchmarks (citing Sotopia) but does not contribute one.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Synthesizes foundational self-improvement/self-correction work it reviews, including: 'Large Language Models Can Self-Improve' (Huang et al., LMSI), STaR (Zelikman et al.), Self-Refine (Madaan et al.), Reflexion (Shinn et al.), RCI, CRITIC, Self-Debugging, Self-Instruct (Wang et al.), Constitutional AI / Self-Alignment (Bai et al.; Sun et al. Dromedary), Self-Reward, ReST / ReST-EM (self-training), and memory frameworks (MemGPT, MemoryBank, TRAN, IML/In-Memory Learning). Conceptually inspired by human experiential learning.

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Cited by and inspires subsequent self-evolution work, e.g. AgentGym / AgentEvol (Xi et al.), R-Zero: Self-Evolving Reasoning LLM from Zero Data (Huang et al.), Guided Self-Evolving LLMs / R-Few (Yu et al.), RISE (self-evolving VLMs), PACE (two-timescale self-evolution for small LM agents), CoMAS (co-evolving multi-agent systems), Alita-G (self-evolving generative agent), Evolving LLMs' Self-Refinement (EvolVE), and later surveys/roadmaps (Lifelong Learning of LLM-based Agents roadmap; Evolutionary Computation in the Era of LLMs; A Survey on Complex Reasoning of LLMs through the Lens of Self-Evolution; Evo-Memory benchmark; LLM-Evolve).

- **citation count**: ~70 (Semantic Scholar, Corpus ID 269294023, as fetched; 155 references; an earlier cached snapshot showed 62). Treat as approximate and growing.


### Other / reserved fields

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Relevant in spirit but not by name: the survey's In-Weight 'Replay-based' updating (ReST / ReST-EM, self-training on filtered self-generated rollouts) is closely related to on-policy/self-distillation and skill-optimization ideas, and it frames self-evolution as iteratively distilling refined self-generated experience back into weights or memory. It predates and does not cite the specific 'on-policy distillation' formulation.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Not quantified as trials-to-gain. The survey reports a qualitative empirical observation that current self-evolution methods struggle to improve after roughly three rounds of self-evolution, suggesting limited iterative sample efficiency / diminishing returns.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- reasoning_model_native
