<a id="r057-a-survey-of-self-evolving-agents-on-path-to-artificial-super-intelligence-full-subtitle-what-when-how-and-where-to-evolve-on-the-path-to-artificial-super-intelligence"></a>
## A Survey of Self-Evolving Agents: On Path to Artificial Super Intelligence (full subtitle: What, When, How, and Where to Evolve on the Path to Artificial Super Intelligence)

**ID:** R057  **Category:** J (Surveys & roadmaps)  **Authors:** Gao, Geng, Hua et al.  **Venue:** arXiv preprint  **Learning locus:** hybrid  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21046

### Basic info

- **name**: A Survey of Self-Evolving Agents: On Path to Artificial Super Intelligence (full subtitle: What, When, How, and Where to Evolve on the Path to Artificial Super Intelligence)

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Huan-ang Gao, Jiayi Geng, Wenyue Hua, Mengkang Hu, Xinzhe Juan et al. (27 authors); lead/corresponding affiliations: Princeton University & Princeton AI Lab (Mengdi Wang), with Tsinghua, CUHK, UIUC, PSU, SJTU and others

- **venue**: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 01/2026 (arXiv preprint 2507.21046, first submitted Jul 2025)

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21046

- **code url**: https://github.com/CharlesQ9/Self-Evolving-Agents (curated paper/resource list, not a single executable method)


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> none (survey/roadmap that taxonomizes reflection mechanisms rather than proposing one). The surveyed methods span verbal-self-critique (Reflexion, Self-Refine), tool/environment-verified, learned-critic / reward-model, search-guided (PromptAgent MCTS), multi-agent debate/collaboration, and population/evolutionary approaches; the survey itself contributes a unifying what/when/how/where framework.

- **feedback source**:

> n/a for the survey itself; it organizes the surveyed signal sources into: self-generated textual feedback, external tools (compiler/interpreter/web/search), unit-tests, environment-reward (scalar/verifiable), ground-truth/oracle labels, and human feedback. A core 'how to evolve' axis is textual feedback vs. scalar reward, and feedback source internal (model-generated) vs. external.

- **iteration structure**:

> n/a (survey). Catalogs the full spectrum: single-shot, iterative-refine (Self-Refine, TextGrad), episodic-retry (Reflexion), tree/MCTS search (PromptAgent), and population/evolutionary search (PromptBreeder, EvoAgent, ADAS). Temporally split into intra-test-time (online, within one task) and inter-test-time (offline/online, across tasks).

- **reflection object**:

> All of them — the survey's central 'what to evolve' dimension explicitly enumerates the objects of evolution: (1) Model/weights (the underlying LLM via SFT/RL), (2) Context = prompt/instructions + memory, (3) Tools (acquiring/creating/managing tools and skills), and (4) Architecture (single-agent workflow and multi-agent collaborative structure). It thus covers output content, reasoning chains, action trajectories, prompt/context, reusable skills/workflows, the agent's own code/architecture, and model weights.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: hybrid

- **requires training**:

> n/a (survey). It explicitly frames self-evolution across three learning paradigms it surveys: in-context learning (no weight update), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL, including online/on-policy and off-policy/DPO), plus nested meta-RL+SFT (e.g., self-edit/SEAL-style intra-test-time SFT driven by RL).

- **reward or critic model**:

> n/a for the survey; it categorizes the surveyed improvement signals into self-as-judge (Self-Refine, SPO pairwise self-preference), trained reward models / outcome-reward models (WebRL ORM), verifiable rewards (math/code), process- vs outcome-based reward granularity, and separate retrospective/critic or memory-manager models (e.g., Memory-R1 RL-trained memory manager).

- **distillation target**:

> All forms — the survey systematizes how reflection/experience is distilled into reusable artifacts: episodic-memory (long-term memory banks, Mem0, A-mem, Memento), reusable-skill/workflow (Agent Workflow Memory, Voyager-style skill library, MUSE hierarchical memory), structured-rules/insights (ExpeL rules, ReasoningBank reasoning strategies, ACE 'playbook' contexts), prompts (APE/ProTeGi/PromptBreeder/SPO), and model-weights (STaR, SELF, SEAL self-edits).

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> Covers both. The survey discusses prompt/scaffold-engineered reflective behavior (Reflexion, Self-Refine, AdaPlanner) AND RL-emergent / weight-update self-improvement (STaR, SELF, SEAL self-edits, LADDER/TTRL test-time RL, WebRL self-evolving curriculum). A guiding thesis is the shift from scaffold-engineered in-context adaptation toward learned/parametric self-evolution on the path to ASI.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> n/a (survey). Surveys the full memory spectrum: short-term/scratchpad, long-term episodic memory banks, skill libraries, structured notes/knowledge graphs (A-mem Zettelkasten-style interconnected networks), and playbook/cheatsheet contexts (ACE). Memory is treated as a first-class 'what to evolve' component (Context = prompt + memory).

- **memory persistence**:

> n/a (survey). Explicitly spans within-episode (intra-test-time), cross-episode/cross-task (inter-test-time experience accumulation), and cross-session/lifelong (long-horizon lifelong-learning evaluation, persistent state across tasks without reset, e.g., EvoAgent's persistent experience pool + continual world model).

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> n/a (survey) but it explicitly catalogs curation strategies: append-only experience logs; self-summarized/curated insights (MemInsight, ExpeL rules); retrieval-gated case banks (Memento); overwrite/evolution via self-relinking and structured ops ADD/MERGE/UPDATE/DELETE (Mem0, A-mem dynamic indexing/linking, Memory-R1 RL-trained manager); forgetting policies (SAGE Ebbinghaus curve, memory decay / right-to-be-forgotten unlearning); and population/Pareto-style selection for population-based methods.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> n/a (survey). Discusses signal granularity as an explicit axis: outcome-level (coarse, end-of-trajectory) vs process-level (fine, per-step) reward granularity; response/step/trajectory-level textual feedback; and agent-level attribution in multi-agent settings. It treats reward granularity (outcome-based vs process-based) as a key cross-cutting 'how to evolve' dimension.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> Covers both as the central 'when to evolve' dichotomy: intra-test-time self-evolution (adaptation during execution of a single task, coupled to the immediate instance, e.g., AdaPlanner, LADDER TTRL, SEAL self-edits) vs inter-test-time self-evolution (learning between tasks from accumulated experience, e.g., ExpeL, AWM, STaR, WebRL).

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> n/a (survey) but covers all: mid-trajectory recovery (AdaPlanner out-of-plan replanning, TrustAgent rule-based in-flight revision), post-hoc revision (Self-Refine, TextGrad), and avoidance/retry-next-episode (Reflexion-style episodic retry, inter-test-time policy updates). It distills strategies from both successful and failed trajectories (ReasoningBank).


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> Survey spans general-purpose and specialized domains. Explicitly: coding/autonomous software engineering, GUI/web navigation, math/reasoning, QA, tool-use, dialogue, decision-making, and specialized verticals — finance, medical/healthcare, education, plus embodied/games (Minecraft, Atari) and multi-agent collaboration.

- **benchmarks**:

> Survey-level coverage of evaluation resources, including: ARC, WebArena, Mind2Web-Live, GAIA, SWE-bench (named in evaluation discussion), AUTOENV-36, MemoryAgentBench (Test-Time Learning dimension), LTMBenchmark, LifelongAgentBench, StuLife, Benchmark Self-Evolving, TRACE, and EvoAgent's 67-task Minecraft + Atari suite. Introduces evaluation paradigms: static, short-horizon adaptive, long-horizon lifelong-learning.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> No single headline number (survey). Illustrative figures it reports: EvoAgent improves overall Minecraft Success Rate from 21.80% to 30.29% (relative gain approx. 105.9%) under long-horizon lifelong-learning evaluation; an architecture/population-based design-search entry reaches 84.7 in the how-to-evolve overview table. The paper's primary contribution is the unified what/when/how/where-to-evolve taxonomy, not a benchmark SOTA.

- **baselines**:

> n/a (survey). Positions itself as the first systematic survey of self-evolving agents; compares conceptually against related paradigms it distinguishes (curriculum learning, lifelong/continual learning, model editing, unlearning) and against prior narrower surveys on LLM agents, memory, or self-improvement.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> n/a (survey provides no head-to-head gain of its own). It tabulates representative methods' reported gains as exemplars (e.g., EvoAgent overall SR 21.80%->30.29%, ~+105.9% relative; roughly doubled SR on Gold/Diamond Minecraft tiers vs baselines with >6x fewer ineffective steps and ~2.7 vs ~7 A100-days).

- **compute cost profile**:

> n/a (survey) but it foregrounds compute as a cross-cutting concern: discusses online/offline and on-policy/off-policy trade-offs (off-policy improves sample efficiency at cost of distribution shift), test-time scaling/inference-time adaptation cost growing non-linearly with adaptation complexity, and proposes efficiency metrics such as Cost-per-Gain (CPG), tokens-per-success, memory growth rate, and training wall-clock (e.g., ~2.7 vs ~7 A100-days for EvoAgent).


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> As a survey it notes its own scope limits: a rapidly forming area with contested conceptual boundaries, framed as a 'guiding synthesis' rather than a review of an established paradigm; no rigid taxonomic boundaries. For the field it identifies open challenges: catastrophic forgetting / stability-plasticity dilemma, robust cross-domain knowledge transfer/generalization, scalability and non-linear compute cost, safety degradation during evolution ('misevolution'), reward hacking under off-policy learning, data governance/privacy in personalization, benchmark saturation and data leakage in continuous evaluation, and immature long-horizon lifelong-learning evaluation.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> n/a (survey) but it makes feedback source an explicit discriminating axis: methods range from intrinsic-only/self-verify (Self-Refine, SPO self-preference, MM-UPT/CoVo self-rewarding RL) through external tool/verifier (compilers, web verifiers, WebRL ORM) to oracle-label/ground-truth and environment-reward. Table 3 classifies each surveyed method's feedback source as internal vs external, surfacing the dependency on external/verifiable signal.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent (survey synthesis). It reports that self-evolution yields measurable gains in many settings (in-context improvement accumulates with experience; memory/skill distillation improves repeated/similar tasks) but warns that performance can degrade as benchmarks evolve, that off-policy self-evolution risks reward hacking, and that continual self-modification risks catastrophic forgetting and safety/alignment drift ('misevolution'); efficacy is conditioned on feedback quality and source.

- **calibration effect**:

> not-measured (survey does not directly study reasoning-model calibration / 'reasoning tax'). It discusses adaptivity, robustness, and safety as evaluation goals and warns of overconfident drift and misevolution, but does not report calibration metrics.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> classifies-failure-mode (taxonomy-style). The survey itself is a taxonomy/roadmap; it organizes failure-related challenges (catastrophic forgetting, reward hacking, misevolution/safety drift, distribution shift, benchmark saturation/data leakage) and surveys multi-agent and step-level/process-level signal granularity, but does not perform per-step or per-agent counterfactual failure attribution.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Field-level failure modes it foregrounds: catastrophic forgetting and stability-plasticity dilemma in continual learning; reward hacking / exploitation of train-deploy inconsistencies under off-policy learning; misevolution (safety/alignment/fairness degradation during evolution, per Shao et al. 2025); distribution shift; superficial/ineffective self-reflection without external verification; benchmark saturation and data leakage during continuous evaluation; non-linear compute blow-up. Relates to MAST-style modes such as superficial self-reflection and inter-agent misalignment in multi-agent co-evolution.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new dataset proposed by the survey itself; it releases a curated GitHub resource repository (https://github.com/CharlesQ9/Self-Evolving-Agents). It catalogs/recommends emerging benchmarks (MemoryAgentBench TTL, LTMBenchmark, LifelongAgentBench, AUTOENV-36, StuLife, TRACE, Benchmark Self-Evolving) and proposes evaluation protocols/metrics (Cost-per-Gain, BWT/FGT, Personal Adaptation Gain, Data Minimization Score).


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Synthesizes and is grounded in prior self-improvement / reflection / memory / agent works it surveys, including Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023), Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023), STaR / Quiet-STaR (Zelikman et al. 2022/2024), ExpeL (Zhao et al. 2024), Agent Workflow Memory (Wang et al. 2024), Voyager-style skill libraries, SEAL/self-edit intra-test-time SFT (Zweiger et al. 2025), WebRL (Qi et al. 2024), DigiRL (Bai et al. 2024), TextGrad, PromptBreeder/APE/ProTeGi/PromptAgent, ADAS, and DPO/RRHF; positioned relative to curriculum learning, lifelong/continual learning, model editing, and unlearning.

- **citation count**: ~39 (Google Scholar via arXiv/OpenReview listing, mid-2026); Princeton research portal listed ~32 — figure is rising and source-dependent


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> Partially. The survey covers self-evolution for general LLM agents and explicitly includes RL-emergent reasoning/self-improvement (STaR, test-time RL such as LADDER, R1-style reward-driven adaptation) but is not specific to o1/R1-style native-reflection models; it treats reflection/evolution as orthogonal to whether the base model is a reasoning model.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Relevant. The survey discusses on-policy vs off-policy learning as a cross-cutting 'how to evolve' axis, off-policy learning from prior policy versions / experience libraries for sample efficiency (with distribution-shift/reward-hacking caveats), and distillation of reflection/experience into reusable artifacts (skills, workflows, rules, prompts, weights) — directly connecting to on-policy distillation / skill-optimization themes.

- **sample efficiency**:

> n/a as a single number (survey). It frames sample efficiency as a design trade-off: off-policy methods improve sample efficiency at the cost of distribution mismatch; intra-test-time methods adapt from as little as a single synthetic example (TT-SI) or focused variant sets (LADDER); proposes Cost-per-Gain / tokens-per-success as efficiency metrics rather than reporting a fixed trial count.


### Uncertain (not determined)

<a id="r058-a-survey-on-the-feedback-mechanism-of-llm-based-ai-agents"></a>
## A Survey on the Feedback Mechanism of LLM-based AI Agents

**ID:** R058  **Category:** J (Surveys & roadmaps)  **Authors:** Liu, Bai, Chen et al.  **Venue:** IJCAI 2025 (Survey Track), pp. 10582-10592  **Learning locus:** hybrid  **URL:** https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2025/1175

### Basic info

- **name**: A Survey on the Feedback Mechanism of LLM-based AI Agents

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Zhipeng Liu, Xuefeng Bai, Kehai Chen, et al. (Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen; Peng Cheng Laboratory; Central South University)

- **venue**: IJCAI 2025 (Survey Track), pp. 10582-10592

- **paper url**: https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2025/1175 (DOI: 10.24963/ijcai.2025/1175)

- **code url**: https://github.com/kevinson7515/Agents-Feedback-Mechanisms (curated paper list, not a method implementation)


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> Survey covering the full spectrum of feedback/reflection types it taxonomizes: verbal-self-critique (internal feedback, e.g. Self-Refine, Reflexion), tool-verified/external (compiler, search engine, game API, world-model feedback), multi-agent-debate (collaborative and adversarial), and human feedback (instructional, corrective, preference). As an analysis/survey artifact it has no single reflection_type of its own.

- **feedback source**:

> Survey organizes feedback by source into four top-level categories: internal/self-generated (intra-task and inter-task), external-tool (compiler/interpreter, search engine, game API, world model, environment reward), multi-agent (peer agents in collaborative or adversarial setups), and human (instructional, corrective, preference). It synthesizes across all of these rather than proposing one.

- **iteration structure**:

> Survey-level synthesis. Reviewed methods span single-shot and iterative-refine (Self-Refine, Reflexion, Voyager); the survey explicitly tags each representative work with an 'Iteration (or not)' column in Table 1. No new iteration structure is proposed.

- **reflection object**:

> As a survey, it discusses reflection over many objects: output content (Self-Refine), reasoning chain (CoT-based internal feedback, SelfCheck), action trajectory (ReAct, Reflexion, ExpeL inter-task experience), reusable skill/workflow (Voyager skill library), and model weights (RLHF/RL-from-compiler-feedback methods like StepCoder, CodeRL, Retroformer). The survey's unifying frame is the 'feedback module' acting on the agent's prior decisions and actions across perception/planning/memory/action modules.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: hybrid

- **requires training**:

> Survey covering both training-free in-context methods (ReAct, Self-Refine, Reflexion verbal RL, ExpeL, AutoGuide use ICL with no weight updates) and gradient-update methods (RLHF/InstructGPT, RL-from-compiler-feedback StepCoder/CodeRL, policy-gradient Retroformer, preference learning DPO-style/Christiano-style RLHF). It does not itself train a model.

- **reward or critic model**:

> Survey enumerates many improvement-signal sources: self-as-judge (internal feedback), external verifiable signals (compiler success, task completion, environment reward), separate feedback/critic models, multi-agent peer evaluation, LLM-as-judge / Agent-as-a-judge, and human reward/preference models. It notes LLM-as-judge suffers positional bias, verbosity bias, and weakness on math.

- **distillation target**:

> Survey discusses several reusable artifacts that reflection can be distilled into: episodic-memory (Reflexion stores self-reflections; Generative Agents memory stream), reusable-skill/workflow (Voyager skill library), prompt/guideline (AutoGuide context-aware guidelines), and model-weights (RL/SFT methods such as StepCoder, Retroformer, RLHF). No single target is prescribed.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> Predominantly covers prompt/scaffold-engineered reflective behavior (Reflexion, Self-Refine, ReAct, Voyager, multi-agent debate), framed as designed feedback modules rather than RL-emergent reflection. The survey predates/does not center R1-style RL-emergent 'aha' reasoning; reflection is treated as an explicitly engineered module within a five-module agent framework.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> Survey covers the memory dimension explicitly: it defines a memory module with long-term memory (stable knowledge) and short-term memory (real-time task info), and reviewed methods use scratchpad/short-term memory, long-term-episodic memory (Reflexion, Generative Agents, RAP), and skill-library memory (Voyager). Tightly coupled with the feedback module in its unified framework.

- **memory persistence**:

> Survey spans within-episode (intra-task feedback, Self-Refine), cross-episode/cross-task (inter-task feedback: Reflexion, ExpeL, Retroformer transfer experience across tasks via stored trajectories and reflections), with cross-task experience integration highlighted as a key strength of inter-task feedback. No production cross-session deployment focus.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> Survey notes that inter-task feedback 'demands substantial memory to store historical task experience' and that the central challenge is combining intra- and inter-task feedback efficiently. Reviewed methods use append-style episodic stores (Reflexion), retrieval over similar past trajectories (ExpeL, RAP), and curated guideline generation/selection (AutoGuide). No unified curation scheme is prescribed.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> Survey-level; spans holistic/outcome-level (most QA and success-rate benchmarks), response-level (Self-Refine output revision), step-level (SelfCheck per-step reasoning checks; DevAI evaluates each stage; AdaPlanner code-splitting), and agent-level (multi-agent feedback attributing roles/responsibilities). It critiques outcome-only benchmarks for ignoring the reasoning process.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> Both, and this is an explicit organizing axis of the survey: internal feedback is sub-divided into intra-task (refine within current task, e.g. ReAct, Self-Refine) and inter-task (transfer experience across tasks, e.g. Reflexion, ExpeL, Retroformer, RAP). Discussion section contrasts their complementary strengths/limits.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> Survey covers both: mid-trajectory recovery (Voyager combining execution errors and self-validation to repair programs in-flight; ReAct interleaving reasoning and acting; QueryAgent self-correction via environmental feedback) and post-hoc/avoidance via retrospection in the next episode (Reflexion, ExpeL using prior-task experience to avoid repeating mistakes).


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> Survey spans QA/reasoning, code generation, web-navigation, embodied/games (virtual worlds, robotics), tool-use, dialogue, multi-agent collaboration, machine translation, financial reasoning, social simulation, and general decision-making/alignment.

- **benchmarks**:

> Survey catalogs benchmarks by domain (Table 2): Reasoning (HotpotQA, ScienceQA, StrategyQA); Virtual World (ALFWorld, IGLU, MineRL/Minecraft); Embodied Action (Franka Kitchen, Meta-World, RT-X); Web Navigation (WebShop, WebArena, Mind2Web, WebVoyager); Code Generation (MBPP, HumanEval, SWE-bench, DevAI); Social Simulation (SocialBench, SocKET); Tool Usage (ToolBench, TravelPlanner, ToolEyes); Multi-agent Collaboration (RoCoBench, PARTNR, VillagerBench); Machine Translation (WMT, FLORES-200); Financial (FiQA_SA, FinQA); Multidimensional (AgentBench).


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Survey (no single headline number of its own). Its experimental comparison (Table 3, on HotpotQA, ALFWorld, WebShop, with some results borrowed from ExpeL and AutoGuide) qualitatively reports: ReAct gives limited gains on complex reasoning (HotpotQA, StrategyQA) but strong performance on sequential decision tasks (ALFWorld, WebShop); Reflexion further improves ALFWorld via iterative learning, with the largest jump between the first and second trials; ExpeL and AutoGuide add stability on long-horizon dynamic tasks. Specific numeric deltas are not legibly recoverable from the OCR of the proceedings PDF.

- **baselines**:

> In its comparative analysis the survey contrasts non-learning methods (CoT, Act, ReAct) against iterative-learning feedback methods (Reflexion, ExpeL, AutoGuide, AdaPlanner) and against traditional scalar-reward reinforcement learning, evaluated on HotpotQA, ALFWorld, and WebShop.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Not quantified numerically. The survey qualitatively argues in-context verbal-feedback methods (Reflexion) are more data- and compute-efficient than scalar-reward RL because they avoid fine-tuning the LLM, and warns that multi-agent feedback sharply raises computational demands and communication overhead as agent count grows. No token/API-call multipliers are reported.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Survey identifies six open challenges: (1) real-time feedback and scaling multi-agent systems (rising compute, communication overhead, lack of standardized protocols such as MCP/A2A/ANP/Agora); (2) integrating multimodal feedback (cross-modal alignment); (3) meta-learning adaptive feedback (feedback conflicts, overfitting to evolving user needs); (4) explainability/transparency of feedback mechanisms; (5) sim-to-real transfer for embodied agents; (6) inherent LLM/VLM limitations (hallucination, bias). It also flags ethical bias risks in human feedback (gender, race, culture).

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> Survey makes external-vs-internal feedback a central axis. It notes external feedback (compiler, search, environment reward, world model) gives insights self-improvement cannot, but its effectiveness 'is highly dependent on the quality and relevance of external information.' It frames internal/self-feedback as limited and recommends external tools, multi-agent debate, RAG cross-validation, and world models to correct hallucinations and reasoning errors.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent. Survey reports intra-task self-refinement enables rapid optimization but is limited by its task-specific nature, while external and multi-agent feedback are needed to correct hallucinations and reasoning errors that pure self-feedback misses; multi-agent negotiation can also converge on incorrect consensus. Efficacy is framed as contingent on feedback source quality rather than uniformly net-positive.

- **calibration effect**: not-measured. The survey does not analyze calibration/overconfidence ('reasoning tax') of reasoning models; it predates that lens and focuses on feedback taxonomy, hallucination, and bias rather than calibration metrics.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a (survey). It does not perform formal failure attribution, but discusses failure modes qualitatively: multi-agent systems risk uncontrolled discussions (mitigated by coordination agents like ChatLLM), reward misalignment among agents (CollabQ), convergence on incorrect consensus (PRD peer-ranking), LLM hallucination/bias, and option bias in QA benchmarks.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Discusses failure modes including hallucination/factual error, reasoning errors, multi-agent reward misalignment and conflict, uncontrolled debate, incorrect-consensus convergence (analogous to MAST inter-agent misalignment), QA option/positional bias, LLM-as-judge verbosity/positional bias, and sim-to-real transfer failure. Proposed fixes: dedicated coordination agents, peer-ranking, RAG cross-validation, world models, multi-agent debate.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new dataset or benchmark released. The survey releases a curated, continually-updated paper list at https://github.com/kevinson7515/Agents-Feedback-Mechanisms (README organizes works by feedback category and benchmarks).


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Synthesizes and builds on prior surveys (Wang et al. 2023 'A survey on LLM-based autonomous agents'; Xi et al. 'The rise and potential of LLM-based agents'; Pan et al. 2024 and Madaan et al. self-correction surveys; Cheng et al. 2024; Durante et al. 2024 Agent AI) and foundational methods it taxonomizes: ReAct, Reflexion, Self-Refine, Voyager, ExpeL, MetaGPT, Multi-agent Debate (Du et al.), InstructGPT/RLHF, StepCoder, Generative Agents.

- **citation count**: 16 (Semantic Scholar, as of 2026-06; influentialCitationCount 0, referenceCount 95)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**: no — the survey is organized around engineered feedback modules and verbal/RL feedback for general LLM agents; it does not specifically target o1/R1-style reasoning models with built-in reflection.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Not quantified. The survey qualitatively argues verbal-feedback methods (Reflexion) are more data/compute efficient than scalar-reward RL (no fine-tuning needed) and notes Reflexion's main ALFWorld gain appears within the first 1-2 trials, but reports no formal sample-efficiency numbers.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- extended_by_or_inspired
- on_policy_distillation_link

<a id="r061-a-comprehensive-survey-of-self-evolving-ai-agents-a-new-paradigm-bridging-foundation-models-and-lifelong-agentic-systems"></a>
## A Comprehensive Survey of Self-Evolving AI Agents: A New Paradigm Bridging Foundation Models and Lifelong Agentic Systems

**ID:** R061  **Category:** J (Surveys & roadmaps)  **Authors:** Fang, Peng, Zhang et al.  **Venue:** arXiv preprint (Univ. of Glasgow / Cambridge et al.)  **Learning locus:** hybrid  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.07407

### Basic info

- **name**: A Comprehensive Survey of Self-Evolving AI Agents: A New Paradigm Bridging Foundation Models and Lifelong Agentic Systems

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**:

> Jinyuan Fang, Yanwen Peng, Xi Zhang, et al. (15 authors); corresponding author Zaiqiao Meng. Lead affiliation: University of Glasgow (with University of Sheffield, University of Cambridge, MBZUAI, NUS, UCL, University of Aberdeen, Leiden University).

- **venue**: arXiv preprint (cs.AI / cs.CL / cs.MA). Not yet peer-reviewed as of the survey version; associated framework EvoAgentX appears at EMNLP'25 Demo.

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.07407

- **code url**: https://github.com/EvoAgentX/Awesome-Self-Evolving-Agents (companion awesome-list / taxonomy repo). Related open-source framework: https://github.com/EvoAgentX/EvoAgentX


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> none (survey/analysis). The survey itself does not propose a reflection method; it taxonomizes self-evolution techniques, several of which use verbal-self-critique, learned-critic-model, search-guided, and multi-agent-debate styles of reflection/feedback (e.g., Self-Refine, Reflexion-style verbal feedback, LLM-as-a-judge, evolutionary search).

- **feedback source**:

> n/a for the survey as an artifact. Across surveyed methods, the abstracted 'Environment' component supplies feedback via proxy metrics covering self-generated signals, external tools (compiler/interpreter/search), unit tests, environment reward, ground-truth/oracle labels, and LLM-based evaluators.

- **iteration structure**:

> n/a (survey). The unified framework abstracts a closed iterative optimisation feedback loop (Execution -> Feedback -> Mutation/Refine) that subsumes single-shot, iterative-refine, tree/MCTS-search, and population/evolutionary structures found in the surveyed literature.

- **reflection object**:

> Survey covers the full spectrum of what is reflected on / modified: prompt/context, reasoning chain, action trajectory, memory, tools, reusable skills/workflows, multi-agent topology/architecture, model weights, and the agent's own code/architecture. The framework formalises this as the optimiser's 'search space' (prompt template, tool selection, LLM parameters, architectural).


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: hybrid

- **requires training**:

> n/a (survey). The taxonomy explicitly spans both training-free in-context/test-time optimisation (prompt optimisation, memory, search) and training-based optimisation (SFT, RL such as PPO/GRPO, DPO/preference) under 'Training-Based Behaviour Optimisation' vs 'Test-Time Behaviour Optimisation'.

- **reward or critic model**:

> n/a (survey). Surveyed signals include none, self-as-judge (LLM-as-a-judge / Agent-as-a-judge), trained reward/process-reward models (e.g., Math-Shepherd, Skywork-Reward), verifiable rewards, and separate retrospective/meta-optimiser models (e.g., Retroformer policy-gradient retrospective optimisation).

- **distillation target**:

> Survey enumerates all reusable-artifact targets: episodic-memory (e.g., A-MEM, Mem0, ReasoningBank), reusable-skill/workflow (e.g., Agent Workflow Memory, AFlow), prompt (prompt optimisation methods), and model-weights (SFT/RL fine-tuning). The framework treats these as alternative loci that the optimiser writes its improvements into.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> Covers both: RL-emergent reflective behaviour (e.g., R1/Absolute-Zero/R-Zero self-play reasoning lines) and prompt/scaffold-engineered reflection (e.g., Self-Refine, Retroformer, evolutionary prompt optimisation). The survey does not privilege one; it organises them under behaviour optimisation vs. structural/workflow optimisation.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> n/a (survey). Dedicates a 'Memory Optimization' subsection (1.3) reviewing short-term/scratchpad, long-term-episodic, skill-library, structured-notes/graph (e.g., GraphReader), and playbook/cheatsheet style memories, plus production memory systems (Mem0, A-MEM, Memory-R1, ReasoningBank).

- **memory persistence**: n/a (survey). Surveyed memory methods span within-episode, cross-episode, cross-task, and cross-session/production persistence; the lifelong-agent framing emphasises cross-task and cross-session adaptation.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> n/a (survey). Reviews append-only, self-summarised/curated (compressive memory), retrieval-gated, RL-managed (Memory-R1), and evolution/self-relinking (A-MEM agentic memory; MemEvolve meta-evolution of memory architecture) curation strategies.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> n/a (survey). Spans the full granularity range across surveyed methods: holistic/outcome-level, response-level, step-level (process reward models, step-wise preference tuning), block-level (code), and agent-level (multi-agent / topology optimisation).

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> n/a (survey). Explicitly distinguishes test-time / intra-task optimisation (refine within a task) from cross-task lifelong evolution (transfer of experience across tasks), the latter being the central motivation ('lifelong agentic systems').

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**: n/a (survey). Covers post-hoc-revision (Self-Refine, self-debug), avoidance via cross-episode experience transfer, and mid-trajectory recovery within the broader optimisation loop; not framed as a single mechanism.


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> General agentic tasks plus domain-specific: code/programming, math/reasoning, QA, web-navigation/GUI, tool-use, decision-making, multi-agent collaboration, and specialised domains - biomedicine (medical diagnosis, molecular/drug discovery), finance (financial decision-making), legal reasoning, scientific research, and climate science.

- **benchmarks**:

> Survey's evaluation section catalogs benchmarks rather than reporting its own: GAIA, AgentBench, SWE-bench, WebArena, BrowseComp, WebWalker, OSWorld, AndroidWorld, Mobile-Bench, API-Bank, ToolQA, MetaTool, MLGym, DataSciBench, MultiAgentBench, plus safety benchmarks (AgentHarm, RedCode, R-Judge, MobileSafetyBench, SafeLawBench).


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Not a results paper. Headline contribution: a unified conceptual framework abstracting the self-evolving feedback loop into four components (System Inputs I, Agent System A, Environment, Optimiser P), plus the 'Three Laws of Self-Evolving AI Agents' (Endure / Excel / Evolve, inspired by Asimov), used to organise single-agent, multi-agent, and domain-specific optimisation techniques from 2023-2025.

- **baselines**:

> n/a (survey). It is positioned relative to prior surveys of LLM agents, agent optimisation, prompt optimisation, and multi-agent systems, distinguishing itself by the unified optimiser-centric feedback-loop abstraction and the lifelong/self-evolving lens.

- **gains vs baseline**: n/a (survey; no empirical gains reported by the paper itself).

- **compute cost profile**:

> n/a (survey; no compute experiments). Conceptually notes that optimisers vary widely in cost (rule-based heuristics vs. gradient descent vs. Bayesian/MCTS/RL vs. learning-based policy) and discusses efficiency as a design dimension of the search space + optimisation algorithm pair (S, H).


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> States that self-evolving agentic systems are an emerging direction with open challenges in evaluation (lack of standardised lifelong/self-evolving benchmarks), safety (must maintain stability during modification - the 'Endure' law), alignment/ethics, controllability of autonomous self-modification, and risk of capability regression; calls these critical to effectiveness and reliability.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> n/a (survey). Catalogs the full dependency spectrum across methods (intrinsic-only self-verify, external-tool/verifier, oracle-label/ground-truth, env-reward) via the abstracted Environment/proxy-metric feedback channel; does not itself adjudicate which works without label leakage.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent (survey-level characterisation). The paper does not run controlled experiments but frames efficacy as contingent on the optimiser design, the quality of environmental feedback, and domain constraints; the 'Excel' law explicitly requires that evolution preserve or enhance existing performance, acknowledging regression risk.

- **calibration effect**: not-measured (survey does not empirically study reasoning-model calibration / 'reasoning tax').


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**: n/a (survey is not a failure-attribution method; it reviews evaluation and safety considerations but does not provide a failure-mode classifier or step/agent attribution mechanism).

- **failure mode addressed**:

> n/a as a method. As a survey it discusses safety/stability failure modes of self-evolution (capability regression, unsafe self-modification, alignment drift) and reviews safety benchmarks; it does not map to MAST's 14 modes.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new dataset/benchmark released by the survey itself. It releases a curated, continuously updated taxonomy/awesome-list repository (EvoAgentX/Awesome-Self-Evolving-Agents) and is associated with the EvoAgentX open-source evolving-workflow framework.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Foundation-model and LLM-agent literature; agent optimisation primitives it synthesises include Self-Refine, Reflexion-style verbal feedback, Retroformer, TextGrad/DSPy, EvoPrompt/Promptbreeder/GEPA (prompt evolution), AFlow/ADAS/GPTSwarm (workflow & multi-agent architecture search), STaR/ToRA (training-based), and R1/Absolute-Zero/R-Zero (RL self-play); Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics (conceptual inspiration for the Three Laws).

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Cited/extended by follow-up self-evolving and lifelong-agent works including MemEvolve (meta-evolution of agent memory), CoMAS (co-evolving multi-agent systems), FLEX (continuous agent evolution from experience), Alita-G, ReasoningBank, Self-evolving Embodied AI, and domain surveys on agentic AI for wireless/edge networks; ~69 citing works as of mid-2026.

- **citation count**: 69 (Semantic Scholar, Corpus ID 280566335, retrieved 2026-06-08; 4 highly-influential citations).


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> Partially. The survey explicitly covers RL-trained reasoning models with built-in/emergent reflection (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-style, Absolute Zero, R-Zero) under 'Reasoning-Based' and RL behaviour optimisation, but is not specific to o1/R1-class models; it treats them as one branch of self-evolution.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Relevant. The taxonomy includes distillation- and RL-based self-improvement (e.g., STaR bootstrapping, Chain-of-Agents multi-agent distillation, self-rewarding LMs, self-play RL), which are on-policy distillation / skill-optimisation analogues, but the survey does not single out on-policy distillation as a named category.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- sample_efficiency

<a id="r062-automatically-correcting-large-language-models-surveying-the-landscape-of-diverse-automated-correction-strategies"></a>
## Automatically Correcting Large Language Models: Surveying the Landscape of Diverse Automated Correction Strategies

**ID:** R062  **Category:** J (Surveys & roadmaps)  **Authors:** Pan et al.  **Venue:** TACL 2024  **Learning locus:** n/a  **URL:** https://aclanthology.org/2024.tacl-1.27/

### Basic info

- **name**: Automatically Correcting Large Language Models: Surveying the Landscape of Diverse Automated Correction Strategies

- **year**: 2024

- **authors**: Liangming Pan, Michael Saxon, Wenda Xu, Deepak Nathani, Xinyi Wang, William Yang Wang (University of California, Santa Barbara). arXiv first submission 2023 (2308.03188).

- **venue**: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics (TACL), Volume 12, pp. 484-506, MIT Press, 2024. DOI: 10.1162/tacl_a_00660.

- **paper url**: https://aclanthology.org/2024.tacl-1.27/ (arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.03188)

- **code url**:

> No standalone official code repository (survey). A companion reading list / curated bibliography exists; the paper is tracked in community lists such as dongxiangjue/Awesome-LLM-Self-Improvement and tianyi-lab style self-correction reading lists.


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> Survey/analysis (not a single method). Taxonomizes the full landscape of automated-feedback correction, spanning verbal-self-critique (self-refine, self-feedback), tool-verified correction (compiler/interpreter/symbolic-solver/retrieval), learned-critic-model approaches (trained reward/critic models, PRM), search-guided generation (beam/tree search with step feedback), and multi-agent-debate. Its own contribution is the conceptual framework, not a new reflection mechanism.

- **feedback source**:

> Surveys all sources. Organized into two top-level classes: (1) self-feedback (the LLM itself as critic, e.g. Self-Refine, Reflexion) and (2) external feedback subdivided into other trained models, external tools (code interpreters/compilers, symbolic solvers, BMC), external knowledge sources (Wikipedia/web/retrieval), and external evaluation metrics. Human feedback (RLHF) is covered for completeness but the survey's focus is automated feedback.

- **iteration structure**:

> Surveys all of them. Distinguishes single-shot (e.g. one-pass post-edit, re-ranking/generate-then-rank) vs iterative-refine (the 'Iter.' column in Table 2 marks iterative vs non-iterative post-hoc methods, e.g. Self-Refine/Reflexion iterative; SelfCheckGPT/RARR non-iterative) and search-based generation-time correction (stochastic beam search, Tree-of-Thoughts). Reflexion is the episodic-retry-with-reset exemplar surveyed.

- **reflection object**:

> Survey covers the full range. Two main targets per the framework's 'Refine Model': (1) the output itself (output content / reasoning chain / code), repaired during or after generation without weight change (generation-time and post-hoc correction); and (2) the model parameters/weights themselves via training-time correction (fine-tuning, self-training, RLHF/RLAIF, model editing). Prompt/context-level correction (e.g. MemPrompt) is also noted. Primary axis 1 of the taxonomy is explicitly 'What gets corrected?' answered at the error-type level: hallucination, unfaithful reasoning, toxic/biased/harmful content, and flawed code.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**:

> n/a (analysis/survey). The survey itself performs no weight update; it organizes the literature precisely along this axis, distinguishing training-time correction (gradient_weight_update) from generation-time and post-hoc correction (in_context_verbal, no weight update).

- **requires training**:

> n/a for the survey itself. As a taxonomy it explicitly classifies surveyed methods by learning method: ICL (in-context, no training), SL (supervised fine-tuning), and RL (e.g. PPO-based RLHF/RLAIF, CodeRL, RL4F, Reflexion's RL variant). The 'When to correct' dimension separates training-time (parameter update via SFT/RL) from post-hoc (no parameter update).

- **reward or critic model**:

> Surveys the spectrum. Its 'Critic Model (Doctor)' abstraction C: X x Y -> F covers: self-as-judge (LLM critiques itself), separately trained reward/critic models (RLHF reward models, PRM, DIVERSE, REFINER), verifiable/tool-derived signals (program executors, symbolic solvers, oracle verifiers like ALGO), external evaluation metrics, and external knowledge. Feedback format is taxonomized as scalar-value vs natural-language.

- **distillation target**:

> Survey-level. Covers the cases where correction is distilled into model weights (training-time self-training: STaR, Self-Improve, ReST, RLAIF distill correct/positively-evaluated outputs back into the model). Also discusses post-hoc correction collecting frequent-mistake/correction pairs to feed periodic training-time correction (a proposed continual-improvement pipeline), and prompt-level memory (MemPrompt). Episodic memory of past errors is exemplified by the surveyed Reflexion.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> Predominantly engineered. The surveyed paradigms (Self-Refine, Reflexion, CRITIC, Self-Debug, debate) are prompt/scaffold-engineered correction pipelines built around the Language-Critic-Refine framework. The survey predates reasoning-model RL-emergent self-correction (o1/R1 'aha'); it instead frames the open question of whether self-repair is an emergent ability of certain large models (citing Olausson et al.'s finding that self-repair gains appear mainly with GPT-4-level feedback).


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> Survey-level (not a single memory design). Discusses scratchpad/iterative refinement (within-episode), episodic memory of prior trial errors (Reflexion), prompt-level memory of past feedback (MemPrompt), and weight-based 'memory' via fine-tuning/self-training. Continual/life-long self-improvement with persistent learning is raised as an under-explored future direction.

- **memory persistence**:

> Survey-level. Most surveyed methods operate within-episode (single task refinement) or cross-episode within a task (Reflexion-style retry). The survey explicitly flags cross-task/continual (life-long) self-improvement and the associated catastrophic-forgetting risk as open, under-explored problems.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> n/a (survey does not propose a memory-curation method). It notes, as future work, that post-hoc correction could be used to collect the most-frequent mistakes and their corrections to drive periodic training-time correction (a form of curated retention), and discusses model editing for targeted, side-effect-limited updates.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> Surveys multiple granularities. Spans holistic/outcome-level (re-rank or accept/reject whole outputs), response-level (post-hoc revision of full output), and step-level / process-level (process reward models like PRM/Lightman, step-wise reasoning verification, stochastic beam search over intermediate reasoning steps, Tree-of-Thoughts). Code is corrected at block/program level using execution feedback. Multi-agent debate operates at agent-level.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> Both, as a survey. Generation-time and most post-hoc methods are intra-task (refine within a single task instance, e.g. Self-Refine). Reflexion and training-time self-training (STaR, Self-Improve, ReST) carry experience inter-task / across instances. The survey treats this implicitly through its training-time vs generation-time vs post-hoc timing axis rather than as a named dimension.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> Survey covers all three. Generation-time correction = mid-trajectory recovery (correct/guide errors as generation proceeds, e.g. feedback-guided beam search). Post-hoc correction = post-hoc revision (fix after a full output is produced). Training-time correction = avoidance (fix the model so future generations avoid the error). Reflexion-style retry-with-reset is the episodic-avoidance exemplar.


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> Survey spans: code generation/synthesis, math & reasoning (arithmetic, deductive/proof, commonsense, multi-hop QA), open-domain QA & fact-checking, machine translation (automatic post-editing), summarization, dialogue/response generation, story/open-ended generation, toxicity/harmful-content/detoxification, controlled text generation, planning, and general alignment. Dedicated application sections: factual correction, reasoning tasks, code synthesis, and other (open-ended generation, MT, summarization).

- **benchmarks**:

> As a survey it does not run benchmarks itself; it aggregates methods evaluated on tasks/datasets such as HumanEval/MBPP-style code generation, GSM8K-style arithmetic reasoning, HotpotQA/multi-hop QA, proof-generation (EntailmentBank-style), machine translation (WMT), summarization, commonsense reasoning, and toxicity (RealToxicityPrompts-style) benchmarks referenced through the surveyed primary works. No single headline benchmark suite is the survey's own.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> No quantitative headline result of its own (survey). Its primary contributions are: (1) a unifying conceptual framework with three roles — Language Model (patient), Critic Model (doctor/diagnosis), Refine Model (treatment); (2) a five-dimension taxonomy — what gets corrected, source of feedback, format of feedback, when feedback is used, how to correct; and (3) categorization of works into training-time, generation-time, and post-hoc correction (Tables 1-2 catalog ~60 representative methods).

- **baselines**:

> n/a (survey has no experimental baselines). It positions itself relative to prior surveys: Fernandes et al. (2023) on human feedback for language generation, and broader alignment/continual-learning surveys; its differentiator is the focus on automated (vs human) feedback for self-correction.

- **gains vs baseline**: n/a — no experimental gains reported; this is a literature survey/taxonomy, not an empirical method.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Discussed qualitatively rather than measured. The survey notes the practical cost trade-offs of each timing strategy: training-time correction is most fundamental but highest compute (rollouts/gradient steps) and infeasible for giant closed-source LLMs; post-hoc correction is more immediate and less costly but adds inference iterations (extra API calls per refinement loop); generation-time correction adds search/decoding overhead. No numeric multipliers are given.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> As stated in Sections 6-7: (1) self-repair is often bottlenecked by feedback quality — Olausson et al. found substantial code self-repair gains only when feedback came from expert humans or GPT-4, raising whether self-correction is an emergent ability of only the largest models; (2) lack of theoretical justification for why self-correction works (tied to calibration/metacognition); (3) no robust quantitative metrics or diagnostic benchmarks to compare self-correction strategies; (4) continual/life-long self-improvement is under-explored and risks catastrophic forgetting; (5) model-editing-based correction lacks generalization and introduces side effects; (6) training-time correction is infeasible for closed-source LLMs and requires 'optimizable' feedback. Scope limit: the survey predates reasoning-model RL-emergent self-correction (o1/R1).

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> Survey-wide, this is a central organizing variable. It explicitly contrasts intrinsic self-feedback against external-tool/verifier, external-knowledge, and oracle signals (e.g. ALGO's oracle verifier, program executors, symbolic solvers). It foregrounds Olausson et al.'s finding that self-repair improvements largely depend on high-quality external feedback (expert humans / GPT-4), and that without good feedback self-correction is limited — anticipating the Kamoi/Huang critique that follows it.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent / often requires-strong-feedback. The survey reports broad empirical effectiveness across many tasks but is candid that efficacy hinges on feedback quality and that intrinsic self-correction without external signals is questionable (citing Olausson et al.). Code correction works well because execution feedback is cheap and reliable; reasoning correction is harder because reliable intermediate references are scarce.

- **calibration effect**:

> Discussed as theory, not measured. Section 7.1 ties self-correction ability to calibration and metacognitive awareness (Kadavath et al. 2022): pre-trained LMs are reasonably calibrated on self-evaluation in few-shot settings, while RLHF-tuned models need temperature adjustment to recover calibration. The survey treats calibration as an enabling factor for self-correction rather than reporting an empirical improve/degrade outcome.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> classifies-failure-mode (taxonomy). The survey provides a taxonomy of the errors targeted for correction — hallucination, unfaithful reasoning, toxic/biased/harmful content, and flawed code — and organizes corrective strategies against them. It does not attribute failures to specific agents or steps in a multi-agent trace (that is the domain of later attribution work like Who&When/MAST).

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets/organizes correction for: hallucination (factual errors, fabricated citations), unfaithful reasoning (conclusion not following the reasoning chain), toxic/biased/harmful generation, and flawed/incorrect code. Relates to MAST-style modes such as superficial/ineffective self-reflection (its discussion of when self-correction fails without good feedback) though it predates the MAST 14-mode taxonomy.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> None. As a survey it releases no dataset, benchmark, or trace corpus; it provides a taxonomy and a curated catalog of ~60 methods (Tables 1-2) rather than a reusable resource. It calls for building diagnostic benchmarks for self-correction as future work.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Prior human-feedback survey by Fernandes et al. (2023); foundational methods it organizes including RLHF (Ouyang et al. 2022), Constitutional AI/RLAIF (Bai et al. 2022b), STaR (Zelikman et al. 2022), Self-Improve (Huang et al. 2022), Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023), Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023), CRITIC (Gou et al. 2023), Self-Debug (Chen et al. 2023d), Tree-of-Thoughts (Yao et al. 2023a), PRM (Lightman et al. 2023), Multiagent Debate (Du et al. 2023), and calibration/metacognition work (Kadavath et al. 2022).

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Directly succeeded by the critical survey 'When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs' (Kamoi, Saxon, et al., TACL 2024, DOI 10.1162/tacl_a_00713), which shares authorship and sharpens the oracle-feedback-dependency critique; also widely cited as a reference taxonomy in subsequent LLM self-improvement / self-correction reading lists and surveys (e.g. Awesome-LLM-Self-Improvement) and follow-on self-correction methods.

- **citation count**: ~160 (Semantic Scholar, read from the paper page in 2026; figure is approximate and growing). The Semantic Scholar Graph API could not independently confirm due to rate-limiting at fetch time.


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> No / predates them. The survey (2023-2024) targets prompt-and-feedback self-correction pipelines for standard LLMs (GPT-3.5/GPT-4 era) and does not cover o1/R1-style models with RL-trained built-in reflection. Its open questions about whether self-correction is an emergent large-model ability foreshadow that line.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Indirect. It surveys self-training methods (STaR, Self-Improve, ReST, RLAIF) that retrain a model on its own positively-evaluated/corrected generations — conceptually adjacent to on-policy distillation / self-distillation of correction behavior into weights — but it does not analyze on-policy distillation as such.

- **sample efficiency**:

> n/a — not an empirical method; no trials-to-gain numbers. The survey notes that post-hoc iterative refinement adds inference iterations and that training-time correction is costlier in rollouts/gradient steps, but reports no sample-efficiency measurements.

<a id="r075-internal-consistency-and-self-feedback-in-large-language-models-a-survey"></a>
## Internal Consistency and Self-Feedback in Large Language Models: A Survey

**ID:** R075  **Category:** J (Surveys & roadmaps)  **Authors:** Xun Liang et al.  **Venue:** arXiv preprint (Renmin University of China + IAAR-Shanghai)  **Learning locus:** hybrid  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.14507

### Basic info

- **name**: Internal Consistency and Self-Feedback in Large Language Models: A Survey

- **year**: 2024

- **authors**: Xun Liang, Shichao Song, Zifan Zheng, et al. (lead affiliation: School of Information, Renmin University of China; LLM Center, Institute for Advanced Algorithms Research (IAAR), Shanghai; corresponding author Zhiyu Li)

- **venue**: arXiv preprint (cs.CL); not formally peer-reviewed at time of survey (v1 Jul 2024, v3 Sep 2024)

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.14507

- **code url**: https://github.com/IAAR-Shanghai/ICSFSurvey


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> calibration/probing (unified 'Internal Consistency' lens spanning latent/decoding/response layers) — survey covers all reflection types: verbal-self-critique (Verbal Critiquing, Self-Refine/Reflexion), learned-critic-model, multi-agent-debate, contrastive-decoding probing, and uncertainty/confidence/consistency estimation. Not a single method; it abstracts them under Self-Evaluation + Self-Update.

- **feedback source**:

> Predominantly self-generated (internal consistency signals from sampling across latent/decoding/response layers; e.g. Self-Consistency majority voting, verbal self-critique, hidden-state/attention-head probing). The survey explicitly notes 'generalized Self-Feedback' can also use other models (SelfEvaluate_N) or external tools (SelfEvaluate_tool), so external-tool and inter-model feedback are also surveyed.

- **iteration structure**:

> Surveys the full spectrum: single-shot (Self-Consistency sampling), iterative-refine (Self-Refine, Reflexion, Self-Debug), tree/search (Tree-of-Thoughts, Graph-of-Thoughts, MCTS-based self-improvement), and multi-agent collaboration/debate. Framework itself is layer-agnostic (Self-Evaluate -> Self-Update loop).

- **reflection object**:

> Survey scope spans multiple objects of reflection/modification. Self-Update can target (a) the output/response content (iterative response refinement), (b) the reasoning chain (Reasoning Topologically: CoT/ToT/GoT), (c) decoding distribution (truthful/contrastive decoding), (d) latent-layer activations (activating truthfulness, attention-head steering), and (e) the model's own weights (fine-tuning on self-selected/self-corrected data, e.g. Self-Improve, LEMA, Mistake Tuning). Unifying lens: 'internal consistency' across latent, decoding, and response layers.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: hybrid

- **requires training**:

> Surveys both training-free and training-based methods: none/in-context (Self-Consistency, Self-Refine, decoding-time methods) and SFT (self-generated data fine-tuning, e.g. Self-Improve, LEMA, Mistake Tuning) plus preference/RL approaches (DPO/RLHF discussed under Preference Learning). Survey itself requires no training (n/a as a method).

- **reward or critic model**:

> Surveys the range: self-as-judge (verbal self-critique, sampling/voting as scalar signal), trained reward/value functions (value function for best-selection), separate models (NLI models, other LLMs in debate), and internal-state probes (latent consistency as an implicit critic). Central abstraction: feedback signal f from SelfEvaluate.

- **distillation target**:

> Surveys multiple distillation/persistence targets: prompt/response (in-context refinement), model-weights (fine-tuning on self-generated/self-corrected reasoning data — Self-Improve, LEMA, Mistake Tuning, Self-improvement via MCTS data synthesis), and student-model distillation (Eq. 8, SelfUpdate_N updating a separate student / LLM-based knowledge distillation in Section VII). No dedicated episodic-memory/skill-library focus (agentic memory is largely out of scope).

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> Primarily covers prompt/scaffold-engineered reflective behaviors (Self-Refine, Reflexion, Multi-Agent Debate, decoding-time interventions). Predates the o1/R1 RL-emergent 'aha' reflection wave (survey v3 is Sep 2024), though its 'Reasoning Paradox' (latent vs explicit reasoning) and future-directions anticipate native/latent reflection. So: engineered-leaning, with forward-looking discussion toward emergent latent reasoning.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> n/a (survey; not an agent with memory). The lens is internal consistency (latent/decoding/response sampling), not episodic memory. Methods reviewed mostly use short-term/scratchpad-style iterative context; long-term/skill-library agentic memory is largely outside the survey's scope (agent memory listed among out-of-scope/related areas).

- **memory persistence**: n/a — surveyed methods operate mostly within-episode (single-task refinement); cross-task persistence appears only via weight updates (fine-tuning on self-generated data). Survey itself has no memory.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> n/a (survey does not propose a memory-curation scheme). For weight-update methods reviewed, the analog of curation is data selection/filtering (e.g. majority-vote best-response selection, GPT-4-annotated corrected rationales in LEMA) used to build fine-tuning datasets.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> Survey spans granularities: holistic/outcome-level (Self-Consistency answer voting), response-level (iterative response refinement, hallucination alleviation), step-level (reasoning-chain critique, topological reasoning over CoT/ToT/GoT nodes), token/decoding-level (truthful/contrastive decoding), latent-level (attention-head / hidden-state consistency), and agent-level (multi-agent collaboration/debate). Explicitly framed by the latent/decoding/response 'Hourglass' layering.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> Covers both. Intra-task: refine within one task (Self-Refine, iterative response refinement, decoding-time correction). Inter-task: transfer via weight updates (Self-Improve/LEMA/Mistake Tuning fine-tune the model so improvement persists across tasks). Emphasis is more on intra-task consistency mining than agentic cross-task experience transfer.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> Mix of post-hoc-revision (iterative refinement of an already-produced response/CoT) and avoidance via learning (fine-tuning to avoid prior mistakes, e.g. 'Learning from mistakes' / Mistake Tuning). Mid-trajectory recovery is less central (predates Agent-R-style in-flight correction). Decoding-time methods act in-flight to steer toward truthful tokens.


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> QA/reasoning (math, knowledge, logic), free-form generation / hallucination mitigation, code generation, dialogue, and general alignment/preference learning. Two flagship task buckets in the survey: Reasoning Elevation (QA) and Hallucination Alleviation (open-ended generation); plus 'Others' (preference learning, knowledge distillation, data augmentation).

- **benchmarks**:

> Common evaluation benchmarks tabulated (Table VI): C-Eval, MMLU, BBH, ARC, WiC, HumanEval, MATH, GSM8K. Other tasks referenced in critique/discussion include TruthfulQA, Game-of-24, Graph Coloring, and planning tasks. Survey also catalogs meta-evaluation methods/benchmarks for Self-Feedback components.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> No single headline number (it is a survey, not an empirical method). Its core qualitative 'result'/claim: Self-Feedback reliably improves internal consistency ('Does Self-Feedback improve internal consistency? Yes'), but whether internal consistency equals correctness 'cannot be directly concluded' — captured by the 'Consistency Is (Almost) Correctness' hypothesis. It organizes 100+ 'Self-*' works under the unified Self-Evaluation + Self-Update framework across latent/decoding/response layers.

- **baselines**:

> n/a (survey). Positions itself against prior surveys that 'predominantly focus on categorization' and against fragmented/biased treatments of 'Does self-correction work' (e.g. it argues Huang et al. and Kamoi et al. give either limited-perspective or overly-complex answers). Provides a unified internal-consistency-based alternative framing.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> n/a (no empirical delta; survey). Conceptual contributions over prior surveys: (1) unified Self-Feedback framework (Self-Evaluation + Self-Update) instead of pure categorization; (2) layer-based 'Hourglass Evolution of Internal Consistency' (latent -> decoding -> response); (3) a more 'insightful' affirmative-but-qualified answer to 'Does Self-Feedback Really Work?'; (4) novel hypotheses: 'Consistency Is (Almost) Correctness' and 'The Paradox of Latent and Explicit Reasoning'.

- **compute cost profile**:

> n/a as a survey; but it discusses cost as a critique axis — e.g. it relays Huang et al.'s point that Multi-Agent Debate is 'resource-heavy' and inferior to (cheaper) Self-Consistency, and that sampling/iterative refinement methods multiply inference calls. No quantified token/FLOP multipliers of its own.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Survey-stated limitations of the field it reviews: (1) self-correction often depends on external/oracle feedback to actually improve (Huang et al. [87], Kamoi et al. [21]); (2) models are better at generating than verifying answers (SELF-[IN]CORRECT, Jiang et al. [137]); (3) self-verifiers produce many false positives (Stechly/Valmeekam on Graph Coloring & planning); (4) self-refinement can amplify self-bias (cites 'Pride and Prejudice'); (5) internal consistency does not guarantee correctness (vagueness/hallucination inherent to probabilistic LMs). Survey-specific: largely pre-o1/R1 reasoning-model era; agentic long-term memory mostly out of scope.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> Explicitly the discriminating variable in the survey's critique synthesis. It distinguishes intrinsic-only / self-verify methods from those needing external-tool/verifier or oracle-label/ground-truth. Key relayed finding: Reflexion-style refinement relying on external truth is 'impractical' when no oracle exists; self-correction works best on decomposable or verifiable tasks (where verification is easier than generation, e.g. Game-of-24), and is unreliable on QA without external signals.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent / requires-oracle. Survey's nuanced conclusion: Self-Feedback DOES improve internal consistency (net-positive on consistency), but improvement in CORRECTNESS is not guaranteed and is task-dependent — feasible for decomposable/verifiable tasks, unreliable (sometimes net-negative/degrading) for intrinsic self-correction on open QA without external/oracle feedback (consistent with Huang et al. 'LLMs cannot self-correct reasoning yet').

- **calibration effect**:

> mixed / partly negative. The survey notes models show 'overconfidence without understanding their capability limits' and relays self-bias amplification under self-refinement; internal-consistency signals can serve self-evaluation/calibration (cites Calibrating Reasoning with Internal Consistency) but consistency is not equal to correctness. Net: calibration via self-feedback is promising but not reliably positive (mixed).


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> classifies-failure-mode (taxonomy). As a survey it organizes the field into a taxonomy (4 tasks: Consistency Signal Acquisition, Reasoning Elevation, Hallucination Alleviation, Others; lines of work in Table IV) and catalogs causes of low internal consistency (inadequate latent reasoning, hallucination snowball effect, stochastic-parrot hypothesis). It does not attribute responsibility to specific agents/steps in a trace.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Targets/exposes: reasoning deficiencies and hallucinations (the two core problems), inconsistent responses to identical queries, overconfidence/miscalibration, superficial or ineffective self-reflection/self-correction (relayed critiques), self-bias amplification in self-refinement, and the latent-vs-explicit reasoning tension ('Reasoning Paradox'). Related to MAST modes such as superficial self-reflection and overconfidence, though the survey predates and does not use the MAST taxonomy.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new dataset/benchmark proposed. Releases an open-source resource hub (paper list, framework figures, the Hourglass/Internal-Consistency experiment code) at https://github.com/IAAR-Shanghai/ICSFSurvey. Tabulates existing evaluation benchmarks (Table VI: C-Eval, MMLU, BBH, ARC, WiC, HumanEval, MATH, GSM8K) and meta-evaluation methods rather than releasing one.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Synthesizes and builds on the 'Self-*' literature: Self-Consistency (Wang et al.), Self-Refine (Madaan et al.), Reflexion (Shinn et al.), Self-Improve (Huang et al.), Tree-of-Thoughts (Yao et al.), Graph-of-Thoughts, Quiet-STaR/STaR, Self-Debug, LEMA (Learning from Mistakes), Mistake Tuning, SelfCheckGPT, Multi-Agent Debate, contrastive/context-aware decoding (DoLa, CAD), and the critique works Huang et al. ('LLMs Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet'), Kamoi et al. (self-correction survey), and SELF-[IN]CORRECT (Jiang et al.).

- **extended by or inspired**:

> Cited by ~53 follow-up works (Semantic Scholar, Jun 2026), including: 'LLMs Know More Than They Show: On the Intrinsic Representation of LLM Hallucinations' (Orgad et al., ICLR 2025), 'Scalable Best-of-N Selection via Self-Certainty' (Kang/Zhao/Song 2025), 'DSVD: Dynamic Self-Verify Decoding' (EMNLP 2025), 'Dynamic Attention-Guided Context Decoding (DAGCD)' (ACL 2025), 'Latent Debate' (2025), 'Alleviating Hallucinations with Scepticism Modeling' (2024), 'Calibrating Reasoning with Internal Consistency' (NeurIPS 2024), and several hallucination/cognition surveys (e.g. Loki's Dance of Illusions).

- **citation count**: ~53 (Semantic Scholar, Jun 2026; cross-checked: Semantic Scholar search snippet ~50, paperswithcode ~52)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> Mostly no / forward-looking. Survey v3 (Sep 2024) predates wide o1/R1 adoption and focuses on engineered Self-* methods, but its 'Internal Consistency' framing across latent/decoding/response layers and 'The Paradox of Latent and Explicit Reasoning' directly motivate study of native latent reasoning in reasoning models; it anticipates rather than targets o1/R1-style built-in reflection.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Indirect. Surveys self-distillation / self-improvement where a model fine-tunes on its own (often self-selected via majority-vote/MCTS, hence on-policy-flavored) generations (Self-Improve, LEMA, Mistake Tuning) and student-model updates via SelfUpdate_N (Eq. 8). This is conceptually adjacent to on-policy distillation / self-training, though the survey does not use that terminology or analyze it as OPD.

- **sample efficiency**:

> n/a (survey; no single trials-to-gain figure). It does relay efficiency-relevant critiques (e.g. Multi-Agent Debate is resource-heavy vs Self-Consistency; sampling/iterative methods multiply inference calls), and its 'Reasoning Paradox' frames efficient use of reasoning resources as an open problem.
