<a id="r076-a-survey-on-llm-inference-time-self-improvement"></a>
## A Survey on LLM Inference-Time Self-Improvement

**ID:** R076  **Category:** J (Surveys & roadmaps)  **Authors:** Dong, Teleki & Caverlee  **Venue:** arXiv preprint (Texas A&M University)  **Learning locus:** in_context_verbal  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14352

### Basic info

- **name**: A Survey on LLM Inference-Time Self-Improvement

- **year**: 2024

- **authors**: Xiangjue Dong, Maria Teleki, James Caverlee (first two authors contributed equally); Texas A&M University

- **venue**: arXiv preprint (cs.CL); not peer-reviewed at time of survey

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14352

- **code url**: https://github.com/dongxiangjue/Awesome-LLM-Self-Improvement (curated reading-list / online resource; the survey itself releases no model or training code)


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> calibration/probing — as a SURVEY it catalogs multiple mechanisms rather than proposing one. Coverage spans: decoding-level steering (constrained/contrastive/MBR/parallel/sampling/tree-search/model-level decoding), context-aware prompting (CoT, Zero-shot CoT, EchoPrompt) and retrieval, and model-aided collaboration (expert/anti-expert, draft, amateur, reward-model-guided search, tool/API use). Verbal self-critique and multi-agent debate are NOT the central organizing axis; the survey's lens is 'frozen-parameter inference-time improvement' broadly.

- **feedback source**:

> Heterogeneous across surveyed methods: self-generated (sampling/self-consistency, contrastive decoding), external-tool (retrieval datastores, tools/APIs), trained reward/value models (RAD, ARGS, TS-LLM, Controlled Decoding), and auxiliary expert/amateur/draft models. The survey itself generates no new feedback signal.

- **iteration structure**:

> Surveys the full spectrum: single-shot decoding manipulations, multi-sample parallel/sampling decoding, and tree/MCTS-search-based decoding (PG-TD, GDP-Zero, RAP, TS-LLM). No single iteration structure — taxonomy spans all.

- **reflection object**:

> Primary object across the surveyed taxonomy is the model's OUTPUT generation process at inference time — specifically next-token selection via logits, the softmax probability distribution, and the decoding objective — plus the prompt/context (prompting and retrieval-augmented context). Explicitly EXCLUDES model weights: the defining constraint is 'relying on the LLM's own frozen parameters without additional training or parameter updating.'


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: in_context_verbal — n/a (analysis/survey). The survey's entire scope is defined as inference-time improvement WITHOUT weight updates (frozen parameters); as a Category-J survey it performs no learning itself.

- **requires training**:

> none (for the surveyed paradigm as a whole — inference-time methods require no fine-tuning of the base LLM). Some surveyed model-aided methods use separately pre-trained auxiliary reward/value models, but the base LLM is never updated. The survey explicitly contrasts this with PEFT (LoRA, DoRA) in Appendix B, arguing inference-time methods avoid the need for a dataset and access to model parameters.

- **reward or critic model**:

> Varies by surveyed method: none (decoding-only methods), self-as-judge (self-consistency / sampling-based reasoning), and trained reward/value models (RAD's reward model, ARGS reward-guided search, TS-LLM's learned value + outcome reward model, Controlled Decoding's prefix scorer). The survey itself uses no critic.

- **distillation target**:

> none — inference-time self-improvement is defined as NOT distilling reflection into any persisted artifact (no weight update, no learned skill library). Improvement is realized transiently during decoding via context, retrieval datastores, or auxiliary models, not stored back into the model.

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> engineered/scaffold-based — the surveyed methods are explicitly designed decoding algorithms, prompts, retrieval pipelines, and model-collaboration scaffolds applied to frozen LLMs. The survey predates and does not center RL-emergent reflection (o1/R1-style 'aha'); reflective behavior here is hand-engineered around a frozen model.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> structured-notes/graph — surveyed under Context-Aware Self-Improvement §3.3 'Retrieval-based': external corpora or constructed key-value/reference datastores (kNN-LM, NEST, REST, RTD, Multi-Input CD). This is a retrieval datastore rather than an episodic agent memory; for decoding-only and most prompting methods, memory_type is none/short-term.

- **memory persistence**:

> cross-task — retrieval datastores persist external knowledge usable across queries/tasks. The survey does not address production cross-session agent memory; persistence here means a static/maintained datastore, not accumulated experience.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> retrieval-gated — for the retrieval-based subcategory, relevant entries are selected via nearest-neighbor / top-k retrieval over a datastore (kNN-LM, REST Trie of frequent candidates, RTD top-k references). The survey's Discussion flags 'Maintenance': datastore-/model-dependent methods require ongoing updating over time, unlike independent decoding methods.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> token-level — the dominant granularity across the surveyed taxonomy is next-token / logit-level intervention (constrained, contrastive, reward-augmented, retrieval-augmented decoding all reweight per-token distributions). Higher-level granularities also appear: response/hypothesis-level (MBR over candidate generations, self-consistency) and trajectory/plan-level (tree-search/MCTS decoding).

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> intra-task — methods improve a single inference/generation for the current input (better decoding, retrieval, or model collaboration on the given query). The survey does not center cross-task experience transfer (Reflexion/ExpeL-style), since its defining constraint is no parameter update and no persisted experience.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> mid-trajectory-recovery — decoding-level interventions correct generation in-flight (e.g., contrastive decoding suppressing hallucination/repetition per token, reward-guided steering, tree-search backtracking). This is in-generation steering rather than episodic retry-then-avoid.


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> Broad NLP/reasoning coverage surveyed: reasoning/QA (CoT, Zero-shot CoT, self-consistency, MCTS reasoning), faithful/factual generation and hallucination reduction (contrastive/retrieval decoding), code generation (PG-TD), dialogue/planning (GDP-Zero, RAP), machine translation (MBR decoding), alignment/trustworthiness (ARGS, URIAL, DecodingTrust), and tool-use/APIs. Applications enumerated in Appendix C / Table 1.

- **benchmarks**:

> As a survey it does not run its own benchmarks; it aggregates results from cited primary works across reasoning (GSM8K-style math/QA), machine translation (MBR), hallucination/factuality, code generation, and trustworthiness suites (e.g., DecodingTrust). No single benchmark is central; per-method benchmarks live in the cited papers.


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> No original quantitative result — this is a survey (Category J). Its contribution is a three-axis taxonomy of inference-time self-improvement (Independent / Context-Aware / Model-Aided Self-Improvement, coined 'ITSI', pronounced 'itsy') over frozen-parameter LLMs, plus a discussion of selection criteria, challenges, and limitations.

- **baselines**:

> n/a — no experimental comparison. Conceptually positioned against (a) train-time scaling / larger-model pretraining and alignment (RLHF, DPO) and (b) parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT: LoRA, ProLoRA, DoRA), which the survey argues still need datasets and parameter access (Appendix B).

- **gains vs baseline**: n/a — no measured delta reported by the survey itself. Gains for individual surveyed methods are attributed to their original papers and not re-benchmarked here.

- **compute cost profile**:

> Discussed qualitatively under 'Trade-Offs in Inference Costs': methods that scale inference (multiple-generation sampling §2.5, tree-search §2.6) cost more wall-clock/tokens at inference than methods that directly manipulate the decoding step; the central premise is trading extra TEST-TIME compute (no training compute) for quality/efficiency. No explicit numeric multiplier is given.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> Survey-stated challenges (Discussion §5): (1) Maintenance — datastore/model-dependent methods need ongoing updates; (2) Amount of model access — e.g., OpenAI Chat API returns only a partial probability distribution, so full-distribution methods are infeasible on closed APIs; (3) Trade-offs in inference cost (latency/compute of multi-sample and search methods); (4) Generalizability — external expert/auxiliary models are domain/task-specialized and need re-creation or fine-tuning for new contexts, with performance tied to auxiliary-model quality; (5) Generation quality — constraint enforcement competes with the LLM's fluency/coherence tendencies; (6) Explainability/interpretability — few works analyze the decoding process at the neuron/attention-head or theoretical level. Authors' own Limitations note: not exhaustive; coverage focused on ACL/EMNLP/NAACL/NeurIPS/ICLR/ICML/arXiv. Ethical considerations: social bias (e.g., Zero-shot CoT can increase harmful outputs), economic equity, environmental sustainability.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> external-tool/verifier — many of the most effective surveyed methods depend on external support: retrieval datastores (Context-Aware) and auxiliary/reward/expert models (Model-Aided). The survey frames a spectrum from intrinsic decoding-only methods (no external feedback) to methods reliant on external models/datastores, and flags that performance is closely tied to the quality of these auxiliary components.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent — the survey emphasizes method selection criteria (model access, maintenance, cost, generalizability, generation-quality trade-offs) rather than claiming uniform net-positive improvement. Efficacy depends on task, available model access, and auxiliary-model quality; constraint-enforcing methods can degrade fluency.

- **calibration effect**:

> not-measured — the survey does not quantify confidence calibration or a 'reasoning tax'. It does note interpretability/explainability gaps and that some decoding/prompting strategies (e.g., Zero-shot CoT) can increase harmful outputs, but offers no calibration measurement.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> classifies-failure-mode (taxonomy) — at the method level the survey provides an in-depth taxonomy of inference-time self-improvement approaches and a structured discussion of their failure/limitation modes (maintenance, model-access, cost, generalizability, generation-quality, explainability). It does not do per-step or per-agent failure attribution (not a Category-I attribution method).

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Decoding/generation-level failure modes surfaced by surveyed methods: hallucination and factual unfaithfulness (contrastive decoding: DoLa, LCD, Anti-LM; retrieval decoding: RTD, Multi-Input CD), degenerate repetition (Look-back, Adaptive Decoding), constraint violation (constrained decoding: NeuroLogic, Control-DAG), and reasoning errors / lack of lookahead (sampling-based self-consistency, tree-search MCTS). Loosely maps to MAST-style 'superficial reasoning'/factuality errors but the survey does not use a multi-agent failure taxonomy.

- **dataset or benchmark released**: none (no new dataset or trace corpus). The authors release a curated, continuously-updated reading list / online resource: https://github.com/dongxiangjue/Awesome-LLM-Self-Improvement.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Synthesizes and organizes prior inference-time / decoding literature, including: Self-Consistency (Wang et al. 2023), Chain-of-Thought and Zero-shot CoT (Wei et al. 2022; Kojima et al. 2022), contrastive decoding (DoLa, Anti-LM, LCD, PMI-Decode), kNN-LM retrieval (Khandelwal et al. 2020) and speculative/retrieval decoding (REST, NEST), reward/value-guided decoding (RAD, ARGS, Controlled Decoding, TS-LLM), and MCTS/planning decoding (PG-TD, RAP, GDP-Zero). Conceptually contrasts with train-time scaling (Kaplan et al. 2020) and PEFT (LoRA et al.).

- **citation count**: 16 (Semantic Scholar, paperId a9d1356dad110f4ad04d223c9fee1eb6fd2e3455, retrieved 2026-06; influentialCitationCount 0)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> no / not-centered — the survey is framed around applying inference-time techniques to standard frozen LLMs (GPT/Gemini-class) and predates centering o1/R1-style models with built-in RL-trained reflection. It discusses test-time compute scaling generally but is not specific to reasoning-model-native self-reflection.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> none / negative-by-definition — the survey's defining boundary is NO parameter update and NO distillation of behavior back into weights; it explicitly contrasts itself with fine-tuning (including PEFT). It is therefore the inference-time counterpoint to on-policy distillation / skill-internalization rather than an instance of it.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- extended_by_or_inspired
- sample_efficiency

<a id="r077-lifelong-learning-of-large-language-model-based-agents-a-roadmap"></a>
## Lifelong Learning of Large Language Model based Agents: A Roadmap

**ID:** R077  **Category:** J (Surveys & roadmaps)  **Authors:** Zheng, Shi, Cai et al.  **Venue:** arXiv preprint (South China Univ. of Technology / Tencent AI Lab)  **Learning locus:** hybrid  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.07278

### Basic info

- **name**: Lifelong Learning of Large Language Model based Agents: A Roadmap

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**:

> Junhao Zheng, Chengming Shi, Xidi Cai, Qiuke Li, Duzhen Zhang, Chenxing Li, Dong Yu, Qianli Ma (equal contribution by first four); lead affiliation: South China University of Technology (SCUT), with Tencent AI Lab and MBZUAI

- **venue**: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (TPAMI), 2026; arXiv preprint 2501.07278 (v1 Jan 2025, v2 Jan 2026)

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.07278

- **code url**: https://github.com/qianlima-lab/awesome-lifelong-llm-agent (curated literature/resource list, not a single method implementation)


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**:

> none (survey). As an analysis object it taxonomizes reflection-related methods it reviews: verbal-self-critique (Reflexion), multi-agent-debate / model-feedback critics (N-CRITICS), tool-verified self-correction (CRITIC), and calibration/confidence-based intrinsic correction (If-or-Else prompting). Self-correction is treated as a Working-Memory sub-capability (Section 6.4) and experience-driven reflection as an Episodic/Reasoning-Action capability (Sections 7.3, 12).

- **feedback source**:

> n/a for the survey itself; it catalogues feedback sources used by reviewed works: self-generated verbal feedback, external-tool feedback (search engine, code interpreter via CRITIC), other-model critic feedback (N-CRITICS), environment reward/interaction feedback, and self-confidence assessment.

- **iteration structure**:

> n/a (survey). It organizes reviewed methods along single-trial vs multi-trial and intra-episodic vs inter-episodic axes, covering iterative-refine (self-correction), episodic-retry (Reflexion across trials), and tree/MCTS search (Tree of Thoughts, RAP, LLM-MCTS) approaches.

- **reflection object**:

> As a survey, it spans multiple objects across its three-module taxonomy: output content and reasoning chain (Working-Memory self-correction, Reasoning Actions), action trajectory and experience (Episodic Memory: self-experience, continual RL), prompt/context (Working-Memory prompt optimization, prompt compression), reusable skill/workflow (skill libraries, Agent Workflow Memory), external knowledge (Semantic Memory: knowledge graphs, documents), and model weights (Parametric Memory: continual instruction tuning, knowledge editing, alignment).


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: hybrid

- **requires training**:

> n/a (survey). It explicitly covers the full spectrum of reviewed techniques: training-free in-context methods (prompting, self-correction, episodic experience reuse), continual SFT (continual instruction tuning), continual RL (continual reinforcement learning of agents), and continual alignment (preference/DPO-style updates) under the Parametric Memory module.

- **reward or critic model**:

> n/a (survey). It surveys multiple improvement signals among reviewed works: self-as-judge (intrinsic self-correction, confidence assessment), separate/other-model critics (N-CRITICS), external verifiable tools (CRITIC), and environment reward (continual RL).

- **distillation target**:

> n/a as a method; the survey frames where experience is consolidated across its memory taxonomy: episodic-memory (self-experience, replay), reusable-skill/workflow (skill libraries, Agent Workflow Memory/AWM), prompt (prompt optimization/compression), structured external knowledge (semantic memory / knowledge graphs), and model-weights (parametric memory).

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> Mostly surveys scaffold/prompt-engineered reflective behaviors (Reflexion, CRITIC, N-CRITICS, self-correction prompting, skill libraries). The v1 (Jan 2025) framing predates wide adoption of RL-emergent reasoning; reinforcement-learning-based self-evolution is discussed primarily as a future direction (Section 15.3, 'Reinforcement Learning for Self-Learning and Evolution') rather than centered on R1-style emergent reflection.


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> Surveys all categories. Its central contribution is a four-type memory taxonomy: Working Memory (short-term/scratchpad), Episodic Memory (long-term-episodic experience), Semantic Memory (external structured-notes/knowledge-graph/document store), and Parametric Memory (knowledge stored in model weights). Also covers skill-library / workflow memory under action and reasoning modules.

- **memory persistence**:

> Covers the full range: within-episode (working memory), cross-episode and cross-task (episodic/semantic memory, continual learning), and toward cross-session production deployment. The survey's explicit goal is cross-task / lifelong persistence that mitigates catastrophic forgetting across an agent's lifetime.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> Surveys multiple curation strategies and flags memory growth as an open challenge (Section 15.2 'Dynamic Memory Management'): append-only experience stores, self-summarized/curated memory, replay buffers (data/feature replay), retrieval-gated access (retrieval actions over semantic/episodic memory), knowledge distillation for consolidation, and proactive pruning/summarization of outdated knowledge. Neuro-inspired consolidation is proposed as a future direction.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> n/a as a single method; the survey reviews methods spanning holistic/outcome-level (trial-level Reflexion), response-level self-correction (N-CRITICS, CRITIC), and step-level reasoning correction (Tree of Thoughts, RAP, MCTS-based reasoning actions). No single localization granularity is proposed.

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> Both, and this is an explicit organizing axis of the survey. Section 12 distinguishes Intra-Episodic Reasoning Actions (single-trial and across-trial within a task, e.g. ReAct, Reflexion, Tree of Thoughts) from Inter-Episodic Reasoning Actions (transfer of experience across tasks/episodes, e.g. ICAL, GITM, Voyager). The lifelong-learning framing emphasizes inter-task / cross-episode experience transfer.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> Surveys both: avoidance via cross-trial reflection (Reflexion reflects on past failed trials to improve the next trial), mid-trajectory recovery via in-flight self-correction (CRITIC, N-CRITICS revise current output using tool/critic feedback), and post-hoc revision. The lifelong lens stresses accumulating experience to avoid repeating failures across episodes.


### Application domain

- **task domains**:

> Broad coverage: web-navigation, embodied/games (Minecraft via Voyager/GITM), tool-use, QA/reasoning, code, dialogue, role-playing, decision-making, plus domain-specific applications in education, law, and medicine. Organized around perception (web/charts/games, multimodal), memory, and action (grounding/retrieval/reasoning).

- **benchmarks**:

> Catalogues benchmarks in two groups. Simple/skill-specific continual-learning: CITB, GLUE, SuperGLUE, NaturalInstructions/SuperNI, WMT, TED Talks, CLLE, zsRE, FEVER, CounterFact, Concept-1K, Biography. Complex agent environments: ToolBench, StableToolBench, APIBench, ToolAlpaca, API-Bank, WebArena, WebShop, WorkArena, VisualWebArena, VideoWebArena, AgentBench, VisualAgentBench, Mind2Web, plus game environments (Minecraft).


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> Survey/roadmap with no single quantitative headline; it claims to be the first to systematically organize lifelong-learning techniques for LLM-based agents into a perception / memory / action three-module framework, and contributes a unified taxonomy plus lifelong-learning evaluation metrics (AP, AIP, FGT, BWT, FWT).

- **baselines**:

> n/a (survey). Positions itself against prior surveys it cites, notably Zheng et al. 'Towards Lifelong Learning of Large Language Models: A Survey' (arXiv 2406.06391) and a continual-learning-for-LLMs survey by Shi et al., arguing those treat LLMs as static black boxes without environment interaction, whereas this survey centers agent-environment interaction.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> n/a (no empirical comparison; survey/roadmap). It does not report performance deltas; instead it formalizes lifelong-learning metrics by which agents could be compared: Average Performance (AP), Average Incremental Performance (AIP), Forgetting Measure (FGT), Backward Transfer (BWT), and Forward Transfer (FWT).

- **compute cost profile**:

> n/a (survey). It discusses compute/scaling qualitatively as open challenges (scalable memory architectures, ever-growing memory volume, dynamic memory management) but reports no inference-token multipliers or training-cost figures.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> As stated for the field/survey: catastrophic forgetting and loss of plasticity (the stability-plasticity dilemma) remain unsolved; perception fails on novel distributions/modalities; memory does not scale gracefully (growth, retrieval, pruning); tree/MCTS reasoning methods unrealistically assume states are retraceable (e.g. irreversible web payments); lack of standardized, realistic, reproducible benchmarks and unified evaluation. As a survey it is a roadmap rather than an empirical contribution, so claims are not experimentally validated here.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> n/a as a method; the survey explicitly distinguishes feedback sources among reviewed self-correction works: intrinsic-only / self-verify (If-or-Else confidence-based intrinsic self-correction), other-model critics (N-CRITICS), and external-tool/verifier dependence (CRITIC using search engine / code interpreter), plus environment-reward via continual RL. It does not adjudicate the Huang/Kamoi 'self-correction needs oracle' critique.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent (as surveyed). The survey presents self-correction as a working-memory capability that improves outputs via iterative feedback (self, other-model, or tool), without quantifying when intrinsic correction fails; it does not take a strong empirical position on net-positive vs net-negative correction.

- **calibration effect**: not-measured. The survey discusses confidence self-assessment (If-or-Else intrinsic self-correction) as a self-correction strategy but does not analyze calibration improvement/degradation or a 'reasoning tax'.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> n/a (the survey is a roadmap, not a failure-attribution method). It addresses failure conceptually via catastrophic forgetting and loss of plasticity and via reflection-on-failed-trials (Reflexion) but provides no failure-attribution taxonomy or responsible-agent/step localization.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Primary failure modes framed at the field level: catastrophic forgetting (loss of past knowledge) and loss of plasticity (inability to adapt) — the stability-plasticity dilemma. Reviewed reflection methods (Reflexion) target repeating past mistakes by reflecting on failed trials; relation to MAST's 14 multi-agent failure modes is not addressed.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> No new dataset or benchmark released. The contribution is a curated, continuously updated resource/literature repository (awesome-lifelong-llm-agent on GitHub) and a survey-level catalogue/categorization of existing benchmarks; no original traces or labeled failure dataset.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Prior lifelong/continual-learning surveys for LLMs: Zheng et al. 'Towards Lifelong Learning of Large Language Models: A Survey' (arXiv 2406.06391, same first author); Shi et al. continual-learning-for-LLMs survey; classic continual-learning surveys (De Lange et al. TPAMI 2021; Wang et al. TPAMI 2024). Core agent methods it synthesizes: ReAct, Reflexion, Tree of Thoughts, Voyager, GITM, CRITIC, N-CRITICS, Agent Workflow Memory (AWM), ICAL, FireAct.

- **citation count**: 72 (Semantic Scholar API, paperId 76aebf01bdfeaf743ac83ac231384a861f7b69ca, retrieved 2026-06-08; influential citation count 2)


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> Not specifically targeted. The v1 framing (Jan 2025) precedes broad reasoning-model adoption; RL-driven self-evolution is treated as a future direction (Section 15.3) rather than a study of o1/R1-style models with built-in reflection. The v2 (Jan 2026) revision may update this, but the core taxonomy is model-agnostic and centers on external memory/action scaffolding rather than native reasoning models.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Indirect. Knowledge distillation and replay are surveyed as consolidation mechanisms for the memory module, and continual RL / experience reuse are discussed, but there is no explicit treatment of on-policy distillation or skill-optimization as a named technique.

- **sample efficiency**:

> n/a (survey reports no trials-to-gain measurements). It motivates lifelong learning partly by sample/efficiency arguments (reusing past experience for faster adaptation, 'Transfer Learning for Rapid Adaptation') but gives no quantitative sample-efficiency figures.


### Uncertain (not determined)

- extended_by_or_inspired

<a id="r078-adaptation-of-agentic-ai-a-survey-of-post-training-memory-and-skills"></a>
## Adaptation of Agentic AI: A Survey of Post-Training, Memory, and Skills

**ID:** R078  **Category:** J (Surveys & roadmaps)  **Authors:** Jiang, Lin, Shi et al. (Jiawei Han group)  **Venue:** arXiv preprint (UIUC, Stanford, Princeton, Harvard et al.)  **Learning locus:** hybrid  **URL:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.16301

### Basic info

- **name**: Adaptation of Agentic AI: A Survey of Post-Training, Memory, and Skills

- **year**: 2025

- **authors**: Pengcheng Jiang, Jiacheng Lin, Zhiyi Shi, et al. (34 authors; Jiawei Han group). Lead affiliation UIUC, with Stanford, Princeton, Harvard, UC Berkeley, Caltech, UW, UCSD, Georgia Tech, Northwestern, TAMU, MGH.

- **venue**: arXiv preprint (cs.AI; cs.CL). arXiv:2512.16301, submitted 18 Dec 2025, last revised 9 Mar 2026 (v3). Not yet peer-reviewed.

- **paper url**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.16301


### Core mechanism

- **reflection type**: calibration/probing

- **feedback source**: self-generated

- **iteration structure**: single-shot

- **reflection object**:

> As a survey, it is an analysis (no single mechanism). It taxonomizes what the surveyed methods reflect on / modify: model weights (A1/A2 post-training), action trajectories and reusable skills/workflows (skill libraries), prompt/context and episodic memory (adaptive memory systems including episodic buffers, reflective databases, structured knowledge graphs), and the agent-tool interaction. The survey itself reflects on the design space of agent adaptation rather than performing reflection on outputs.


### Learning paradigm

- **learning locus**: n/a (analysis/survey)

- **requires training**: none

- **reward or critic model**: none

- **distillation target**:

> Survey-level: it catalogs all distillation targets used by surveyed methods — model-weights (post-training via SFT/DPO/RLVR), episodic-memory (episodic buffers, reflective databases), reusable-skill/workflow (skill libraries such as Voyager, EXPEL, JARVIS-1, CREATOR, ASI), and structured-rules/notes (knowledge graphs, curated reasoning strategies as in ReasoningBank). The survey treats long-term memory as a special case of T2 (agent-supervised tool adaptation).

- **emergent vs engineered**:

> Discusses both: A2 end-to-end RL produces RL-emergent behaviors (self-correction, adaptive search depth, query refinement never explicitly supervised, e.g., DeepSeek-R1 'aha'-style emergence), while memory/skill systems and scaffolds are prompt/engineered. The survey explicitly contrasts RL-emergent strategic behavior (A2) against engineered modular tool/memory adaptation (T1/T2).


### Memory mechanism

- **memory type**:

> Survey covering multiple: long-term-episodic (episodic buffers), structured-notes/graph (reflective databases, structured knowledge graphs), skill-library (executable-code skills, abstract heuristics, API/MCP protocols, synthesized tools, full-trajectory stores), and playbook/cheatsheet (curated reasoning strategies, e.g., ReasoningBank). Memory is framed as a special case of T2 agent-supervised tool adaptation.

- **memory persistence**:

> cross-session (production). The survey emphasizes persistent memory and reusable skills accumulated across episodes, tasks, and sessions (motivated by systems like OpenClaw that accumulate persistent memory and reusable skills); covers within-episode through cross-session.

- **memory curation mechanism**:

> Surveys multiple curation strategies: self-summarized/curated (memory curators store concise transferable snippets — reusable strategies, code snippets, problem-solving insights — rather than full transcripts; ReasoningBank distills generalizable strategies from both successful and self-judged failed experiences, extracting preventative lessons from failures), retrieval-gated (RAG-style retrieval of memory/skills to guide future tasks), and overwrite/evolution (skill refinement across sessions). Append-only raw-trajectory storage is contrasted as the less effective baseline.


### Reflection granularity & timing

- **error localization granularity**:

> Survey-level: the central A1-vs-A2 axis IS an error-localization axis. A1 (tool-execution-signaled) gives step-level/per-action dense feedback (e.g., code execution pass/fail, retrieval recall); A2 (agent-output-signaled) gives holistic/outcome-level sparse feedback on the final output with difficult credit assignment. Multi-agent/agent-level localization also discussed (lightweight subagents).

- **intra task vs inter task**:

> Primarily inter-task: the survey's framing of adaptation is improving an agent/tools across tasks and sessions (transfer of experience via memory, skills, and weight updates). Memory and skill systems explicitly transfer experience across tasks/sessions; post-training transfers learned skills inter-task.

- **failure recovery vs avoidance**:

> Survey-level / mixed: covers methods spanning mid-trajectory recovery (RL-emergent self-correction within trajectories in A2) and avoidance/learning-for-next-time (memory of failures, e.g., ReasoningBank's preventative lessons from failed experiences applied to future tasks).


### Application domain

- **task domains**: code (software development), QA/reasoning, web-navigation, computer-use, tool-use, decision-making, and scientific domains including drug discovery; general agentic AI. Deep research is a highlighted application domain.

- **benchmarks**:

> Maps benchmarks onto A1/A2/T1/T2 paradigms. Mentioned suites include SWE-Bench (software development), WebArena and Mind2Web/web-navigation, OSWorld (computer use), GAIA (deep research/tool-use), and medical/general QA benchmarks; scientific tool benchmarks (SciToolAgent). Verifiable-execution metrics (pass@k, recall) vs holistic-utility metrics (final-answer correctness).


### Evaluation results

- **headline result**:

> No single model result (survey). Representative synthesis: s3 (a T2 search subagent) reaches 58.9% average generation accuracy using only 2.4k training samples — 70x less data than Search-R1 (an A2 agent needing ~170k examples) and 33x faster wall-clock training — and generalizes better (76.6% vs 71.8% on medical QA). Illustrates that T2 tool adaptation can match A2 with orders of magnitude less data.

- **baselines**:

> As a survey it contrasts the four adaptation paradigms (A1, A2, T1, T2) against each other and against prompting-only / monolithic retraining; representative head-to-heads include T2 (s3) vs A2 (Search-R1). Also positions itself against prior AI-agent surveys as the first survey centered specifically on adaptation.

- **gains vs baseline**:

> Survey-reported deltas for cited systems: s3 (T2) achieves 70x data efficiency and 33x faster training vs Search-R1 (A2) at comparable/better accuracy (58.9% avg; 76.6% vs 71.8% medical QA); SciToolAgent's knowledge-graph tool retrieval reaches 94% tool-selection accuracy, a 15-20% improvement over GPT-4o without tools. Core thesis: T2/T1 modular tool adaptation can match A1/A2 weight-update gains at far lower cost while avoiding catastrophic forgetting.

- **compute cost profile**:

> A central comparative axis. A1/A2 (agent weight updates) are expensive (RL rollouts, gradient steps, GPU training) and risk catastrophic forgetting — likened to 'going back to college'. T1/T2 (tool/memory adaptation, frozen agent) are cheaper, faster, modular, and hot-swappable. Quantified: T2 method s3 uses 2.4k samples (70x less than A2's 170k) and trains 33x faster; T2 attains data efficiency by learning only procedural skill, not domain knowledge + reasoning + tool-use jointly.


### Limitations & critique

- **known limitations**:

> As a survey it documents field-wide limitations and open problems: catastrophic forgetting in continual/open-ended adaptation; reward hacking / specification gaming (paradigm-dependent); unsafe exploration during on-policy RL in real environments; safety-guardrail erosion under aggressive RL (DeepSeek-R1 reasoning around refusals); difficult credit assignment under sparse A2 rewards; non-stationary agent-tool co-adaptation dynamics; and evaluation gaps (static single-score benchmarks fail to measure adaptation dynamics, stability, and safety trajectories). Survey-specific limits: rapidly moving field, no new experiments of its own.

- **oracle or external feedback dependency**:

> Survey-level: explicitly organizes methods by feedback dependency. A1/T1 rely on external-tool/verifier or verifiable execution rewards (compiler pass/fail, recall, formal proof); A2/T2 rely on holistic output signals (final-answer EM, LLM-as-judge) and are characterized as more susceptible to reward hacking because of greater degrees of freedom. The A1-vs-A2 supervision-signal axis is the paper's primary discriminator.

- **self correction efficacy**:

> task-dependent. The survey concludes adaptation strategy should match the domain: A1 (execution-based) dominates software development (deterministic test suites); A2 + T2 dominate deep research and computer use (non-deterministic / no test suites); T1 + T2 dominate drug discovery (sparse delayed wet-lab feedback). No universal winner; effectiveness is paradigm- and domain-dependent.

- **calibration effect**: not-measured (survey). It discusses safety degradation under aggressive RL adaptation (reasoning around refusal mechanisms) and reward hacking, but does not present a dedicated calibration/'reasoning tax' measurement.


### Failure analysis

- **failure attribution capability**:

> classifies-failure-mode (taxonomy). The survey taxonomizes adaptation failure modes — catastrophic forgetting, reward hacking/specification gaming (with paradigm-dependent susceptibility: A1 hard to game, A2 sparse-reward susceptible, T2 tool-level reward hacking), unsafe exploration, parasitic tool adaptation, and safety degradation — but does not provide an automated step/agent attribution method.

- **failure mode addressed**:

> Catastrophic forgetting (continual adaptation), reward hacking / specification gaming (e.g., trivially passing self-generated tests, manipulating evaluation state), tool-level / parasitic reward hacking in T2, unsafe exploration during on-policy RL, and safety-guardrail erosion. Conceptually overlaps with MAST-style modes (e.g., reward-hacking ~ task-derailment/specification gaming) but the paper uses its own adaptation-centric failure taxonomy rather than MAST's 14 modes.

- **dataset or benchmark released**:

> n/a. The survey does not release a new dataset or benchmark; it proposes an evaluation framework (four lenses: benchmark landscape mapped to A1/A2/T1/T2, adaptation-signal metrics, adaptation dynamics, safety) but does not publish a new resource.


### Relations

- **builds on**:

> Positions itself relative to and builds on prior AI-agent surveys (which it cites as refs [1,15,16,17,18]); synthesizes foundational adaptation lines: DeepSeek-R1 (RLVR / on-policy RL for reasoning and tool use), Search-R1 / ReSearch / DeepResearcher (A2 search agents), s3 / AgentFlow / DynamicRAG (T2 tool adaptation), HuggingGPT / ViperGPT / SciToolAgent (T1 tool integration), Voyager / EXPEL / JARVIS-1 / CREATOR / ASI (skill libraries), and Mem-alpha / ReasoningBank (adaptive memory). Frames OpenClaw-style persistent memory/skills as motivation.

- **citation count**: 13 (Semantic Scholar, as of June 2026; influentialCitationCount 0). Recent preprint, so count is low and rising.


### Other / reserved fields

- **reasoning model native**:

> Partially: the survey explicitly covers reasoning models with built-in/RL-emergent reflection (DeepSeek-R1 self-correction, adaptive search depth as emergent A2 behavior) and how RLVR post-training induces such behavior, but it is a general adaptation survey not exclusively about o1/R1-style models.

- **on policy distillation link**:

> Strong relevance. The survey foregrounds on-policy RL with verifiable rewards (DeepSeek-R1) as a pillar of adaptation, and its T2 paradigm (agent-supervised tool adaptation, e.g., s3) is closely related to skill/procedure distillation from a frozen agent's outputs — distilling reusable procedural skills into lightweight tools/memory rather than into core weights, directly relevant to on-policy distillation / skill-optimization threads.

- **sample efficiency**:

> Survey emphasizes sample efficiency as a key trade-off axis: T2 (s3) reaches comparable accuracy with 2.4k samples vs A2 (Search-R1) ~170k (70x more data-efficient) and 33x faster training, because T2 learns only procedural skill on a frozen, knowledgeable generator.
